Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:24:14 BST
23:24:14 KST

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
- Published
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.
Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies.
Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine.
Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.
Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".
"We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote.
He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
- Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people 
  - Published1 hour ago
Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small".
He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US".
"Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms."
The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.
The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.
The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace.
"We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace."
Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.
Putin said he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Its diesel production has fallen by nearly 30%, according to International Energy Agency estimates.
Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.
But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying they were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".
"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.
- Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? 
  - Published20 hours ago
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, and the details of exactly how Russia will supply this fuel to the global market is unclear.
But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.
With the looming US elections - which will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.
Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.
Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

Why is the US sanctioning the International Criminal Court?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:19:43 UTC
23:19:43 KST

Why is the US sanctioning the International Criminal Court?
The sanctions targeting the ICC, which prosecutes humanitarian crimes, are the latest move by the US against the court.
The United States has sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), hours after one of its former judges was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in what the Nobel committee said was, in part, a show of support for institutions under attack.
South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who is currently a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also in The Hague, was announced winner of the prize on Friday.
Nobel Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice,” the committee said.
The US move follows sanctions it has already imposed this year on judges and other personnel at the ICC.
Here’s what we know:
What has the US announced?
On Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the latest set of US sanctions targeting the ICC, this time focusing on the court itself, which was established in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” he said in a video shared on social media.
The Trump administration claims that the ICC has gone beyond its remit by pursuing non-member countries. In 2024, the Trump administration condemned the court when it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for suspected war crimes in Gaza. It also previously opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan.
The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction. However, abuses committed by citizens of non-statute states in ICC territories or countries can still be prosecuted.
“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement, adding that if the US allies failed to “rein in the court”, the US would “continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”.
What other sanctions has the US imposed on the ICC?
These sanctions are just the latest in the US’s campaign against the ICC. Previous measures have targeted dozens of ICC judges and prosecutors, the UN special rapporteur for Palestine, Francesca Albanese, and Palestinian rights groups which have provided evidence of war crimes committed by Israel to the court.
In August, ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior lawyer Abdoulaye Sey were also sanctioned by the US, in what Rubio said was the US’s unwavering mission to protect Americans from this sham of a court”.
Any assets they hold in the US are frozen, and US companies are limited in conducting transactions with them.
>What do the latest sanctions mean in practice?
The sanctions targeting the court could see companies that provide services to it penalised. They will also freeze any ICC assets held in US territories.
However, they have given US companies a six-month grace period to wrap up any existing business with the court. There are also some other exemptions allowing for certain transactions.
William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London, told Al Jazeera that the court has been “developing a plan B” to get around potential sanctions for more than a year.
This includes migrating to European alternatives to US software, and ending its relationship with insurance company Axa, which does business with the US.
“How significant this will be remains to be seen,” he said. “Obviously for the institution, it’s going to complicate things considerably.”
What have the responses to this been?
“What Trump is trying to do is to make the world safe for American and Israeli war criminals,” Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University and former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera.
The ICC itself released a statement condemning the US move, which it said was an attempt to “obstruct the course of justice” and intimidate those who work or cooperate with the court.
“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” it said, calling on its 125 states parties to take action to ensure it can continue its work.
“History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it added.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply alarmed” by the decision, adding that it was “a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice”.
The foreign ministers of the UK, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan all said they “strongly disagree” with the sanctions, and warned of the significant impact they would have on the court.
Netanyahu thanked Trump for his leadership on social media, and accused the ICC of being a “political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide”.
Is the US eroding the system of international law?
The US targeting of the ICC threatens the rule of law, as international courts and tribunals must be able to operate without the threat of sanctions.
The US itself has repeatedly ignored international law under President Trump. Its joint attack on Iran with Israel in February was criticised by observers as being in violation of both US law and Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, while the US military abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from Caracas in January was also condemned as illegal.
The Trump administration has also launched strikes against alleged drug smuggling boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific, killing more than 200 people in what UN human rights experts warn are “extrajudicial and unlawful“.
Under Trump, the US has also pulled out of international organisations and agreements, from the Iran nuclear deal (the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action) and the Paris Climate Agreement during Trump’s first term, to the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, more recently.
“What Trump is doing is obstructing justice,” Roth said of the ICC sanctions. “If you look at Article 70 of the Rome Statute, it makes it a crime to intimidate or threaten court officials because of their official duties.”
“But the court remains strong, it is very capable of doing its work,” he said, adding, “there’s important work for the court to do to protect victims in places like Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, Afghanistan, the Philippines. This is work that should continue, and it will.”

China Focus: Scientific expedition warns of accelerated glacier melting in NW China's Xinjiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:19:39 CST
23:19:39 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Scientists with China's Third Xinjiang Scientific Expedition announced on Saturday that they had found more than 24,000 glaciers in the region and warned of accelerating melt there.
Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in northwest China ranks first in glacier reserves in the country, followed by Xizang Autonomous Region in southwest China. At a press conference in Urumqi, Xinjiang's capital, the expedition team released the latest data, saying Xinjiang is home to 24,202 glaciers, covering 23,629 square km.
The glacier study is part of a five-year expedition, which was launched in 2021 by the Ministry of Science and Technology. The previous two were conducted in the 1950s and 1980s.
The expedition carried out studies on Xinjiang's ecology, land and agriculture, biodiversity and biological resources, mineral, energy and water resources. Forty-six national research institutions joined the work, with over 6,000 person-times of expedition members.
While the two earlier surveys centered on basic, census-based static resource inventory, this mission yields fresh first-hand data on Xinjiang's climate, ecology and resources.
From the 1990s to 2020, Xinjiang has lost 2,167 square km of glacier area, and most parts of this glacier-rich region are experiencing rapid melting, according to the expedition team.
Global warming is the main cause, said expedition member Li Zhongqin, a glacier researcher at the Northwest Institute of Eco-Environment and Resources under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS).
The region has been warming faster than the global and national averages. The expedition team noted that over the past three decades, Xinjiang's temperature has been rising at a rate of 0.34 degrees Celsius per decade, roughly 1.7 times the global average and 1.13 times the national average.
The surface of lakes and wetlands in Xinjiang has grown by roughly one-third, also partly due to glacier melt, Li said.
Glaciers are vital to Xinjiang as the sources of many rivers in this inland region. Faster melting can increase river runoff, but it can also cause ice avalanches and raise the risk of floods and mudslides, Li told Xinhua, adding that glacier collapses are likely to become frequent in this region.
Strengthening of monitoring efforts is necessary to respond to these risks. Li and his colleagues have used remote sensing satellites and drones to track glacier movement and temperature changes.
Another highlight of the expedition was joint cross-border glacier research, including the identification of glaciers in Tajikistan, which neighbors southwestern Xinjiang, and the publication of an atlas of that country's glaciers.
Scientific cooperation between the two countries stems from the common challenge of glacier melt, said Li Zhi, a researcher at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography under the CAS. She and her colleagues have launched a UNESCO-recognized project that focuses on assessing glacial changes in Tajikistan, predicting future glacier trends and studying the risks of glacier-related disasters.
Tajikistan has many glaciers, and melt could lead to disastrous events, such as glacial lake outburst floods, which may endanger local residents, she added.
Besides glacier melt, the expedition also focused on other common regional challenges, such as water scarcity and desertification, and carried out joint scientific research with Central Asian countries. ■

Astronomers identify host galaxy of most distant fast radio burst
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
22:19:29 CST
23:19:29 KST

CAPE TOWN, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Astronomers have identified the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever detected, using South Africa's MeerKAT radio telescope and NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO) said.
In a statement issued Thursday, SARAO said the discovery, published in the journal Science, involved FRB 20240304B, detected on March 4, 2024, by the MeerTRAP team, an international collaboration that uses MeerKAT to search for FRBs and other transient radio signals.
The radio telescope precisely localized the burst and indicated that it was extremely distant, but astronomers needed to identify its host galaxy to measure the distance accurately. The galaxy was too faint to be detected by ground-based telescopes, so the team turned to Webb, whose infrared instruments detected the galaxy and measured a redshift of 2.148.
According to the study, the burst traveled for more than 10 billion years before reaching Earth, and occurred when the universe was only about 3 billion years old, roughly a quarter of its present age. The finding more than doubles the previous distance record for FRBs.
The host galaxy was also unexpectedly small, with a mass about 1,000 times lower than expected for a typical FRB host, although it was actively forming stars.
"We thought it would be a big, nicely formed galaxy with lots of stars, and instead it was a little dwarf galaxy, although it was actively forming stars," Manisha Caleb of the University of Sydney, lead author of the study, said in the statement.
The galaxy was observed during "cosmic noon," when star formation across the universe was at its peak, and most of its stars may have formed within just 30 million years. This makes a neutron-star merger an unlikely explanation for the burst, as binary neutron stars typically take at least a billion years to merge.
Instead, the researchers believe the burst may have resulted from an energetic event, such as a starquake in a young magnetar, a neutron star with an extremely powerful magnetic field formed following the collapse of a massive star.
"What is particularly exciting about our result is that we've now demonstrated that we can identify and study an FRB from when the universe was young," Caleb said. ■

Abbas postpones Palestinian legislative elections to September 2027
Unknown

2026-10-10

Abbas postpones Palestinian legislative elections to September 2027
November 2026 vote delayed and joint presidential and legislative elections set for next year, president says in decree.
President Mahmoud Abbas has postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council for almost another year.
According to the decree, legislative elections planned for next month will be combined with a presidential vote and set for September 11, 2027, Wafa, the official Palestinian news agency, said on Saturday.
The long-awaited parliamentary vote was originally set for November 28, with a presidential election expected in early 2027.
The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met on Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote.
The Palestine Liberation Organization’s (PLO) Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in occupied East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
Israeli interference, including military raids, settlement expansion and settler violence in the occupied West Bank, has made a fair vote in November impossible, Wafa reported.
The agency also cited Israel’s systemic withholding of Palestinian tax revenues and its restrictions on electoral candidates and international observers entering Gaza and occupied East Jerusalem, as reasons.
As for Gaza, it said that the lack of progress on reconstruction and on deploying an international stabilisation force factored into the decision as well.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority’s (PA) credibility among Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
On Friday, the Israeli Minister of Foreign Affairs, Gideon Saar, accused Abbas of “fooling the international community” by planning to cancel promised elections.
A source told the AFP news agency on Thursday that Palestinian factions, including Abbas’s Palestinian National Liberation Movement – also known as the Fatah party – had agreed to hold a “national dialogue” before legislative elections and that they wanted to postpone the vote.
The last parliamentary elections held in the Palestinian territories were in 2006, when Hamas defeated Fatah, which dominates the PA. The split led to factional fighting and Hamas later seized control of Gaza.
Ninety-year-old Abbas won the last presidential election in 2005. His term should have ended in 2009, but he has ruled by decree since then. In June, he signed a decree calling for the presidential election to be held in early 2027.
Mustafa Barghouti, secretary-general of the Palestinian National Initiative party, told Al Jazeera there is great disappointment among the Palestinian people over Abbas’s decision to postpone the elections.
“At this moment, everything is concentrated in the hands of the executive authority,” he said.
“There is no independent judiciary, no parliament, that can issue laws and legislations,” Barghouti added, saying it is “totally unacceptable” that Palestinians have been denied elections for two decades.
“There is a great need for reform from the perspective of the Palestinian people.”

Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:10:24 UTC
23:10:24 KST

Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’?
Fighting is intensifying between the Yemeni government forces and the rebel Houthi group.
Fighting continues to intensify in Yemen as the internationally recognised government forces push a military offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, which controls part of the country.
Speaking at the United Nations Security Council on Friday, the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, said the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”.
Government forces are particularly looking to retake the important Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital trading chokepoint that has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have all but halted shipping.
At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in September, the UN’s migration agency (IOM), said.
Fierce battles across several fronts have prompted concerns from rights groups that Yemen has essentially returned to civil war after the relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014.
Amid the US-Iran war, Yemen’s worst fighting in years threatens to destabilise the region further, experts say. Here’s what we know:
What’s the latest on the ground?
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea. Riyadh has increasingly relied on it for oil exports amid the US-Iran war, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sunday, the Yemeni government announced the start of the operation “Dawn of Yemen”, which aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa.
On Saturday, it said it had conducted more than 2,750 precision strikes during military operations over the previous 24 hours, resulting in the “neutralisation” of more than 1,400 Houthi fighters.
The spokesperson for the armed forces, Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, said in a statement carried by Saba news agency that the operations also targeted high-value military assets deep within Houthi-held territory.
He added that ground forces “successfully” breached Houthi defences, recaptured operationally significant positions, secured their field gains and continued to advance the offensive according to operational plans.
The Bab al-Mandeb strait emerged as yet another front in the US-Israel war on Iran when the Houthis declared a blockade on ships linked to Saudi Arabia in July.
While the Houthis said that was in retaliation for ongoing Saudi blockades on Yemen, analysts viewed the move as calculated to provide more leverage for Iran amid on-and-off negotiations with the US – a close ally of Riyadh.
Battles are now raging around the strategic southern cities of Mocha and Dubhab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb. The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides currently claim control of the shipping lanes.
The Houthis, who have developed sophisticated weapons systems, including ballistic missiles, have also targeted Saudi Arabia with missile and drone attacks. On Friday, Saudi Arabia’s aviation authorities said three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, had been killed and several others wounded in Houthi strikes on the international airport in Riyadh – the first such deaths in the kingdom since fighting resumed. Several airlines suspended flights.
The coalition forces also heavily bombarded Sanaa, on Friday, with several injuries reported, including a child. Both sides are also fighting to control Taiz.
What led to the original civil war?
Civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis took control of Sanaa and imposed their own government in the capital. The seizure came amid dissatisfaction with the ruling government and following a revolution three years earlier.
A coalition of armed forces and local armed groups backed by Saudi Arabia launched military operations and restored the internationally recognised government in Aden. Fighting resulted in the deaths of between 150,000 and 227,000 people, while millions were displaced.
While the Houthis controlled much of the north, the Yemeni government controlled the southern regions.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 saw a lull in fighting and allowed aid to reach the deprived population, which has faced famine since 2016.
In 2023, the Houthis, who form part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” alliance of proxy armed groups, began disrupting shipping in the Red Sea in response to Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip. In March this year, the Houthis fired missiles at Israel amid the war on Iran, officially entering the US-Israel war with Iran which began in February.
Tensions escalated when the group declared a naval blockade of Saudi ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July, shattering the relative calm in the country since 2022. It followed the announcement with a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back Yemeni coalition forces from the strategic port city.
In September, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, leader of the Yemeni government’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a military offensive to “restore state authority”.
Is this a return to war?
Analysts say the scale of fighting means Yemen has fallen back into civil war as both sides come under scrutiny for targeting civilians.
As the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, declared that the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”, civilians, including women and children, are the ones bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.
The envoy stressed the need for the UNSC to support urgent mediation once more, although analysts have pointed out that recent gains by Yemeni government forces could mean they are more determined to push through the ongoing offensive, rather than agree to a settlement.
But “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now”, Grundberg warned.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, said: “It is beginning to resemble the 2015 Saudi-led coalition war on Yemen, when Sanaa and various other provinces were attacked relentlessly around the clock.”
A number of sites in Sanaa have been targeted, he said, including Sanaa International Airport. Several industrial facilities, including a chips factory in the north and a sponge factory in the south, have also been hit.
At least four telecommunications infrastructure sites have been struck in the capital and throughout areas controlled by the Houthi movement. Mount Attan in Sanaa was also hit by 10 air raids.
Mawry reported that, according to Saudi coalition officials, strikes have destroyed 136 military targets in areas under Houthi control, including military sites, launch pads and radars belonging to the Houthi group.
“Meanwhile, the Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of targeting public infrastructure and telecommunications facilities, warning that the campaign risks plunging the country back into a humanitarian crisis similar to the one experienced from 2015 to 2022,” Mawry said.
Will the United States take action in Yemen?
The US, which has previously indicated that it does not want to get involved in the Yemen conflict, nevertheless on Friday called on the Houthis to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, while demanding that Iran end its support for the group.
Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Yemen, Jeff Bartos, the US ambassador to the UN for Management and Reform, said Washington was “gravely concerned” by the Houthis’ recent escalation, including attacks on civilian infrastructure and airports.
“The pattern remains unmistakable. The Houthis act as instruments of Tehran to threaten freedom of navigation, undermine regional stability, and terrorise innocent civilians,” Bartos said.
“We demand that the Houthis cease their attacks against the legitimate governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia and we demand that Iran cease all support to the Houthis,” he added.

Abbas delays Palestinian elections to 2027, marking 20 years without a vote
Unknown

2026-10-10

Palestinian Authority president postpones legislative elections another year, marking 20 years without a vote
President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.
Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority's credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas' party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas' presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.
The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.
Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas' Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.
The West Bank has grown increasingly violent in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority's control are both regularly reported.
Though the U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year outlined a future role for the authority, its immediate role was left mostly undefined as Hamas has continued to govern and the technocrats under the Board of Peace remain in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza to transition power.
Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election. But behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan. Dahlan had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas and was exiled in 2010 after a falling-out with Abbas.
"Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.

Russia, With Uganda’s Help, Backs UN Resolution Calling Unilateral Sanctions Unlawful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:03:00 UTC
23:03:00 KST

Russia and Uganda have helped secure a UN Human Rights Council resolution declaring unilateral coercive measures contrary to international law, giving Moscow another diplomatic argument against sanctions imposed over its invasion of Ukraine.
Adopted by 27 votes to 16, with four abstentions, the resolution extends for three years the mandate of the special rapporteur examining the negative human rights effects of such measures. Uganda sponsored the draft on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement, alongside Russia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Neither sponsor is currently a Human Rights Council member, so neither participated in the vote. Their role nevertheless illustrates how Moscow can influence UN proceedings beyond the Security Council, where it holds a permanent seat and veto.
What the resolution says about sanctions
The resolution’s preamble declares unilateral coercive measures contrary to international law, international humanitarian law, and the UN Charter. Its operative provisions renew the rapporteur’s mandate and request continued institutional support.
The text does not itself overturn sanctions against Russia or determine the legality of individual restrictions. It sustains a UN mechanism focused on their adverse human rights effects, whose work Moscow can invoke when challenging economic pressure.
That broad framing leaves important distinctions between sanctions unresolved. The EU’s restrictions on Russia target military-industrial capacity alongside revenue and other resources supporting the war. They also include exemptions and safeguards for humanitarian needs and essential civilian supplies.
‘I Love the Smell of Russian Gas’: Controversial Polish Politician Backs Nord Stream
While those provisions do not eliminate the need to investigate civilian harm, assessing it requires examining the purpose, scope, and implementation of particular restrictions.
For Moscow, a general condemnation offers a broader argument against measures adopted outside the Security Council, where Russia can block their authorization.
Russia’s veto limits collective action
As a permanent Security Council member, Russia can veto substantive resolutions, including those authorizing sanctions against it.
Moscow demonstrated its willingness to obstruct action concerning its own conduct on Feb. 25, 2022, vetoing a draft resolution that condemned its invasion and demanded the withdrawal of Russian forces.
The Human Rights Council resolution does not explicitly declare that only Security Council sanctions are legitimate. However, treating council authorization as a prerequisite would make sanctions against Russia dependent on overcoming Russia’s own veto.
Moscow thus benefits from two complementary positions: it can prevent Security Council action while supporting arguments elsewhere in the UN against pressure imposed outside that body.
This selective approach also appears in Russia’s broader use of international law. Moscow invokes legal protections when discussing Russian speakers abroad, yet disregarded the International Court of Justice’s March 2022 order to suspend the military operations it began in Ukraine on Feb. 24.
Moscow can also block the next UN chief
Russia’s institutional leverage extends to the selection of the secretary-general.
As Kyiv Post’s examination of the succession process explains, a successful candidate needs a Security Council recommendation supported by at least nine members and vetoed by none of the five permanent members.
That gives Moscow the power to block a candidate to succeed António Guterres. It does not require Russia to vote in favor, since a permanent member’s abstention does not prevent a recommendation, but any candidate must avoid a Russian veto.
Changing the underlying rules presents another obstacle. Under Article 108 of the UN Charter, amendments require adoption by two-thirds of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent Security Council members.
Russia can therefore obstruct Charter amendments that would remove its privileged position. A change in UN leadership alone would leave that constraint intact.
Some backers had also supported Ukraine
The sanctions resolution’s supporters have markedly different voting records on Ukraine.
Of the 27 governments backing the text, 16 also supported the General Assembly’s February 2023 resolution calling for a just peace and Russia’s withdrawal. They included Brazil, Colombia, Indonesia, Egypt, Kenya, and the UAE.
On the Ukraine-sponsored resolution adopted in February 2025, however, only five of the same countries voted in favor: Egypt, Gambia, Indonesia, Mauritius, and Thailand. Eighteen abstained, Burundi and Sudan voted against, and Benin, Bolivia, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo did not vote.
Brazil, Colombia, Kenya, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE, and Zambia were among those that moved from supporting the 2023 text to abstaining in 2025. The latter resolution reaffirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity, recalled the demand for Russian withdrawal and called for accountability for crimes committed during the war.
These votes concern different texts but they do show that condemnation of Russian aggression does not necessarily translate into support for economic pressure on Moscow.
Scrutiny of Russia continues
Other decisions made by the council show the limits of Moscow’s influence.
During the same session, members voted 21-5, with 21 abstentions, to renew the special rapporteur’s mandate on human rights inside Russia.
Independent scrutiny of Russian abuses therefore continues alongside the sanctions mechanism Moscow supported.

Belief in supernatural evil is linked to blaming the system for poverty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
14:00:30 UTC
23:00:30 KST

People who believe in supernatural evil are more likely to blame society for poverty, while those who believe in a supportive deity are less likely to do so. These findings come from a recent survey of South Korean adults published in the Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion. The research reveals how specific theological ideas intersect with political ideology to shape public views on social inequality.
Sociologists use the term stratification beliefs to describe how people explain why some individuals are wealthy and others are impoverished. In this field of study, explanations for poverty are generally divided into two main categories. Individualistic beliefs place the blame on the poor themselves, citing a lack of effort, talent, or financial discipline. Structuralist beliefs fault the broader economic and social systems, pointing to issues like discrimination, low wages, or underfunded schools.
How a person explains poverty often predicts their support for welfare programs and redistributive economic policies. Past research has examined how religion influences these views, but most studies have focused simply on whether a person belongs to a specific denomination. Researchers often categorize people as Catholic, Protestant, or Buddhist without examining the specific nature of their personal faith.
To address this gap, sociologists Jong Hyun Jung and Muhan Chen of Sungkyunkwan University, along with Harris Hyun-soo Kim of Ewha Womans University, designed a study focused on specific supernatural beliefs. They wanted to understand how belief in a supportive divine presence compares to a belief in supernatural evil when it comes to predicting attitudes toward poverty. The team also sought to test these relationships outside of a Western context.
They chose South Korea for its unique blend of religious traditions, where Buddhism, Protestantism, and Catholicism coexist alongside a large population of people with no religious affiliation. Supernatural belief in South Korea is also moderate compared to heavily Christian nations like the United States. This environment provided a distinct cultural backdrop to see if previous theories about religion and economics hold true in a different setting.
The researchers analyzed data from an online survey of 1,632 South Korean adults conducted in August 2024. The participant pool was recruited to match the national population in terms of age, gender, and geographic region. Because the survey included questions about a person’s relationship with God, the researchers excluded respondents who stated they completely disbelieved in a deity.
The survey asked participants to rate their agreement with statements measuring two distinct theological concepts. Belief in divine support was measured by asking if respondents felt they had a warm relationship with God and if God was responsive to their personal needs. Belief in supernatural evil was measured by asking participants if they believed in the existence of demons, hell, and the devil.
Participants then rated the importance of various causes of poverty. To measure individualistic views, the survey asked about factors like personal irresponsibility and a lack of thrift. To gauge structuralist views, respondents evaluated the role of low wages, prejudice, and a failure of private industry to provide enough good jobs. The researchers also asked participants to rate their own political orientation on a scale from very liberal to very conservative.
When the researchers analyzed the data, they found that neither religious belief was associated with individualistic explanations for poverty. People who reported a warm relationship with God were no more likely to blame poor individuals for their circumstances than those with weaker divine beliefs. The same held true for those who firmly believed in demons and hell.
The authors suggest that this lack of association might stem from the charitable aspects of religious involvement. Believing in a supportive deity might increase a person’s sense of compassion for others. This humanitarian impulse could prevent believers from harshly judging those who fall below the poverty line, even if their faith encourages self-reliance in other areas of life.
A different pattern emerged when the researchers looked at structuralist explanations for poverty. Belief in divine support was negatively associated with blaming systemic and economic issues. In other words, individuals who felt closely supported by God were less likely to view poor schools or low wages as the primary drivers of poverty.
This result aligns with an academic concept known as the insurance effect. Some sociologists argue that religion provides psychological comfort and a sense of security that functions much like a social safety net. People who rely on a divine figure for support during hard times might feel less need for government intervention, prompting them to discount systemic explanations for economic hardship.
Conversely, belief in supernatural evil was positively associated with structuralist views. Respondents who expressed a strong belief in the devil, hell, and demons were more likely to blame society and economic systems for poverty. The researchers interpret this through the lens of a spiritual warfare worldview, which sees the universe as a battleground between good and evil.
In this worldview, adversarial supernatural forces are thought to be actively working to harm humanity. Believers might view oppressive social structures, rampant discrimination, or failing schools as manifestations of these dark forces. As a result, they may attribute the suffering of the poor to these external, corrupt systems rather than pointing the finger at the individuals experiencing the hardship.
The research team also looked at how political orientation interacted with these supernatural beliefs. In general, conservative respondents were much less likely to endorse structuralist explanations for poverty than liberal respondents. This aligns with a wide body of existing political science research.
However, a strong belief in supernatural evil modified this trend among political conservatives. For respondents who leaned conservative, higher levels of belief in demons and hell were linked to a sharp increase in structuralist views of poverty. In fact, conservatives with the strongest belief in supernatural evil were nearly identical to liberals in their tendency to blame the system for poverty. Belief in supernatural evil did not have this effect on liberal respondents, who generally favored structuralist explanations regardless of their religious views.
The researchers note several caveats to consider when interpreting these results. The survey captured a single snapshot in time, meaning the data cannot prove a specific directional relationship between the variables. It is entirely possible that a person’s preexisting views on poverty and inequality shape how they interpret their religious faith, rather than the other way around.
Cultural differences also provide important context for these results. Research in psychology indicates that people in East Asian societies often lean toward environmental and situational explanations for human behavior, whereas Westerners frequently favor individualistic explanations. This cultural baseline in South Korea might suppress any potential link between religious beliefs and individualistic views on poverty, a dynamic that could look entirely different in the United States or Europe.
Additionally, the concepts of God and evil carry different meanings across varying religious traditions. A devout Buddhist and a practicing Protestant might interpret survey questions about supernatural forces in entirely different ways. Future research will need to untangle how specific doctrinal teachings within different faiths interact with public opinions on wealth and inequality.
The study, “Belief in Supernatural Agents and Lay Explanations About the Causes of Poverty,” was authored by Jong Hyun Jung, Muhan Chen, and Harris Hyun-soo Kim.

In September 2026, the Ukrainian military destroyed more than 4,700 aerial targets and neutralized more than 48,000 tactical-level drones, the press service of the Ukrainian Air Force said on its Telegram channel on Saturday.
In particular, 24 Kh-101 cruise missiles, eight Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, 12 Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 guided air-to-surface missiles, six Iskander-K cruise missiles, and eight Zircon anti-ship missiles were destroyed during the month.

Trump lifted Russian fuel ban after Zelensky rejected his demands – Axios
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:58:10 UTC

Trump lifted Russian fuel ban after Zelensky rejected his demands – Axios
US President Donald Trump has approved a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian fuel exports. The move came after Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky ignored multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, Axios has reported, citing a US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
Trump has persistently blamed Ukraine, and Zelensky personally, for exacerbating the global fuel crisis, accusing authorities in Kiev of deliberately targeting Russian refining facilities and driving up prices for American consumers. Despite repeated warnings from Washington, the Ukrainian leader pledged earlier this month to ramp up the long-range strikes.
“The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the US, too,” the US official told the news outlet.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly warned Ukrainian negotiators during eight hours of talks in Miami earlier this week that Trump planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner threatened to cut off US intelligence sharing with Kiev if it continued to ignore Trump’s requests to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, but the US official denied that any such threat had been made.
The media outlet cited the official as saying that the dispute over the diesel deal emerged as the US mediators conducted constructive talks on ending the conflict with Ukrainian and European diplomats. The negotiations reportedly focused on finalizing security guarantees for Ukraine from the US, Europe, and NATO, as well as new territorial proposals.
The official added that Witkoff and Kushner had presented postwar plans covering Ukraine’s reconstruction, military funding, and budget deficits, while participants discussed Kiev’s potential EU accession, its future relationship with NATO, and a possible postwar security framework between Europe and Russia.
Trump and Putin held a phone call on Friday, shortly after which the US Treasury Department announced a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian fuel trade, allowing diesel to be sold, delivered, and exported, including into the US, until at least April 7, 2027.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and a million tons thereafter, with up to three million additional tons available “within a short period of time.”
The Kremlin said Moscow was ready to supply oil and petroleum products to global markets, adding that this would benefit the world economy. Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak also confirmed that Russia would lift diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, with the process to begin “immediately.”
Russia had previously extended restrictions on diesel, ship fuel, and gas oil exports until October 31 to stabilize the domestic market amid seasonal demand from the harvest. Fuel producers are barred from exporting until October 31, while fuel resellers face a ban until January 31, 2027. Gasoline exports are also prohibited until the end of January.

When streets become a workplace: Gaza workers convert tents into offices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:50:05 UTC
22:50:05 KST

When streets become a workplace: Gaza workers convert tents into offices
Gaza doctors, lawyers, and teachers have converted tents into offices to maintain a livelihood.
Khan Younis, Gaza – Dr Mohammed al-Khalidi, a specialist in prosthetics and orthotics, sits in a modest tent in al-Mawasi, southern Gaza. It has been his place of work since his clinic on al-Bahr Street in Rafah was destroyed by Israeli bombing in April 2024. His second and third clinics in Khan Younis’s Old City, southern Gaza, were subsequently destroyed by Israel in May 2025.
After this triple heartbreaking setback, al-Khalidi salvaged whatever medical equipment he could find and moved into his new office, a tent, where he has received patients for the past two years.
This transitory space reflects a new reality in Gaza since Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave began in October 2023. Offices, clinics and shops have been wiped out in waves of Israeli air raids over the past three years, leaving professionals to conduct their work from tents or on the road.
This phenomenon emerged in December 2023 following the displacement of Khan Younis residents to a narrow strip of coastal land between their hometown and Deir el-Balah.
After a ceasefire, repeatedly broken by Israel, was announced for the enclave in October 2025, more of these tent offices, surgeries and shops emerged across Gaza as professionals sought to continue their practices.
Challenges
Working within these canvas confines presents multiple challenges for al-Khalidi. There is limited space, unreliable electricity, and the intense heat and loud noises to deal with.
The setting bears little resemblance to his previous practice in a bricks-and-mortar office, but he still feels this arrangement is better than suspending services altogether.
There is a massive need for prosthetics in Gaza, where between 5,000 and 6,000 people have undergone amputations between October 2023 and October 2025.
“Working from a temporary space is nothing like working in a fully equipped clinic, but for me, it is better than stopping the service altogether,” al-Khalidi told Al Jazeera.
“Patients who need prosthetic limbs or orthotic devices cannot always wait until conditions return to normal. Some have lost a limb during the war, while others need follow-up care or adjustments to devices they rely on in their daily lives.”
More than four-in-five buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed since Israel’s genocidal war began in 2023, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS), creating a real estate crisis.
The lack of office space has seen rental prices reach unaffordable levels for most Gaza professionals. But resilience, necessity, and duty have encouraged Palestinians to find solutions to this situation. Tents are now where lawyers meet clients, doctors treat patients, and traders sell their wares.
Repeated displacement
After Omar al-Tawashi, a civil engineer and construction auditor, saw his office destroyed in an Israeli air strike in August 2024, he began work from his home in July 2025. But that too met the same fate, so he shifted operations to a tent in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, to continue his work.
“My move to a tent was not a professional choice. It was a direct result of the destruction of the place where I used to work, compounded by the rental crisis, which made finding an alternative office extremely difficult,” he said.
“In some cases, rents have risen to more than 10 times their pre-war levels, making a new office beyond my means”.
The tent is not a suitable environment for his engineering work, but there is no alternative for al-Tawashi.
“There is heat, cold and noise, and none of the privacy needed when discussing projects or reviewing technical files,” Omar said. “But stopping work would mean losing my source of income”.
In the crowded market in Nuseirat camp, central Gaza, accountant Mahmoud Shaheen receives clients inside a small tent amid the sound of neighbouring vendors and passers-by.
Shaheen was once responsible for a Gaza-based company’s accounts, but the office was destroyed in an Israeli air strike in November 2025.
“Moving to a tent was not so much a professional choice as a response to a reality imposed by the war,” he told Al Jazeera.
With the start of the new school year in Gaza last month, tents have been pitched across the country as substitutes for schools destroyed in Israeli air raids or converted into refuges for the displaced.
School starts
Teacher Palestine Hussein has been forced to adapt to this new reality. She previously taught English at an educational centre in Bureij in central Gaza, which she had spent years building.
It was destroyed in seconds when an Israeli air raid destroyed the educational facility, so she now teaches children from a tent at al-Balata, a camp for displaced Palestinians in Nuseirat.
There is a lack of seats for the students, ventilation, or protection from the noise and heat. But despite these challenges, Hussein is determined to provide children in the camp with some form of education.
“Although the tent may appear to be a temporary place, to me it represents an attempt to hold on to what remains of my profession and rebuild my dream from scratch, even with the most basic resources,” Hussein told Al Jazeera.
New reality
Trader Khalil al-Tahrawi saw his clothing store in Nuseirat destroyed by Israeli bombing in October 2023. After salvaging surviving merchandise from his destroyed shop, he displayed his goods – mostly men’s T-shirts and jeans – at a small tent in the Nuseirat market.
He pays $350 a month in rent for the small patch of pavement to sell the clothing, which he removes every night to protect them from thieves.
“This routine makes the work even more difficult and consumes my time and energy,” al-Tahrawi told Al Jazeera.
Repeated power cuts, unreliable internet and shortages of equipment have complicated efforts by Gaza’s business community to rebuild during this period of a relative decrease in bombing.
Customers, too, are changing their consumption patterns, heading to certain towns or camps for a particular good or service. Often what they find are prices more inflated than during Israel’s siege on Gaza before Israel’s genocidal war.
One customer, Mohammed Zweid, a 24-year-old IT worker, looks through a market in Nuseirat. “Accessing professionals in tents and temporary spaces is better than having no service at all,” he told Al Jazeera. “The transformation has changed not only where services are provided, but also how they are experienced.”

‘4-year-olds sleeping in the woods’: police expose suspected child-begging ring in northern Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:48:15 UTC
22:48:15 KST

Israeli police detained more than 40 people near Nazareth in a major crackdown on a suspected begging network that brought Palestinian women and children into Israel, including mothers who allegedly spent entire days soliciting money at busy intersections while holding infants in extreme heat.
The operation, carried out Friday by Northern District Police and Border Police officers, targeted apartments and makeshift shelters in wooded areas near the northern Israeli city. Among those found were children as young as four and five who police believe had been sent to intersections to collect money for adult organizers.
"We saw difficult and heartbreaking scenes," Inspector Tal Krispin, an officer with the Nazareth Police municipal policing unit, told ynet. "I questioned 21-year-old mothers who stood at intersections around Nazareth with babies less than a year old, begging all day in extreme heat of more than 40 degrees."
According to Krispin, some women could collect as much as 3,000 shekels in a single day. "They deliberately bring babies to attract attention and sympathy from drivers," he said, describing findings from police questioning.
Investigators believe most of the women came from the Jenin area of the northern West Bank, while others traveled from Nablus. Police suspect Israeli and Palestinian intermediaries arranged their entry into Israel and distributed them among busy intersections in Nazareth, Wadi Ara and Ahihud.
The alleged operation also involved young children who approached vehicles stopped at traffic lights, knocked on windows and asked motorists for money. Police believe the children were expected to hand over their daily collections to the adults who had sent them out to beg.
Many of the children were found living in wooded areas or temporary encampments near the intersections, according to police. Investigators are examining the roles of the adults suspected of organizing their activities and collecting the money.
The operation resulted in the detention of more than 40 people suspected of being in Israel illegally. Adult suspects were taken for questioning at the Nazareth police station, and a court extended the detention of several of them. Police said some women had previously been arrested multiple times but returned to Israel to continue begging.
Children below the age of criminal responsibility were transferred to Palestinian Authority representatives following coordination with the Israeli military. Adults being returned to Palestinian-controlled territory were taken to checkpoints, Krispin said.
The crackdown follows years of complaints about women and children approaching cars at major intersections across northern Israel. Around Nazareth, where tens of thousands of motorists travel through busy junctions, the practice has become a familiar sight, with young children moving between vehicles and mothers carrying infants approaching drivers for donations.
Beyond concerns about the suspected exploitation of children, local officials have warned that their presence on heavily traveled roads poses safety risks for both the children and motorists.
Shlomit Shichor-Reichman, head of the Jezreel Valley Regional Council, welcomed the police operation after what she described as dozens of requests for enforcement.
"After dozens of appeals I submitted on the issue, it is good to finally see decisive action to restore law and order at our intersections and throughout our region," she said, praising the Northern District Police and Brig. Gen. Ran Ofir.
Shichor-Reichman also described the presence of people staying in Israel illegally at major intersections as a security concern, warning that it could create opportunities for nationalist violence. She urged authorities to focus not only on those begging but also on the suspected organizers arranging their entry into Israel.
"Beyond the appalling exploitation of children, the presence of people staying in Israel illegally at major intersections constitutes a serious violation of sovereignty," she said.
She called on police to continue pursuing the intermediaries allegedly operating the network, saying enforcement should target those responsible for organizing the activities rather than end with the detention and removal of women and children found at the intersections.

London Halal Forum kicks off, spotlighting global halal economy opportunities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:44:17 UTC
22:44:17 KST

Aysu Bicer
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
The London Halal Forum has kicked off on Saturday, bringing together entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers and industry leaders to explore opportunities across a growing range of sectors.
The forum is organized by Halal360, a joint initiative of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce and Development and the Halal Products Development Company (HPDC), with Anadolu serving as its global communications partner.
Under the theme Halal Tayyib for Humanity, the forum will examine the halal economy’s expansion beyond certification and food products into investment, tourism, technology, supply chains, branding and international trade.
In his opening speech, Hassan Khalawi, Secretary-General of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture, said London offers an ideal environment for the halal industry to grow through creativity and international connectivity.
“We need the creativity and we need the connectivity, and this is what we can build and find easily here in London,” Khalawi said.
He stressed that the halal economy is moving beyond its traditional focus on food to encompass a wider range of Muslim lifestyle sectors, including media, technology and Islamic art.
At the forum’s second edition, held just 11 months after the inaugural event, organizers introduced three concepts focusing on halal lifestyle, halal technologies and Islamic art.
Khalawi said the aim is to take these initiatives beyond London and develop them in markets worldwide, highlighting plans for a halal reception in Paris and the upcoming ASEAN Halal Forum in Bangkok.
“What is next is to take that from here to the rest of the world,” he said, underlining the importance of international partnerships in expanding the industry.
Khalawi thanked the forum's partners and sponsors for helping "create creative halal concepts everywhere" as the intitiative expands globally. He noted that with the global Muslim population projected to reach between 25% to 30% by 2050, it is vital from a business perspective to understand the importance to "cover all lifestyle sectors."
'Halal has become more than a religious requirement'
For his part, Fahad bin Suliman Alnuhait, CEO of HPDC, said halal has become more than a religious requirement, emerging as a global benchmark for quality, safety and trust.
He said Saudi Arabia is seeking to transform its position from one of the world’s largest halal import markets into a producer and exporter under its Vision 2030 economic diversification strategy.
Alnuhait highlighted HPDC’s role in supporting this transformation through investments, industrial development and international cooperation.
Over its first three years, the company made more than six investments, enabled six factories and helped bring three international company headquarters to Saudi Arabia, he added.
The company also supported the creation of more than 3,000 direct and 5,000 indirect jobs, while delivering 75 advisory projects and undertaking 10 international government projects to support halal strategy development across Organization of Islamic Cooperation member states, he explained.
Alnuhait said the London Halal Forum provides an important platform for connecting markets, producers and consumers, strengthening the halal value chain and creating new business opportunities.
“It's a bridge,” he said, describing the forum’s role in connecting European and UK markets with global opportunities.
Following the opening speeches, plaques were presented to sponsors. Anadolu Deputy Director General for Administrative and Financial Affairs Oguz Enis Peru received the plaque on behalf of Anadolu.

Aysu Bicer

Global financial and business leaders, policymakers and industry experts will gather in London on Oct. 13-14 for the 5th Annual AlBaraka Summit to discuss the role of Islamic finance in economic development.
The two-day event, held under the theme Ethics in Action: Rebuilding Foundations and Advancing the Global Impact of the Islamic Economy, will take place at JW Marriott Grosvenor House.
Anadolu will serve as the summit's global communications partner.
The gathering will bring together government ministers, scholars and representatives from Muslim-majority and non-Muslim-majority markets to explore ethical investment, financial inclusion, innovation and sustainable economic growth.
Discussions will focus on translating Islamic economic principles, including justice, accountability, risk-sharing and social responsibility, into practical outcomes across financial markets, regulation, technology and economic development.
The agenda will cover Islamic banking and capital markets, policy and regulation, social finance, Takaful, Waqf and Zakat, digitalization and entrepreneurship.
Participants will also examine the role of international financial centers in advancing the Islamic economy, the organizers said.
'Putting ethics into action'
"The Islamic economy has always been about more than financial products. Its foundations connect economic activity with justice, accountability and responsibility to society," Yousef Hassan Khalawi, secretary-general of the AlBaraka Forum for Islamic Economy, said in a statement.
"The challenge before us is to ensure those principles are not simply discussed, but put into action," he added.
Khalawi said London's position as a major international financial center made it an important venue for discussions on the future of Islamic finance.
"London provides an important setting for that conversation, connecting Islamic finance with one of the world's leading international financial centers," he said.
A panel of Islamic banking chief executives on the first day will examine policy, regulation and the sector’s global direction, including the evolution of regulatory frameworks, the role of ethics in public policy and priorities for the industry’s next phase.
The summit aims to explore how Islamic finance can strengthen its contribution to economic development by connecting financial activity with ethical principles and broader social responsibilities.

As the detentions mounted, opposition leaders accused the government of suppressing dissent. BJP defended the police action and the SIR process, accusing the protesters of attempting to create unrest.
NEW DELHI: Delhi witnessed an extraordinary security clampdown on October 10 as police moved to prevent the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed protest against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Jantar Mantar. What began with barricades, transport restrictions and preventive detentions escalated into a day of mass arrests, street demonstrations, reported clashes and a fierce political confrontation over the right to protest.By late afternoon, Delhi Police detained more than 3,000 people across the national capital. Those detained included CJP leaders, YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor Arvind Kejriwal, former Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee, student activists, lawyers and other opposition leaders. Two police personnel were reported injured in incidents involving stone-pelting.As the detentions mounted, opposition leaders accused the government of suppressing dissent. BJP defended the police action and the SIR process, accusing the protesters of attempting to create unrest.CJP later announced to continue the agitation as it vowed to march again to Jantar Mantar on Sunday.Here is how the day unfolded for protesters, from the security measures before sunrise to the political confrontation that followed.
Early morning: Delhi tightens security, detentions begin
Delhi Police denied permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar, citing procedural lapses and law-and-order concerns. Authorities planned to deploy around 35,000 police and paramilitary personnel, with barricades, checkpoints, metro restrictions and mobile internet curbs in parts of central Delhi. Services to and from New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin stations were expected to be particularly affected.Police personnel wearing body cameras and drones were deployed for surveillance.Police also detained 30–40 people with criminal records as a preventive measure. At least 600 people had been detained across Delhi by 9am.
Morning: CJP leaders and Dhruv Rathee detained
CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained inside an aircraft shortly after it landed in Delhi from Mumbai. CJP called the action pre-planned and demanded their immediate release.YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was also detained from his Gurugram residence. CJP accused the government of targeting young people who questioned its actions.CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh and content creator Kavya Karnatac were also reported detained. CJP later alleged that Ratna Singh was being held inside a car surrounded by around 35 police personnel and the deputy commissioner of police. Police also placed several Congress workers and members of other political parties under house arrest ahead of the demonstration.Meanwhile, BJP president Nitin Nabin accused Rahul Gandhi and CJP associates of attempting to destabilise the country for political gains, alleging that their actions were driven by foreign forces.
Late morning: Students, lawyers and activists detained
More than 400 SFI members, other student activists and lawyers marching from the Supreme Court towards Jantar Mantar were detained. SFI and Left party workers staged protests at INA and near the BJP headquarters as the protest crackdown continued.Former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan was also reported detained.Student leader Neha Bora, CPI(ML) Liberation general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya, and activist Prashant Bhushan and Yogendra Yadav were among those detained near INA market while heading towards the protest. Bora had led a march from Jor Bagh towards Dilli Haat-INA.CJP named Ajinkya Shinde to lead the protest in a pre-recorded video. Following the announcement, Ajinkya urged protesters to turn any location where police stopped them into their “Jantar Mantar”.Congress MP Shashi Tharoor described the situation as an “undeclared Emer-GenZ”. He criticised the heavy security deployment, train cancellations, metro closures and restrictions on movement.
Afternoon: Kejriwal and Mamata detained
Former Delhi CM Arvind Kejriwal, former Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee were detained while heading to join the protest. Mamata said they had been taken around in a prisoner van for two hours. She announced a sit-in at Dwarka North police station and said she would join the INDIA march on Monday.Congress leaders Mallikarjun Kharge and Priyanka Gandhi criticised the crackdown ahead of the planned protest. Kharge accused the Modi government of suppressing dissent, saying it had turned the “mother of democracy” into a "muzzled democracy”. Meanwhile, Priyanka alleged that the government had curtailed constitutional rights.Police officials reported stones being pelted at a bus carrying detained protesters in Jhandewalan. Two police personnel, including a Pink Force member, were reported injured. Another officer was injured in alleged stone-pelting near Baba Kharak Singh Marg in Connaught Place, where police said a scuffle broke out as they tried to disperse protesters.By late afternoon, the reported detention count had risen from at least 600 in the morning to around 1,000 by afternoon.
BJP defends SIR, criticises opposition
BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra accused Rahul Gandhi of attempting to drag the President into a street protest. The party defended the police action, describing it as a victory for democracy over “mob rule”. Nabin had earlier accused the protesters of trying to destabilise the country.
