Verstappen wins F1 Singapore Sprint after Russell crashes out of lead
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
20:33:16 CST
21:33:16 KST

By F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
SINGAPORE, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Red Bull's Max Verstappen claimed his first Formula 1 victory in Singapore on Saturday, winning a rain-hit Sprint race that saw Mercedes' George Russell crash out of the lead and McLaren teammates Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri collide on the final lap.
Verstappen, who started from pole position, finished ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, with Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli taking fourth after benefiting from the late McLaren collision.
The victory marked Verstappen's first win of any kind at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, previously the only venue on the current Formula 1 calendar where the four-time world champion had never won.
Singapore's first-ever Sprint race was also its first Formula 1 contest held in daylight, but a torrential downpour shortly before the start forced a delay, echoing the disruption caused by heavy rain at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
After two formation laps, the 20-lap race began from a standing start on a track that remained wet in places, particularly along the main straight, despite some sections having already dried.
Russell made the better getaway from second on the grid, sweeping past Verstappen to take the lead, while Hamilton surged from sixth to third.
However, Russell's advantage lasted barely a lap. The Mercedes driver lost control exiting the final corner and spun into the barriers along the pit straight, damaging the right-rear of his car and bringing out the safety car.
"Sorry," Russell told his team over the radio.
The incident compounded a difficult weekend for the Briton, who is already set to start Sunday's Grand Prix from the back of the grid after incurring penalties for exceeding his allocation of power unit components.
Russell's retirement handed the lead back to Verstappen, with Hamilton and Leclerc second and third.
The opening laps descended into further chaos as Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez collided near the back of the field, eliminating both drivers.
Isack Hadjar also retired after reporting an engine braking problem, while Franco Colapinto stopped on track. Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas were among the other casualties, and Arvid Lindblad came under investigation for driving in the wrong direction while recovering from a spin.
With Russell's damaged Mercedes and debris being cleared from the circuit, the remaining cars were briefly directed through the pit lane before racing resumed at the end of lap six.
Verstappen controlled the restart and gradually established himself at the front, and with Hamilton unable to mount a serious challenge, the Dutchman eased to victory.
"The start was horrendous again, so that's definitely something that we need to improve on because if you have something like that tomorrow, that's your race over, if nothing crazy happens," said Verstappen, who had battled back to win last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia after having initially lost the lead at the start.
"Not ideal, but we got a bit lucky with what happened with George out of the last corner.
"And after that, you just want to keep it calm and under control, because you know that you can't pass around here, especially around here in these conditions with the intermediate.
"I'm happy to win here in the Sprint, but I also know that I want to win tomorrow [in the grand prix], not today."
Although a dry racing line began to emerge as the race progressed, drivers remained on intermediate tyres, with the limited number of laps remaining making a switch to slicks increasingly unattractive.
Overtaking opportunities were also scarce on Singapore's narrow street circuit, and with only eight championship points available to the winner, drivers had little incentive to risk damage ahead of qualifying for Sunday's main race.
By lap 16, Alex Albon had also retired, leaving just 14 cars running and making it the most attrition-hit Sprint race in Formula 1 history.
The closing stages appeared set to pass without further incident until Norris attempted to overtake teammate Piastri on the inside during the final lap.
The two McLarens made contact and spun, with Piastri forced to retire and Norris recovering to finish eighth, taking the final championship point.
Norris apologized to his team over the radio.
"Thought I was fully alongside, ran out of space," the Briton said.
The collision allowed championship leader Antonelli to finish fourth and collect five points, two more than he would have earned in sixth.
Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson finished fifth, ahead of Haas driver Ollie Bearman and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, with Norris completing the points-paying positions.
The qualifying session for Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix takes place later on Saturday. ■

He said the government was collaborating with provincial administrations and relevant stakeholders to integrate mental health services into primary healthcare facilities, educational institutions and community-based platforms.
Sharif stressed the need for early diagnosis, timely treatment and a supportive environment that allows people to seek help without fear of discrimination or social pressure.
He said children, young people, women and disadvantaged groups, as well as communities affected by poverty, displacement, emergencies and climate change, required particular attention.
The prime minister urged Pakistanis to build a society where people could discuss mental health openly and receive the support needed to lead healthy and fulfilling lives.
The theme of this year's World Mental Health Day is "Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change," highlighting the importance of incorporating the perspectives of people experiencing mental health conditions into policies and services. ■

Book on history of vehicle license plates in Iran unveiled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:30:54 UTC
21:30:54 KST

Book on history of vehicle license plates in Iran unveiled
TEHRAN – A book tracing the history of vehicle license plates in Iran, from the arrival of automobiles to the introduction of the country’s national registration system, was unveiled on Saturday at the Mostazafan Foundation’s headquarters in Tehran.
Titled Nomreh Aval (First Number), the book was prepared through a joint initiative involving the Applied Research Center of Iran’s Traffic Police, the Historical Car Museum of Iran and the Dafineh Museum Institute, which is operated by the Mostazafan Foundation.
Hamidreza Soleimani, managing director of the Foundation’s Museum Institute, said the publication was the culmination of at least 12 years of research by the institute and its research team.
“The technology that entered Iran also changed our social contracts,” Soleimani said, explaining how the introduction of automobiles and traffic regulations reshaped public behavior. Street signs, for example, now guide how vehicles should move and interact on roads, he noted.
He described the book as the first comprehensive reference on the history of vehicle license plates in Iran, saying it could serve researchers and automobile enthusiasts.
Soleimani also highlighted the research potential of the Historical Car Museum of Iran, which houses 320 historic vehicles, each with its own story and historical significance.
The book examines the evolution of vehicle registration plates in Iran, beginning with the arrival of automobiles and the establishment of the first numbering systems, and continuing through the introduction and adoption of national license plates.
According to its publishers, the work draws on historical research, documentary evidence and reliable sources, particularly archival materials held by Iran’s classic car museum. It brings together information that, in many cases, had not previously been compiled in a single publication, aiming to provide a documented account of how vehicle plates developed over time.
Reza Sakhaei, head of the Applied Research Center of the Law Enforcement Command’s Traffic Police, said vehicle license plates might initially appear to be a simple administrative matter, but they also reflect aspects of Iran’s modern history.
He added that vehicle registration and identification systems now serve purposes beyond their original function.
Sakhaei also discussed plans to develop smart glasses for traffic police officers, saying the technology could help officers monitor vehicles and drivers. The proposed device would incorporate a camera similar to those worn on police uniforms, with additional functions allowing users to move menus to the palm of their hand, he said.
Sakhaei described the newly unveiled book as a contribution to preserving Iran’s historical identity and collective memory.
Ainollah Jahani, the book’s technical supervisor, said the research had also brought to light unusual old vehicles, some of which could be used for museum displays and, in certain cases, might still be operational.
The publication adds to the research potential of Iran’s historic automobile collections, documenting how a practical system of vehicle identification evolved alongside the country’s transportation infrastructure and changing social practices.

Estonia's central bank adds stone barrier to after multiple vehicle strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

Estonia's central bank adds stone barrier to after multiple vehicle strikes
After multiple instances of the building being hit by vehicles, the Bank of Estonia has installed street-side rock barriers.
The Bank of Estonia (Eesti Pank) is located on Kentmanni and Estonia pst. in central Tallinn, and has seen around 20 instances in as many years of drivers, generally those driving under the influence of alcohol, hit its exterior wall.
Part of the issue is the central bank's building lies adjacent to a left turn, if coming from Freedom Square (Vabaduse väljak) and its traffic lights, around 150 meters away. Vehicles have been known to speed along this stretch of Estonia pst. and run out of road at the turn, hitting the bank building.
"For the past 20 years, drivers speeding across Freedom Square have rammed the bank building's wall around twenty times. There have been accidents on the curve by Eesti Pank where a drunk driver has driven into the bank's wall. To prevent this, a stone barrier has now been brought there, " the bank said.
The Saaremaa-quarried dolomite blocks will prevent stray vehicles hitting the bank itself. The blockes are irregular shapes and will be "greened" by the next summer.
The bank's management also recalled the April 2007 "Bronze Soldier Night" riots, though the building remained adequately protected during those incidents.
Much of the bank's real estate is state owned, noted Rait Roosve, adviser to the Bank of Estonina board.
"We have quite a lot — or let's say, an unbelievably large amount of property in the Eesti Pank quarter, and that property doesn't belong to us, it belongs to the Republic of Estonia, or to put it more precisely, to the people of Estonia, and we have an obligation to guard and protect it at the maximum level," he said
Since the area is public urban space, the Bank of Estonia says it cannot cannot and does not want to build a wall there. At the same time, the row of blocks being installed must ensure the safety of ordinary traffic and stop cars and small trucks.
It is not, however, a national defense structure, ;the stones will not be sufficient to defend the building from armored vehicles such as tanks, for instance..
"This is Estonian national stone, limestone, specifically dolomite, and these have been brought from Kaarma on Saaremaa. It will certainly slow a tank, but considering the mass of these dolomite blocks and the mass of a tank, purely physically or mechanically the victory is certainly on the tank's side. But it also won't allow a tank to ram straight into our wall," Roosve continued.
The project, carried out in cooperation with Tallinn city government, will be completed by the end of next week. Grasses planted by the stones should conceal them come next summer, making the area in front of the bank on Kentmanni tänav greener, planners say.

Why is US turning to Russia for diesel despite sanctions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:16:12 UTC
21:16:12 KST

Why is US turning to Russia for diesel despite sanctions?
President Donald Trump’s annoucement comes amid surging fuel prices and looming US midterm elections.
United States President Donald Trump says he has agreed a deal to release stocks of diesel fuel from Russia to try to ease high fuel costs in the US before November’s midterm elections.
However analysts told Al Jazeera that the deal will likely have little effect on easing the global energy crisis while European countries could refuse to buy from Russia altogether.
The agreement comes despite years of sanctions on Russia over its war on Ukraine, the latest of which were announced last month by the US and specifically targeted buyers of Russian oil.
Here’s what we know:
What has Trump agreed with Putin?
On Friday night, Trump announced on social media that after a “highly successful discussion” with Russian President Vladimir Putin, it had been agreed that Russia would “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global marketplace.
Another 500,000 tonnes would be released in November, and a further 1 million tonnes sometime after that, Trump said. He added that, based on the current condition of its diesel refineries, Russia would then deliver another 3 million tonnes of diesel.
Trump claimed that this move, along with what he described as “total control” by the US of the Strait of Hormuz, would bring down diesel prices in the US and the rest of the world.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” he wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform.
Trump later thanked Putin for the deal, telling reporters outside the White House on Friday: “To be honest, we have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel which is what we want.”
Putin said in a statement on Friday that Russia “confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large”.
Why is there a global diesel crisis?
Global fuel prices have surged as a result of both the US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine. Tehran has largely closed off the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas supplies had been shipped in peacetime, since the US and Israel first launched strikes on Iran in February.
The recent attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, another key oil export route from the Gulf, as well as attacks by Yemen’s Houthis around the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb strait have compounded supply disruptions.
Meanwhile, oil refineries and energy and port facilities have come under heavy attack in both Russia and Ukraine.
Global fuel inventories have plummeted, and diesel prices reached record highs in both the US and Europe in September.
Last week, the Group of Seven countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of emergency reserves of diesel and crude oil after a US pressure campaign on the European Union in which the Trump administration threatened a US ban on its diesel exports.
Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera last week that the impact of the G7 release “would be short-lived given that this is just a temporary solution to the supply crunch”.
How has the diesel crisis affected the US?
Surging diesel prices in the US saw the national average rise to a record $6.52 a gallon (3.79 litres) in September, more than twice the price from a year earlier. The national average is currently $6.20, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
The US is the world’s largest diesel exporter. Its inventories have fallen sharply since the Iran war began and remain below normal levels despite refiners increasing their output.
In September, US lawmakers and Trump floated restricting diesel exports in a bid to lower consumer costs. Trump also called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt attacks on diesel fuel targets, accusing him of causing a shortage after Ukraine ramped up its strikes on Russia’s oil industry this year, aiming to disrupt its energy industry, which it uses to fund its war effort. Trump did not single Russia out for similar treatment over its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Trump is particularly concerned about bringing down the price of diesel before the US midterm elections. The Iran war is already deeply unpopular and many small-business owners in his MAGA (Make America Great Again) support base rely on diesel being affordable.
Consumers are feeling the effects of rising prices as diesel is used by truckers to transport food and products and by farmers operating machinery. The latest Pew Research Center polling indicated that the economy is the most important issue for 84 percent of registered voters.
States that voted for Trump and typically support candidates from his Republican Party, like Iowa and Kansas, are now seen as battlegrounds in the November 3 elections, putting Trump under pressure to avoid a Republican defeat.
What does this mean for US sanctions on Russian oil?
The US banned imports of Russian oil and gas in 2022 under the Biden administration in response to the invasion of Ukraine in February that year.
A sweeping Russian sanctions law passed in Congress last month and signed by Trump also targets countries that buy Russian oil and gas. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 expanded existing sanctions and aimed to pressure Putin by targeting officials, banks and shadow tankers that facilitate the Russian energy trade.
It also gave Trump the power to impose 100 percent tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil and natural gas.
After Trump’s announcement on Friday, the US Department of the Treasury said the Office of Foreign Assets Control was “immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market”.
Isn’t Russia having a fuel crisis of its own?
Yes, it is, giving analysts reason to doubt that Russia will be able to release as much diesel as Trump is promising.
Neil Atkinson, former head of the International Energy Agency’s oil industry and markets division, told Al Jazeera that he is sceptical about Russia being able to do this.
“In the very short term, it’s very hard to see how Russia can deliver the volumes that are talked about in the deal other than at the expense of its domestic market,” he said.
Russia was previously the world’s second-largest diesel exporter after the US. But Russian diesel and gas exports in the third quarter of this year were at 190,000 barrels per day compared with 690,000 barrels per day in the second quarter and 850,000 barrels per day in the first quarter, explained Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a maritime intelligence analyst with the shipping analytics company Windward, citing data from the commodities tracker Vortexa.
Russia, therefore, banned diesel exports in July in a bid to meet domestic demand and in late September expanded the ban until the end of October.
Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy facilities have also contributed to the fuel crisis in Russia. Putin has admitted that 1 percent of Russia’s gross domestic product has been affected by Ukrainian attacks.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said its air strikes have destroyed more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity. In July, it also struck hundreds of Russian shadow fleet tankers in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, affecting the delivery of gas to Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.
Bockmann told Al Jazeera that Russian domestic shortages were “so acute that over the third quarter for the first time we saw Russia import gasoline and diesel and gas oil”.
She added that “as recently as this week”, a ship carrying diesel and gas oil arrived in the port of Vysotsk.
Last week, Russia said it would consider a partial lifting of diesel export restrictions in the case of overproduction. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told the Russian parliament that the domestic market was balanced and “if diesel production exceeds domestic demand, we will consider partially reopening exports.”
Russia typically produces double the diesel needed to meet its domestic needs, according to the International Energy Agency. It has different standards of diesel suitable for different temperatures. Its summer-grade diesel for temperatures over 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) may be released to make way for the winter and Arctic grades needed domestically in the coming months.
How has Ukraine reacted?
Trump’s announcement came as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, were meeting with Ukrainian officials and European negotiators in Miami, Florida, to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.
Zelenskyy reacted to the announcement, saying it was “a weak decision by strong partners”.
He said the deal “plays into Russia’s hands,- allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.
Can Russian diesel ease the pressure on global prices?
On Friday, Putin said he was “convinced [the agreement] will have a positive impact on the entire global economy”.
The Russian president also noted that “an agreement was reaffirmed to maintain personal contacts between the presidents of the two countries and to continue cooperation across their respective administrations, security services and agencies.”
Analysts said the agreement will do little to address the global energy crisis, however.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera that the Trump-Putin deal to release Russian diesel is a short-term solution and “another classic Trump deal”.
“Announce an ‘agreement’ with an unpleasant dictator with impressive headline numbers and no certainty that any of the objectives will be achieved,” he said. “Even if some of the diesel does make it out of Russia, it is only a short-term solution given the globe’s daily consumption of diesel is around 30 million barrels,” which is roughly the total amount that could be released under the outlines of the deal that Trump announced.
Bockmann also told Al Jazeera that it is unclear how much impact releasing Russian diesel will have on reducing prices and global shortages.
“I’m not sure how effective the issuing of the general licence will be in allowing volumes to be imported at levels that are going to impact the domestic price of diesel in the US,” she said.
Atkinson said the volumes announced by Trump – even if Russia could manage to provide them – “don’t really move the needle very much” on prices because the US uses about 3.7 million barrels of diesel a day.
There are also indications that European countries may not even buy diesel from Russia.
“It’s very hard to see how a European government could, in all morality, buy oil from Russia when the whole point of the last four years is that Europe has been trying to wean itself off Russian oil and gas supplies as soon as practical,” Atkinson said.

Ukraine National Bank delegation heads to IMF, World Bank Annual Meetings
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:15:50 EEST
21:15:50 KST

A delegation from the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU), led by NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyy, has departed for Bangkok, Thailand, on a working visit to participate in the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group (WBG), scheduled for October 12-18, 2026, the central bank said in a statement on Facebook.
Meetings are planned with the leadership and representatives of the IMF and the World Bank, including IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and World Bank Vice President Antonella Bassani.
Consultations with the heads of several central banks and representatives of the European Commission and international financial institutions are also scheduled, along with participation in investment conferences and the 10th Ministerial Roundtable on Ukraine organized by the World Bank.
According to Interfax-Ukraine, a delegation from the Ministry of Finance, led by Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko, will also attend the Annual Meetings.
The Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group are the main global financial forum, bringing together central bank governors, finance ministers, representatives of international financial institutions and businesses to discuss and address the world's most pressing financial and economic challenges. They are usually held in Washington, D.C., at the headquarters of the IMF and the World Bank Group, for two consecutive years, with the third year's meetings taking place in another member country.
Speaking in Singapore this week, Georgieva identified persistently high energy prices, record government debt, and risks associated with the artificial intelligence investment boom as the main challenges to the global economy to be discussed at the meetings. According to her, the global economy is being affected by two opposing forces: a shock in the energy sector caused by reduced supply and a sharp increase in economic demand associated with the development of artificial intelligence.
"Our World Economic Outlook will show that… The largest hits to growth this year are in economies ravaged by war: a war on Ukraine in its fifth year, a war in the Gulf in its eighth month, and too many other raging conflicts, destroying lives and causing global economic damage," Georgieva said.
She added that a less pronounced slowdown was also being observed in a number of other vulnerable countries, particularly those dependent on energy imports and with limited fiscal and monetary policy capacity to mitigate such shocks.
However, economic growth is likely to accelerate in some countries thanks to artificial intelligence, which is rapidly becoming one of the key factors determining countries' positions in the global economy, Georgieva noted.
"Global investment-to-GDP in AI will reach and likely exceed the amounts that went into building the railroads, the electricity grid, or the telecommunication network. We estimate AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of world goods trade and rising," she said.
AI-related demand is supporting investment, particularly in countries such as the United States, China, and India, Georgieva noted. However, she added that this growth is largely bypassing most other countries, increasing the risk of widening economic inequality around the world.
As for rising oil prices, Georgieva said the impact of the energy shock on the global economy remained limited for now. However, oil prices were still hovering around $100 per barrel, contributing to higher inflation, interest rates, and government bond yields, which in turn were driving up fiscal deficits, public debt, and debt-servicing costs.
"And, to quote from Game of Thrones, winter is coming. Price pressures may build further as countries replenish reserves and demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season," the IMF managing director said.
In July, the IMF forecast that the global economy would grow by 3% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027. Georgieva did not say in her speech on Wednesday whether these forecasts would be revised.
"Putting all of it together, my message to the world's economic policymakers next week will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them," Georgieva concluded in her Singapore speech, citing fiscal consolidation and structural reforms among those actions and tools.

The West’s Azerbaijan Paradox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

On Sept. 25, three US senators sent an unusually clear and specific message about Azerbaijan.
Senators Peter Welch, Thom Tillis and Tim Kaine called on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to make the release of Azerbaijan’s political prisoners a condition of a deeper strategic partnership with Baku.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In their letter, the senators specifically called for the immediate release of Ali Karimli, leader of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, alongside other prominent political prisoners.
(It is worth noting that the letter mentions seven other names in addition to Karimli, although the true number of political prisoners is closer to 300+. Other prominent individuals not specifically mentioned in the letter include Ulvi Hasanli, Mamad Ibrahim, Azer Gasimli, and Bakhtiyar Hajiyev).
The senators’ intervention is extremely timely and should be supported on both sides of the Atlantic.
This is because the crucial question confronting Western governments is no longer simply whether they should speak more forcefully about human rights in Azerbaijan.
Yes, Azerbaijan is one of the most authoritarian countries in the world, and according to V-Dem and Freedom House scores, it’s even below countries like Russia.
But there’s also another, more realpolitik side to all this.
The fundamental question is as follows: can the West build a durable strategic partnership with a government that is imprisoning some of the Azerbaijanis most committed to their country’s integration with the democratic West.
Russian Drones Sink Turkish-Owned Grain Ship as Ankara Pushes Black Sea Security Deal
Can the West really build any meaningful strategic partnership with the very same regime that constantly hedges its bets, is very happy to help Russia escape sanctions and remove its oligarchs from the sanctions list, and is actively pursuing a deeper and deeper strategic partnership with China?
Or is it finally time to fully support imprisoned pro-West, pro-Euro-Atlantic liberal democrats currently in jail for standing up to the corrupt and despotic rule of the Aliyev regime?
The European Parliament has understood this contradiction better than most.
Following Karimli’s arrest, in its Dec. 18, 2025 resolution, it condemned his detention and called for the immediate and unconditional release of Karimli and of all political prisoners in Azerbaijan.
The European Parliament has urged the EU to consider measures against officials responsible for repression and argued that progress on any future partnership agreement with Azerbaijan should depend on tangible improvements in human rights and the rule of law.
Yet the response from Europe’s executive leadership has been demonstrably (and embarrassingly) less forceful.
That silence is extremely damaging because of how it is perceived by the Aliyev regime.
They now think that they can absolutely dismiss any concerns about human rights, believing that there will not be any meaningful pressure on them.
Western policy towards Azerbaijan rests on a pragmatic calculation: Azerbaijan supplies energy to Europe, occupies an important geographical position between Europe and Central Asia (the Ganja corridor as part of the Middle Corridor), and is an important participant in the emerging peace settlement with Armenia.
These are indeed legitimate strategic interests.
But strategic realism should not mean treating authoritarian stability as permanent stability.
Because, unlike the wealthy Gulf monarchies in the Middle East, the Azerbaijani regime is extremely repressive but not very stable at all. In the past 10 years, there have been multiple riots in Ganja, Guba, Ismaili, etc. In spite of billions spent on security forces, in each of these instances, the Aliyev regime found it difficult to maintain order.
What if next-gen Z-fueled protests, the likes of which we saw in India, Bangladesh, and Nepal, were to arise in larger cities like Baku, and in a country sandwiched between hostile Russia and an increasingly aggressive Iranian regime?
In a geography of such hostile interventionist powers, the last thing that Azerbaijan needs is a spontaneous, uncontrolled revolt caused by the extreme corruption and economic mismanagement of the regime.
But this doesn’t mean that Azerbaijan’s fate is a choice between spontaneous uprisings destabilizing the country, or an ever-increasing authoritarianism.
A democratic alternative
There is another Azerbaijan.
It is a country whose democratic civil opposition has historically looked towards Europe, NATO, and the wider Euro-Atlantic community rather than Moscow.
Indeed, Karimli himself has repeatedly advocated Azerbaijan’s integration with the European Union.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he has written explicitly in support of Ukraine and warned that Russian victory would whet Moscow’s imperialist appetite and strengthen authoritarianism throughout the former Soviet space.
In February 2022, and mere days before the invasion, when the whole civilized West was uniting against Russian aggression, President Ilham Aliyev flew to Moscow to sign a treaty of alliance with Russia.
Karimli was the opposition leader who stood up against this national embarrassment and pointed out that Azerbaijan must stand together with Ukraine and the Western, Euro-Atlantic community.
And so, this is precisely what makes his imprisonment a strategic question for the West, not merely a humanitarian one.
If Azerbaijan eventually becomes more democratic, there is every reason for Western governments to want the political forces emerging from that transition to regard Europe, Britain and the United States as partners.
Yet what lesson are Azerbaijani democrats supposed to draw today?
They see the European Parliament speaking for them. They now see American senators doing the same.
But they also see Western governments pursuing ever deeper relations with President Aliyev while organized democratic opposition is systematically dismantled.
Meanwhile, Baku is treating the very same West with increasing contempt, and Aliyev himself recently described the European Parliament as a “den of bribery”.
(It is worth noting that in a few instances when such bribery did take place, it was the Aliyev regime itself that fueled and enabled these instances of corruption and bribery in Europe. It is all very well documented in Azerbaijan’s ‘‘caviar diplomacy” investigations.)
And at the same time, the regime is developing relationships elsewhere.
In 2025, Azerbaijan and China elevated their relationship to a “comprehensive strategic partnership.” And in September this year, Azerbaijan’s State Security Service signed a security cooperation agreement with China’s Ministry of Public Security.
The two governments have pledged greater cooperation between law-enforcement and security institutions.
Then there is the extraordinary recent affair involving Alisher Usmanov.
France had been pressed by Azerbaijan over the EU sanctions imposed on the Russian-Uzbek billionaire, whom the EU had previously described as having particularly close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The EU subsequently removed Usmanov from its sanctions regime. The following day, Aliyev pardoned a French citizen imprisoned in Azerbaijan.
This incident should therefore dispel the comforting assumption that Azerbaijan’s current government is naturally or irreversibly anchored in the Western geopolitical camp.
In fact, the very opposite is true: the Aliyev regime is not even trying to hide its order-taking from the Kremlin and its desire to please Putin at any cost.
The cost here is immediate and relevant to Ukraine: had Aliyev agreed to release the French citizen without conditioning it on a Russian oligarch’s sanctions release, the whole incident around sanctions on Russia would have been avoided. And Putin would not have as much leverage over European sanctions targeting its regime.
And this then makes the distinction between Azerbaijan and its government essential.
Azerbaijanis should not be written off as belonging naturally to some Russian, Chinese or authoritarian sphere of influence. Azerbaijan has a secular society, deep connections with Europe and a democratic tradition stretching back to the establishment of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic in 1918.
Given genuinely competitive elections, freedom of assembly, independent media and functioning political institutions, Azerbaijan could become one of the West’s most natural partners in the South Caucasus.
But that possibility becomes more remote every time another journalist is imprisoned, another civil-society organization is dismantled or another opposition politician disappears behind prison walls.
Karimli has now been detained since November 2025. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International has raised serious concerns about his treatment and detention conditions. And Karimli’s lawyers have witnessed firsthand how continuous sleep deprivation and drinking-water restrictions have led to his deteriorating health.
(It is worth noting that the Aliyev regime has been extremely cruel in one other respect: keeping political prisoners facing other, more serious health risks in jail for as long as possible and only releasing them just before their health enters the terminal phase. Most recently, a prominent journalist Evez Zeynalli was suffering from cancer, and yet authorities refused to release him until the very last moment, when they realized he was about to die. Unfortunately, that day came on Sept. 28, 2026.)
The preliminary investigation against Karimli has now reportedly been completed, bringing the prospect of a full trial closer.
There is therefore little time for quiet diplomacy without consequences.
Turning engagement into leverage
The administration in Washington, and leaders in Brussels should both act on the bipartisan senators’ proposal and make the immediate release of political prisoners part of negotiations over a strategic partnership.
European leaders should reinforce the position already taken by their own parliament. Britain, with its substantial economic relationship with Azerbaijan, should add its voice.
This does not require abandoning the current engagement with Baku.
But it does require using engagement as leverage.
Western governments should communicate privately and publicly that Azerbaijan can have a deeper relationship with the democratic world, but that such a relationship cannot be built on the imprisonment of democratic opponents.
The immediate objective should be simple: release Karimli and Azerbaijan’s other political prisoners.
To this effect, both Washington and Brussels should be willing to use any leverage against the regime itself, including targeted sanctions, asset freezes, and travel bans against the leaders of the Aliyev regime.
But the larger objective is more important still.
The West should make clear that its partnership is not merely with whoever occupies the presidential palace in Baku today.
It is with Azerbaijan and its people.
And consequently, with the possibility of a democratic, sovereign and genuinely Euro-Atlantic Azerbaijan tomorrow.

Ukraine and Finland condemn Trump’s deal to import Russian diesel
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
15:09:44 EEST
21:09:44 KST

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo has condemned an agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to American and global markets, describing the decision as a major disappointment.
Speaking to Finnish broadcaster Yle on Saturday, Orpo questioned whether the agreement would have any significant effect on fuel prices, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Washington of providing financial support to Russia during its war against Ukraine.
The agreement, announced by Trump on Friday, provides for Russia to deliver more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes thereafter.
Trump also announced plans for an additional three million tonnes, depending on the condition of Russian refineries damaged by Ukrainian attacks.
The US Treasury subsequently issued a temporary licence permitting imports of Russian diesel until 7 April 2027, easing sanctions introduced to restrict Moscow's energy revenues.
Orpo told Yle's Ykkösaamu programme that the announcement was a "terrible disappointment", although he stressed that the agreed quantities represented only a fraction of US diesel consumption.
He also questioned whether Russia would fulfil the deliveries and said he did not expect the agreement to have much impact on American or global markets.
Zelenskyy described the agreement as a gift to Putin and "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy wrote on X, warning that Russia would repay the diesel with further attacks.
The announcement coincided with talks between Ukrainian, European and American representatives in Miami aimed at ending the war.
Trump defended the arrangement as necessary to reduce fuel costs following disruptions caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran, which began in February.
According to figures from the American Automobile Association reported by Reuters, average US diesel prices reached $6.28 per gallon on Thursday, approximately 70% above their level before the conflict.
Diesel prices have become a concern for the administration ahead of the 3 November congressional elections, particularly because of their effect on farming, transport and consumer costs.
The agreement also attracted criticism from American lawmakers. Republican congressman Don Bacon called for stronger sanctions against Russia rather than measures that would increase Moscow's revenues.
Energy specialists questioned the potential benefits for consumers.
In an interview with Finnish newspaper Ilta-Sanomat, Hanna Kalenoja, a transport specialist at the Finland Chamber of Commerce, said the agreement would primarily redirect existing Russian diesel exports rather than increase global supplies.
Russia has continued exporting diesel despite production disruptions caused by Ukrainian strikes on its refineries.
Kalenoja explained that the agreement would determine whether available Russian fuel reached the United States and its allies instead of Asian markets, where much of it has previously been sold.
She told IS that Finnish motorists were unlikely to see meaningful reductions in diesel prices as a result of the agreement.
Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, also questioned the potential price benefits, telling the Associated Press that the agreement would provide Russia with additional export revenue without substantially reducing diesel costs in the United States or Europe.
Seigle said Russia was seeking buyers for its summer-grade diesel as domestic demand shifted towards winter and Arctic fuel grades.
Kalenoja identified Washington's willingness to ease sanctions on Russia in response to energy costs as a concern for Europe, where governments have maintained restrictions on Russian energy imports.
Meanwhile, the Finnish government continues discussing measures to help households and businesses facing higher fuel prices.
Orpo told Yle that proposals include tax changes, commuting deductions and support for professional drivers, but ministers have yet to agree on a package.
The prime minister also announced plans to propose ending tourist visas for Russian citizens across Europe at next week's European Council meeting, citing concerns about possible Russian sabotage operations.

Twelve people, including three children, were reportedly killed in a Russian strike on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
A six-year-old girl was among those reported killed after a strike damaged a residential apartment block. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, said her birthday would have been at the end of the month.
Fourteen others were wounded in the attack on the industrial city, whose outskirts lie less than 30 kilometres from the frontline. Local governor Mykhailo Semikin said Russia hit several locations simultaneously in the early hours of Saturday.
Emergency workers continued search-and-rescue operations at the damaged buildings, pulling survivors from the rubble.
Zaporizhzhia, which had a pre-war population of more than 700,000, has experienced repeated strikes during the conflict, with Ukrainian authorities reporting an increase in attacks in recent months.
Ukrainian officials said nearly 80 civilians had been killed in Russian strikes over two days earlier this week.
Zelenskyy hits out at Washington
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had marked the lifting of diesel sanctions by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House.
He said Moscow reads any easing of pressure as a signal that it can keep bombing cities. "Different signals are needed," he said.
Trump's decision comes as his administration tries to curb fuel prices, which have risen sharply during the US conflict with Iran. Ukraine has advocated maintaining economic pressure on Moscow as part of negotiations aimed at ending the conflict.
Trump has also criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he says have driven up global prices. Kiev says it wants a total halt to energy strikes by both sides.
On Saturday, parts of Kiev and the surrounding region were left without power, bringing the city's metro to a complete halt for the second time this week.
Peace efforts stall
The latest strikes came after Ukrainian and European officials held talks with US negotiators in Miami on Friday, aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Trump announced the diesel deal while the talks were under way, a move Zelenskyy said caught Kiev by surprise.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said after a call with Trump that an immediate resumption of peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow.
Separately, the Russian-installed governor of the Russian-controlled Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine said four civilians were killed and five wounded in Ukrainian attacks on Saturday.

Outrage after Syrian universities bar women from several majors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:06:20 UTC
21:06:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Outrage in Syria after universities bar women from several degree programmes
Syria’s university admission rules have sparked anger after women were excluded from several degree programmes, including law, social sciences and business administration, prompting concerns about their access to higher education under the country’s new government.
The Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research published admission requirements for the 2026-2027 academic year on 30 September. The lists allocate places at universities and technical institutes according to students' secondary-school results and preferences, while restricting admission to certain programmes based on gender.
The restrictions cover military, security and civilian fields. Programmes reserved for men include legal studies at the newly established National University of Defence Sciences, as well as law, social sciences, business administration and economics at its Damascus faculties. Some technical programmes, including radio and television production at a media institute in Idlib, are also restricted to male applicants.
Other affected fields include mechanical, electronic, computer, mechatronics, marine and aeronautical engineering, alongside programmes at military and security institutions.
Some programmes remain open to women, including early childhood education, nursing, midwifery and selected cybersecurity courses. The restrictions vary by institution and location, and women can still study subjects such as law and engineering at other universities, including Damascus University.
Not all the restrictions are new. Some technical institutes have historically admitted only men, including the Oil and Gas Institute in Deir Ezzor, according to a former higher education ministry official cited by AFP. Some institutes also fall under ministries other than higher education, which set their own admission requirements.
The ministry has not explained why women have been excluded from the affected programmes, according to AFP, which said it had sought comment from the authorities.
The rules have fuelled wider concerns about women’s rights and their opportunities in education and employment since the overthrow of former dictator Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Educator Ahlam Othman told AFP that the restrictions represented "another obstacle" for women in Syria, adding that Syrian women already faced discrimination and oppression.
Social media users have also criticised the decision, arguing that restricting access to certain subjects could limit women’s ability to understand and defend their rights.

"The Syrian authorities’ decision to bar women from higher education in most fields – particularly the study of law – aims to prevent them from learning about their rights or defending them legally, thereby excluding them from social and professional life," one user wrote on X.
Author Rime Allaf, who wrote It Started in Damascus: How the Long Syrian Revolution Reshaped Our World described the restrictions as "primitive" and unjustifiable, warning that they would affect society more broadly.
Sally Obeid, a founding member of the Syrian Christian Congress, condemned the rules as an example of exclusionary policies, writing on X: "Syria will not be ruled by a mindset that begrudges women the right to think!"
Women remain underrepresented in Syria’s transitional institutions. Hind Kabawat, minister of social affairs and labour, is the only woman in the transitional cabinet.
The transitional parliament has 22 women among its 206 sitting members. Seven were indirectly elected through electoral bodies, while 15 were appointed by President Ahmed al-Sharaa.

Astronaut Pikachu logs 67 days and 1,040 orbits aboard ISS – now catch him on Earth
- Astronaut Pikachu spent 67 days and 1,040 orbits on the ISS, then returned to Earth and began a Europe tour to promote space exploration.
- ESA and The Pokemon Company launched a World Space Week campaign with a travelling exhibition and Pokemon Go events at six European science and space museums.
- French astronaut Sophie Adenot filmed Pikachu’s ISS tour, and ESA said the project aims to inspire future generations through a fun, engaging space experience.
AI generated
After 67 days and 1,040 orbits on board the International Space Station (ISS), Pikachu is back on Earth and on tour across Europe to stoke interest in space exploration.
The spacesuit-clad, yellow, plush space traveller was at the orbiting laboratory from April 11 to June 17 with crew members from the European Space Agency (ESA).
A YouTube video posted on Oct 6 that has since been viewed over a million times shows French astronaut Sophie Adenot giving the plush toy a tour of the ISS.
Pikachu is seen being guided through the station, with visits to its water dispenser, laboratory freezers and crew quarters.
Adenot closes the video by telling Pikachu that, even in space, “you have a tendency to hide everywhere”.
“Yeah, I know you like this game,” she tells him.
Adenot returned to Earth on Oct 8, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off California aboard SpaceX’s Dragon capsule with three other Crew-12 astronauts.
Her 237-day mission set a record for the longest single spaceflight by a European astronaut.
Pikachu’s space adventure is part of a wider ESA-Pokemon collaboration marking World Space Week from Oct 4 to 10.
The partnership includes a travelling, family-friendly exhibition combining space science with Pokemon storytelling. Displays explain how Europe launches spacecraft, supports astronauts, studies the sun and explores the solar system.
“Inspiring future generations is a key part of ESA’s mission,” said Josef Aschbacher, the agency’s director-general. “Through this collaboration with Pokemon, we are unlocking new ways for people across Europe to connect with space through a unique and engaging experience.”
For fans who prefer their scientific outreach with something to catch, Pokemon Go offered an Astronaut Pikachu through one-star raids and timed research at six European science and space museums.
The locations included London’s Science Museum; Cité de l’espace in Toulouse, France; Deutsches Museum in Nuremberg, Germany; Museu de les Ciències in Valencia, Spain; Space Expo in Noordwijk, Netherlands; and Euro Space Center in Transinne, Belgium.
The event ran through Oct 10. A rare Shiny version of Astronaut Pikachu was also offered.
Pikachu joins an elite club of plush space travellers that include Snoopy, who was on NASA’s uncrewed Artemis I lunar mission, and Grogu, the mascot on SpaceX’s Crew-1 flight.

Mari-Liis Jakobson: Are we sailing to the end with a minority government?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:05:00 UTC
21:05:00 KST

Mari-Liis Jakobson: Are we sailing to the end with a minority government?
Can Estonia's current minority government make it to the finish line or are we heading toward early elections, asks Mari‑Liis Jakobson.
Politics watchers have no reason to be bored. The first signs of the election campaign are already visible on the streets, the Riigikogu is processing the state budget, and the opposition is preparing yet another no‑confidence motion against the prime minister. All this in a context where the governing parties have lost their parliamentary majority and the opposition is threatening early elections.
For those who have tuned out of politics for a while: as of Thursday evening, the governing parties — Reform Party and Eesti 200 — hold 50 of the Riigikogu's 101 seats, meaning less than half. In theory, MPs not belonging to the government have a good chance of voting down coalition‑backed bills. This is loudly demanded by MPs from Isamaa, Center Party, and EKRE, while the Social Democrats have said they are willing to support the budget under certain conditions.
The budget bill currently under consideration is weightier than usual, because if the Riigikogu fails to pass it, this leads to early elections. True, the constitution says early elections must be called if the government cannot pass the budget within two months after the start of the fiscal year — meaning by February 2027. But regular elections are already scheduled for March. If a no‑confidence motion against the prime minister succeeds, it leads to forming a new government, but not necessarily early elections.
In this light, I wanted to steer the debate a bit more toward research‑based understanding and briefly introduce what political science has found about minority governments.
First, what exactly are minority governments and why are they sometimes chosen?
Generally, it is more comfortable to govern with a secure majority, allowing you to implement promises made to voters. Sometimes, however, the coalition that would form is so diverse and contradictory in its goals that it is simpler and more logical to proceed without a parliamentary majority and rely on cooperation with opposition parties on issues where views overlap.
Minority governments are quite common in the Nordic countries, where the spectrum of parties entering parliament is broad. But they have also been used elsewhere — for example in Spain, Romania, the United Kingdom, and even in Estonia, when Andrus Ansip's minority government hoped to pass certain issues with the support of the Estonian Greens. Research shows minority governments are not necessarily less effective than majority governments.
Minority governments can differ greatly in structure and effectiveness. Sometimes such cooperation is covered by formal agreements; sometimes it is more ad hoc. Some minority governments have stable partners; others change them frequently. The circle of cooperating parties also varies. Sometimes minority governments rely on small regional parties; other times on parties with more radical views.
For example, Sweden's outgoing minority government led by Ulf Kristersson relied on the so‑called Tidö Agreement with the Sweden Democrats, who were not part of the government but provided parliamentary support.
The government's interest in such cooperation is obvious. But why are partners who remain outside the government willing to cooperate?
Every political move has a political cost. Entering government makes you more visible, gives your members political posts, and allows you to directly shape policy. At the same time, as a government member you are responsible for decisions your voters may dislike, and in many eyes you share blame for any blunders the state makes.
As a supporter of a minority government, you do not get political posts, but you also do not have to support all government decisions or share responsibility for them. And from time to time, in exchange for your support, you can negotiate a decision that pleases your voters.
Research shows that parties supporting minority governments generally perform better in elections than small coalition partners — though not necessarily better than parties that remain in opposition.
Parties that support the government on a case‑by‑case basis and are not tied to cooperation agreements tend to do best in elections. Minority governments also appeal to some voters because they create a sense that voter preferences are taken into account more than in majority governments. This is likely the strategy the Social Democrats and Reform Party are hoping for.
The rest of the opposition continues to beat the drum of early elections. This is a familiar tune, played mainly to highlight the government's weakness in a more dramatic light. The campaign‑covered cityscape amplifies this message: look, things are serious. But most likely election day will still be 7 March, no matter what is said.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Operations Plan Germany: How the Bundeswehr trains for NATO collective defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:02:00 UTC
21:02:00 KST

How the German military trains for NATO defense
October 10, 2026
In a residential district of Hamburg at midnight, the streets are quiet and deserted. Suddenly, the silence is shattered: Several helicopters circle the night sky, and flashing blue lights illuminate the darkness. A long convoy of vehicles moves through the streets. Soldiers stand atop armored Bundeswehr vehicles, their machine guns at the ready. For local residents, it is an unusual, perhaps even unsettling sight in an otherwise peaceful port city.
"Red Storm Charlie" is the name of the exercise that will bring parts of Hamburg, northern Germany's largest city, to a standstill for three days. The Bundeswehr, police, and civilian organizations are jointly testing how well prepared they are to respond in a crisis.
The scenario centers on a deteriorating security situation on NATO's eastern flank. NATO troops, represented in the exercise by Bundeswehr soldiers, arrive at the port of Hamburg, Germany's largest seaport, before moving eastwards through the Hanseatic city.
Acts of sabotage and demonstrations, also included in the scenario, hamper their advance. With around 1,700 participants, including 500 soldiers, the exercise held in late September 2026, was the largest of its kind to date.
"Red Storm Charlie" forms part of a classified strategy known as the "Operationsplan Deutschland" (Operations Plan Germany). Through this document, the Bundeswehr is preparing for the possibility of a Russian attack on NATO territory. The Operations Plan Germany is an integral element of NATO's broader defense planning and is closely aligned with the Alliance's overall defense framework.
In the event of war or a major crisis, not only the city of Hamburg but Germany as a whole would assume a pivotal role as a logistics hub for hundreds of thousands of NATO soldiers, weapons, and pieces of heavy equipment. "This is a highly detailed and strictly classified plan that specifies exactly where NATO allies would arrive in Germany, including which ports they would use and which routes would be required for their transit across the country," security expert Aylin Matlé of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) told DW.
Germany as a transit country for NATO troops
The Baltic states are widely regarded as the region where NATO considers a Russian attack most likely. In such a scenario, the alliance would concentrate large troop contingents from its 32 member states there. To reach the region, soldiers from southern and western Europe would need to pass through Germany. "In concrete terms, this means that around 800,000 soldiers and 200,000 vehicles would have to move through our country within six months. Those are the calculations," says Marcel Bohnert, a Bundeswehr officer who contributed to the first version of the Operations Plan.
Speaking to DW in a personal capacity rather than as a representative of the Bundeswehr, Bohnert explained: "We must ensure that soldiers can use our roads and ports safely. That is why we take care of all their needs: We arrange accommodation, provide food, ensure their security, and guide them through our transport network."
The plan also covers transport in the opposite direction, from east to west, including the evacuation of wounded soldiers and civilians fleeing the conflict. Its development was commissioned by Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As Germany's highest-ranking military officer, Breuer is far from alone in his concern that Russia could target additional countries. Germany is already confronting a wide range of Russian hostile activities, from cyberattacks to acts of sabotage directed against the Bundeswehr.
Defense Minister Pistorius: 'Moscow is testing our response'
A new dimension of the threat emerged with the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. An explosive-laden drone was deployed there and failed to detonate only through luck. The German government holds Russia responsible. "The threat is becoming more tangible. It is serious, acute, and increasingly visible. This is exactly what the Russian president wants. Moscow is testing our response," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told the Bundestag on September 23.
The Bundeswehr is also addressing this threat through the Operations Plan Germany, which is continuously being refined and updated. Lessons learned from exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are incorporated into the plan. According to Bohnert, the plan also serves as a deterrent: "We hope to discourage Russia from further aggression by demonstrating our strength through the rapid build-up of military capabilities and the highly organized, swift deployment of forces to the borders."
Roads and bridges need upgrading
How well prepared is Germany for its role as a military logistics hub? Matlé identifies one major vulnerability in the country's ageing and, in some cases, deteriorating infrastructure. Germany, she argues, must address the maintenance and repair of the bridges, roads, and transport routes required for troop movements "far more quickly and comprehensively." "Some of this infrastructure dates back to the Cold War and was not designed to accommodate heavy loads or military equipment."
A further challenge lies in striking the right balance between confidentiality and public involvement. To guard against acts of sabotage, sensitive details such as the precise transit routes for NATO troops must not fall into Russian hands. At the same time, the plan can only succeed through close cooperation between the Bundeswehr and civilian society, including local and regional authorities, the police, and relief organizations. "Parts of the plan must be publicly accessible because we need support from society, as well as from ministries and governments, to make it work," said Bohnert.
Could the AfD pass on sensitive information?
The debate over the confidentiality of the more than 1,000-page document recently resurfaced after the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) emerged as the strongest party in recent elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Security experts expressed concern that the party, which is classified in part as right-wing extremist and is regarded as Russia-friendly, could pass information from the plan to Moscow if it were to assume the office of state premier. The Defense Ministry rejected these concerns, noting that no federal state is given access to the complete document. Instead, the sensitive sections of the Operations Plan are shared only in excerpts and strictly on a need-to-know basis.
According to observers, however, the growing number of hybrid threats is underscoring the need for secrecy. During the "Red Storm Charlie" exercise in Hamburg, accredited journalists were not informed of routes or locations until the very last moment because of concerns over potential disruptions and acts of sabotage.
This article was originally written in German.

Edge Control: the art exhibition using hidden camera images to explore race and beauty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:00:57 UTC
21:00:57 KST

In her essay The Oppositional Gaze: Black Female Spectators, writer and philosopher bell hooks explains that the relationship between Black people and the act of “looking” has been traumatic since slavery. Black people, many of whom are still subject to the constant surveillance that originated during enslavement, have historically been punished with severe consequences, such as lynching, for looking back at those who subjugate them. Despite these risks, hooks writes, they rebelled by secretly looking at white people, as well as their surroundings, rejecting the white gaze as the singular framework of reality. We can, as bell hooks writes, “interrogate the gaze of the Other but also look back, and at one another, naming what we see”.
I thought of this analysis when I visited Edge Control, artist Deana Lawson’s latest photography exhibition at the Gagosian gallery in New York City. Edge control refers to the gels and pomades that slick the hairs along the edges of a Black woman’s hairline, but in Lawson’s exhibit, the phrase takes on an additional meaning. It’s at once a styling product for Black haircare devotees as well as a tool to examine the beauty industry, consumerism and how surveillance and race intersect.
To explore these intersections, Lawson uses photos of alleged beauty supply store shoplifters, presented in large scale and outside their original contexts. As a warning to customers, many beauty supply stores post surveillance photos of alleged shoplifters caught in the act of stealing products. The stores, which almost exclusively sell Black haircare products within Black neighborhoods, are rarely owned by Black people. The small, indistinct images tend to fade in the background amid the various colors of shampoo bottles and hair accessories.
Lawson’s images, however, are large portraits framed by mirrors, forcing the onlooker to simultaneously see themselves looking at these shoplifters. The viewer is small and narrow while the shoplifters are life-size, and what was once quiet, passive spectatorship immediately becomes active participation. This evolution is further emphasized once a viewer moves to the middle of the gallery room where two holograms stand, revealing Black women’s bodies that shift depending on the viewer’s angle. These pieces demonstrate how Lawson manipulates perception: these alleged shoplifters are not frozen in time, they are in motion, just as the viewers are.
The notion of wrongdoing is questionable as the exhibition becomes a house of mirrors exploring who is and is not being watched. Lawson accomplishes exactly what bell hooks wrote about – the rebellious gaze – by looking at her subjects, challenging viewers to evaluate them, and therefore exploring how perception functions within a space full of unequal power relations.
The exhibit’s official description proclaims that Lawson does not intend to cast moral judgment over these images, but rather “foregrounds the implications of agency and transformative potential of beauty products within our late capitalist society”. Lawson is not trying to villainize or glorify these shoplifters, but she does protect them. The shoplifter photos are evasive – the original images are low resolution, some of the shoplifters are masked and a few of the photos are so blurry that the viewer is unable to make out the subject’s face. Lawson’s deliberate refusal to clarify these images causes the viewer to contemplate what or who they are looking at. Who is the regular customer and who is the criminal?
She aims for neutrality in the depiction of her subjects by making the artistic decision to show them in stark contrast to other Black people whose images were not gathered from surveillance cameras. On the right wall opposite Lawson’s shoplifter images, the photographer’s signature style portraits hang: lush images of Black men and women in very private settings.
In all these artworks, the subjects’ gaze always meets the viewers’, reinforcing their humanity and leveling the playing field. In fact, due to their size, the subjects seem to be looking down at you. In the early 20th century, Black photographers would immortalize their Black subjects in suits, nuns’ habits or graduate gowns to usher in a new form of race pride – and respectability – into the mainstream. Lawson’s subjects are casually dressed – if at all. She’s not interested in a dignified kind of Blackness, but rather the beauty of Blackness within the mundane. By placing all of these images together within the same space, Lawson forces the viewers to view Blackness through a continuum of life in all of its contradictions, rather than a flat binary of good and bad behavior.
The relationship between the Black subjects on both sides of the room is contingent upon the viewer’s own judgment. How different is the Black female shoplifter near the braid extensions aisle from the naked Black woman squatting with her knees apart? How different is the Black male shoplifter from the Black man with a busted eye posing with others in a living room? However the viewer judges these subjects reveals their own biases. But in this exhibition, one’s biases are not private, inconsequential flaws. They’re ideological constraints that must be confronted.
Edge Control succeeds at capturing the extreme vulnerability of people who are being surveilled without their knowledge in active pursuit of beauty. At the same time, Lawson narrows the gap between spectator and participant as the viewer is confronted with multiple gazes–including their own–so that no one person is valued differently than the other. With power being briefly reassembled, parity is achieved.
- Edge Control is on view at the Gagosian in New York City until 24 October

====================================================================================================

In three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
12:00:56 UTC
21:00:56 KST

There was a world before 7 October, 2023, and now there is a world after. For Gaza, for Israel, for the wider Middle East, and for everyone else too. Not all hinge points in history are obvious at the time. Three years on from the day it began, and precisely one year since a supposed ceasefire was agreed, this one is now impossible to ignore.
The before-and-after pictures tell part of the story. An update to Google Maps, released last week, underscores just what three years of relentless Israeli military onslaught has done to Gaza. Satellite images show how entire towns have been reduced to rubble. Mosques and hospitals, visible three years ago, have now disappeared. Meanwhile the once-empty shoreline is now crammed with tents. This is what it looks like when an attempt has been made to destroy a people.
For Israel, too, there has been a before and after. Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had cultivated a sense of security, even of impregnability. The ease with which Hamas carried out its terrorist attack, killing 1,200 Israelis, including hundreds of young people at a music festival, destroyed that belief for ever.
Three years on from 7 October, both Israel and Gaza have changed beyond recognition. But the consequences of Hamas’s attack and Israel’s brutal response, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, have spread far wider.
Under the pretext of protecting its own borders, Israel has launched wars and military offensives across the region, sending troops into Syria; effectively annexing parts of southern Lebanon, deploying the same tactics there that it used in Gaza; and starting, with the US, an unwinnable war with Iran that has spiralled into a regional conflict affecting all six Gulf states.
The Iran war has sparked a new conflict between the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, which this week triggered a mutual defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey, dragging two other countries into the maelstrom. Across the Red Sea, some of the same combatants are involved in the war in Sudan and a fresh conflict inside Ethiopia.
More than a dozen countries across two continents are now entangled in a rising number of wars, with overlapping participants and numerous competing interests.
But there is something else, more insidious, that has changed. The rule of international law, tenuous as it was, has been openly replaced by military might. In 2022, western leaders – building a coalition rightly opposed to Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – made moral appeals based on the violation of international law. In Gaza, they encouraged and supported Israel, even when it was clear that the rules were being broken. That hypocrisy has not gone unnoticed, not just in the global south but among many millions of citizens in the west.
We have watched this happen in real time. Despite the ban on international journalists, anyone with a phone knew what was happening in Gaza from the early days of Israel’s response. Hundreds of Palestinian journalists have reported on the bombing of hospitals and schools, the bombing of cafes and wells, the killings at food distribution points, the deaths of children and babies. War crimes have never before been broadcast in real time, relentlessly, every hour of every day, around the world.
Gaza has also changed how wars are fought. Israel has pioneered the use of AI to select targets, accelerating our descent into a future for which we are unprepared.
All of this was allowed to take place in a time when the west could still argue that the “international rules-based order” existed. It may have been destroyed by Donald Trump, but we cannot forget that the dismantling began under Joe Biden. It was Biden who ensured the flow of weapons to Israel continued uninterrupted, Biden who insisted that every United Nations security council resolution calling for a ceasefire was vetoed, and Biden who attacked the international criminal court when it sought to indict Netanyahu for war crimes.
US support for Israel has always been strong and, on the whole, unquestioned. But even Republican presidents have understood they have influence over Israel’s actions and have been prepared to use it.
Ronald Reagan suspended an arms deal in 1981 after Israel annexed the Golan Heights. A year later, his administration stopped supplying cluster weapons to Israel after Menachem Begin’s government used them in populated areas during its invasion of Lebanon. In 2002, the killing of 15 Palestinians in Gaza was enough for Colin Powell, the then secretary of state, to announce a review of Israel’s use of American arms.
Israel was also given a free pass by every other member of the G7, including those run by centrists or centre-left politicians. French president Emmanuel Macron, German chancellor Olaf Scholz, Justin Trudeau in Canada and Australia’s Anthony Albanese all initially gave Israel their backing.
Only António Guterres, the much-maligned UN secretary general, emerges with a modicum of credit. Less than three weeks after 7 October, he called Israel’s response “collective punishment of the Palestinian people” and demanded an immediate ceasefire.
The one ray of hope for the future is that our shared understanding of what has happened over the past three years means that in many countries the political winds have shifted.
Before Andy Burnham even entered Number 10, he apologised for how Labour had handled the early days of the conflict. The UK now has a prime minister who was one of the few western politicians to call for a ceasefire just weeks after 7 October. Ed Miliband’s willingness to accurately describe Israel’s actions in the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” indicate a change in attitude that could lead to more concerted international action against Israel.
In the US, support for Israel has fallen through the floor. For a Democrat who wants to be president in 2028 there is no credible path to the White House that doesn’t involve support for the Palestinian cause. And yet, we cannot simply close our eyes and hope that a change in America will magically restore the world to how it was on 6 October 2023.
Nor should we pretend that the previous era was one we should wish to return to. Did we enter a new world on 7 October, or did we just notice where we were? In the three years before the Hamas attack, the wars in Tigray and Sudan saw many of the same trends play out.
In Tigray, the northernmost part of Ethiopia, a war between the central government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front killed 600,000 people. There were brutal massacres, forced starvation, widespread use of drones – and absolutely no accountability. In Sudan, too, hospitals have been hit by drones, women have been raped, children have been shot dead. Again, we could see it happen. Again, there were no consequences.
Gaza, though, has undoubtedly accelerated the trend, normalising the immoral. The wars that have begun, that have spiralled out of control and pulled more countries and more actors into their orbit, cannot easily be stopped. There is a momentum to this conflict, a hardening of positions, as each new outrage leads to a response. When there is impunity, when there is no price that those responsible will ever pay, there are terrifyingly few levers to pull. If war crimes go unpunished, they only escalate.
And so a family in Addis Ababa fears the sound of a drone crashing into their home. A village in Lebanon is evacuated, destroyed and the land made uninhabitable. A mundane job at Riyadh airport becomes a daily deadly gamble. A crew of badly paid seafarers pray to their gods as they cross through the strait of Hormuz. The dreams of millions of children shrink from university, fame or fortune, to the brute reality of survival.
And in Gaza, crammed into tents, deprived of enough food and water, two million Palestinians are still living under the brutal rule of Hamas and the daily threat of death from a military force that fears no consequences.
This is our world now. We need to recognise that, if anything is going to change.
- Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer
