Feature: Spanish jets leave Ämari — but the Baltic mission goes on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:25:00 UTC
17:25:00 KST

Feature: Spanish jets leave Ämari — but the Baltic mission goes on
NATO's Baltic air mission is now over 20 years old and was recently upgraded to a defense posture — making it high time to visit Ämari Air Base to catch up on developments.
The mission is held on a rotational basis and planes from Turkey's Air Force were joined from late August to early October by those of Spain's Air Force.
Four Spanish EF-18M Hornets left Ämari Air Base on October 9, five weeks after arriving, and the crews gathered on the apron to see them off.
If you had told me previously there were Spanish Hornets in Estonia, I would likely have thought you were talking about the effects of climate change. However, these are state-of-the-art multirole fighter planes we are talking about here, and they are leaving that very morning ERR News visits.
This provides the last chance to see the Spanish contingent, but the first chance to understand what a five-week rotation actually means.
Maj. Antonio Mancebo Marín stands at the edge of the apron and watches his aircraft leave. The four EF-18M Hornets have been parked at Ämari for some weeks, but unlike many military ground vehicles they do not require being transported back home by road, rail or sea, and the pilots can fly them back themselves.
On the morning they are due to fly home to Spain, personnel gather on the tarmac to see them off in suitably enthusiastic manner. Some carry national and unit flags. This is a mood that is closer to celebration than it is to routine. Around three crew members support every aircraft too. The jets are heading back home to sunny Zaragoza, a journey of around four hours including a mid-air refuel over Germany.
Next the jets begin to taxi. While on civilian flights you are kept well away from jet exhaust, on a military base you get much closer, enough to feel the heat coming off the engines as well as the noise, despite being issued ear defenders. There is a smell of burnt aviation fuel that lingers in the air after they have passed by, the pilots giving their own signature farewells through the closed canopies.
One of the planes is held up — a hydraulics issue which would affect control surfaces, the Spanish Air Force's helpful press officer tells me. It, too, is soon on its way once this gets fixed. The base at Ämari is not small — about twice the land area of nearby Keila. A car is needed to get from the entrance to the apron. Fortunately the weather is fittingly glorious and sunny too. Liaison and flight plan filing with civilian air traffic control takes place well before the take-off, so we can be sure the flights won't interfere with anything.
The takeoff itself is not something you can prepare for. Four fighters going up in pairs make a sound you feel in your body as much as hear, and the length required to take off is considerably shorter than with civilian airliners. But soon the last plane is on its way — they are flying direct to Spain from Estonia.
The pilots are gone but many of the personnel remain until at least the next day, sometimes more, packing up equipment, and making sure everything is in good order for the next arriving deployment.
The mission
The Spanish detachment had arrived at Ämari in late August and left by or on October 9 — joining a Turkish Air Force deployment already there. Around 110 personnel came with the aircraft, most of them from Zaragoza, particularly from Wing 15 and the Air Deployment Support Squadron of the Ejército del Aire y del Espacio, the Spanish Air Force.
"The detachment comprises around 110 personnel, and the pilots are only its most visible element," the air force had said in a written statement. "Behind every flight are specialists in maintenance, weapons, operations, logistics, communications, force protection, medical support and administration. Without them, no aircraft would take off."
The Spanish and Turkish detachments share the base but retain their own national command structures. Daily coordination covers flying schedules, airspace, flight safety, alert duties and joint training.
"We use the same procedures and command-and-control structure," the press officer tells me. "Sharing the base has made that cooperation very natural and has allowed us to learn from each other."
Baltic Air Defense has changed much since Spain's first deployment here over a decade ago. What was once primarily peacetime surveillance, identification and interception is now integrated into a broader defensive posture — a posture designed to address both manned and unmanned threats, with closer links between fighters, surveillance systems, command-and-control centers and ground-based air defenses.
Drones are the clearest example of that shift. Maj. Mancebo, the unit's commander, says roughly 20 percent of training in the Baltics now relates to drones, including seek-and-destroy drills.
With their small size, around 2 meters maximum, these naturally present a different target which must be adapted to.
"The message is that no one without authorization may fly in NATO airspace," Maj. Mancebo says.
This is not an abstract matter either. In August this year, a Spanish Hornet just like the ones departing Ämari downed a Russian-made drone, this time in the skies over Romania.
As for Baltic airspace, the mission here has long conducted interception missions of foreign aircraft too, if they stray too near to, or occasionally briefly even inside, Estonian airspace.
Scrambling to identify and intercept is "a professional and highly controlled task" the press officer said. "In the cockpit, we focus on the behavior of the aircraft and on carrying out the instructions received, rather than on its nationality."
"When directed, we approach safely, identify the aircraft visually, report what we observe and monitor or escort it as required. Operating close to national borders demands discipline, situational awareness and strict adherence to established procedures. An interception is a defensive measure intended to maintain safety and awareness, not a provocation," he went on.
As for what a typical day might look like, this "depends on whether you are assigned to Quick Reaction Alert, a training mission or mission planning. A normal day includes intelligence and weather briefings, checking the status of the aircraft, reviewing the tasking and coordinating with operations, maintenance and the control agencies.
"Alert crews remain ready to respond when directed. At the same time, we regularly fly air-defense and Close Air Support training missions with our Allies, both by day and at night. These activities allow us to practise identification, interception, air-to-air refueling, support to forces on the ground and coordination among aircraft and control agencies."
Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) is maintained around the clock. The Air Force could not give exact readiness times for operational-security reasons, but from being roused from sleep by the alarm in a QRA scramble to being airborne is about 15 minutes, meaning pilots and ground personnel alike have to have everything well drilled. The actual order to launch comes from the Combined Air Operations Center at Uedem in western Germany.
"Every mission begins with detailed planning and ends with a debrief, where we review its execution and identify ways to continue improving," the press officer notes.
As of the end of the rotation, the detachment had flown over 200 hours without incident — something the commander describes as one of the mission's main successes.
Including the recently departed contingent, Spain has now deployed fighters to Ämari five times: in 2015, 2017, 2022 (combined with the German Air Force), 2023 and then this year.
The host nation
For all its state of the art equipment and trained personnel, the detachment could not have operated from Ämari without Estonian support, the Air Force was explicit about that.
"Estonian host-nation support is fundamental," the officers tell me. "It includes airfield infrastructure and services, air traffic coordination, fire and rescue capabilities, security and daily logistical support."
Estonian personnel also provide local knowledge and can help the Spanish integrate into the base and the wider NATO command-and-control system.
"We could not sustain our operations from Ämari without their continuous support and close cooperation."
The plane
The Spanish Air Force deployment consisted of four EF-18Ms. This is the Spanish version of the McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornet.
The air force describes it as a mature, reliable and highly capable aircraft, well suited to air-defense missions, with sensors and communications that allow it to integrate into NATO's command-and-control system.
The plane designation follows the U.S. F-for-Fighter, B-for-Bomber format, regardless of manufacturer. In the Spanish variant the designation is EF-18M: originally an F/A-18, when sold to Spain it became EF-18, with the M subsequently added to stand for "Modernized (MLU)." The "E" stands for España.
Spain's Hornets are also unusual in one further specific respect. When the aircraft were purchased, Spain was the only user nation granted permission in the contract to modify the planes itself. Most of those modifications were software-related, and over time they produced this distinct EF-18M version.
Also unusually, the Spanish Hornets carry European weapons on an American airframe, which means integration work has to go through the relevant defense industries.
As for operating in Estonia, the regional environment puts specific demands on the aircraft. The press officer cited rapidly changing weather, reduced visibility, dense airspace and the proximity of several borders — conditions the crews train for regularly, while Maj. Mancebo notes that colder conditions bring challenges too. "Planes suffer in the cold," he said.
Maj. Mancebo would have no other plane than the EF-18M, which he describes as superb and his favorite jet to fly. Past experience includes time on a more vintage plane, the F-5, which comes in as a worthy second favorite. As for planes he would like to fly but has not yet, the F-22 Raptor figures highly.
The people
As noted, around 110 personnel came from Zaragoza, particularly from Wing 15 and the Air Deployment Support Squadron, though several other units contributed.
"The pilots are only the most visible element," the press officer says. "Behind every flight are specialists in maintenance, weapons, operations, logistics, communications, force protection, medical support and administration."
Life on deployment means long working days and time away from families. The air force says morale is maintained through a sense of purpose, team cohesion, physical training, shared activities and regular contact with home. "Knowing that every member of the detachment contributes directly to the mission also brings the team together."
Not all of the time is spent on base. The commander mentions Tallinn's Old Town and Patarei Prison among the highlights of places personnel visited during what free time they had during the deployment.
As to what he would say to those back home, the press officer points to the families as much as the crews. "Every sortie represents the effort of a large team and the support of our families, who also make this mission possible," he said.
And a message to Estonia: "Spain's commitment is real and practical. We are here with our personnel and aircraft, ready to contribute to the protection of Allied airspace because Estonia's security is also Spain's security."
The goodbye
Maj. Mancebo was clear about how he felt.
"We are happy to go back to our families, but sad to leave," he said. "I would have loved to stay another month."
The EF-18Ms have gone now. Life at the base at Ämari goes on, however.
The walk back away from the base brings a curious blend of state-of-the-art and traditional, too: I spot an old woman out mushrooming in the copious forest that surrounds the base. Along the public road leading up to the gate lies a Soviet-era cemetery where pilots from another epoch lie buried below headstones shaped like the vertical stabilizer from a MiG-17.
The Spanish crews have packed up, their planes long gone, and the Turks are still at Ämari. That is how the Baltic air mission works: it does not stop, it just changes flags.
With thanks to Staff Sergeant Siim Verner Teder and Junior Sergeant Triin Musting of the Estonian Air Force (Õhuvägi) for facilitating the visit.

EU budget slashed by €159B in new Irish proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:22:16 UTC
17:22:16 KST

BRUSSELS — The bloc’s next seven-year budget suffered a €159 billion cut from the Commission's original proposal, according to a new plan unveiled Saturday.
The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, proposed cutting around 8% to the bloc’s total budget from 2028 to 2034 to appease a German-led camp demanding major cuts.
The Irish negotiating document, or negobox, envisages cuts of €122 billion in current prices from the previous negobox presented by the Cyprus presidency in June. It sets the scene for fraught discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during a summit next week.
Advertisement
The bloc is split between frugal countries demanding cuts of several hundred billions to the nearly €2 trillion proposal on the table and a rival camp of southern and eastern states, known as the Friends of Cohesion, opposing reductions.
In a concession to the Friends of Cohesion, Ireland shielded farmers’ subsidies and regional payouts, that account for half of the total budget and are politically sensitive, from any cuts.
Instead, the bulk of the reductions came from foreign aid which was cut by €38 billion; competitiveness which was axed by €75 billion and the EU’s administrative costs which were reduced by €10 billion.
Dublin also scrapped a rainy day fund, known as the "EU Facility cushion," that allowed the European Commission to deploy cash to tackle unforeseen emergencies throughout the seven-year budget cycle.
Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne, who leads the negotiations, defended the proposal as a balanced compromise between 27 countries.
“We protected … the traditional policies of the Union, which are very important for the European Union and the single market. But we also very much look to the future,” Byrne told reporters.
Advertisement
However, Ireland’s proposal is unlikely to satisfy the frugals, who have warned against disproportionate cuts to new EU-wide priorities such as competitiveness, defense and development funding.
“The Irish proposal is a disappointment and not even close to a landing zone. The steep increase in MFF spending compared to today is unaffordable and financially not viable at all. By favouring policy priorities of the 20th century the proposal fails to prepare the EU for the 21st century,” an EU diplomat said.
They added: “This negobox is no basis for an agreement among member states. We urgently need more financial realism and less financial La La Land.”
Germany and its allies criticized the previous Cyprus Council presidency for cutting only €32 billion in the last negobox in June.
The new negobox will also be a hard sell to the European Parliament.
“The Irish Presidency has delivered little progress, no meaningful new solutions and a weaker budget,” the European People Party’s budget negotiator Siegfried Mureșan wrote in a statement shortly after the proposal was published.
Advertisement
He added: “Parliament is not bluffing: the budget proposed by the Irish Presidency will not receive our consent.”
The EU’s 27 ambassadors will react to the negobox during a meeting on Sunday, where they will also prepare the leaders’ discussion on Thursday.
Governments are racing to agree on a budget deal among themselves by the end of the year, before elections in France, Poland and Italy threaten to disrupt the negotiations.
Tax tweaks
The Irish presidency made no major changes to a package of five new EU-wide taxes, or own resources, that were proposed by the Commission last year to generate a total of €66 billion for the budget.
This comes as a disappointment for countries such as France, which had been pressuring Dublin to add the European Parliament's proposed levies on digital giants, online gambling and crypto firms to the negobox to increase the potential revenue.
Some of the Commission's ideas — including a corporate tax, known as CORE, and a levy on polluting firms (ETS) — have been challenged by EU governments for more than a year of negotiations and are seen as unlikely to come to fruition.
Advertisement
Despite pressure to drop the most criticized options, Ireland has kept the five taxes on the table and merely suggested technical changes to overcome opposition.
It suggested phasing in ETS contributions for poorer countries that are overwhelmingly hit by the tax, and increasing EU budget contributions from a levy on carbon imports that is accepted by most governments.
Tensions on own resources will come to a head during Thursday's leaders' discussions. The president of the European Council, António Costa, said he intends to "fix" a package of potential taxes that are acceptable to governments during that meeting.

Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least 17 people, including three children, in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhya and disrupted electricity and water supplies in Kyiv on October 10, Ukrainian authorities said.
Rescue workers continued searching for survivors as Russia reported attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities.
The death toll from the morning Russian attack on Zaporizhzhya currently stands at 17, with 16 others injured, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the regional defense council, said on Telegram. Search-and-rescue operations were continuing, with six people still unaccounted for, he added.
Authorities have declared October 11 a day of mourning in Zaporizhzhya.
Rescuers pulled a woman alive from the rubble of a destroyed building and were taking her to hospital, the acting head of the regional military administration, Mykhaylo Semikin, said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said as many as 12 people could still be trapped under the rubble.
Ukrainian authorities shared images of what they said was the aftermath of the attack, including badly damaged residential buildings.
The State Emergency Service said a Russian aerial bomb destroyed an entire entrance section of an apartment building and damaged other buildings and private homes. Rescuers extinguished a fire and continued searching through the rubble for possible survivors, it said.
Zaporizhzhya has been a regular target of Russian aerial strikes, with attacks intensifying in the past few months.
Russian attacks injured seven people in Kyiv’s Obolon district and disrupted electricity and water supplies in the capital on October 10, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Five of the injured were hospitalized, three of them in serious condition.
The strike hit a boat station in Obolon, according to Klitschko.
Ukraine’s Energy Ministry said attacks on energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding area had left parts of the region without electricity. Repair crews would begin restoring power as soon as security conditions allowed, the ministry said.
Klitschko said damage to an energy facility in the Kyiv region had worsened the capital’s electricity supply and disrupted water service. Specialists were working to restore water, he added.
The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched 160 attack drones against the country overnight, including 110 jet-powered Shahed drones.
By 9 a.m. local time, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 117 drones, including 82 jet-powered drones, the Air Force said. Hits were recorded at 14 locations, while falling debris was reported at 10 others.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said on October 10 that Russian forces had struck energy facilities used by Ukraine’s defense industry, as well as drone-production workshops and storage sites.
It also said Ukrainian military deployment sites in 151 areas had been hit over the preceding 24 hours.
The ministry’s claims could not be independently verified.
The ministry also claimed on October 10 that Russian forces had destroyed a bulk carrier at sea that it claimed was transporting military cargo for Ukraine’s armed forces to the port of Odesa.
The ministry did not provide further details about the vessel or the circumstances of the alleged strike.
Separately, Leonid Pasechnik, the Russian-installed governor of the occupied Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine, said on October 10 that four civilians had been killed and five wounded in Ukrainian attacks over the preceding 24 hours.
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.
Trump's Diesel Deal Sparks Criticism
The latest attacks came a day after US President Donald Trump’s announced that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports, with hundreds of thousands of tons of fuel expected to reach global markets.
Zelenskyy criticized the move, calling it a “gift” to Putin and warning that allowing Russia to earn more from fuel exports could help sustain its war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy also said the latest strikes reinforced his argument that easing pressure on Moscow could encourage further attacks.
Elsewhere, US, Ukrainian, and European officials held talks in Miami on October 9 in a renewed diplomatic effort to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
US envoy Steve Witkoff described the discussions as constructive, saying they covered ways to de-escalate the conflict before winter, energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees, and Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction. The talks ended without a breakthrough.
Germany said on October 10 that it would continue supporting Ukraine and pursuing new European Union sanctions against Russia despite the diesel agreement between Washington and Moscow.
Government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin remained committed to its existing sanctions and was working with European partners on additional measures.
The European Union, meanwhile, will continue reducing its dependence on Russian fossil fuels and does not want to help finance Moscow’s war against Ukraine, a European Commission spokesperson told RFE/RL on October 10.
“Europe knows too well the hidden costs linked to over reliance on Russian hydrocarbons,” the spokesperson said, adding that the EU continued to believe a cease-fire protecting global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia was needed.

====================================================================================================

Paraguay will not renounce friendship with Israel despite political costs, VP tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:21:07 UTC
17:21:07 KST

For a country separated from Israel by more than 11,000 kilometers, Paraguay has proved an unusually close friend over the Jewish state’s history.
While governments across the world have spent the past three years disassociating themselves from Israel’s war against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran, the South American nation has taken a different course, restoring its embassy to Israel’s capital, deepening security cooperation, and defending the Jewish state’s right to protect itself.
That friendship was on display yet again this week, when Paraguayan Vice President Pedro Alliana arrived in Israel alongside Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez Lezcano and Environment Minister Rolando de Barros Barreto, and the timing of the delegation’s visit was intentional. Three years after the Hamas massacres of October 7, 2023, Paraguay wanted to make clear where it stood.
For Alliana, who sat exclusively with The Jerusalem Post during his visit, the relationship extends well beyond diplomatic gestures.
“Paraguay is building a strategic alliance with Israel in which we share values and principles of democracy, the rule of law, human rights, and freedom,” he told the Post. “Our relationship with Israel is founded on these values and principles, and we also defend Israel’s right to defend its territory.”
Paraguay, Israel discuss expanding cooperation in healthcare, technology, and security
On Wednesday, Alliana and Ramírez met with Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar in Jerusalem, where the two sides discussed expanding cooperation in healthcare, technology, security, and other fields. Meetings with Israel’s prime minister and president followed on Thursday.
The Paraguayan delegation also visited Yad Vashem, laying a wreath in the Hall of Remembrance, before participating in commemorations marking the anniversary of October 7.
“Since the October 7 massacre, Paraguay has stood firmly by our side,” Sa’ar said following the meeting. “We remember who stands with us in difficult times, and Paraguay has proven itself to be a true friend.”
Alliana was equally emphatic, stating, “Three years ago, Hamas carried out brutal acts of terrorism. The terrorist organization murdered, raped and kidnapped innocent Israelis.”
Paraguay’s support has not always been without consequences. Asked whether standing so firmly alongside Israel had carried a diplomatic or political cost, Alliana acknowledged that it had, telling the Post, “There are, evidently, political costs on many occasions. However, above the circumstances of the moment and any tensions that may arise are these values and principles, which Paraguay will not renounce.”
The relationship between Israel and Paraguay stretches back to the earliest years of the Jewish state. Paraguay voted in favor of the United Nations partition plan in November 1947, supporting the proposal to establish Jewish and Arab states in British Mandatory Palestine. Formal diplomatic relations followed in 1949.
Yet the friendship has faced political upheavals, most notably in recent years over the location of Paraguay’s embassy.
In May 2018, then-Paraguayan president Horacio Cartes moved the Paraguayan Embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, following the United States and Guatemala. Four months later, his successor, Mario Abdo Benítez, reversed the decision, prompting Israel to close its embassy in Asunción.
The diplomatic dispute lasted for years, until President Santiago Peña took office in 2023 and moved to restore the relationship. In December 2024, Peña personally attended the reopening of Paraguay’s embassy in Jerusalem, a powerful diplomatic gesture at a time when Israel was facing growing international criticism over the war in Gaza.
Israel has since reopened its embassy in the Paraguayan capital.
For Alliana, the challenge now is ensuring that the status quo survives changes of government.
The 52-year-old vice president, a former president of Paraguay’s Chamber of Deputies and longtime leader of the governing Colorado Party, intends to seek the presidency in the 2028 election.
His candidacy, the former national team basketball player and seasoned politician explained, is also a commitment to preserving the relationship with Israel.
“My candidacy for the presidency of the republic for the next term follows that same path: ensuring continuity in a close, firm, and lasting relationship,” he said.
Alliana pointed to Peña’s personal attendance at the embassy inauguration, the foreign minister’s visit earlier this year, and his own presence in Israel during the October 7 commemorations as evidence of that commitment.
The message was one of continuity. Having experienced how quickly diplomatic decisions can be reversed, Paraguay’s current leadership wants its relationship with Israel to endure beyond individual administrations.
There is another, less familiar dimension to Paraguay’s affinity with Israel, one rooted in the country’s own history of extraordinary suffering.
Shared history of national tragedy strengthens Paraguay's bond with Israel
There is also a deeper historical dimension to Paraguay’s strong relationship with Israel, rooted in a national tragedy that continues to shape the country’s collective memory.
More than 150 years ago, Paraguay endured one of the most devastating conflicts in the history of the Americas: the War of the Triple Alliance, fought between 1864 and 1870.
The conflict, in which Paraguay fought an alliance of Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay, remains one of the most devastating wars ever fought in the Americas.
By the time the fighting ended, Paraguay lay in ruins. Its economy was shattered, much of its territory had been occupied, and an enormous proportion of its population had perished.
The precise death toll remains a subject of historical debate. Some estimates suggest that Paraguay lost around 60% of its population, while others place the figure lower. What is not in doubt is that the destruction of the country’s adult male population was so severe that it left a demographic and social legacy that lasted generations.
For Paraguayans, the war remains a defining episode in their national history, a catastrophe that threatened the country’s very existence.
The conflict is seen among Paraguayans as an attempt to exterminate the Paraguayan people, and they draw analogies with the historical suffering of Jews and Israelis.
The circumstances of the War of the Triple Alliance and the Holocaust were, of course, very different, but the analogizing offers insight into how Paraguayans understand their country’s relationship with Israel.
Both nations carry memories of catastrophic loss within their national consciousness, alongside a determination to preserve their independence and ensure their survival.
For Paraguay, whose history includes the experience of seeing its population decimated and its future placed in jeopardy, Israel’s insistence on defending itself against threats to its existence has a particular resonance.
Against this historical backdrop, the Paraguayan delegation’s visit to Yad Vashem and its decision to commemorate October 7 in Israel is even more significant.
Israel’s bridge in Latin America
Paraguay’s ambitions extend beyond its own bilateral relationship with Jerusalem.
Across Latin America, Israel’s diplomatic position has undergone considerable changes in recent months. Argentinian President Javier Milei has long been one of Israel’s most outspoken international supporters, but recent developments in Colombia and Venezuela have opened the door to renewed engagement after years of strained relations. Colombia and Israel fully restored diplomatic, security, and economic ties after President Abelardo de la Espriella’s inauguration in August, while that same month, Israel and Venezuela agreed to resume consular relations after 17 years of severed ties under the Chavez and Maduro regimes.
Alliana believes Paraguay has an important role to play in encouraging Israel’s reintegration process on the continent.
“Paraguay has been promoting closer relations between Latin America and Israel, based on the strategic alliance that I have mentioned on several occasions,” he stated. “We have served as a bridge for dialogue, which has allowed us to bring Israel closer to the region.”
He pointed to a videoconference organized this year by Foreign Minister Ramírez, bringing together Israel’s foreign minister and his Latin American counterparts.
The initiative, Alliana explained, allowed Israel to present its position directly to regional governments, including during particularly challenging periods.
Paraguay is also part of a relatively small group of countries that maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan rather than the People’s Republic of China, a long-standing foreign policy commitment that has occasionally placed it at odds with prevailing regional trends.
Asked whether Paraguay’s foreign policy was increasingly based on shared values rather than broader diplomatic consensus, Alliana rejected the suggestion that it was ideologically driven.
“The foreign policy of the Republic of Paraguay, and of our government, is based on the values and principles I have mentioned and is in no way aligned with ideological considerations,” he said.
For Paraguay, its relationships with Israel, the United States, and Taiwan form part of a diplomatic outlook that the current administration regards as consistent and principled.
The recent changes in Venezuela are of particular interest. For years, Caracas was among Iran’s closest partners in the Western Hemisphere, providing the Islamic Republic with a valuable political and strategic foothold in South America.
Alliana welcomed the developments following American intervention in Venezuela and President Peña’s engagement with interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez, but he also emphasized the need for a democratic transition based on respect for human rights, the release of political prisoners, and full participation in elections.
The objective, he said, is to establish a clear road map that would allow Venezuelans themselves to determine their country’s future.
Paraguay takes firm stance against Iran's growing influence in Latin America
The changing political landscape of Latin America also raises questions about Iran’s influence in the region, a subject on which Paraguay has taken a particularly firm position.
Paraguay has designated Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as terrorist organizations. The country’s concerns are rooted partly in the long-standing activities of Hezbollah-linked networks in Latin America, particularly around the tri-border region shared by Paraguay, Brazil, and Argentina.
The region has attracted international attention for decades over allegations of illicit financing, smuggling, and activities linked to terrorist organizations.
For Alliana, the response requires close intelligence and security cooperation with Israel, the United States, and neighboring countries.
“Paraguay has been taking a series of measures,” the vice president said. “First, we have significant intelligence cooperation with Israel, the United States, and other allied countries in our region.”
He highlighted a status of forces agreement with the United States, which he linked to military cooperation and support for Paraguay’s armed forces and police, while also referencing regional security initiatives involving Chile and Bolivia, including cooperation with the government of Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz.
These arrangements, he said, have allowed Paraguay to work more closely with its neighbors on operations against terrorist organizations, transnational organized crime, and Iranian activities in the region.
His remarks suggest that Paraguay regards the Iranian threat as an operational security concern requiring international coordination, rather than simply a matter of diplomatic disagreement. The relationship with Israel is therefore important in practical terms, particularly in intelligence sharing, cybersecurity, and counterterrorism.
“The fight against terrorism is one of the areas in which Israel is at the forefront and is the first line of defense against terrorist groups that are causing so much harm around the world,” he said.
Security cooperation may dominate much of the political relationship, but Paraguay also sees substantial opportunities in Israeli technology and expertise.
In meetings with Sa’ar, the Paraguayan delegation discussed cooperation in cybersecurity, water management, agriculture, healthcare, and technological development.
Paraguay possesses major freshwater resources, yet the efficient management of those resources, particularly for agriculture and irrigation, remains an area where Israeli expertise could prove valuable.
Healthcare is another priority for the landlocked South American country. During Wednesday’s meeting, the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding on health cooperation, opening the way for technology transfer and further professional training.
“[The MOU] will enable technology transfer, the specialization and training of Paraguayan doctors in Israel, and the training of technicians in various technological fields in Israel to become part of this broader agenda,” Alliana explained.
Educational exchanges have also become an important component of the relationship. Israel’s MASHAV international development cooperation agency has provided training and scholarships to Paraguayan professionals, with Alliana’s delegation emphasizing the participation of nearly 400 people over the past two years.
Trade is another bilateral area which continues to expand. Paraguay has become an increasingly important supplier of beef to Israel, with Alliana citing growth from $85 million to $300m. annually over the past three years.
“Our vision is clear: Paraguay and Israel must work together to significantly expand the bilateral relationship,” he said.
For Paraguay's leadership, the relationship with Israel also fits into a wider vision of the country’s place in international affairs.
Alliana pointed to Peña’s participation in the Sharm el-Sheikh peace summit in Egypt, where he said the Paraguayan president was the only Latin American head of state invited to witness the signing of the ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas.
The vice president cited US President Donald Trump’s personal invitation to Peña to participate in the event as evidence of Paraguay’s growing diplomatic standing and its potential role in international efforts involving Israel.
“We have been and continue to be a bridge for engagement in the region,” he said.
The country’s friendship with Israel has already survived diplomatic reversals, regional disagreements, and mounting international pressure, but its current leaders now want to ensure the relationship becomes a permanent feature of the country’s foreign policy.
As Alliana looks toward the 2028 presidential election, he is presenting that continuity as part of his political vision.
Meanwhile, his government’s efforts to deepen cooperation in security, healthcare, technology, and regional diplomacy reflect how much Paraguay values its friendship with Israel and the strength it sees in that relationship.
“Paraguay is working with Israel on a long-term relationship that extends into the future,” the vice president said. “We have a shared view of the challenges we face.”
For Israel, in a world where genuine friends have sometimes seemed in short supply over the past three years, Paraguay’s friendship is one worth cherishing.

Russia announced Saturday that it was beginning to lift domestic restrictions on diesel exports following U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement Friday of an agreement to purchase Russian diesel, marking a significant policy reversal after years of American pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Axios reported overnight, citing a U.S. official familiar with the matter, that Trump decided to pursue the agreement with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored repeated American requests for Kyiv to stop attacking Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv appeared unwilling to comply with Trump's demands even after the agreement. Ukraine launched an overnight attack on Russia involving some 500 drones, according to the report, including a strike on an oil facility in the Rostov region.
The American official criticized Zelensky, saying he was misreading the situation and that continued Ukrainian attacks on refineries were undermining the trust the Ukrainian president had built with Trump over the past six months.
Zelensky sharply criticized the U.S.-Russia agreement Friday, accusing Washington of exploiting negotiations with the Ukrainian delegation as cover for its own dealings with Moscow.
"I believe our team is simply being used as cover. This is certainly not fair and not how partners should treat each other," Zelensky said.
Ukrainian media reports noted that officials in Kyiv doubted the agreement would achieve Trump's objective of lowering global fuel prices. They nevertheless acknowledged that the deal itself weakened Ukraine's negotiating position.
Russian petroleum exports have been restricted by both international sanctions and domestic export bans imposed after Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities disrupted production and caused fuel shortages inside Russia.
Now, according to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the country's energy sector, Moscow is beginning to lift those restrictions ahead of schedule.
Trump announced on his Truth Social platform that he had reached the agreement during a phone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The two leaders had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.
Instead, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and an additional 1 million tons shortly afterward. Russia would then supply another 3 million tons within a relatively short period, he added.
Warm exchanges between Trump and Putin
Senior Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the conversation to Russia's state-run RIA Novosti news agency.
"The conversation lasted an hour and a half, and neither side wanted to be the first to hang up," Ushakov said. He added that Trump had expressed his willingness to continue speaking with Putin that evening, overnight and the following day.
Putin's economic adviser Kirill Dmitriev, meanwhile, posted several messages on social media thanking Trump for the agreement. One of the posts consisted of a single word: "Diesel."
Ushakov and Kremlin-aligned media sought to portray the agreement as evidence of a new phase in relations between Moscow and Washington, arguing that it demonstrated Russia could no longer be considered internationally isolated.
Describing the personal exchanges between the two presidents, Ushakov said Trump had warmly congratulated Putin on his 74th birthday earlier in the week. Trump wished Putin success and conveyed greetings from first lady Melania Trump, Ushakov said.
"Vladimir Putin thanked his American counterpart for the congratulations and warm words," the senior Russian official said, adding that Moscow appreciated the attention Trump and his team were devoting to dialogue with Russia despite domestic U.S. issues and developments in the Middle East.
On the ground, however, Russian attacks deep inside Ukraine continued to exact a heavy toll on civilians.
Overnight, Moscow launched a missile attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia. According to Ukrainian media reports, at least seven people were killed when a residential building suffered a direct hit. Local authorities said another 14 people were missing.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s former military secretary said the Prime Minister’s Office falsified records related to Oct. 7, 2023, including altering the recorded time of a key phone call, Yedioth Ahronoth’s Ynet news outlet reported Thursday, citing an interview aired on Channel 12.
“I will give everything I know, leave my impressions and let them understand the reality,” Avi Gil said in the interview. “The past few weeks have set me on a different path and signaled to me that I need to come out and tell the truth.”
Gil, 54, who served as Netanyahu’s military secretary from July 2021 to May 2024, told Israel’s Channel 12 that a stenographer in the Prime Minister’s Office approached him in January 2024 and said she had been instructed by Netanyahu’s chief of staff to change the time of a four-minute call from 6.40 am (0340GMT) local time to 6.29 am (0329 GMT).
“She told me, ‘I’m not allowed to change it. The computer shows and says 6:40 to 6:44,’” said Gil, accusing the head of Netanyahu’s office of manipulating telephone records.
“Those are facts, and there is no dispute about them,” he added.
Gil said he immediately documented the stenographer’s account in a handwritten note to the attorney general and recommended that any future commission of inquiry obtain the original recordings rather than rely solely on transcripts, according to the newspaper.
“This is changing a transcript, changing the truth,” he said. “Factually, there was an instruction to change the time of a call.”
Gil also said Israeli security officials had repeatedly recommended targeted military operations in the Gaza Strip before Oct. 7, but the political leadership rejected that course.
“There were recommendations from time to time to carry out targeted operations in Gaza. Those recommendations were not accepted,” he said.
Gil confirmed an earlier report that then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar warned Netanyahu in July 2023 that Israel faced the danger of war.
Bar told Netanyahu, “I am giving you a warning of war today. I cannot give you an exact day and hour, but this is the warning,” according to the warning previously reported by Yedioth Ahronoth.
Gil stressed that the warning was not specifically about an impending attack from Gaza.
“Was there a specific, focused warning from Gaza? Absolutely not,” he said.
Gil also rejected claims that the intelligence available during the preceding night would normally have required Netanyahu to be awakened immediately, saying the information repeatedly described the situation as “routine” and did not indicate immediate urgency.
He also said he could not confirm reports that Netanyahu had received warnings from Egypt or the United Arab Emirates before Oct. 7, noting that he was not in the office on dates linked to the reported Emirati contact.
Netanyahu denied the accusations made by his former military secretary and blamed Gil for failures surrounding Oct. 7.
The dispute comes as campaigning intensifies ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 general election.
Israel's genocidal war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since October 2023 and injured over 175,000, according to Palestinian figures. Tel Aviv has also destroyed 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.
The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in November 2024 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.

Bathurst 1000: Zach Bates wins Top 10 Shootout, qualifies on pole at Mount Panorama
In short:
Zach Bates has qualified on pole for Sunday's Bathurst 1000, topping the time sheets during the Top 10 Shootout at Mount Panorama.
Qualifying king Brodie Kostecki failed to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions, finishing second.
What's next?
ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.
Supercars rookie Zach Bates — not qualifying king Brodie Kostecki — will start the Bathurst 1000 in pole position.
Kostecki was on track to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions after laying a mighty lap of two minutes and 4.4912 seconds as the fifth driver in Saturday's top-10 shootout.
Proven race winners Will Brown, David Reynolds and Anton De Pasquale tried, but failed to beat Kostecki's time.
But provisional pole-sitter Bates refused to waver, proving his mettle as the last driver with a searing lap around the famous Mount Panorama track.
A day after becoming the fastest Gen3 racer, the 22-year-old clocked 2:04.2062 to deny Kostecki by 0.285 seconds.
Bates had earlier become the first to go below the 2:04 benchmark in the Gen3 era after taking provisional pole with a time of 2:03.9376.
In just his second pursuit of the holy grail of Australian motorsport, Bates is the third rookie to claim pole position after Klaus Ludwig (1987) and Marcos Ambrose (2001).
The Canberra local is the son of former rally and Supercars driver Rick Bates, and the nephew of four-time Australian Rally champion Neal Bates.
His surprise success comes after his mother Alison Drower died from cancer weeks before his Bathurst 1000 debut last year, in which he finished 10th as part of the Triple Eight Race Engineering wildcard with the great Craig Lowndes.
Team 18 driver De Pasquale will start in the second row with fourth-fastest Cooper Murray, while series leader Matt Payne was 10th.
But Grove Racing star Payne will be far from disheartened, given he had started from 18th en route to last year's epic wet-weather triumph with former co-driver Garth Tander.
Reynolds will start on the grid in eighth after a family of ducks threatened to derail his bid for a second Bathurst 1000 title.
Tickford co-driver Mark Winterbottom was forced to a sudden halt when ducks were spotted crossing the track at Conrod Straight during practice on Friday.
Winterbottom's sudden braking caught out Reynolds' co-driver James Courtney, who locked up and slammed into the rear of the Tickford Ford Mustang.
But both cars were able to return to complete the 60-minute practice session before the shootout.
Defending Supercars champion Chaz Mostert was among the big names to miss out on the top-10 shootout and will start from 16th for the best qualifying result in the Toyota Supra.
Payne's teammate Kai Allen fell agonisingly short in 11th, while title contender Broc Feeney was 12th ahead of Cam Waters in 13th.
Kostecki's rookie teammate Rylan Gray will start from the back row with Ryan Wood after the duo crashed out in separate incidents in Friday's first practice session.
ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:16:49 UTC
17:16:49 KST

A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona
The football club founded in a West Bank refugee camp has built a global movement of solidarity.
London, United Kingdom – Nearly 200 people packed into Edami, a small Lebanese bakery in east London, to celebrate a decade of Lajee Celtic, a grassroots sports club based in a Palestinian refugee camp in the occupied West Bank.
What began as a football project has grown into an international symbol of solidarity.
In London, the room was filled with Palestinian flags, the aroma of Edami’s freshly baked manousheh, and Lajee Celtic shirts – which have been worn by celebrities, including football icon Eric Cantona and the actor Hannah Einbinder.
Martin, a Lajee Celtic organiser, travelled down from Glasgow for the celebration in September. He first visited Aida Camp, in the occupied West Bank, more than 10 years ago, a trip he described as life-changing.
“I don’t think anyone would really have expected that the project would have been as successful as it’s been,” said Martin, who requested to be identified by his first name. “But Celtic is a unique football club with its foundation, its Irish identity, the diaspora community, its universal support and then the values, which tie so much of that together.”
The relationship between Aida Camp, where Lajee is based, and Celtic supporters developed over years.
Mohammed al-Azzeh, director of the Lajee Centre, which provides services to the youth of the camp, remembers how it all began.
“We’d built up relationships with friends from Scotland and Ireland who had visited Palestine, and then in 2012, I travelled to Glasgow for the first time. We started to have conversations about creating a football academy,” he recalled.
By 2015, the idea was taking shape when a group of footballers from the camp travelled to Belfast to play a game.
Then came the 2016 Champions League draw. Celtic were paired with Israeli side Hapoel Be’er Sheva.
Supporters ignored warnings that displaying Palestinian flags could result in a fine. As the teams emerged, the stadium was transformed into a sea of Palestinian flags, an action led by Celtic ultras, the Green Brigade.
UEFA subsequently fined Celtic.
The Green Brigade responded by launching the Match The Fine For Palestine campaign. Not to pay the fine, but to support Palestinian organisations, including with the formation of a football academy in Aida Camp.
For al-Azzeh, it was a turning point.
“The support and solidarity shown in that game was really a pivotal moment,” he said. “And that’s what ultimately led to Lajee Celtic becoming what it is today.”
The team has brought together young Palestinians from villages around Bethlehem, refugee camps and communities in Hebron and Jerusalem.
“It means a lot, for us as Palestinians, to be in one place and meeting each other,” al-Azzeh said. “It becomes about more than just playing football.”
Lajee Celtic is competing in organised football for the first time. The club had been due to enter the Palestinian league three years ago, but the competition was cancelled when Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza began. Now, despite restrictions on movement between Palestinian cities and the wider disruption to football, the club has entered the Thousand Martyrs Cup, named after the 1,014 athletes killed in Gaza since October 2023.
Bassil Mikdadi, journalist and founder of Football Palestine, said that international reach has given Lajee Celtic a significance beyond the club itself.
“Lajee Celtic is a blueprint for ways in which fans of European clubs can directly support those on the ground in Palestine. It’s connective tissue,” he said.
For Martin, the popular shirts are more than merchandise.
“When people buy these shirts, they do so knowing that the money is funding football, sports and general youth development in Palestine. And then when the same people wear these shirts, whether they’re in Glasgow or London or New York, they’re each making their own individual solidarity action.”
Lajee Celtic created a link between clubs and communities inside Palestine and supporters and campaigners abroad.
“It has this kind of cross-cultural, cross-border solidarity,” he said.
That connection has become increasingly important as Palestinian football has struggled to continue since the genocide in Gaza.
For Mikdadi, the survival of grassroots clubs is essential: They are the groundwork for the national team.
“The success of the Palestinian national team in recent years … the base of that success has always been players provided by clubs in the West Bank and Gaza,” he said.
The club’s ambitions stretch beyond football. It has expanded into sports such as boxing and table tennis, while creating opportunities for young Palestinians across Palestine and the diaspora.
“Fundraising campaigns come and go all the time. But when you create a football club and when you have that sort of tangible idea at the heart of it, then you are creating a journey,” said Martin.
Mohammed al-Azzeh recalled a meaningful memory on a beach in Cape Town, South Africa, where the team played two friendlies in 2025.
Samir al-Amir, a coordinator with Lajee Celtic, had spent more than 19 years in Israeli prisons. When he travelled with the team to South Africa, it was the first time he had been able to leave the walls and checkpoints of the West Bank.
Al-Azzeh remembers watching him on the beach.
“He was acting like a young boy because it was the first time seeing the sea,” he said. “Without Lajee Celtic, I’m not sure Samir would have ever had that opportunity. That illustrates why the project is so important,” he said.

The vow comes as energy market analysts question Moscow’s physical ability to fulfill the commercial commitments announced by the White House, citing extensive degradation across the Russian petrochemical sector caused by repeated Ukrainian interdiction operations.
According to data cited by the Financial Times, Russian refineries are currently operating at approximately 60 percent of their installed capacity due to operational halts, emergency repairs, and equipment deficits resulting from Ukrainian strikes.
“The biggest question for me is: where are they going to get the diesel from?” said Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at energy intelligence firm Kpler. “Russia does not have an export problem. It has a refining problem.”
Russian refining deficit
Industry data highlights the extent of the contraction across Russia’s downstream petroleum sector over the past year.
Russia Exploits School Knife Attacks for Disinformation
Prior to 2025, Russia exported an average of 2.6 million metric tons of diesel fuel per month by sea, according to Kpler records.
However, maritime shipments fell precipitously throughout 2026 as successive Ukrainian drone waves damaged primary distillation units, cracking facilities, and storage hubs across European Russia and western Siberia.
With domestic refining capacity constrained, the Kremlin enacted strict restrictions on petroleum product outflows in July, effectively prohibiting domestic diesel exports to prevent localized fuel deficits and inflation within the Russian domestic market.
Outside rare exceptional consignments, seaborne diesel exports have effectively ceased.
The Financial Times also noted that the US has historically accounted for a negligible share of Russian refined petroleum consumption.
Washington has not imported Russian diesel fuel since July 2022, following early sanctions enacted in response to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. During periods when American importers did purchase Russian diesel, volumes averaged approximately 77,000 metric tons per month, peaking at 210,000 metric tons in January 2022.
The Trump diesel pact
The dispute over refining strikes follows Trump’s announcement on Truth Social that Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter.
Trump indicated that deliveries could scale up to 3 million tons within a short timeframe, though he acknowledged that shipments would depend on the condition of Russian refineries.
The US president claimed that the bilateral deal, alongside US naval operations in the Strait of Hormuz, would quickly alleviate fuel costs for American consumers and global markets amid volatility fueled by the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Following Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The regulatory exemption was granted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, which aimed to expand statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
The sanctions waiver granted Moscow an economic accommodation it had sought since its July export ban, when Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov asserted that Russian fuel could ease international benchmarks only if granted unrestricted market access.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukrainian officials to suspend strikes on Russian petroleum facilities, attributing high diesel benchmarks to Ukrainian interdiction rather than shipping disruptions in the Middle East.

'All human emotions': French astronaut Sophie Adenot returns to Earth
French astronaut Sophie Adenot said she experienced “the full range of human emotions, from the most joyful to the most difficult” during her eight months in space, speaking on Saturday in Cologne, Germany, in her first public appearance since returning to Earth.
French astronaut Sophie Adenot went through "all human emotions, from the most joyful to the hardest" during her eight months in space, she said back on solid ground on Saturday in Germany.
Adenot splashed down in the Pacific Ocean Thursday off the coast of California in the Dragon capsule that carried Crew-12, having returned to Earth from a mission on the International Space Station (ISS).
Read moreExclusive: French astronaut Sophie Adenot recounts her ‘miracle’ mission from orbiting ISS
She had spent a total of 235 days in space, breaking the record for the longest uninterrupted orbital stay by a European astronaut.
At 400km away from Earth, Adenot could see there are "no divisions, no borders" but "just a precious planet that we all share", she said Saturday on the tarmac of the European Space Agency (ESA) training centre in Cologne, occasionally in tears.
The 44-year-old astronaut looked visibly weakened on her arrival in Germany and was assisted by two ESA physicians.
In space, the body adapts to the absence of gravity, which leads to bone loss, muscle wasting, cardiovascular deconditioning and even visual problems.
Adenot must now begin an intensive recovery program of about three weeks to regain her pre-flight condition.
"It's a cocktail of astonishing emotions, it's incredible. It's great to be back on Earth, but it also comes with its share of challenges, especially physiological ones," she told a press conference.

Report: Trump struck Russia energy deal after Zelensky ignored requests to halt attacks on refineries
An unnamed US official says Ukraine’s strikes strained ties with Trump, while Kyiv alleges his envoys threatened to cut off intelligence sharing
President Donald Trump decided to strike a diesel supply deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky disregarded six US requests to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, Axios reported, citing a US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
“Zelensky is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the good will that he has built with Trump over the last six months,” the official told Axios.
According to the official, Trump wanted Ukraine to stop the strikes unilaterally because they were contributing to high fuel prices in the US.
Zelensky, however, told Trump and his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that Ukraine was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries if Moscow stopped targeting Ukrainian power plants.
The dispute also produced conflicting accounts of the pressure Washington placed on Kyiv. A Ukrainian official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could end US intelligence sharing if Ukraine continued to disregard his requests.
The US official denied that any such threat was made. Instead, the official said, the envoys emphasized that Washington was supplying Ukraine with munitions and intelligence, and argued that Kyiv should avoid actions that hurt American consumers.
Zelensky told Axios after the announcement that the agreement caught him by surprise. He described it as “not fair and not honest” and an unjustified gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump unveiled the surprise energy agreement on Friday following a call with Putin, saying Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million tons afterward.
He also said Russia would deliver a further 3 million tons within a short period, depending on the condition of its refineries. Trump presented the agreement as a way to lower diesel costs, highlighting the burden on farmers, ranchers and truckers.
His administration temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports to enable the deliveries, relaxing restrictions intended to limit Moscow’s revenue from energy sales during its war against Ukraine.
Hours after Trump announced the deal, a large fire broke out at the Novoshakhtinsk oil terminal in Russia’s Rostov region following Ukrainian drone strikes, in an apparent indication that Kyiv was continuing to target Russian energy infrastructure.

Simon de Pury: ‘The art market is ripe for disruption’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Simon de Pury: ‘The art market is ripe for disruption’
The star auctioneer Simon de Pury built his reputation by selling masterpieces to the world's wealthiest collectors. At 75, he tells Swissinfo the business model that made him famous has reached its limits: the art market's future depends on technology and tearing down its walls of exclusivity.
In the art world, Simon de Pury is something akin to a rock star, having been called the “Mick Jagger” of auctioneers. However, the comparison between the 75-year-old auctioneer (and art dealer, collector, photographer and DJ) and the youthful-looking 83-year-old Jagger is based more on de Pury’s public performances than on his looks and attire, although both men still sport rich and well-cared-for manes.
Impeccably dressed in his signature navy Caraceni suit, de Pury defies the typical image of the high-end art auctioneer with a style finessed over the course of a career spanning more than half a century.
In the documentary The Hammer, which premiered at the Zurich Film Festival in September, he appears completely at ease, cracking jokes with a selective audience of art collectors making six or seven-figure bids. One is left with the impression that this gentleman is an indefatigable social beast.
But de Pury confesses that even today he still gets nervous taking the stage. “I was very shy as a teenager and at the start of my career, at [auction house] Sotheby’s, conducting auctions was a challenge to overcome my shyness”, he tells Swissinfo in an interview at the luxury Baur au Lac hotel after the festival premiere of The Hammer.
Born into a patrician Genevan family, de Pury admits there is another, more reserved side to his personality and his private life. “That’s surely my Swissness,” he says. Home for him, though, is Monaco, where he has lived since 2000. In the documentary, there are only hints of a private life seen through discreet family pictures of his wife and four children.
Life of a salesman
The film follows the star auctioneer around several world capitals. Yet his career has gone far beyond hitting the hammer and visiting artists. He stayed with Sotheby’s for 16 years before being invited by Baron Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza to curate his private collectionExternal link – then one of the largest in the world – and oversee its transfer from his villa in Lugano, Switzerland, to its current site, the Museum Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.
In 2000, de Pury acquired Phillips auction house (est. 1796), and renewed the old house’s standing in the market by focusing on contemporary art. In 2012, he sold it to the Mercury Group, a holding owned by two Russian oligarchs. Since then, de Pury has been on his own: his companyExternal link consists of only one assistant.
“When I sold Phillips, I thought I would never conduct another auction,” he says. “And now, at my advanced age, I conduct more auctions than I have ever conducted before.” In the week before we met in Zurich, he completed auctions in Dallas, Venice, Basel and Monaco; the next day he was off for another week of non-stop action.
Being at the high-end of the art market, and with an outstanding carbon footprint, de Pury still keeps his eyes open for new trends and shows a genuine concern about the elitism that pervades this exclusive universe. So much so that he has not shied away from embracing new technologies to expand access to artworks.
Swissinfo: The art market has changed continuously throughout your 50-year career. There are now new players: big galleries, global galleries, global art fairs and new big markets such as China. Do you miss the old art world a little bit?
Simon de Pury: No, I don’t. I feel that the art market is at a fascinating juncture and that it needs complete disruption. The art market is one that has best resisted all technological innovations, but now it’s at a stage where it has to embrace them. You can resist change, but at some point, change takes over. And I think this is what’s going to happen now.
Though the art market is much larger than when I first started my career, it remains small in absolute terms and still has huge growth potential. Art is universal in the same way that music is universal.
I feel that the art world has made itself difficult to access and has intimidated people, and that new technologies will make the market, and the knowledge that comes with it, accessible to everyone.
Swissinfo: You’re operating within the market in a very central position. And as we can see in the film, you are also working to cut off the intermediaries by putting the artists more directly in contact with their buyers. This is also a sort of disruption, isn’t it?
SdP: Auctioneers are going to be derelict because they are intermediaries. I’m excited to see how the art world will successfully transform the live auction experience by gamifying it, by making it accessible so that everybody can participate.
If a mega collector walks into Sotheby’s or Christie’s, then the expert will tell them all about a certain object and share their expertise. But that expertise can be shared with everyone. And with knowledge comes the hunger. The key is education; the more you know about a subject, the more you want to know, and the more you want to get into it. Spreading the knowledge is absolutely essential.
I think the disruption will probably not come from the traditional players, but from people with the tech savvy, with gaming savvy. And then, of course, you will need the expertise of the art market.
But if you bring the best of these elements together, you can completely revolutionise the art market. The current model is a result of the vision of Peter Wilson, who became chairman of Sotheby’s in 1958, and everything that he foresaw has happened. But now I think we’ve reached the limits of what that business model could bring. It now needs complete disruption.
Swissinfo: There is a new generation of collectors coming up. A big part is inheriting the collection of their parents, and they’re not selling it. Also, there are new players like tech billionaires and the emerging Asian market. Do you think they can play a role in this disruption?
SdP: It’s very important for the art market to always renew itself and renew its pool of buyers and collectors. Every year a whole range of very important collectors pass away.
I’ll give you an example. Take hip hop. I was fascinated by that whole jewelry in the scene, the bling jewels that they were wearing. It was a very innovative thing culturally in a field where there is not that much innovation.
Back then the big hip hop moguls were buying big cars, expensive watches, jewelry, and not buying any art at all. And then that changed. Who made that change?
The first one was Kanye West. I know that it’s a controversial name now, and he is indeed indefensible. However, he really was the first to ask contemporary artists like (Takashi) Murakami [in Graduation, West’s third studio album in 2007] or George Condo [My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy in 2010] to design his album covers, and the first to collect art.
And then a number of key hip-hoppers like Jay-Z, Pharrell Williams, Puff Daddy, and many more all followed in his footsteps and focused on African American art. For a long time, the only African American artist with a high-profile in the market was Jean-Michel Basquiat, as if he was the only “artist of colour”. And then there has been this whole wave of fantastic artists like Mark Bradford, Kerry James Marshall… it’s a long list of artists whose market value has risen exponentially.
The tech community, with one or two exceptions, has not really entered the market yet in a way like the hedge fund guys, who became big collectors when they started making big money.
Swissinfo: Although many of them saw art much more as an investment, and not for the love of art.
SdP: Possibly, yes. But I feel it’s very important that the tech people get into the art market more actively, and they will when they understand that the only way to leave a long-term legacy is through art and culture. You can innovate all you want, but this will never leave as big and long-lasting an imprint as art and culture.
Another very important world that I love and that hasn’t entered the market yet is football. You only need somebody like [Norwegian footballer] Erling Haaland to start collecting to create a movement.
In the same way that hip-hoppers became tastemakers, football players will become tastemakers because whoever spends the most becomes a tastemaker. The same could go for the tech community. That’s why taste will always change and evolve.
Swissinfo: As for new markets, China is now the world’s second-biggest art market. But does China play a significant role today since Chinese collectors, in general, buy mostly Chinese art?
SdP: Initially, yes. The Chinese case is very interesting because, at the very start, some of the biggest collections of Chinese art were built by non-Chinese. [Swiss businessman] Uli Sigg was the key figure behind Chinese art. And when [Swiss curator] Harald Szeeman, at the head of the Venice Biennial in 1982, for the first time made a whole focus on Chinese art, it was all artists that had been discovered by Uli Sigg. And only then the Chinese started really collecting actively, and they moved on to also buying top Western artists.
More
Uli Sigg wants to help Chinese people ‘view their own art.’ Simple, right?
Swissinfo: But mostly Old Masters, right?
SdP: Yes, classical and modernist masters such as Modigliani but also cutting-edge contemporary art. During the Covid pandemic, when we could only look at art on the iPad and iPhone, the Chinese played a big role [in buying online].
That has quieted down at the moment, but I would say that Asian buying is absolutely key for the future of the art market. You always have to see which parts of the world are economically the strongest. Creativity usually flourishes in economically strong areas. I’m always fascinated to see how an economic upswing brings a cultural upswing.
Swissinfo: Where do you think this is happening now?
SdP: There is a new category of oligarchs that has been created in America. This will have an impact on the market as well as on future tastes.
The market has also become much more global. Some of the best contemporary art over the last few years has been made in Africa. There is this fantastic art fair called 1-54 [London, New York and Marrakech]External link, which has launched the careers of a number of African artists… so, location no longer is key for artists.
Swissinfo: Still, most of African art is still dealt in America and Europe. There are no big dealers or big players coming from Africa.
SdP: There are however quite a few African collectors now. I was two weeks ago in Rwanda, and I went to the Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art that has just opened. The person behind it, Kami Gahiga, is partially working for Art Basel in charge of all African collectors. It’s all globally connected.
Swissinfo: We observe a consolidation of the market in which the bigger galleries and players are surviving and thriving while the mid-sized galleries, which include the ones dealing with Latin American and African art, have felt quite a squeeze. How do you see the picture right now for the mid-size and smaller galleries? That’s where usually new and original talent comes from.
SdP: That’s why I think that the market is ripe for disruption. Yes, there is a squeeze; it’s very difficult for the vast majority of galleries to cope financially. This means most galleries can no longer afford to go from art fair to art fair – and to be accepted by an art fair, you need to have a physical location as well.
It’s a model which is problematic because only the top players will be able to continue participating in it; a vast number of galleries will be left out. In the case of auction houses, whenever they become a little less profitable, they raise their commission, which is not a sustainable business. If I have to sell an object between 0 and $3 billion, I have to leave at least 28% on the table – these are absurd margins.
The market has to find ways of bringing these margins down. That will widen the market. And greater efficiency in selling will have to come through technology.
Swissinfo: And you’ll be happy to be part of this disruption, right?
SdP: As long as I am alive and kicking, I would love to be part of it, yes.
More
Art Basel keeps its lead as art fairs go corporate and scramble for markets
