A year of 'ceasefire' in Gaza, Israel killed over 1,450 Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:37:27 UTC
15:37:27 KST

One year ago, US President Donald Trump declared the war in Gaza over. Twelve months on, Palestinians are still being killed, Israeli troops are still occupying huge areas of the enclave, and families are still queueing for hours for a single meal.
Here is where the October 10, 2025 ceasefire stands.
Israel got its captives, and Gaza got no peace
Three days after the deal was announced, the Palestinian resistance group Hamas released the 20 remaining living captives, delivering the first and most immediate demand of the agreement.
Gaza has also stayed silent for a full year. Not a single rocket has been fired from the Palestinian side since the truce took effect. Palestine has held to the terms it could meet on the ground, while Israel has kept up near-daily strikes and violated the ceasefire with little consequence.
The US military set up a command post with allies near the border to monitor the truce. A year on, the monitoring has produced no accountability, and no one has stopped Israel from attacking.
A 'ceasefire' that kills nearly every day
Israel said it has scaled back its attacks. The Palestinians under its bombs would struggle to recognise the claim.
Israeli strikes have killed some 1,450 Palestinians since the truce began, according to Gaza's health ministry, whose figures the United Nations considers accurate. That is a death toll of a war, recorded during what was supposed to be peace.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, locked in a tight election race, is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Yet he has vowed to kill everyone involved in the October 7 attack.
On the anniversary he boasted that 4,000 of 6,000 Hamas members had been killed. His war has killed more than 73,600 Palestinians since October 2023, in a brutal war that rights groups and UN officials have described as genocidal.
A leader who campaigns on killing, and who is accused of war crimes, is not committed to a ceasefire.
Occupying 70 percent of the Palestinian enclave
Under the terms of the truce, Israeli forces were allowed to remain in 53 percent of Gaza. A year later, official accounts show they control about 70 percent.
That means the occupier has not withdrawn. It has advanced beyond the lines it agreed to, swallowing more of a territory already reduced to rubble.
Almost every building in Gaza was damaged or destroyed by Israel's near-constant bombardment, and the people who lived in them have nowhere to return to.
Disarmament pretext
The deal's second phase promised a political transition away from Hamas. Technocrat Ali Shaath was named to head the new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, and Hamas said in July it was dissolving its governing body and handing over administration.
Hamas still runs security through civilian police in the limited areas of Gaza not under Israeli occupation. The resistance group announced it would give up its weapons and, according to Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza Peace Board's high representative, agreed to transfer civilian and security authority to a UN-recognised transitional administration. But it has not yet disarmed.
The handover depends on that administration being able to function, and it cannot do so while Israel bars Palestinian technocrats from entering Gaza and the promised international security forces have yet to deploy.
With no functioning body to receive its weapons, Hamas's armed wing has refused to disarm until the next phase of the Gaza ceasefire is implemented. Netanyahu rejects this and demands verifiable decommissioning of all weapons, down to individual guns, before Israel withdraws.
Whatever the failings of the transition, Israel has used them as a pretext. It has refused to reciprocate with any withdrawal, turning a phased deal into a one-sided demand and holding territory hostage to conditions it keeps raising.
Reconstruction: big promises, no money
Trump created a "Board of Peace" and recruited former British prime minister Tony Blair and Bulgarian diplomat Nickolay Mladenov as key figures. In January, he promised $10 billion in US funding to a board he controls, and Gulf allies pledged more.
No money is known to have reached Gaza reconstruction. In September, the board proposed a $2.45 billion recovery plan, to span six months. For now it remains a slide in a presentation, while two million people live among ruins.
The human cost: hunger that never left
Behind the diplomacy are people like Niyaha al-Masri, a 35-year-old mother of eight in Khan Yunis. Every day she spends six hours or more queueing at a community kitchen, because without it her family would have "nothing at all". Her husband was wounded in both legs by an air strike. The family of 10 lives in a tent and eats one meal a day.
In August 2025, the UN-backed IPC declared famine in Gaza. The UN lifted the declaration in December after two months of improved supplies.
The World Food Programme’s Shaun Hughes says the situation is still "extremely serious", with 1.4 million of Gaza's roughly 2.1 million people acutely food insecure and 200,000 of them one step below famine.
Nutrition is failing, too. Medecins du Monde found that 93 percent of pregnant or breastfeeding women showed symptoms of anaemia, and only 17 percent had a varied enough diet. Hughes warned that repeated acute malnutrition in children is something people "just don't recover from".
Masri's children dream of fruit and spend their days gathering scraps of nylon and cardboard to patch their tent. "I swear to God, this isn't normal," she said.
A ceasefire in name only
The truce did what Israel wanted: its captives came home and its border fell quiet. For Palestinians, it has brought continued killing, shrinking land, hunger and an empty promise of rebuilding.
A year on, Israel has yet to withdraw from Gaza, and no one has been held to account for breaking the terms it signed.

Türkiye’s seismic research vessel Oruç Reis has reached waters off Kyrenia as surveys continue for a planned natural gas pipeline linking Türkiye and Turkish Cyprus, with operations targeted to begin in 2028.
The project envisages two pipelines along a 101-kilometer route from Anamur in the southern province of Mersin to Teknecik, east of Kyrenia. The route includes 97 kilometers beneath the Mediterranean and four kilometers on land.
Oruç Reis is mapping seabed conditions along the proposed route.
The current survey program runs through Oct. 25, while engineering studies are expected to be completed by the end of the year.
Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz and Turkish Cypriot Prime Minister Ünal Üstel signed a memorandum of understanding for the project on July 10.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said at the signing that the system would be designed to transport gas in both directions.
Alongside supplying Turkish Cyprus, it could eventually carry gas from future discoveries in the Eastern Mediterranean to Türkiye and onward to Europe.
The gas supplied from Türkiye would initially be used for electricity generation.
Bayraktar said the project would help meet growing demand and reduce reliance on imported petroleum products.
The surveys come as Greece prepares to resume work on a separate electricity interconnector linking Crete and Greek Cyprus, with a later extension to Israel.
Türkiye says surveys and cable-laying in areas where it asserts continental shelf rights require prior coordination with Ankara.
Athens has rejected seeking Turkish permission for the work.

Türkiye sets rules for under-15 social media ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:33:44 UTC
15:33:44 KST

Türkiye has published regulations barring social media platforms from serving children under 15 and requiring users to verify their age through the e-Devlet government portal.
The rules, prepared by the Cyber Security Directorate and published in the Official Gazette on Oct. 10, take effect on Nov. 1.
Platforms must complete age verification for existing accounts by March 31, 2027.
Registration requests from children under 15 will be rejected, while existing accounts found to belong to users below that age will be closed.
Verification will use a digital token generated through e-Devlet and uploaded to the platform.
The token will indicate whether users meet the 15 and 18 age thresholds without containing names or other identifying information.
Accounts belonging to users aged 15 to 17 must remain private, with no option to make them public.
Platforms will be prohibited from offering livestreaming or displaying personalized advertisements on these accounts. Infinite-scrolling feeds will also be banned.
Teenagers will only be able to receive messages from accounts they follow. Their follower and following lists will be hidden from other users.
Platforms must also provide parental controls allowing parents to manage account settings, monitor and limit screen time, and approve purchases and other paid transactions.

Hind Rajab Foundation asks ICC to investigate Israeli doctors over alleged Sde Teiman torture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:28:59 UTC
15:28:59 KST

The Hind Rajab Foundation accused Israeli medical personnel and senior health officials of complicity in the alleged torture, abuse, and deaths of Palestinian detainees at the Sde Teiman detention facility, announcing on Thursday that it had submitted a request to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague to investigate their involvement.
The request names medical professionals, hospital administrators, senior Health Ministry and Defense Ministry officials, and leaders of the Israel Medical Association (IMA) in connection with alleged abuses at the facility since October 7, 2023.
Among those the Hind Rajab Foundation is seeking to have investigated are former health ministers Moshe Arbel and Uriel Buso, IMA chairman Prof. Zion Hagai, IMA director-general attorney Leah Wapner, and Dr. Yosef Walfisch, chairman of the IMA's Ethics Bureau.
According to the foundation, the alleged acts could constitute war crimes, crimes against humanity, and even genocide.
The submission was filed under Article 15 of the Rome Statute, which allows organizations and individuals to provide the ICC prosecutor with information about alleged crimes and request that it be examined. The submission is not an indictment, nor does it constitute a decision by the court to open an investigation into any of the individuals named.
Allegations of medical abuse at Sde Teiman
The timing of the move is not coincidental. From October 7 to 10, the World Medical Association (WMA) is holding its General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, with representatives of the IMA also participating.
Hagay chairs the WMA's Socio-Medical Affairs Committee, while Wapner serves on its advisory committees.
At the center of the submission is the field hospital established at the Sde Teiman detention facility following the October 7 attacks.
According to the Hind Rajab Foundation, the Health Ministry was responsible for establishing and operating the hospital, while the medical personnel working there were placed under the authority of the Military Police.
The organization refers to guidelines it claims were issued by the Health Ministry in December 2023, including provisions for treating detainees while they were handcuffed and blindfolded, prohibiting medical personnel from identifying themselves by name, restricting transfers to civilian hospitals, and allowing involuntary medical treatment.
The foundation also relies on previously published testimony, including an Associated Press report in which medical personnel described surgeries performed without adequate pain relief.
It also cites a letter written in April 2024 by a doctor who worked at Sde Teiman, warning that two detainees had undergone leg amputations following injuries caused by prolonged shackling.
A separate section of the submission is devoted to the Israel Medical Association.
The Hind Rajab Foundation accuses the association's leadership of providing what it describes as professional and ethical backing for conditions at the detention facility.
It cites a letter published in April 2024 in the American Journal of Bioethics by Hagay, Walfisch, and Malka Boro of the IMA, in which they maintained that detainees at Sde Teiman were receiving appropriate medical care.
The authors noted that Walfisch had visited the facility as part of a delegation of medical ethics experts and acknowledged that isolated violations of ethical rules might occur. However, they maintained that, to the best of their knowledge, the doctors were fulfilling their professional obligations.
The foundation's director-general, Dyab Abou Jahjah, criticized the participation of Israeli representatives in the Rotterdam conference.
According to Abou Jahjah, the WMA must explain why it continues to host an organization that he claims provided institutional backing for torture.
Israeli Medical Association faces international pressure
In early July, the IMA announced that more than 5,000 doctors from 46 countries had signed a petition opposing efforts to remove it from the WMA.
In its statement, the association argued that the campaign represented an attempt to bring politics into medicine and that the accusations against it included false or disputed claims.
The IMA has previously opposed calls for its suspension, arguing that disagreements over government policy should not affect cooperation between medical professionals.
At the WMA's meeting in Portugal last year, the Israeli association also succeeded in blocking an attempt to suspend its membership.
However, the Hind Rajab Foundation has made clear that its submission to The Hague is only the beginning of a broader initiative.
In its statement, the organization warned that it was preparing individual case files against Israeli doctors and medical professionals who also hold foreign citizenship, with the intention of filing complaints against them with prosecuting authorities in their countries of citizenship.
Through this initiative, the foundation seeks to expand its legal activities targeting Israeli military personnel to include members of the healthcare system, in an effort to subject them to criminal proceedings outside Israel.

====================================================================================================

Premature birth may cause lifelong kidney damage, Israeli researchers find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:28:51 UTC
15:28:51 KST

Imagine starting life with a permanent biological deficit that you won’t discover until decades later. For the 15 million babies (one in 10 births) born each year prematurely, this is the hidden reality of kidney health. Until now, scientists knew that early arrival doubled the lifetime risk of chronic kidney disease, but the underlying biological culprit remained a mystery.
Prematurity is defined as a live birth before 37 weeks of pregnancy. Thanks to improvements in treatment and research in this field, the rate of live premature births has increased dramatically within the past decades. But preemies can suffer from an increased rate of adult diseases, when organs such as the kidney have not developed well in the uterus.
A groundbreaking joint study by researchers at Hadassah-University Medical Center in Jerusalem’s Ein Kerem and at Monash University in Melbourne has finally uncovered the cellular mechanism behind the shortfall – and, crucially, pinpointed the narrow therapeutic window where intervention might protect these vulnerable organs for life. The signs precede the diagnosis by many years.
Dr. Morris Nechama of Hadassah’s pediatric nephrology unit and the Faculty of Medicine of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem led the study, together with Athar Amleh, a doctoral student from the Palestinian Authority carrying out her doctoral research at Hadassah, whose scholarship was funded by the Yad Hanadiv Foundation.
Amleh designed and carried out the experiments and is the first author of the paper. Dr. Oded Volovelsky, director of Hadassah’s pediatric nephrology, and Prof. Alexander Combes of the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute in Melbourne, Australia worked with them.
The new study just published in iScience, under the title “Preterm birth disrupts nephron progenitor cell dynamics predisposing to renal disease,” provides the authoritative answer of why the kidneys of premature babies remain vulnerable for life.
Using an advanced mouse model, the research team has identified the exact cellular disruption caused by premature birth that limits the development of kidney filtration units – opening up a specific, limited period during which action must be taken for future preventative treatments.
A healthy human relies on roughly one million microscopic filtration units built entirely before or around birth, which never regenerate. The study reveals for the first time how premature birth short-circuits this delicate developmental window, leaving millions of adults going through life with a lower kidney reserve that they never knew they were missing.
The cellular mechanism leaves the kidney with too few filtration units and the short window of time in which intervention may be possible. The findings could make possible a technique to protect the kidneys of babies born prematurely, the researchers said.
“We have known for years that children born prematurely reach adulthood with more vulnerable kidneys, but we didn’t know exactly what went wrong and when. Here, we saw it happen in real time: nephron progenitor cells enter distress within the first hours after birth, and their timing is disrupted. They try to compensate later, but the window has already closed,” Nechama said:
Health effects from premature birth
In an American study of 15-year-olds who had been born prematurely, about half already had high blood pressure, protein in the urine, or smaller-than-normal kidneys. Thus, many people go through life with kidneys that started out with less reserve, without knowing it, until something begins to go wrong.
A healthy kidney consists of about a million tiny filtration units called nephrons in each normal human kidney. The creation of human nephrons ends by the 35th week of gestation, but this number varies greatly between different individuals. They don’t regenerate after birth. Some babies are born with more and some with fewer, Volovelsky explained in an interview with The Jerusalem Post; a person born with fewer nephrons carries a smaller kidney reserve throughout life.
Preterm birth is increasingly recognized not merely as an acute neonatal event but as a lifelong determinant of renal health. But the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving this developmental programming have remained elusive, often confounded in clinical settings by two or more medical conditions that occur at the same time in a person – such as sepsis, medications that harm the kidneys, or having received steroids after birth.
The human nephron, the basic functional unit of the kidney, is a structure that produces urine in the process of removing waste and excess substances from the blood. At present, little can be done clinically to increase the number of nephrons.
Epidemiological studies have already shown that children and adults born prematurely suffer more often from high blood pressure, protein in the urine, and reduced kidney function. Until now, it was not clear why.
“Our research, using a mouse model of premature birth, provides the answer. The researchers examined the progenitor cells that give rise to nephrons and found that the sudden, early transition from the womb to the outside world disrupts the delicate timing of their development and maturation. The cells enter a state of stress and lose the opportunity for repair. We believe the findings are relevant to human babies as well,” Volovelsky added.
“Immediately after premature birth, the progenitor cells enter a state of cellular stress, triggering an emergency molecular response known as the unfolded protein response. At the same time, the genes responsible for differentiation into mature nephrons are suppressed. In other words, the cells focus on survival instead of building.”
A day later, they try to compensate for the delay with a faster wave of division and differentiation, but the compensation comes too late.
“One surprising finding of our study is that in the preterm animals, the period of nephron building lasts about 24 hours longer than usual, yet this extension does not fill the gap. The result is a permanent nephron deficit, clearly measured about a month after birth and already accompanied by signs of declining kidney function,” Volovelsky noted.
In a later examination, at an age equivalent to adulthood, the kidneys of these mice showed signs of chronic damage: the glomeruli (filtration bodies) had enlarged to compensate for their small number, protein appeared in the urine, and markers of kidney tubular damage accumulated. In other words, damage caused in the first days of life keeps unfolding for decades.
“We accompany children born prematurely in the clinic and see the result years later, sometimes only in adolescence. This study indicates that the first few days after birth are not only a period of survival but also a period in which the kidney’s reserve for life is set. It’s a perspective that can change what we monitor and how we monitor these children. Preemies should be monitored for kidney disease as they get older.”
An additional finding is a difference between the genders. “The impairment in nephron number and kidney function was significant in males but not in females, consistent with previous evidence that male fetuses are more susceptible to adverse perinatal conditions, and it may help in assessing risk in the future,” the pediatric nephrologist stated.
Identifying the stress response in progenitor cells as the point of failure suggests a possible intervention window in the first few days after premature birth. If this stress response can be curbed in time, it may be possible to preserve some of the nephrons that are lost today.
The researchers emphasize that this is an early stage; the study identifies the mechanism and the timing, but a treatment that prevents the damage has not yet been tested, and that is the goal of their next study.
Nechama and Volovelsky said their research could eventually revolutionize the care of kidney disease. The notion that nephron numbers can be restored with timely intervention in experimental models gives hope to the important struggle to find a cure for kidney diseases.
The study grew out of an Israeli-Australian collaboration supported by AUSiMED, an Australian charity that promotes joint medical research between the two countries.
The collaboration continued without interruption throughout the war, with the lab work in Jerusalem and the bioinformatic analysis in Melbourne advancing in parallel, in daily coordination across the time difference and the security situation. For the teams, it was also proof that international medical research can keep working under the most difficult conditions, they said.

Alabama's Emergency Management Agency (EMA) issued a warning to residents after hurricane Isaias made landfall on Thursday evening.
Isaias weakened to a post-tropical cyclone on Saturday, having rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, the US National Hurricane Center said in its latest advisory.
US President Donald Trump told reporters that hurricane preparation were "under control," adding that "We are watching it very closely."
The hurricane has produced high winds, downed power lines, and caused travel delays, including the closure of all roads through Houston county, Alabama.
"Widespread damage and power outages are likely as this system passes through the state. All actions to protect property should have already been completed for the southern half of Alabama and should be completed across the northern half by 10 pm," Alabama's EMA warned.
Additionally, the Florida division of the EMA extended a tornado watch for parts of North Florida until Saturday morning.
National Hurrican Center warns of potential for flooding
The post-tropical cyclone, crossing over southern Alabama after making landfall earlier near Destin, Florida is about 55 miles (89 km) south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kmh), the agency added.
The center warned of possible storm surges, urban and river flooding and flash floods across the region, with considerable impacts likely across much of southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle into southwest Georgia.
Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland through Saturday even after it becomes post-tropical, the NHC said.
Isaias is expected to cross Alabama and go into the Tennessee Valley over the weekend, the NHC said.
More than 412,000 people in Florida and nearly 243,000 in Alabama lost power as the storm hit shore, according to power outage tracking firm PowerOutage.us.
"Emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X.
Florida's emergency services urged residents to shelter in place and watch for hurricane conditions across the north of the state.
Post-tropical cyclone Isaias is about 55 miles (88.5 km) south-southwest of Montgomery, with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kmh), NHC said.
Continued weakening is expected, but Isaias will continue to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the agency added.

Fund bill sets out repayment terms for affected investors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:28:26 UTC
15:28:26 KST

About 350,000 investors in funds under liquidation could recover their net principal through advance payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras under a bill before parliament, ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) parliamentary group leader Abdullah Güler said.
Güler put the number of affected investors at roughly 455,000, explaining that inflation compensation would be calculated separately at the final settlement.
“Think of it as an advance payment,” he said.
Under the proposal, investors whose net investment is below 1 million liras could receive that amount, while those with larger investments could receive an advance capped at 1 million liras. Payments would depend on available assets and verified entitlements.
If available cash is insufficient, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) could prioritize investors with the smallest balances or set a common minimum advance.
Where fund assets fall short of the value of investors’ holdings, repayment calculations would use actual cash invested and withdrawn, adjusted for inflation through the liquidation date.
The adjustment would reflect the average change in the consumer price and domestic producer price indices, with withdrawals deducted from the earliest investments first.
Further payments would follow as assets are sold and money recovered.
Güler said no public funds would be used.
The bill also addresses responsibility for losses caused by unlawful transfers of fund assets.
The portfolio management company that founded or managed the fund would bear primary liability. If recovery from the company proved impossible, other individuals and entities found responsible by the SPK could be held personally liable.
Leaving office would not remove responsibility for transactions and decisions made during their tenure.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) would collect recovered money in separate accounts for each fund.
Where appointed as trustee, it could sell seized assets before the conclusion of court proceedings.
Investors found by the SPK to have participated in market abuse or acted with those responsible would be excluded from repayments.
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek told daily Sabah that investigators had identified more than 187 billion liras in allegedly unlawful gains made by 141 individuals and 73 companies through Tera, Pusula and Hedef funds.
He said their details had been sent to the TMSF, which had begun issuing repayment notices.
The nine-article bill, submitted on Oct. 9, covers funds ordered into liquidation by the SPK on Sept. 17 whose liquidation remains unfinished when the legislation takes effect.
Güler said the proposal was scheduled for consideration by parliament’s Plan and Budget Commission the following week, before proceeding to the General Assembly.

‘Cockroaches’ are back in the streets: Here is why India faces a new wave of protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:27:02 UTC
15:27:02 KST

‘Cockroaches’ are back in the streets: Here is why India faces a new wave of protests
The protests in the Indian capital New Delhi demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, have intensified, with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a satirical youth movement joining the cause on Saturday.
Delhi’s police have moved to snuff out the protests even before they begin. They detained CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke from inside a plane when he landed in Delhi on Saturday morning. And YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, a known critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, was detained from his residence in Gurugram.
Central Delhi has been turned into a fortress. Prohibitory orders are in place and permission for further demonstrations have been denied. Local reports say 20,000 police personnel are now on Delhi’s streets. The capital’s stadiums have been turned into makeshift detention centers. And the internet has been cut.
Up to 250 long-distance trains arriving in Delhi have been cancelled. Restrictions have been imposed on public transport, including on Delhi’s metro system – prompting India’s Supreme Court to intervene.
The approaches to Jantar Mantar – an 18th century astronomical observatory in central Delhi, which has served as a site for the protests – were sealed earlier this month.
However, Delhi police have so far avoided the heavy-handed approach they had taken against the CJP in July, when the movement humbled Modi’s government and forced the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Why does the opposition want the election panel chief to resign?
The opposition parties allege that the Election Commission’s country-wide voter revision exercise is helping Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) stay in power, and win elections in state after state.
The Election Commission of India started its special revision of voter lists in the world’s largest democracy last year, starting with the northern Bihar state. The aim was to identify, and remove, the names of dead voters, those who have moved locations, have registered for vote in more than one constituency, or those that simply could not be traced.
About 130 million names have been removed or flagged for removal so far, figures cited by the BJP itself show. If that figure sounds big, remember that India has a 1.4 billion population. The final decisions on removing many of these names are yet to be made.
However, India’s opposition parties allege that legitimate voters, including people from minority communities and groups less likely to back the BJP, have been removed.
They claim the name removals means India’s elections are no longer a level playing field. The opposition says the exercise has already skewed the results of state elections held in April, with the BJP and its alliance winning three of the five states.
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has gone so far as to call it “vote theft,” arguing that any laws passed by lawmakers elected through “stolen” votes lack legitimacy. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have denied manipulating the rolls for political gain.
The BJP maintains that the exercise is only for removing ineligible voters. Home Minister Amit Shah has said it is also intended to prevent “infiltrators” – an euphemism for illegal immigrants, mainly from neighboring Bangladesh – from voting.
The election panel contends that any wrongly excluded voters can request to be added back to the rolls, and further appeal any adverse decisions.
The long-simmering controversy flared up last month after the Indian Express daily reported that the two other members of the election panel had objected to many of Singh’s decisions on voter registration, deletions, and control of electoral databases. The panel acknowledged the objections, but said those internal differences were normal and its final decisions were unanimous.
Opposition Congress party leads the charge in Delhi
The Congress-led opposition took the issue to Delhi’s streets earlier this week. The protests received unexpected energy when Rahul Gandhi and his sister Priyanka Gandhi, led from the front. Dramatic scenes unfolded, with Rahul climbing atop police barricades and waving the national flag, and the siblings then dodging the police and entering the office complex of the state broadcaster All-India Radio in an attempt to reach the Election Commission office next door.
Police detained them and several other lawmakers briefly on October 6, and again the next day. Cases were filed against them for alleged obstruction and assaults on officers.
But Rahul Gandhi has remained unfazed and pressed on. He said there were already 45 first information reports (FIRs), the formal complaints that start police investigations, against him. “Every FIR is a medal for me,” he taunted, adding that he wanted the figure to reach 100.
Through the week, the opposition lawmakers have managed to dodge the heavy police presence in central Delhi and sustain the momentum through impromptu sit-ins at various locations, like at the memorial of Mahatma Gandhi. Demonstrations have also taken place in several states, and opposition leaders have sought to raise the issue with Indian President Droupadi Murmu.
What happens next?
Kumar remains in office. He can only be removed after a parliamentary process and a two-thirds majority vote in both the houses of the Indian Parliament. That seems a bridge too far – the opposition alliance holds just 184 of the 543 seats in the Lok Sabha.
The opposition’s only other option is to raise the pressure on Kumar through public protests and force him to resign.
The CJP’s role is crucial. Its last protest was successful because it resonated across India. Can they get the same popular support this time is the key question.
Gyanesh Kumar’s future, and that of the CJP, depend on it

Professor Rıfat Atun has become the first Turkish academic to hold a deanship at Harvard University.
The Turkish Cypriot academic took office on Aug. 1 as dean for education and innovation at Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
His responsibilities cover the school’s degree and non-degree programs, including efforts to introduce artificial intelligence and other technologies into teaching.
He previously served as vice dean for non-degree education and innovation.
Atun also holds the Julio Frenk Professorship of Public Health Leadership and is a professor of global health systems. His research focuses on health system performance, financing, reform and the adoption of new technologies.
He has advised the World Health Organization, the World Bank and G20 presidencies on health policy and reform, and previously chaired the Stop TB Partnership’s coordinating board.
Atun has published more than 500 papers, according to his Harvard profile. It lists him among Clarivate’s highly cited researchers for 2020–2025 and Stanford–Elsevier’s most influential scientists for 2021–2025.

Introduction
 
In today’s complex and rapidly evolving era, managing a nation cannot be achieved solely through political power; rather, it requires leadership that charts the path forward with profound insight into knowledge, the future, and human needs. 1. Mastery of Modern and Interdisciplinary Knowledge: One of the most prominent characteristics of Iran’s Leader is his extensive knowledge across diverse fields. He is not confined to political matters alone; his record demonstrates scholarly mastery in areas such as engineering sciences, resource management, modern agriculture, and even the social sciences. This interdisciplinary knowledge enables him to engage in expert and impactful dialogues with technical specialists and professionals during decision-making sessions—acting not merely as a politician, but as an informed analyst.

Conclusion:
The leadership of the Islamic Republic of Iran exemplifies a model of "knowledge-based leadership"—a model in which politics is intertwined with science, and strategy with human understanding. Yemen’s Taiz under siege again as food and fuel prices rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:20:53 UTC
15:20:53 KST

Yemen’s Taiz under siege again as food and fuel prices rise
Houthi advances and the closure of vital roads into Taiz have triggered shortages, reviving memories of earlier siege.
Taiz, Yemen – Taiz is under siege, but 37-year-old Iskandar Abdullah already knows what it’s like to live under one.
The city, a major population centre in Yemen’s southwest, endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, as the Iranian-backed group attempted to capture the city from local pro-government forces. The Houthis continued to maintain a partial siege in the following years through their control over other access points into the city.
“They were difficult days,” Abdullah recalls, even as the Houthis begin a new siege on Taiz following their capture of territory to the south of the city, cutting off the main road to government-held territory. “We witnessed the horrors of the siege and experienced the bitterness of life in all its terrifying details.”
“I hope those painful days never return.”
In early September, the Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of Taiz governorate. The group soon established full control over the port city of Mocha and the district of Dhubab, where the Bab al-Mandeb strait – through which 12 percent of global trade passes – is located.
The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen’s populous northwest, including the capital Sanaa, since the country’s war started in 2014, did not stop their military attacks at the Red Sea. Even as government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October and regained some of the territory lost, the Houthis pressed forward in the countryside surrounding Taiz.
The Houthis successfully captured the town of al-Turbah by October 4, severing the only remaining main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.
Taiz residents, like Abdullah, are now worried that the city is about to face a prolonged full-scale siege. Abdullah remembers how difficult life was between 2015 and 2016, when pro-government forces were confined to an enclave in the centre of the city.
Locals endured “horrors, as well as appalling humanitarian and economic conditions unlike anything experienced by any other Yemeni governorate during the war”, according to Abdullah.
“People lacked even the most basic necessities of life, including drinking water, food, fuel and medicine,” he said. “The only exceptions were supplies smuggled across rugged mountain terrain, carried on the backs of people and donkeys, including oxygen cylinders for the sick and wounded.”
Shortages
The siege was eventually broken in 2016 when pro-government forces recaptured territory south of Taiz city. In 2024, under domestic and international pressure, the Houthis agreed to reopen another important route into the city from the east, connecting it to Sanaa and other Houthi-controlled areas of northern Yemen.
However, with the recent resumption of fighting, the vital crossing has been closed following attempted incursions by Houthi fighters, according to security sources who spoke to Al Jazeera.
The closure has severed a crucial route that had become essential for Taiz residents – much of the city’s food supplies had entered through the crossing.
Nabil Jamil, director-general of the planning and development office in Taiz governorate, said that the current siege on Taiz is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.
“This time, the siege does not only affect the governorate’s main roads, but also most of the secondary roads connecting the rural districts themselves,” Jamil said.
Jamil said that approximately 2.8 million people had been living in government-held areas of Taiz governorate, alongside another 200,000 people who have been recently displaced by the fighting along the coast and rural Taiz.
“All of them will face humanitarian hardship and deteriorating living conditions as a result of the siege,” he said.
Less than a week into the renewed siege, the city’s streets appeared almost deserted because of a fuel shortage, which had previously entered the city through the al-Turbah route from Aden.
On the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol rose from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 Yemeni riyals ($58).
Meanwhile, markets and grocery shops have seen a surge in demand, as residents rush to stock up on food amid fears that supplies would disappear from shelves because of the siege.
Some residents have accused traders of hoarding and monopolising essential goods in the absence of any effective market oversight.
“Food markets in Taiz have witnessed a noticeable increase in the prices of basic commodities, particularly wheat and flour, while the prices of vegetables and fruits have doubled, as the siege has made it difficult to bring these products into the city,” said Wafiq Saleh, a journalist specialising in economic affairs.
“Traders in the city have food stocks sufficient to last several months,” he added. “Nevertheless, some traders began raising prices as soon as the fighting intensified on the outskirts of the city.”
Humanitarian fears
Fighting is continuing in the Taiz countryside, and there is hope among locals that government forces will be able to retake the areas lost to the Houthis in recent days, or continue their forward momentum in areas to the west of Taiz city, and break the siege from that direction.
But for now, the Houthis appear to be on the front foot in the areas to Taiz city’s south.
Salman al-Maqrami, a journalist specialising in Houthi affairs, believes the primary objective of the Taiz siege is to undermine the cohesion of the forces opposed to them in the city, which has long been a hotbed of hostility towards the group.
“Therefore, there is no doubt that [the Houthis] are seeking revenge against this population that opposes them,” he added.
The fall of Taiz would also be symbolic for the Houthis, allowing the group to present itself as being able to threaten any area under government control, even if the population is hostile.
However, Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and the head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization (JRDO), pointed out that the effect of any such battle for Taiz – including a longstanding siege on such a large city – would be detrimental to civilians.
“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” Sharyan said.
He warned of the enormous humanitarian cost of the renewed siege, “particularly for patients, children, women and the elderly, given the difficulties in accessing hospitals, medical services, and medicines”.
“Restrictions on travel and movement will also affect students, patients, employees and families who depend on travelling between different areas of the governorate and beyond,” he added.
Sharyan called on the international community, human rights organisations and humanitarian agencies to take a clear position that “guarantees residents access to their basic needs, ensures that roads and crossings remain open to civilians and goods, and allows patients to reach healthcare services, in a manner that safeguards human dignity and fundamental rights”.
Jamil said that local authorities in Taiz had sent a letter to the United Nations seeking assistance in addressing the crisis and its humanitarian consequences.
Local authorities’ priorities include opening safe roads and corridors for civilians, especially those who need to travel for medical treatment, and allowing medicine and food to reach Taiz.
“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.

Hong Kong to expand community recycling after shelving waste-charging scheme

Hong Kong will strengthen its community recycling network with measures such as round-the-clock automated collection points after scrapping its waste-charging scheme due to strong public opposition, the environmental chief has said.
Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan on Saturday also pledged to review the permitted profit levels of the city’s two power companies when their control agreements with the government expire in 2033. He added that the government would boost clean energy imports from mainland China.
Tse expressed confidence that Hong Kong would achieve the four binding goals on environmental protection outlined in the city’s first five-year plan, unveiled last month.

French policing under scrutiny as student protest injuries mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:09:59 UTC
15:09:59 KST

French policing under scrutiny as student protest injuries mount
PARIS/ARGENTEUIL, France, Oct 10 - Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a broken jaw and multiple smashed teeth when he was struck by a tear gas canister directed towards him at close range by a police officer last week during student protests in France, his parents and family lawyer said.
The teenager had been sitting on a wall looking at his phone metres away from the protest in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumone, the lawyer said. An officer approached him and struck him with a baton, prompting Eden to respond with a kick, according to the local prosecutor. A second officer then fired a tear gas grenade with a Cougar launcher, hitting him in the face.
"(The officer) shot him in the mouth and left him lying on the ground, without even calling the emergency services," said lawyer Elsa Marcel. The family, who asked for Eden's second name to be withheld to protect their privacy, has filed a complaint for attempted murder, she said.
A police spokesperson said they do not comment on ongoing investigations. The prosecutor's office said in a statement that the student had confronted the police and the officers tried to push him back. The officer was placed under formal investigation on charges of assault by a public official resulting in permanent disability or disfigurement on Tuesday, eight days after the incident.
The case is one of 24 under investigation by the IGPN internal police watchdog linked to the policing of a more-than-two-week-long wave of student unrest over conditions in schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has described the demonstrations as the most violent in decades.
The police response has renewed calls for the withdrawal of the use of rubber bullets and grenade launchers, which are not used by police in many other European countries and have been repeatedly criticised in recent years by rights groups, including Amnesty International and UN human rights experts, as dangerous and disproportionate.
It has also sparked anger among the public and fanned support for a protest movement that is the latest manifestation of deep-seated discontent with President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of a 2027 election.
Via interviews and reviews of legal documents, Reuters has documented 28 cases of injuries suffered due to police force, of which 15 are among those under investigation by the IGPN. They involve the use of rubber bullets, stun grenades, tear gas, batons and charges on horseback.
In two cases, a person's eye has been lost or injured due to rubber bullets. In another, a 15-year-old in Lens had his hand blown off — likely by a stun grenade, according to interior minister Laurent Nunez, who paused the use of stun grenades pending an investigation into the case.
Nunez said on Wednesday in a radio interview that about 200 students had been injured, but that it was very rarely the result of police action. “Our primary role is, of course, to protect high school students,” he said.
Authorities said that 700 police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked. The police have arrested 6,877 people, mostly minors.
“France is an anomaly in terms of its use of arms and the number of victims — we have four irreversible injuries in the space of 12 days, and they are minors,” said Sebastian Roche, researcher on policing at the French National Centre for Scientific Research.
“It is a level that is unknown in (France’s) contemporary history,” he said.
CALLS TO BAN 'LESS LETHAL' WEAPONS
Roche said that France stands out in Europe for its use of "less lethal" weapons such as rubber bullets and stun grenades. Such weapons are generally not used for public order policing in Britain, Italy and Germany, aside from Hamburg, and although permitted in Spain, have caused fewer injuries than in France, said Roche.
In the Paris suburb of Argenteuil, a 16-year-old student on his way home after finding his school closed was shot by police, injuring his left eye, which may be permanently damaged, his lawyer Sophia Kerbaa told Reuters. It is not clear if he was hit by a rubber bullet or something else, she added.
A video viewed by Reuters showed the boy bleeding from his eye.
“He was in the wrong place at the wrong time ... he is injured and in shock,” Kerbaa said.
The prosecutor investigating the case said that, according to the police account, the injured student “seemed to correspond” to one of two young people who had directed fireworks at police officers, who responded with rubber bullets.
The interior ministry did not respond to questions on the case, or that of Eden.
Human rights advocates, including Amnesty International, and some politicians have called for “less lethal” weapons to be banned permanently, while police unions say the police need these weapons to enforce order in violent situations and to ensure their own security.
“We must withdraw the use of rubber bullets and ... aim for zero injured students. That will allow us to de-escalate,” Mayor Bally Bagayoko of the left-wing France Unbowed party told Reuters. Bagayoko joined the protests in his town Saint-Denis, saying he wanted to protect young people from the police.
Thierry Clair, a police union representative, said that serious injuries such as Eden’s, or another child losing his hand, were tragedies, but should not call into question France’s policing techniques. He said the problem came instead from the intensity of the violence being committed by some young people who stoked tensions.
“How do we respond when people are moving towards confrontation? If we remove intermediate force options, all we are left with is lethal force,” Clair told Reuters. “That is simply inconceivable.” REUTERS

Germany's firewall against the far-right AfD feels the heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:04:53 UTC
15:04:53 KST

Germany's firewall against the far-right AfD feels the heat
BERLIN, Oct 10 - Chancellor Friedrich Merz's warning this week that extremism was entering Germany's parliamentary system was the latest in a series of signs that mainstream parties' "firewall" to isolate the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has begun to buckle.
This week, at least four lawmakers from mainstream parties in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt appear to have defied party orders and voted to give the AfD, which wants to restrict immigration and restore energy ties with Russia, its first regional assembly speaker.
The ballot was secret but suspicion immediately fell on the 15 members of Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) in parliament, who had been told to abstain.
Karin Prien, deputy chair of the national CDU, said if CDU lawmakers were to blame, "there must be consequences".
The AfD itself, which has been leading the CDU in nationwide surveys for more than a year and declared its aim of winning a national election due in 2029, hailed a "political turning point".
"For the first time, it was clear that the so-called 'firewall' doesn't have to be stronger than the freedom of action of members of parliament," said Martin Reichardt, head of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt.
COULD AFD WIN A NATIONAL ELECTION IN GERMANY?
The AfD's record victory last month has alarmed rivals, who consider it an anti-democratic party opposed to the values that helped Germany to rebuild after World War Two and renounce the horrors of Nazism and its nationalist, racist ideology. The AfD rejects their label of "extreme right" as a slur.
Across Europe and beyond, the result, which left the AfD just short of an absolute majority in the state parliament, was seen as one of the clearest indications yet that it could win a national election in 2029.
Merz's coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats in Berlin has been under increasing strain, riven by disagreements and sliding in opinion polls as voters, like many across Western Europe, blame the mainstream parties for declining living standards.
On Wednesday, the parties held talks to iron out differences over issues including pensions and tax, and said they were "determined not to hand our country over to extremists".
Set up over a decade ago during the euro zone debt crisis, the AfD has grown from a fringe movement into the most popular party in Germany in opinion polls.
Yet parts of the AfD - including its Saxony-Anhalt branch - have been designated as extremist by German security services, meaning that they are considered to be opposed to constitutional principles of human rights, democracy and the rule of law.
The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), the domestic intelligence agency, compiled a 1,100-page confidential report last year that found the AfD incited resentment of migrants, as well as racism and Islamophobia.
For its part, the AfD says it is restoring German national pride and values, and ensuring that migrants are not prioritised at the expense of German citizens.
So far, the "firewall" approach - under which the established parties have refused to cooperate with the AfD - has kept it from joining any coalition government.
In Saxony-Anhalt, where it needs three more seats for a majority, it is still unclear how it can form a government after talks over a possible coalition with the populist far-left BSW made no progress.
FEARS OF COOPERATION WITH AFD
However, the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund, who dismisses the firewall as "childish", says he can persuade enough members of other parties to defy party orders to enable him to be confirmed as state premier by the end of the year.
In this week's speaker ballot, the AfD's Tobias Rausch won 48 votes - four more than the combined total held by the AfD and the BSW.
Merz has ruled out any arrangement with the AfD, which he says aims to destroy the CDU, and the issue is expected to be discussed at a CDU's leadership meeting on Sunday and Monday.
But whether it remains realistic to refuse to cooperate with a party attracting almost a third of the vote, and more in the formerly communist eastern states where it is strongest, has become an urgent question.
CDU deputy leader Prien said any sign of accommodation could open divisions that could "jeopardise the very existence of the entire party".
The AfD has gained ground nationwide but remains weaker in western Germany than in the east, and appears unlikely to repeat its Saxony-Anhalt result in state elections next year.
However, the problems that have helped create the conditions for its rapid rise resist easy answers. War in Ukraine has cut off the supply of cheap energy that fuelled Germany's economy while competition from China has eaten away at its once-invincible industrial base.
Economists warn continually that fundamental reforms are needed to pensions and taxes to meet the needs of an ageing population, while deep divisions remain between the eastern and western regions, almost four decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Marking the anniversary last week of German reunification in 1990, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier acknowledged that many felt overlooked by the political system and that a generalised feeling of insecurity had undermined confidence.
But, in an unusually bleak assessment, he said the bitter political climate was threatening to send Germany back into the chaos that ended the democracy of the prewar Weimar Republic.
"Today is about the survival of democracy," he said. "We must stand up for what remains important." REUTERS

UN warns of rising civilian toll in Ukraine as Russian strikes kill 100 in a week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:04:45 UTC
15:04:45 KST

The UN condemned a sharp escalation in attacks on civilians in Ukraine, reporting that more than 100 people were killed and at least 429 injured over the past week as Russian strikes hit residential areas, passenger buses and critical infrastructure.
Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, told the UN Security Council on Friday that attacks by the Russian Federation had reached “a new horrifying level” since the council’s briefing September 23.
“We strongly condemn all attacks against civilians,” said Khiari.
He said the pattern of escalating attacks had contributed to a "significant increase" in civilian casualties this year, with every month recording more casualties than the corresponding month in each of the previous three years.
Beyond the immediate loss of life, he warned that repeated attacks on Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure were disrupting life for millions.
The official also expressed concern about reported attacks on telecommunications networks, retail businesses, food suppliers and logistics companies.
“All attacks on energy infrastructure and on population centers must cease immediately,” said Khiari, stressing the urgency of protecting vulnerable civilians before winter sets in.
Black Sea attacks threaten shipping
Khiari also expressed concern about civilian deaths and injuries resulting from intensified attacks by Ukrainian forces inside Russia.
The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded reports of 3,890 civilian casualties in Russia between January and September, including 496 deaths and 3,394 injuries, said Khiari.
“All attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a violation of international humanitarian law and must end immediately,” he added.
Khiari warned that the consequences of the war were increasingly extending beyond Ukraine and Russia, threatening regional security and international trade.
"Particularly worrisome, in the Black Sea, attacks on civilian vessels have multiplied and expanded in geographic scope," he said.
He welcomed diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions and securing safe civilian navigation in the Black Sea, urging both to negotiate credible and sustainable arrangements.
Khiari warned that attacks on ports, transport networks, grain facilities and other agricultural infrastructure were contributing to rising global food prices.
He urged Russia and Ukraine to halt the escalating attacks on civilians and pursue renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.
“The current cycle of escalating attacks against civilians must end now before the civilian toll reaches new, devastating levels,” he said.
Diplomacy and dialogue must prevail and be given a genuine chance to succeed, he noted.
“It is time to end this war,” Khiari added.

‘If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we’re screwed’: Labour insiders voice fears over budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:00:51 UTC
15:00:51 KST

In the days since Labour’s annual conference, party insiders have been sharing a word cloud produced by the pollsters More in Common, which shows the phrases voters most associate with Andy Burnham.
Such polling is rarely flattering for politicians, and the prime minister’s version had its fair share of negatives. But one of the most prominent words in the cloud – and the one that has caught the imagination of Labour strategists – was “trying”.
At a cabinet away day at Chequers on Monday and a meeting for special advisers on Thursday, the idea that the government was doing its best to improve people’s lives – despite the difficult economic backdrop – was a golden thread.
“The public think the only person that can reach those levers is you,” said a government insider. “They justifiably ask, can you do it or not? And if not, they’ll look for an alternative. We have to avoid the sense of things being out of our control.”
A party strategist said: “Voters don’t want us to put our hands up in despair; they want us to roll our sleeves up. They don’t want us to be helpless in the face of global stuff; they want answers.” But will this prime minister be able to provide them?
At conference, Burnham set out his big vision for the future – on social care and the pensions triple lock, the EU and electoral reform. The party faithful lapped it up and polling suggested the “Burnham bounce” had continued.
But while Labour MPs are relieved to have a leader with a clear political direction, many worry that offering big promises for after the next general election will not be enough to scratch the itch for dramatic change.
Downing Street believes part of the answer is what it describes as “everyday fixes” – cost of living measures that might not, on their own, amount to very much, but added up can make a difference and show the government is trying.
Overseen by the No 10 policy unit and the Cabinet Office’s cost of living taskforce, each department has “incubators” where proposals are dreamed up. Many are in the works, such as rules around car-parking apps and unbranded school uniforms.
They might not grab the media headlines, but strategists say they pick up engagement online, with 85m views across all social platforms last week alone. There will be more announced in the two-and-a-bit weeks running up to John Healey’s first budget on 28 October.
“We want to show we can tackle the everyday frustrations that people assume are part of life,” one adviser said. But several admitted they had some qualms about the drumbeat of small interventions.
“We risk looking twee, frankly, if we aren’t successfully thinking about how to tie it to the bigger picture of structural change. Public control, tax, that is what we want to be able to point to as well as the everyday things.”
Another added: “We need to tread carefully. We have very small interventions now and huge ambitions for three years’ time. We also need medium-scale changes in the medium term, and that is what is missing at the moment.”
The government faces a difficult budget, with inflation and soaring borrowing costs as a result of the Iran war thought to have blown a £12bn hole in the public finances, forcing the chancellor to consider tax rises and spending cuts to fund plans to ease the cost of living.
The statement, which is expected to be “low key”, will focus on fiscal devolution, with a household support package centred on cutting energy bills and more help for small businesses. Next year’s spending review would require more revenue, sources said, but details would have to wait.
A No 10 aide said: “The budget is a moment of peak attention and potentially peak peril. We’re not able to do everything we want to, so we have to level with people and say we can’t fix everything all at once, but we’re trying.”
But for some MPs, there is a growing nervousness at the low level of ambition at this budget, especially on cost of living measures, which the Burnham government has made its main test.
One said: “If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we are screwed. As things stand, this looks like a Reeves budget with better vibes. I hope this isn’t all there is. But I really fear that actually it is.”
Treasury insiders acknowledge the need to “kickstart” longer-term changes at the budget – and that a “low-key” statement with the big decisions put off until next year may not be enough for the public. “The budget will be our first punch in the face moment,” a government aide said.
There was a “bit of friction” between the prime minister’s office and the Treasury over balancing fiscal responsibility with hope, the source added. “No 10 wants to signal intent: that we won’t get everything immediately, but we’ll get there.”
There were lingering questions about “how this all adds up when we’re under grey skies”, another adviser added. “It’s impossible to see how anyone can square the additional spending we need given the tightness of the fiscal envelope.”
Ministers and advisers are expecting a barrage of attacks from the Tories and Reform UK on welfare. But they believe the Milburn and Timms reviews, which will be published shortly after the budget – will help them fight back.
Downing Street expects the days after the budget to be “bumpy” but is optimistic that Burnham’s communication skills will help to make the case, and that the public will continue – for now – to give him the benefit of the doubt.
A source said: “We’ll take a bit of a hit over the budget. It’s going to be a tough couple of weeks. But then we have a run to the 10-year plan. If we get that right, we can potentially go into next year with people saying: ‘Yes, it’s difficult, but we trust this guy.’”
At the cabinet away day, Burnham told ministers: “Politics has become too suffocating. We need greater ambition. The country is not where it should be and nothing simple gets us out of that. We need to show a journey and a longer-term plan.”
Ministers were presented with polling that showed support for Labour’s social care policy, including adjusting the pensions triple lock, went up by a quarter after voters were shown a video of the prime minister explaining his plan.
A party strategist told them: “On social care and the triple lock we need to continually make the case, time after time. When we make the case we have the power to persuade.”
There is a political axiom that if you’re explaining, you’re losing. But Labour strategists are pushing back on that idea. The prevailing view inside government is that Burnham is the only one who can go out and make the case – on all of his big promises – to the country.
Not everybody inside the party thinks it will work. “I don’t know how convinced I am about giving people essentially the same message as before: we want to do more but we’re constrained,” one insider said.
But ministers hope that by focusing on policies which signal intent, they can get through these difficult months. “We need more time to lean into the big things we can do, like public control, but we need to be honest with voters. We set ourselves a target of tackling the cost of living, but so many things are out of our control.”
No 10 insight work shows that people were still prepared to accept the Iran conflict as an explanation for why things are so tough, rather than viewing it as an excuse. At the away day, Healey told his colleagues: “We are recognising those pressures, being honest about what we can do and taking practical action wherever possible to give people some breathing space at the budget.”
When parliament returns after conference recess on Monday, Burnham will give a statement, updating MPs on the past few weeks and taking questions. Throughout, he will aim to show the public he is on their side.
But one senior Labour figure cautioned: “We all hope that he has a plan for what comes next. The sense that he gets it and that he’ll keep trying won’t last for ever.”

UK savings: 5% interest rate deals may not last, say experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:00:50 UTC
15:00:50 KST

National Savings and Investments (NS&I) has increased the returns on some of its accounts, with many now paying more than 5% for the first time in nearly three years.
Competition in the savings market has been growing, leading to some of the highest interest rates for years.
However, in the current climate, attractive deals do not always hang around for long, says Rachel Springall at the financial data website Moneyfactscompare.co.uk. If a provider attracts enough savings cash it will pull a product from sale.
NS&I has upped the rates on its “British savings bonds”, which are rebadged versions of its guaranteed growth bonds and guaranteed income bonds. They offer a fixed interest rate over their one-, two-, three- or five-year bonds.
The deals are available to new customers and those with existing accounts that are maturing. With the growth version, interest is added each year and paid when the bond matures, while with the income version, interest is paid monthly.
Looking at the growth bonds, the new interest rate on the one-year product is 4.99% (up from 4.82%), while the two-year rate has risen to 5.07% (was 4.81%). The three-year rate has gone up from 4.83% to 5.1%, while the five-year rate has been increased to 5.17% (was 4.85%).
Those are pretty competitive rates, though as Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at the advice firm AJ Bell, says, “you can still make more money elsewhere”.
At the time of writing, the top-paying one-year fixed-rate bond was paying 5.12%, while the highest-paying five-year fixed bond was offering 5.37%. But getting the very highest rates sometimes means signing up with less-well-known names. The one-year deal is from Union Bank of India (UK), while the five-year version hails from GB Bank.
If you have a very large sum that you need to stash somewhere – for example, the proceeds of a house sale or an inheritance – these NS&I bonds have one big thing in their favour: you can invest up to £1m per person in each bond issue. The minimum investment is £500.
As NS&I says, “most banks only guarantee your savings up to £120,000,” whereas it is backed by the Treasury and is “the only provider that secures 100% of your savings above this amount”.
Also, it means you are putting your money into the government’s savings bank, and “your savings will be invested back into supporting the UK”.
Money invested in NS&I’s British savings bonds cannot be withdrawn before the end of the fixed term.
That will not suit everyone, and it is a good idea to keep some money in a high-paying easy access account to cover things such as unexpected bills. Earlier this month the digital bank Starling announced that people who sign up for its Easy Saver account will enjoy a table-topping 5% interest rate. This account offers unlimited penalty-free withdrawals, but that rate (made up of a 2.5% variable standard rate, plus a 2.5% fixed interest bonus lasting for six months) only applies to those who open, or have opened, a Starling current account on or after 1 October. The rate applies on balances of up to £25,000.
Starling customers who signed up before then can benefit from a 4% rate when opening a new Easy Saver. That includes a 1.5% fixed interest bonus for six months.
Meanwhile, the savings provider Marcus by Goldman Sachs this week upped the interest rate on its one-year fixed-rate savings account from 4.3% to 4.75%.

UK accused of giving people of Gaza false hope over new refugee safe route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:00:50 UTC
15:00:50 KST

The Home Office is facing claims it gave false hope to the people of Gaza after it emerged that a new safe route for Palestinian refugees will only be open to those who have already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, announced the reopening of a resettlement scheme for refugees at Labour’s annual conference last month. A statement from her department said: “Around one in four referrals will be for Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, fleeing war and persecution.”
But the body administering the scheme has confirmed it would only refer “a very small number of extremely urgent cases”, all of which would be processed in Jordan and Lebanon.
The umbrella alliance Communities for Palestinians (CFP) said this crucial detail was not in Mahmood’s speech or subsequent Home Office statements, giving people in Gaza and their supporters the belief that they could also apply.
Vicky Moller, a co-founder of CFP, said: “The applause at Shabana’s announcement at conference was at the prospect of a resettlement scheme for Palestinians fleeing war and persecution. People understood that would mean rescuing people from Gaza.”
The Home Office has pushed back at the claims, saying the UK resettlement scheme that Mahmood has reopened has always been for people from outside their country of origin.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “To qualify for refugee status under international frameworks, individuals must be outside their country of origin.
“Palestinians who remain in Gaza would not initially be in scope for these routes. However, Palestinians who have fled Gaza could be referred to the UK through the International Refugee Assistance Project [Irap].”
Restrictions on eligibility for the scheme emerged after an exchange of emails between the CFP and Irap, which has been tasked with making referrals.
According to Irap’s website, it will refer “a very small number of extremely urgent humanitarian cases to the UK for consideration for resettlement”, adding: “These cases will be referred to Irap by humanitarian organisations in Jordan and Lebanon and Irap will then hold interviews to determine if these cases can be referred to the UK government.”
The programme focuses on “extremely vulnerable refugees whose lives have become unsustainable in Jordan or Lebanon”.
The non-profit’s website added: “Irap does not know how many people the UK government will accept under the Palestinian resettlement programme. This is ultimately a decision for the UK government and depends on funding as well as local authorities’ capacity.”
Other safe and legal routes administered by the UK have allowed small numbers of people to enter the UK from their country of origin, including previous schemes for Afghan refugees.
Palestinian refugees fall outside the remit of the refugee convention and UNHCR.
Unrwa was instead set up to serve Palestinian refugees who were defined as any person whose “normal place of residence was Palestine during the period 1 June 1946 to 15 May 1948 and who lost both home and means of livelihood as a result of the 1948 conflict”.
As a result, Palestinian refugees live in what refugee charities and NGOs refer to as Palestine – in other words, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip – as well as second countries such as Syria, Lebanon and Jordan.
Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said ministers should recognise the particular circumstances that meant Palestinians could be refugees while living in their own country.
“The government is right to commit to safe and legal routes. They provide a vital way for refugees to reach safety without having to put their lives in the hands of smuggling gangs,” he said.
“But the warm words have to be accompanied by ambition, and that means supporting people in the thousands, not the hundreds. They must also recognise the particular circumstances of Palestinian refugees and be accessible to them no matter where they are in the world.”
A renowned expert in asylum systems has said resettlement programmes are usually designed as a solution for people who have already left their own country.
Dr Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the UK government’s safe and legal route was always going to mean taking Palestinians from neighbouring states such as Egypt, Jordan or Lebanon.
“The Syrian scheme worked the same way: the roughly 20,000 people resettled to the UK between 2014 and 2021 all came from countries around Syria, with nobody to my knowledge being flown directly from Syria,” he said.
“Bringing people directly out of Gaza would be a different kind of programme, closer to an emergency evacuation … And crucially, such an emergency evacuation in Gaza would depend on Israel and Egypt letting people leave and on the Home Office finding a way to do security and biometric checks with no visa centre in Gaza.”
