How much fibre do you really need? Here’s what an expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
01:18:06 UTC
10:18:06 KST

IN BRIEF:
- Fibre-maxxing has swept the algorithm, but it has multiple health benefits.
- Experts say it's important fibre is consumed as food, and not supplements.
Are you getting enough fibre in your diet?
The recommended daily fibre intake is 30g for men and 25g for women, but Australian men and women consume on average about 21g and 18g of fibre per day, respectively. So, you're probably not.
Dietitians have been calling for Australians to increase their fibre intake for decades, and now the challenge has made its way to social media.
Enter the fibre-maxxer: A person committed to hitting, and even exceeding, their daily fibre target.
Online fibre-maxxers promote eating more fruits and vegetables and increasing dietary fibre intake by adding seeds, grains and vegetables to regular foods. This includes putting chia seeds in soft drinks, beans on avocado toast, grains in homemade bread, or adding a cup of legumes to rice.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Can you have too much fibre?
Program director of human nutrition and associate professor at Adelaide University, Evangeline Mantzioris, said that while fibre-maxxing was probably "one of the more positive" social media-fuelled food trends, some elements could be "problematic".
"We actually do need to increase the amount of fibre in our diet," Mantzioris told SBS News.
She said the daily intake suggestion of 25 to 30g per day was based on attaining the best health outcomes, including a reduction of colon cancer, "which is one of the most preventable diseases we have".
"But I understand some are suggesting intakes up to 50 grams a day, possibly more, and there isn't a lot of good evidence that having such extremely high levels may provide any additional benefits."
While there is no upper limit on how much fibre you can eat, more fibre means your body produces more flatulence.
"One of the biggest problems, I guess, is gas, right? No one wants to be gassy out in public."
Another issue, Mantzioris said, is fluid intake.
It was imperative to drink a healthy amount of fluids throughout the day, as without fluids, high fibre can cause constipation, rather than ease it.
"I describe it as it's a bit like trying to clean the bathroom with a dry sponge or a wet sponge. The wet sponge is going to work a lot better than the dry sponge," she said.
"Any increase in fibre will result in an increase in wind, and what we normally tell people to do is to do it slowly."
Don't "go from nothing to 40 grams of fibre in one day". Instead, Mantzioris said, gradually increase high-fibre foods in your diet. This will also help ensure it is a "sustainable" transition for your gut microbiome, the complex community of trillions of microorganisms that live in your digestive tract.
"We know that the bacteria in our gut use that fibre for their survival, and we know that the fibre that comes from whole foods like fruit, vegetables, legumes, beans, nuts, and seeds gives you the healthiest type of microbiome possible", as opposed to the bacteria that thrive on "sometimes foods", which are unhealthy for your body.
"So it's sort of like this lovely symbiotic relationship between your bacteria and you, and the more healthy food you give them, the better off they are, and the better off you are."
Why fibre should come from food
"It's all about balance," Mantzioris said, stressing that fibre intake should come from food, not supplements, which she said some fibremaxxing influencers might be recommending.
"By using supplements, you're missing out on all of the additional nutrients that are in the foods that they originally come from."
She said the best way to avoid "overdosing" on fibre would be to get it from food.
"And get it from a range of different foods — there are a lot of different types of fibres, and they each play a different role in our bodies."
"It's important to eat beans, to eat fruit, eat vegetables, and to eat cereals, to get the maximum benefits from all the different types of fibres, as well as the nutrients that come with all those foods that we know promote health," she said.
What is fibre?
Fibre is a nutrient found in many foods that reduces your risk of chronic disease and keeps your digestive system healthy.
Adequate dietary fibre is essential for proper gut function. It has also been related to risk reduction for some chronic diseases, including heart disease, certain cancers and diabetes.
There are three kinds of fibre: soluble fibre, which slows down digestion, like oats and barley; insoluble fibre, like whole grains, which bulks your stool and speeds up the movement of food through your digestive tract; and resistant starch, found in boiled and cooled potatoes, which ferments in your gut and acts as a prebiotic to feed beneficial bacteria.
Mantzioris said there were "a few reasons" why fibre intake was so consistently low in Australia.
Only about 5 per cent of Australians are meeting the minimum requirements for vegetables in their diet, at 5 serves a day.
"And of course, fibre vegetables are a great source of fibre," Mantzioris said.
She pointed to the ever-increasing popularity of high-protein diets, or "the protein craze".
"When you're consuming more of one food, you're dropping out another essential food group, which is providing you with essential nutrients."
"They're focusing on their protein intake, and we know that roughly 98 per cent of Australians meet their protein requirement".
Beans, she said, were a great example of a high-protein food with multiple benefits.
"The benefit of that protein source is that it also gives you the fibre, and all the antioxidants that we need to fight disease, to reduce oxidative stress in the body and reduce inflammation."
"Every different colour you have in the plant foods represents a different nutrient that's useful for the body."
Finally, she said, "There's an aversion to carbohydrates in our society."
"People see carbohydrates as the problem food when it comes to trying to manage their weight — and all of the carbohydrate-rich foods also provide us with a lot of fibre."

Brazil prosecutors sue Shell for US$108 million over deadly 2024 floods
- Brazil prosecutors filed a US$108 million lawsuit against Shell’s Brazilian unit over the deadly 2024 floods in Rio Grande do Sul.
- The floods, caused by heavy rain, killed nearly 200 people and displaced 500,000. Prosecutors say Shell should answer for its climate impact and emissions.
- The case, backed by Instituto Preservar, is seen as a major step in climate litigation. Experts say it is the first suit by a national prosecutor against an oil major for a climate disaster.
AI generated
BrasIlia – Brazilian prosecutors on Oct 9 filed an unprecedented lawsuit against oil giant Shell’s subsidiary in the country, demanding US$108 million (S$138 million) in compensation over deadly 2024 floods.
Torrential rains sparked historic flooding in southern Brazil in April and May that year, leaving nearly 200 people dead, 500,000 more displaced and massive damages.
According to the lawsuit, Shell’s liability should match its contribution to global warming – estimated at 2% of historical global greenhouse gas emissions.
“This civil suit is aimed at holding the defendant company accountable, in terms of its environmental and climate-related responsibilities, for collective material and moral damages stemming from the extreme weather event that hit Rio Grande do Sul state,” public prosecutors said, according to court documents seen by AFP.
They said the British energy giant should be held responsible because of its past and current greenhouse gas emissions associated with exploration, production and sale of fossil fuels.
The US$108 million in compensation accounts for both material and moral damages.
The filing of a new climate-related suit by Brazilian prosecutors – in conjunction with Instituto Preservar, a Brazilian non-governmental organisation – marks a new phase in the global battle in the courts against oil giants.
“This is the first time a national public prosecutor is suing an oil major for a climate disaster,” Maria Antonia Tigre, director of global climate litigation at the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, told AFP.
Shell is already being sued in Britain by victims of a typhoon in the Philippines. AFP

What is celebrated on October 10 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:58:38 EEST
09:58:38 KST

What is celebrated on October 10 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, Standardization and Metrology Workers’ Day is observed. Around the world, it is World Mental Health Day, World Migratory Bird Day, and World Homeless Day.
On Saturday, October 10, Ukraine observes Standardization and Metrology Workers' Day, while around the world it is World Mental Health Day and World Migratory Bird Day. Orthodox believers commemorate the holy martyrs Eulampius and Eulampia on this day, UNN reports.
Standardization and Metrology Workers' Day
The holiday was established by a decree of the President of Ukraine in 2002. It is a professional holiday for specialists who ensure measurement accuracy, product quality control, and compliance with technical standards in industry, medicine, and other fields.
World Mental Health Day
It has been observed annually on October 10 since 1992. Its aim is to draw attention to psychological well-being, access to assistance, and overcoming prejudice against mental disorders.
What other international holidays are observed on October 10
This year, October 10 also falls on World Migratory Bird Day. It is observed on the second Saturday of May and October to remind people of the need to protect migratory birds, their routes, and their natural habitats.
Other commemorative dates include World Homeless Day, intended to draw attention to the problem of homelessness, and World Porridge Day, dedicated to promoting this dish and addressing nutrition issues.
Church Holiday and Folk Traditions
According to the New Julian calendar, on October 10 the Orthodox Church honors the martyrs Eulampius and his sister Eulampia. According to church traditions, they lived in Nicomedia and suffered because they refused to renounce the Christian faith.
In folk traditions, this day was associated with preparations for winter. Household heads finished their autumn work, checked their supplies, and prepared their homes for the cold. They also tried to predict what the coming winter would be like based on the weather.
Name days on October 10 according to the new church calendar are celebrated by Andrii, Anton, Vasyl, Kyrylo, Pavlo, Serhii, Stepan, Yukhym, and Yakiv.

Three men found guilty of murders of Australian surfer brothers and US friend in Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:50:52 UTC
09:50:52 KST

The parents of Australian surfing brothers murdered in Mexico have said “no outcome can ever undo this tragedy” after three men were convicted of the 2024 killings.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.
The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States.
Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time.
The judge ruled the three Mexican defendants acted with premeditation.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
“They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.”
She burst into tears when the guilty verdict was pronounced.
Speaking outside the court after the verdict, Martin Robinson thanked family and friends for their support, and also thanked the judge, court staff, the Australian embassy in Mexico and the Australian federal police.
He said: “No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honouring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were. They will never be forgotten.”
Debra Robinson said: “I don’t feel any different today as I did yesterday or I will tomorrow, because … Callum and Jake are not here. A verdict is a good thing, but it doesn’t bring them back.”
She said she had no feelings towards the three guilty men. “I have tried to hold on to the memory of my children, my sons, and I try really not to think about them. And I don’t actually want them to have any notoriety. We don’t actually really speak their names. They’re not part of our grief really.”
Martin Robinson said a foundation in their sons’ names would carry on their legacy.
The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.
Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States.
“The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.”
Sentencing is scheduled for 16 October.
The prosecution requested 210 years’ imprisonment for each of the accused, though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.
The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
In November 2025, Ary Gisell Silva, the then-girlfriend of the main defendant, was sentenced to two decades in prison after admitting that she instigated the robbery.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

Berlin and Paris clash over joint main battle tank project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:46:42 UTC
09:46:42 KST

Berlin and Paris clash over joint main battle tank project
Paris and Berlin are contradicting each other on the fate of a much-heralded joint main battle tank development project. French Chief of Defense Staff General Fabien Mandon has claimed Germany withdrew from the program, while the German government says the opposite.
Known as the Main Ground Combat System (MGCS), the project was launched back in 2018 with the aim of replacing both the French Leclerc and German Leopard 2 main battle tanks. It was a collaboration between the Amsterdam-headquartered KNDS – the EU’s largest tank maker – the German Rheinmetall weapons manufacturing giant, and the French Thales industrial group. Berlin even purchased a 40% stake in KNDS in June, with another 40% held by Paris, when the project was still in full swing.
On Thursday, Mandon told French lawmakers that the plans for the project had essentially fallen through. “The outcome isn’t good. We had hoped to build a future tank in cooperation with the Germans, but unfortunately, we have to acknowledge that the Germans have withdrawn from the project,” he said during a hearing on next year’s budget.
According to Le Monde, the chief of the defense staff said Berlin made a political decision to halt cooperation. He reportedly stated that “the two army chiefs of staff had co-signed a joint document outlining their shared needs,” but the two neighbors were “no longer dealing with purely military choices.”
A German Defense Ministry spokesperson denied that claim, stating that Berlin merely wants to “adjust” the program to include the “lessons” of the Ukraine conflict. “We remain committed to equal partnership in the MGCS and are focusing on future technologies for armored combat,” the official said, according to Reuters.
Madon himself stated in a press release published after the hearing that an industrial proposal submitted in early 2026 “was incompatible with the need to replace the current tanks by 2037,” prompting Berlin to opt for a national effort to replace its Leopard 2 tank.
The general also maintained that a decade of work had “not been in vain” and the MGCS project was not scrapped but rather “pushed back to the late 2040s.” Paris would now launch its own national development of “an interim” replacement for its Leclerc tanks, he added.
The MGCS was intended to become a comprehensive platform for land warfare, with multiple weapon systems derived from it. The troubled project has reportedly been plagued by delays linked to political and industrial disputes. It is said Paris was aiming for a lighter combat vehicle suited for African deployments, while Berlin sought better heavy armor suitable for a major conflict, including with Russia.
The total cost of the project remains unclear, although a French parliamentary budget report suggested that Paris authorized a total of €212 million ($237.3 million) for the program over 2025 and 2026. The German government has not published any specific figures related to the project’s funding, but said in 2024 that the two partners were “each contributing 50% of the costs.”
Another major Franco-German armament program collapsed just months ago. Dubbed the Future Combat Air System (FCAS), it aimed to produce a next-generation fighter jet by 2040. The venture failed in June after an estimated €3.2 billion in sunk R&D costs due to irreconcilable disputes between aircraft makers Dassault and Airbus.

Anthropic AI model sent fake murder tip to Philadelphia police

Anthropic AI model sent fake murder tip to Philadelphia police
SAN FRANCISCO - An artificial intelligence model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide to Philadelphia police, US authorities said on Oct 9, criticising the company for taking two months to report the incident.
The Philadelphia Police Department said the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings.
According to Anthropic’s account, as relayed by police, the model was running a test that involved interacting with randomly selected websites when it reached the site and filed false information about an unsolved murder.
The AI model presented itself as someone who might have knowledge of the case.
The incident echoed other recent cases, including one where an OpenAI agent undergoing a security evaluation broke out of its testing environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face.
The episode heightened concerns about the AI industry’s increased use of AI agents, systems programmed to take multi-step actions without human supervision.
Anthropic published a report on Oct 9 outlining multiple types of “unintended” actions that its models have taken, including the incident involving the Philadelphia Police Department website.
Other organisations impacted included the White House and other US government agencies, the report said.
The newly revealed incidents “had minimal real-world impact” and were “significantly less severe” than other cybersecurity incidents previously reported, Anthropic said.
The company outlined four categories of incidents that it found during an internal review of its Claude model: exploiting “basic” coding flaws, submitting forms on websites, bypassing requirements for tokens or fees, and using short URLs to get around other limits.
Anthropic has turned off internet access for Claude during all internal testing for now “until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures... reliably catch behaviours like these,” the report said.
Police said the tip, dated July 18, was flagged as spam and never reached the department’s Real-Time Crime Center for vetting.
They added that there was no sign that police systems had been breached or department data compromised.
Anthropic discovered the incident on Sept 28, shut down the automated testing process responsible and added a new validation step for future tests, police said.
The company alerted the department on Oct 7, and the two sides met the following day.
“The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the department said.
Police said their safeguards had limited the impact, but that these “do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide”.
“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the statement added. 
Anthropic also said it briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved, reported Bloomberg.
On Oct 9, Trump administration officials said they were now requiring that AI companies notify affected parties and address security incidents involving their models.
“Earlier today, Anthropic contacted the SI Force to disclose the details of various prior incidents that it discovered in late September involving the unauthorised and fraudulent use of government and other systems,” the White House said in a statement from the Super Intelligence Force, a new government unit tasked by US President Donald Trump with overseeing AI development and safety.
“The company informed us that these events occurred in the past, the activity has ceased, and there is no ongoing similar activity,” the statement said.
Axios reported on the government requirement earlier. AFP, BLOOMBERG

The Most Valuable Part of Your Course Isn’t the Content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:20:50 UTC
09:20:50 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
By the looks of my LinkedIn feed, courses have had more farewell tours than Cher.
When I posted “Apparently courses are dead again,” the comments focused on something I have been thinking about for a while: why the good stuff inside a course gets stuck there.
You spend hours figuring out how to explain a feature. That explanation lives in module three. Meanwhile, someone in Product is writing it again for a tooltip, possibly unaware your version exists.
Every new place customers learn becomes another place someone has to rebuild work the company already paid for.
And the list of places that need it keeps growing.
Learning happens everywhere now
Your customer is trying to figure out your product. Where do they go?
An onboarding checklist might get them started, while a tooltip explains something along the way. When they get stuck, they search the help center or ask the support bot. They might visit your academy, assuming they know it exists.
They might also end up on YouTube, watching someone named ProductWizard92 explain a feature your team spent six weeks building a course about.
Increasingly, they ask ChatGPT, Claude, or Perplexity, which will happily explain your product whether you’ve given them anything useful to work with or not. Confidence has never been the issue there.
The customer needs help. They’ll look wherever they think they can find it, and customer education owns only some of those places.
Meanwhile, our attention habits are changing. Gloria Mark’s research at UC Irvine found that the average time people spent on a screen before switching fell from about two and a half minutes in 2004 to 47 seconds in more recent measurements.
That measures screen switching, so please don’t use it to declare that humans can no longer learn from anything longer than a TikTok.
But put those habits alongside all the places customers can now get answers, and the pressure makes sense. People want help close to the moment they need it, with as few detours as possible.
Which brings us back to the recurring course funeral.
Are courses dead?
This conversation keeps coming back up for a few reasons:
- Some of it is LinkedIn. “X is dead” gets attention. “X still serves a useful purpose, depending on the circumstances” sounds like something you’d scroll past on your way to a fight in the comments. (guilty 🙋🏼♀️)
- Some of it is vendor positioning. If you sell in-app guidance, declaring courses outdated is a pretty convenient way to introduce the thing you sell.
But get past the headline, and the argument becomes much less dramatic. Even Appcues, which sells in-app guidance, recognizes a role for structured courses when customers need to understand complex concepts.
So, are courses dead? No. Courses still give customers room to work through complex concepts, practice, and get feedback.
But customers also need help in the product, the help center, and the support chat. And the expertise that makes a course useful could improve those experiences, too.
The problem is how these experiences fit together.
The course designer may have discovered why customers misunderstand a feature and what helps them get past it. The person writing the tooltip has to figure that out again.
And that brings me to the part I find much more interesting than whether courses are dead.
The missing layer
I think instructional expertise gets stuck in the same place as the content.
Suppose your academy teaches customer success managers how to evaluate AI-generated churn predictions. Product explains the risk scores in a walkthrough. Support documents how the scores are calculated.
Everything is accurate. But a customer sees “85% churn risk” and immediately offers a discount, without investigating whether the prediction warrants action.
The course teaches that judgment. The customer hasn’t taken it.
Each team did its job, but something important got lost between the experiences.
And that’s the problem I keep coming back to. The instructional expertise that helps people make good decisions is often trapped inside the course.
You designed an exercise that teaches CSMs to question a prediction before acting. Someone can see the exercise, but they may not understand why it matters.
Was it essential practice? An example? A desperate attempt to break up forty slides?
Those are very different reasons. And when someone asks AI to turn the course into a ten-minute presentation, that distinction matters.
Knowledge, design, and expression
The course contains three things that are worth separating:
- Knowledge: How the prediction model works, which signals it uses, and what the scores mean.
- Design: What this audience needs to do with that knowledge, where they’re likely to struggle, and the instructional decisions intended to help.
- Expression: The scenario, wording, activity, and format used in this particular experience.
The design includes the reasoning behind those decisions. Why investigate an account before choosing an action? Why assess someone’s judgment instead of asking them to define a risk score? What should change for partners, whose job is to explain the feature to buyers?
That reasoning gives another team something useful to work with when the original activity doesn’t fit.
Separating knowledge from presentation has a long history in structured content and single-source publishing. Instructional designers also capture their decisions in storyboards, curriculum maps, and design documents.
So the reasoning may already exist. It may also be in a document called `Churn_Course_FINAL_v6_final_USE_THIS_ONE`.
The question is whether the person building a walkthrough can find it. And finding the original design isn’t enough. They need to understand why a decision mattered and when the same reasoning applies to a different audience.
A CSM needs to practice evaluating a prediction before acting. A partner might need to practice explaining uncertainty to a skeptical buyer. The activity changes, but the underlying instructional insight can apply to both.
That’s the opportunity I’m interested in: making instructional expertise available across teams, with enough context for people to decide how it applies to the experience they’re building.
Of course, making instruction reusable has a long history of sounding easier than it turns out to be.
And there’s a reason for that.
We tried this 25 years ago
In the late 1990s, while some of us were trying to keep a Tamagotchi alive, the e-learning industry was trying to solve content reuse.
Courses were expensive to build. Software developers could create a component once and use it in different applications. Surely instruction could work that way, too?
Enter the learning object.
David Wiley, whose work helped shape the field, defined a learning object as any digital resource that can be reused to support learning.
The idea was to create smaller pieces of instruction, like explanations, activities, quizzes, and simulations. Store them in shared repositories. Then assemble them into whatever learning experience you needed.
Everyone compared them to Legos. Even today, you can see the appeal. Dig into the bin, grab an explanation, add an activity, snap on an assessment. Congratulations, you have a course.
You’d build the explanation once instead of rebuilding it five times. Updates would be easier. Costs would come down. Teams could spend more time improving instruction instead of recreating content they already had.
Standards were developed. Repositories were built. But easily assembling instruction from interchangeable pieces never became widespread practice.
Because a learning activity depends on things a Lego brick doesn’t: who’s using it, what they already know, and what they’re supposed to learn.
Those dependencies made the pieces much harder to swap.
The three paradoxes
Over time, Wiley explored several tensions that made learning objects difficult to reuse. Three feel especially relevant to customer education today.
And yes, this is the part with academic terminology. Stay with me.
The reusability paradox
A short video showing how to create a report could fit into onboarding, a help article, or a course. But someone can follow every click and still not know which report they need.
Build a lesson that explains how to choose a report, gives learners practice, and provides feedback, and you’ve added much more instructional support. You’ve also created something harder to drop into all those places.
That’s Wiley’s reusability paradox: as learning objects become larger and more instructionally complete, their opportunities for reuse narrow.
Smaller pieces travel easily, but someone still has to design the learning around them. Larger experiences include more of that work, but fit fewer situations.
“Build once, reuse everywhere” leaves out a fairly important question: who’s doing the assembly?
The revisability paradox
The more research-based instructional design a resource contains, the more expertise it takes to revise without weakening the learning.
Take the report lesson. A basic explanation of report types is fairly easy to edit. A lesson with carefully chosen examples, practice, and targeted feedback requires more care because those elements work together.
Someone revising it might see two nearly identical examples and delete one. Fair enough. It looks repetitive.
Except comparing those examples was how learners were supposed to notice the difference that determines which report to use. That repetition had a job.
Wiley compared revision to playing Jenga blindfolded. You can see the pieces. You may have no idea which ones are holding the learning together.
That’s the revisability paradox: adding instructional design can make a resource more effective while making it harder to revise without the expertise to understand those decisions.
The localization paradox
Finally, Wiley’s localization paradox describes how this can play out when someone adapts a resource for their own context. A team shortens the lesson for onboarding, removes that comparison, and checks that the remaining information is accurate.
Without understanding what the comparison contributed, they may never realize their edit weakened the instruction. Everything still looks fine.
These paradoxes make an important distinction clear. Having access to an existing resource doesn’t mean you know how to reuse it effectively.
And they raise a fair question about the idea I’ve just proposed.
Would making instructional reasoning portable eliminate these trade-offs? No, not automatically.
But AI is changing that calculation.
What’s changed?
For years, adapting instruction meant someone had to read the original material, figure out what mattered, and rebuild it for another audience or format.
AI can now do parts of that work in seconds. Give it an explanation of the churn prediction feature, and it can produce versions for customer success managers, partners, and executives before you’ve decided which iced coffee to order.
Whether those versions help anyone learn is a separate question. But the time and effort required to produce them have changed considerably.
And that’s happening alongside a few other shifts.
Machines are using our content, too
Help articles, product documentation, and educational resources increasingly supply information to AI assistants.
The product keeps changing
For teams shipping frequent updates, keeping education accurate is a recurring job. A feature changes, and someone needs to work out what that means for the course, the help article, the walkthrough, and the bot.
Customers can get answers from people you’ve never met
Public AI assistants, YouTube creators, consultants, and partners can all explain your product. They may be working from excellent information. They may also be working from a screenshot and a blog post from 2022.
Either way, your customer can find them.
Together, these shifts mean product knowledge is being reused and adapted more frequently, in more places, by more people and machines. AI makes it easier to produce another version of an explanation. But that also creates more opportunities to lose the instructional reasoning behind it.
But the same technology making adaptation easier could also help teams preserve and apply that reasoning.
Instead of giving AI only the finished course, what if teams could give it the design decisions behind the course, too?
Making instructional expertise portable
Go back to the churn prediction feature.
Product updates the churn prediction model. The scores are calculated differently now, which means the academy, help articles, walkthroughs, partner materials, and support bot may all need attention.
Each team still needs to interpret the change for its audience. But what if they could also access the instructional reasoning behind the existing experiences?
Alongside the updated product knowledge, teams could access what CE has learned: customers often mistake predictions for facts, and they need practice evaluating the evidence.
Product could use that insight when explaining the score in the dashboard. The partner team could build practice around explaining uncertainty to a buyer. Each team applies the reasoning to its audience.
Some of that guidance may already exist in storyboards or design documents. But can another team find it and understand when it applies? Giving someone access to a folder only gets you so far. Depending on the folder, possibly nowhere.
The opportunity is to make CE’s reasoning available wherever teams build customer learning, with enough context to apply it and enough expertise to judge the result.
Where AI and tools fit
This is where AI gets interesting to me. It could help people retrieve relevant instructional guidance and apply it to a new context, as long as the reasoning is captured clearly enough.
Instead of asking it to “turn this course into a presentation,” you could supply the product knowledge, the audience, what they need to accomplish, and the design decisions that matter.
For partners, that might mean preserving practice in explaining uncertainty while replacing the account intervention scenario with a buyer conversation.
Now there’s a basis for evaluating the result. Did the adaptation address the known misconception? Did it give partners useful practice? Does the feedback help them understand where their explanation fell short?
A polished presentation can still fail every one of those checks. Fonts are very forgiving that way.
AI can help apply instructional decisions across formats. Deciding what customers need to learn, and whether an experience helps them learn it, still takes expertise.
Which makes the future of customer education a lot more interesting than “now you can make courses faster.”
What this means for customer education
Customer education looks different at every company. Some teams own the academy. Others also manage help centers, in-app education, webinars, certifications, or partner enablement.
Whatever the scope, doing that work teaches you things about your customers.
You learn where they get confused, which explanations help, and which concepts need practice. You discover that someone can pass a quiz about a feature and still have absolutely no idea what to do with it on Monday morning.
That knowledge is valuable wherever customers encounter the product.
Making it available across the organization could become a much bigger part of CE’s role.
I came across Justin Seeley’s L&D Agency Radius framework this week. Its five areas of agency, Create, Diagnose, Orchestrate, Systemize, and Influence, offer a useful way to think about CE’s future.
As CE teams spend less time creating learning experiences, they can spend more time diagnosing, orchestrating, and then systemizing those insights and design decisions available for repeated use.
This could give CE more influence across the customer experience without requiring the team to own every touchpoint. Which is good, because “congratulations, you now own everything” is a terrible career development plan.
There’s still plenty to test. What does another team need to understand an instructional decision? Which guidance can travel across audiences, and which needs rethinking? Does making that reasoning available lead to better learning?
I’ve seen shared standards help teams produce learning experiences at scale. That gives me a reason to explore this idea. Demonstrating that portable instructional reasoning improves outcomes across customer touchpoints takes more evidence.
For now, I see a promising direction: CE’s expertise could inform far more of the customer experience than its production capacity allows it to build.
So, are courses dead?
No. Please cancel the memorial webinar.
Courses still matter. They give customers room to understand complex concepts, practice, and get feedback. But customers are learning in more places than ever, often through experiences CE doesn’t own.
And that’s the opportunity. CE has spent years figuring out how people learn to use products. We all agree that expertise should help Product design better walkthroughs, Support answer questions more effectively, and partners explain features with greater confidence.
Each experience needs its own design, but each team could benefit from what CE has already learned.
The course doesn’t have to go everywhere. The thinking behind it should.
We’re exploring new ways to bring this design layer closer to the production flow. But we’re interested- have you thought about this? How are you handling it?

Is it legal for the US to livestream the Fort Hood shooter's execution? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:15:54 UTC
09:15:54 KST

The Pentagon said on Thursday that it would livestream the firing squad execution of the man who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, raising questions about the legality of the unprecedented announcement.
Here's what US law says about public executions and death by firing squad.
Is death penalty by firing squad legal in the US?
Yes. The US Supreme Court said in a unanimous 1879 decision that execution by firing squad is not "cruel and unusual punishment" prohibited by the Constitution.
The justices last year cleared the way for South Carolina to carry out its first execution by firing squad in decades.
Five states currently allow executions by firing squad: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah. The Trump administration earlier this year said it would allow execution by firing squad in the federal prison system.
The US Army also once regularly carried out executions by firing squad of US soldiers found guilty of desertion or other offenses. Hundreds of US soldiers were sentenced to death during the Civil War from 1861 to 1865.
Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the president is the only person who can approve a death sentence for a member of the US armed services. President Donald Trump, on October 5, signed off on the Pentagon's plan to execute the Fort Hood gunman, Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist.
Can executions be broadcast?
Executions in the US were once public spectacles, but in the last century have been carried out in correctional facilities away from the public eye.
In 1936, a man convicted of rape was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a public hanging in Missouri.
A US law prohibits the recording or broadcasting of executions in the federal prison system. But military regulations have not applied that same prohibition to military executions. Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder by a military jury in 2013, following a court-martial trial.
State laws regulate who can witness executions, generally limiting access to authorized officials, family members, legal counsel, and a handful of media representatives.
Courts have long rejected lawsuits brought by media organizations seeking broader public access to executions.
In 2001, a judge denied a request by an internet company to livestream the lethal injection execution of Timothy McVeigh, an anti-government militant who bombed a federal building in Oklahoma City in 1995, killing 168 people. The Justice Department did provide a restricted, closed-circuit television broadcast exclusively for survivors of the bombing and victims' families.
Could Hasan challenge his execution in court?
While Hasan has exhausted his direct appeals within the military justice system, he can still challenge his underlying conviction and sentence in the federal civilian court system.
Such a challenge, known as a federal habeas corpus proceeding, provides another layer of review before a death sentence is carried out.
Even if unsuccessful, such a challenge could stall the execution, potentially for years. Hasan's execution is currently set for December 3.

The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returned to its home port in San Diego, California on Thursday after a 322-day deployment, as roughly 5,000 sailors reunited with their families, including 122 new fathers meeting their children for the first time.
The carrier arrived at US Naval Air Station North Island to cheers from family members and friends who had gathered to welcome the crew home after nearly 11 months away.
Fathers of babies born during the deployment disembarked first in keeping with the US Navy’s tradition.
The Navy said 64 fathers serving aboard the carrier were meeting their babies for the first time, while the ship's commanding officer, Capt. Daniel Keeler, said the number rose to 122 when the carrier's air wing was included.
“There are 122 new dads that are going to walk off the ship today,” Lt. Cmdr. Tyler Barker, the carrier's public affairs officer, said at a news conference Thursday, according to Military Times. “From the air wing and from my ship, they're waiting to meet their children for the very first time.”
Families and loved ones of the sailors came from across the US
“We would have come in anywhere his ship was coming in,” Lisa Bisson, who traveled from Maine with her family to welcome her son Joseph home from his first deployment, told the San Diego Union Tribune.
The carrier departed San Diego in November 2025 for what was initially expected to be a shorter deployment. It was later redirected to the Middle East as the US and Israel launched military operations against Iran on February 28, extending the deployment.
The Lincoln spent a record 265 consecutive days at sea without a port visit, according to the Associated Press. The carrier was relieved by the USS George Washington in August before beginning its journey back to California, with stops in Thailand and Guam.
The extended deployment also drew scrutiny over the crew's living conditions. The Navy later told lawmakers that eight sailors assigned to the carrier strike group had attempted suicide during the deployment.
On Wednesday, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited the carrier and presented the crew with the Presidential Unit Citation, the military's highest unit-level award for valor.
The carrier strike group's operations included thousands of combat missions and attacks on Iranian military assets during the war.

3 men found guilty of killing American and Australian brothers on surfing trip in Mexico
A local judge on Friday found three men guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.
The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raúl Hernández in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, alias "El Kekas," Irineo Francisco "N" and Ángel Jesús "N" were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson and American Carter Redd Rhoad.
The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.
Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them," CBS News' partner network BBC News reported. Debra Robinson and her husband, Martin Robinson, were at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson said, BBC reported.
The three friends traveled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 50 miles from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well.
García, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Irineo Francisco "N" and Ángel Jesús "N."
During the monthlong trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that García confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9 mm pistol.
Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.
The state prosecutor's office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and "instigated one of her companions to rob them," which was carried out the following day.
The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims' cellphones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to "aggravated robbery with violence" and "vehicle theft with violence" in an expedited proceeding. However, García and his two accomplices decided to go to trial.
The judge will announce the final sentence on Oct. 16. The Baja California State Attorney General's Office requested for each defendant the "exemplary sentence" of 210 years in prison.

New Israeli documentary captures Soroka's fight to save lives on October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:15:24 UTC
09:15:24 KST

‘As someone who went through October 7 at its ugliest, its most difficult, I never would have thought I would be exposed to such powerful cruelty. It haunts me and will continue to haunt me,” Dr. Sabry El Sayed says during an interview in The Shift (Ha Mishmeret).
El Sayed, the deputy head of the ear, nose and throat department at Soroka Medical Center in Beersheba, features in this latest episode of the KAN 11 series, Real Time (Zman Emet), which commemorates the third anniversary of the massacre by Hamas and which can be seen on Kan.org.il, as well as on YouTube.
This moving episode, which is good enough to be a standalone hour-long documentary, details what happened that day at Soroka, the hospital that received the lion’s share of the day’s casualties from all locations.
These included the Nova music festival, the military bases, Sderot, Ofakim, the highways, and the kibbutzim. Soroka Medical Center staff treated a staggering 674 people that day. Some they saved, some they couldn’t.
At the same time, many of them worried about the fates of family members who were in places that were attacked and about their staff members who could not make it to work. One member of the staff lost her son, a soldier, in the fighting, and came to the hospital to identify his body.
Soroka doctor recalls colleague killed while treating October 7 victims in Be'eri
El Sayed talks about his concern for his colleague, Dr. Daniel Levy, an ENT resident who lived in Kibbutz Be’eri. When the attack began, Levy’s family stayed in their safe room, but he went to the dental clinic to treat the wounded and was killed.
He and El Sayed stayed in touch throughout most of the morning. The moment El Sayed realizes he has lost his colleague is especially powerful in a series full of them.
Looking at the day’s events through one hospital is brilliant because Soroka became a kind of microcosm of everything that went on that day, both the chaos and the horrific injuries, and the staff describes it as a battlefield in which they fought for the lives of their patients.
The series’ creators, Keren Galit, Nadav Ben Tzur, and Adi Ben Dor, make it clear from the outset that all the patients and staff shown through hospital security footage gave permission for their names and faces to be shown.
The episode tells a wide variety of true stories. There are dazed, barefoot female border observers holding rifles who were rescued from the Nahal Oz military base, in need of medical treatment, while we learn the majority of their fellow soldiers have been killed. We see Ziv Abud learning that her boyfriend, Eliya Cohen, was kidnapped from the Nova music festival into Gaza.
Worried parents, desperate for information when nothing was coming from official channels, line up to learn whether their children had been admitted, although staff say that in the chaos of the day, many patients have been admitted anonymously because they cannot speak and there is no time to search for ID. Doctors use their own cellphones to call the patients’ families when they can.
Soroka staff recall waves of wounded arriving as October 7 attacks unfolded
The staff also describes being only dimly aware of the bigger picture, and learning about it in waves. First came those wounded from the roads, and later some of the special forces soldiers.
Much later in the day, those wounded at the Nova music festival and in the kibbutzim arrived. One doctor chose not to wear scrubs and to carry his revolver in his jeans pocket, recalling that he expected that the terrorists would likely arrive at the hospital soon.
As if this did not suffice, about a year and a half later, the hospital was hit by an Iranian missile. However, through a combination of foresight (some departments were evacuated) and luck, no one was seriously harmed.
A strange coda to the broadcast of this episode is that after Roni Singer, the host of Real Time, uploaded a promo for it to TikTok, the platform removed the clip, saying it violated policy about spreading false information, though it didn’t specify how.
It’s a strange world where a meticulously sourced documentary can be flagged as false, while so many ludicrous and libelous rumors go viral.

The Escape was directed by filmmaking duo The Paz Brothers (JeruZalem, The Golem, Plan A) and written by Ariel Cohen (The Golem).

Yoel (Tako), the cult’s heir apparent, dreams of escaping with his family and eventually teams up with an ex-Mossad search-and-rescue operative to break free.
But the cult’s charismatic leader (Ivanir) – and an alliance with a drug cartel – turn the rescue into a deadly war. Clearly, the creators were inspired by news reports about the Lev Tahor cult, which has brought members to Mexico and Guatemala.
Although it quickly fizzled in theaters, if the Practical Magic sequel made you want to see the 1998 original again, you can catch it on Disney+ or Apple TV+.
It’s still great fun, with Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock playing the descendants of a long line of witches whose lovers and husbands soon end up dead.

Why won’t the world call Russia’s theft of Ukrainian children genocide? A Ukrainian lawyer has the evidence, and says only the will is missing.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:13:10 UTC
09:13:10 KST

Kateryna Rashevska can trace exactly how one Ukrainian child disappears into Russia: the occupied-territory orphanage, the foster placement with a Kremlin-connected family, the re-education camp, the military uniform, the draft notice that arrives at sixteen. A legal expert at Ukraine's Regional Center for Human Rights, she has filed submissions to the International Criminal Court, documented the cases behind recent EU sanctions, and spent years building the argument that this is not only a war crime but genocide.
The law, she says, is ready. In less than five years of war, Russia has forcibly transferred at least 20,651 Ukrainian children from occupied Ukraine, a crime that has already put President Vladimir Putin and his children's-rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova in the dock of the ICC. The 1948 Genocide Convention lists the forcible transfer of children as one of the acts that constitute genocide, and the ICC's Ukraine investigation has been mandated to examine the charge since 2022. More than 150 states have signed that convention. None has been willing to say the word about Russia.
"We don't need to change any legal framework," Rashevska says. "We simply still lack the political will to call the crimes by their proper names." She presses the point because, for her, justice is not an afterthought but a deterrent: "Without justice, Russia will feel this resentment in several years, and they will repeat their actions."
And the court that could deliver that justice is collapsing. The ICC is in the deepest crisis of its existence: its prosecutor, Karim Khan, removed, 13 of its judges and prosecutors sanctioned by the United States, and on 9 October 2026 the court itself sanctioned by Washington for the first time, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing to dismantle it "brick by brick." The court called the move unprecedented and warned that "history will judge this moment."
Meanwhile the children remain. Of the more than 20,000 taken, only 2,665 have been returned, as of 7 October 2026. The rest are placed in Russia's adoption system and foster homes, taught to forget they are Ukrainian, to love Russia, and to be willing to die for it: Rashevska cites 344,000 Ukrainian children drawn into the Movement of the First and 55,000 into the Yunarmiya youth army.
Euromaidan Press spoke with Rashevska on the sidelines of GLOBSEC 2026 in Prague about the machine Russia built to steal a generation, and why the world still won't name it.
Alya: You say that Russia’s forcible transfer of Ukrainian children is the crime of genocide. In international law, genocide is defined by Article 6 of the Rome Statute. What would it take to change this legal framework to include the deportation and militarization of Ukrainian children? And is the Office of the Prosecutor in any position to do that work under current US sanctions and Karim Khan’s leave?
Kateryna: We don’t need to change any legal frameworks to prosecute what the Russians are doing with Ukrainian children. Militarization and political indoctrination, as well as Russification of young Ukrainians, is a part of Russia’s bigger strategy to destroy Ukraine as a sovereign state and to subjugate everything in the Ukrainian nation to the Russian influence and control. I don’t see legal problems; we simply still lack the political will to call the crimes by their proper names.
The UN’s 1948 Genocide Convention posits that all states that signed the convention, 154 as of today, should act to stop it—not only those affected by genocide. If the international community recognized what the Russians are doing as a crime of genocide, it would mean that yet another time in history the international community was not able to prevent genocide, to recognize some early warnings, to react properly to what the Russians did, for example, in occupied Crimea or Donbas before 2022. It is not easy, and the international community and world political leaders should be mature enough to face all these challenges, recognize that they were involved in the commission of these crimes through silence and inaction, and finally stop it.
So that is why, according to the Rome Statute, the Office of the Prosecutor can start an investigation of the crime of genocide in the Ukrainian context. It is possible: the ICC’s Ukraine-situation investigation in March 2022, supported by 43 states, included not only war crimes and crimes against humanity, but also the crime of genocide. So we have all the legal tools and means, but politically it is very difficult.
Recently, there has been a global shift towards this—in the context of the war between Arabian states and Israel, not Ukraine. But for example, Israel’s attacks against Gaza’s education have already been termed "scholasticide," so as a part of the genocidal intent, as a part of the crime of genocide. So for us lawyers and human rights defenders, this is the task—to push the international community to do the same with Russia. It is not easy because Russia is one of the five "world policemen" expected to maintain this international legal order.
I believe that, perhaps in decades, but we will see how Russia’s actions will be recognized as the crime of genocide. The forcible transfer of children from one group to another group is the fifth universally recognized element of the crime of genocide.
Alya: Your organization was involved in documenting this. How does this pipeline actually work?
Kateryna: Yes, let's take Olga Druzhinina, who fostered four children from the occupied territories of Ukraine. Her story is very interesting: first, it seemed that she could be just an ordinary Russian brainwashed by TV shows about children from Donbas. But then we found that Olga is very close to [former Russian President] Medvedev, and through Medvedev to President Putin. Olga is the head of one non-governmental organization, "Semia Arktiki" [Family of the Arctic], and this organization aims to find foster parents for orphans— now including orphans from occupied territories of Ukraine. The co-head of this organization also fostered Ukrainian children.
It is a very well-built, pre-planned architecture of people involved in the commission of this crime—not some sporadic reaction to the full-scale invasion. They planned to do it. And I will not be surprised if, in the future, we find that these families also adopted children from Crimea or from Donbas even before 2022.
Her husband is a veteran of the Russian Armed Forces. He participated in many wars of the Russian regime, including the wars in Chechnya. It was clearly against the child's best interest to be sent to the family of this Russian serviceman and his wife. So their case was widely publicized. We recorded many different details. Later, we found photos of these children in the "Warrior Center" camp in Novosibirsk, and her foster daughter from occupied Ukraine wearing a St.George’s [Russian imperial] ribbon and in military uniform.
So the Ukrainian identity of these children was completely eradicated. It was prohibited to mention that they were Ukrainians, and the main goal of this family was to repress their unloyalty to the Russian state, to re-educate them, mold them into Russian patriots. Unfortunately, I don’t know the fate of these teenagers from Mariupol, but as far as I know, they were not returned to Ukraine. And now they are already young adults—meaning they will soon be conscripted into the Russian army. They have this military duty because they were forcibly given Russian citizenship. And young children also remain under the control of Olga and his husband.
Olga and her husband are members of the so-called "Putin Team." They were recognized many times as the best family of the Yamalo-Nenets region. The governor of Yamal-Nenets is also Putin's person. His candidacy was supported by Putin for re-election to this position. And this governor has many times mentioned that Ukrainian children from the occupied territories of Ukraine were accepted by foster families from his region, even without the proper documents.
It is very difficult to influence their behavior without sanctions. In this sphere of foster care, the balance between placing children in Russian institutions and Russian families is hard to find. Russia presents only two options for the forcibly transferred Ukrainian children: Russian boarding institutions or Russian foster families. And of course, ordinary people think: a family is better than a boarding institution. The truth is that there is a third option: just return these children to Ukraine, to their homes.
And I would like to highlight that, according to the order of Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, these children from institutions will not be returned to boarding institutions in Ukraine. They will inevitably be placed with a foster family, and they can participate in choosing this family or changing it. Ukraine is doing its best to guarantee that its actions comply with the Convention on the Rights of the Child, but unfortunately, Russians are very hard to persuade to return these orphanage children.
Alya: On 11 May 2026, the EU Council sanctioned 16 individuals and seven entities for the systematic unlawful deportation, forced transfer, and forced assimilation of Ukrainian children, including through indoctrination and militarized education. Your organization pushed for these sanctions. Are they working?
Kateryna: In January–February 2026, we criticized the European Union’s sanctions policy. New persons were being added to lists, but we found that the level of coordination and harmonization of sanctions policies was only 5%. Only 13 individuals and three organizations were under sanctions in all jurisdictions analyzed by us: Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States, the European Union, Switzerland, and Japan. It was terrifying because sanctions exist, yet they are riddled by many loopholes and are actually inefficient.
Trending Now
That is why we started persuading them to do something with this system. And on 11 May, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union synchronized their sanctions packages: the people are included in all jurisdictions. For us, this is a big achievement.
Another achievement: a shift in their perception of where this vertical of guilty persons ends. Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova—okay; ministers, children's rights ombudspersons at the regional level, heads of the occupation authorities—okay. But what about the "ordinary" Russian people who fostered poor Ukrainian children and now contribute to their militarization? The 11 May sanctions saw the United Kingdom and Canada listing ordinary Russians, like the family from Yamalo-Nenets that fostered four Ukrainian children, including teenagers from Mariupol, and then sent them to re-education camps of the "Center Warrior" to be militarized as Russian soldiers.
If these results of our work seem small, we must remember that for the Russians, it is a very sensitive issue. They are mad because of the sanctions—and this was visible when the “Yolochka” boarding institution in occupied Crimea’s Simferopol, called a “concentration camp” by ordinary Russians, was sanctioned. Already in December 2014 [after Russia’s occupation of east Ukraine], the first Ukrainian orphans were sent to Russian foster families from this “Yolochka.” 12 years later, children from Kherson boarding institutions also went through “Yolochka.”
Alya: You've documented over 20,500 deported children. How many of that cohort are approaching Russian conscription age?
Kateryna: It is hard to tell because the way the Ukrainian side is collecting statistics is not good enough. So you should address this question to the competent bodies of Ukraine.
But according to our calculations, just to describe the situation in general: all Ukrainian teenagers under Russian control start receiving draft notices at the age of 16. According to the Russian legislation, it should be at the age of 17, but they're so afraid that these children will escape or will return to Ukrainian-controlled territories, that they start this process in violation of their own legislation.
Everything is organized around schools. They’re not about education under occupation, but have become additional buildings of the military commissariat. Specific teachers are responsible for this conscription process. Boys aged 16-17 are being brought to the military commissariat in organized groups. You cannot escape, you cannot refuse, because you will hear “knock-knock” on your door: the occupation authorities and your teacher will ask: “Where are you? You should go.”
Another problem: Russia and Belarus started exchanging data, meaning that if this child receives a draft notice at the age of 18, he will not be able to cross the border—which matters because the checkpoint of Mokrany-Domanove between Belarus and Ukraine is the main point of returning Ukrainian children from Russian control. Every year, the Russians amend their legislation to impose more obstacles to the repatriation process.
So the only way for a Ukrainian teenage boy to escape is to do this several days before a "povestka" [draft notice] comes to his house at 16 years.
According to our intelligence, since 2014, 48,000 Ukrainians from occupied territories were forcibly mobilized by Russians, including those from occupied Crimea. Some of them participated in the "special military operation.” Around 20% of all prisoners of war in Ukrainian camps for Russians are originally Ukrainians who were forced to sign a military contract. Many of them were forced, manipulated, or brainwashed, so it was not done of their own will.
But I would like to highlight that the average age of a Russian soldier is 35. This is not the war of young Ukrainians who reached the age of majority and were sent to the battlefield as cannon fodder. We see that the Russians’ main goal is to rebuild the army degraded by the Ukrainian side during the first month of the full-scale invasion, to have officers and other qualified personnel who will develop a strategy and conquer more and more territory. That is why they're investing in all these military patriotic movements and centers.
That is why I was really impressed when I saw that their All-Russian championship on drone racing will be for children aged seven. Should we next expect that children in kindergartens will assemble and disassemble a rifle? Their society is very militarized. This is the biggest problem. And now, Russian soldiers are those who are teaching Ukrainian children to fight tomorrow.
Alya: Thank you so much, Kateryna, for your time.

Libya's military seizes narcotics after firefight with smugglers

Libya's military seizes narcotics after firefight with smugglers
TRIPOLI, Oct 10 - Libya's military brigade seized more than 1.3 million narcotic pills after a firefight with smugglers in a southeastern town that injured three soldiers, the military said on Friday.
The north African nation has become a major regional transit hub for synthetic drugs and other narcotics en route to domestic users and elsewhere in the continent, the UN said in January.
In a statement, a military media unit said the Subul al-Salam infantry brigade in Kufra, about 1,700 km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Tripoli, targeted hideouts used by traffickers of narcotics and illicit goods.
Pictures it posted showed soldiers standing around tens of transparent plastic small bags filled with round white pills bearing the number one and a sentence in black that read "made in Germany".
The brigade operates under the Land Forces General Staff and owes responsibility to the military commander Khalifa Haftar of the eastern-based Libyan National Army.
The statement gave no value for the drugs seized.
Drug gangs have exploited the tumultuous situation in the country since 2011, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime said in a January report.
Libya plunged into a prolonged period of internal conflict and division after former ruler Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a NATO-backed uprising that year.
Five people were handed death sentences by a court in the Western Mountains region, about 160 km (100 miles) southwest of Tripoli, for importing more than 2 million pills of psychotropic substances, the attorney general said in October. REUTERS

Putin, Trump hold phone talks on Ukraine crisis, energy supply
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:02:57 CST
09:02:57 KST

MOSCOW/WASHINGTON, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Russian President Vladimir Putin held a telephone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday, during which considerable attention was paid to prospects for resolving the Ukraine crisis, the Kremlin said.
On global energy developments, Russia reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to U.S. and global markets, according to the Kremlin.
"I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy," Putin said.
The talks also covered the situation surrounding Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations. The two sides reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining personal contacts between the presidents and continuing cooperation between their respective administrations, intelligence services and other agencies.
Trump also confirmed the phone call in a post on Truth Social.
"I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote.
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," he added.
Trump expressed confidence that the supplies would help bring down global diesel prices quickly.
Following the phone call, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said that Russia will begin lifting restrictions on diesel fuel exports ahead of schedule.
Novak said that Russia stands ready to supply additional diesel volumes to the U.S. market and other partners.
On the same day, the U.S. Department of the Treasury issued a temporary general license allowing the sale, delivery, offloading and importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel to the global market.
In a separate comment to reporters, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov described the phone call between the two presidents as friendly, substantive and 1.5 hours long.
"Considerable attention was paid to prospects for resolving the conflict in Ukraine. Putin spoke in detail about the measures we are taking in response to terrorist attacks by the Kiev regime, which has opted for escalation and is prolonging the conflict in every possible way," Ushakov said.
He said that Russia's armed forces hold the full initiative and are advancing in the zone of the special military operation, adding that Kiev's attempts to strike deep into Russian territory to halt the advance of Russian troops along the entire contact line stand no chance of success.
Ushakov noted that the previous presidential discussion considered the possibility of resuming trilateral talks after the State Duma elections, but the situation has since changed.
"By attempting to sabotage our elections, launching a massive drone attack on Moscow, other cities and polling stations on the main voting day, and targeting individuals involved in organizing the vote, Kiev has effectively scuttled the chance for an immediate restart of negotiations," Ushakov said. ■

Powerful quake, aftershocks rattle Panama as authorities mobilize response
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:02:54 CST
09:02:54 KST

A damaged building is pictured following an earthquake in Sona, Veraguas Province, Panama, Oct. 9, 2026. A major earthquake struck Panama on Friday. (Xinhua)
PANAMA CITY, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- A powerful earthquake and a series of strong aftershocks rattled Panama on Friday, sending residents into the streets, disrupting water supplies and briefly halting flights as the government mobilized emergency personnel and resources.
The University of Panama's Institute of Geosciences measured the initial quake at magnitude 7.2. It struck at 12:56 p.m. local time (1756 GMT) at a depth of 4 kilometers. By 5:30 p.m. local time, more than 40 earthquakes had been recorded, including over a dozen with magnitudes above 5.0. A quake at 3:25 p.m. had a magnitude of 6.9.
The the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) initially reported the first quake as magnitude 8, then revised it to 7.6 and later to 7.7.
In Panama City, Xinhua correspondents saw crowds pour out of buildings and gather along streets and in open spaces. Some people struggled to contain their emotions as they recalled the shaking, and others wept.
"Very, very strong. Even the building was swaying," said Tina Smith, who gathered outside with her colleagues. She said they were all safe.
Leonor Samudio, a local resident, said previous evacuation drills had helped staff at Caja de Ahorros, a Panamanian savings bank, respond to the emergency.
"We waited for the strong shaking to subside before starting to evacuate the building through the emergency stairs," she said. "We're waiting for instructions. Thankfully, we're all well."
Chelsy, a woman from Chiriqui province, described a tense scene as people rushed to leave.
"It was a very stressful moment, with people running," she said. "The good thing is that we have evacuation procedures, so we were all able to get out safely."
Amy, a foreign resident who has lived in Panama City for five years, said she had never felt such a strong quake during her stay.
"It's the first time I've evacuated the building for this," she said. "We had one in August, but it was not this strong."
The initial panic gradually eased, but recurring aftershocks kept many people outdoors. Some public places closed, traffic backed up on several roads, and residents of high-rise buildings said they were afraid to return home.
Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino said he had ordered agencies to promptly report the earthquake's effects and deploy personnel, resources and aid to affected communities. He said the entire government had been mobilized and that he would take part in response and coordination efforts in the hardest-hit areas.
As of 5:30 p.m., no deaths or missing persons had been reported, though some people were injured. The Chinese Embassy in Panama said it was in contact with Chinese institutions and the local Chinese community to check on their safety, with no casualties reported among them so far.
The quakes disrupted some public services. Panama's national water and sewer authority said earthquake-related power failures had halted or reduced production at several water treatment plants across the country.
Tocumen International Airport resumed flight operations after temporarily suspending services and evacuating people as a precaution. Airport officials said inspections had found no damage that would prevent operations from resuming.
Commercial areas also reopened, and immigration and customs staff returned to their posts. The airport said it would ask the national civil protection agency to conduct further inspections.
The country's Education Ministry canceled afternoon classes nationwide and suspended work at its administrative offices.
The Panama Canal Authority said canal operations remained normal. It activated emergency procedures and began inspecting facilities.
According to USGS's 2026 list of magnitude-7-or-stronger earthquakes, the earthquake was the fifth magnitude-7-or-stronger earthquake to hit Latin America this year, following two in Venezuela on June 24, one in Mexico on July 17, and one in Colombia on Aug. 10.
Panama lies along the Pacific "Ring of Fire," a roughly 40,000-km-long belt of volcanoes and seismic activity encircling the Pacific Ocean.
Panama's civil protection agency said it was assessing areas near the epicenter for possible damage. ■
