‘We’re being used as a front,’ Zelensky says of Trump’s diesel deal with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:02:06 UTC
09:02:06 KST

Russia and the U.S. have agreed on a deal to supply Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets. President Donald Trump announced the agreement on the evening of October 9 after a phone call with Vladimir Putin. Trump called the talks “highly successful.” Putin confirmed that Russia is ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the U.S. and global markets.
The U.S. said it is easing sanctions on Russian diesel. The Treasury Department has already issued a temporary license allowing sales of Russian diesel on the global market through April 7, 2027, despite U.S. sanctions. Washington previously eased sanctions on Russian oil temporarily because of a market crisis caused by the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran.
Russia has also begun lifting restrictions on diesel exports, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said. Sanctions and domestic export bans restrict exports of Russian oil and petroleum products worldwide. A ban on diesel and marine fuel exports by producers, for example, remains in effect through the end of October. Russia imposed it amid Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and a domestic fuel crisis caused by Ukrainian attacks over the summer.
Trump said the two sides agreed on the “immediate” delivery of more than 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel. Russia will supply another 500,000 metric tons in November, followed by an additional million metric tons. Novak said Russia is ready to supply additional diesel to the U.S. market as early as October. Exports are also expected to rise in November and December as refineries resume operations after repairs.
Ukraine criticized the diesel deal between Moscow and Washington. President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media that any easing of sanctions on Russia without agreements on de-escalation shows “obvious weakness.” “Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis,” he said.
The deal comes as talks on ending the war resume. A Ukrainian delegation is reportedly meeting with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami on October 9 and 10. Reuters reported that the national security advisers of the U.K., France, and Germany, along with representatives of NATO and the EU, were invited to the talks. Axios reported that the U.S. negotiators plan to present the Ukrainian delegation with “new ideas and proposals” and then discuss them with Russia. No details of the proposals were given. “I think our team is simply being used as a front. That’s certainly dishonest, and it’s certainly no way to treat a partner,” Zelensky told reporters after the U.S. announced the diesel deal.
Russian authorities asked the U.S. to lift sanctions as part of talks on an “energy truce,” sources told The Kyiv Independent on the eve of the diesel deal. Officials in Kyiv said Ukraine was ready to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Russia agreed to stop striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Trump, who is under pressure over rising U.S. fuel prices ahead of the congressional midterm elections, has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil facilities. He said the attacks were causing global fuel shortages and price increases.
Putin rejected the idea of an “energy truce” with Kyiv on October 2. Speaking at the Valdai forum, he said stopping the strikes alone would not solve the problem of high diesel prices in the U.S. and around the world unless sanctions on Russia were lifted.

Intercommunal clashes kill 71 people in South Sudan
Government security forces regain control of Rumbek town after outsiders attempted to take control of the area.
Intercommunal clashes have killed 71 people in South Sudan’s town of Rumbek, in Lakes State, the caretaker government said in a statement.
“According to initial security reports, approximately 71 people were reportedly killed,” including four soldiers, the South Sudanese interim Ministry of Information said in a statement on Friday. The exact number of fatalities has yet to be verified.
According to AFP, witnesses said a group of people from outside Rumbek tried to take control of the town and briefly succeeded. The attackers withdrew when police and military reinforcements arrived. Two witnesses said the fighting moved outside the city limits.
The government statement said, “Rumbek town is currently under the control of Government security forces, and efforts are ongoing to restore normalcy”.
The caretaker government strongly condemned the violence and urged all communities to “exercise maximum restraint and refrain from acts of retaliation that could further escalate tensions”.
Interim government
On September 22, South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country’s first election since its independence in 2011. Kiir appointed a caretaker administration as the country prepares for its first-ever national elections.
His decree ended a power-sharing arrangement set up under a 2018 peace deal that halted a five-year civil war in which about 400,000 people were killed.
Intercommunal conflict has continued across South Sudan, resulting in multiple deadly clashes.
On September 17, 26 people were killed, and 82 were injured during days of fighting in a disputed region on the border between South Sudan and Sudan.
In early March, intercommunal violence left at least 169 people dead after dozens of armed men attacked a town.

The arrangement stands to generate substantial new revenue for Moscow at a time when Ukraine and its European partners have been pressing for maximum economic pressure to cripple the Kremlin’s war machine.
Speaking to journalists Friday evening, Zelensky sharply questioned Washington’s approach, challenging how the US could credibly mediate peace while simultaneously offering Putin sudden economic relief.
Ukraine seeks ceasefire as Trump cuts deal with Moscow
According to President Zelensky, Ukraine’s negotiating team traveled to Florida to seek a pathway toward ending Russia’s full-scale invasion – or, at the very least, securing an initial ceasefire.
“Right now, our Ukrainian team, our negotiating team, is in Florida, holding talks with the American team about ending this terrible war – or, at the very least, achieving a ceasefire,” Zelensky said.

He emphasized that an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure could provide an urgent first step toward a broader de-escalation, particularly as relentless Russian strikes threaten Ukrainian homes, the power grid, and essential services ahead of winter.
“An energy ceasefire could be the first step toward a broader ceasefire. This is extremely important for our people, for our families.”
The high-level Ukrainian delegation in Florida includes Presidential Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov, First Deputy Chief of Staff Serhiy Kyslytsia, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia. They have been holding talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, alongside representatives from Britain, France, Germany, the EU, and NATO.
But as those sensitive negotiations unfolded in Miami, Trump was pursuing an entirely different conversation with the Kremlin.
“At this very moment, while our team is talking with the American team in Florida, the president of the United States is having a conversation with the Kremlin leader – the leader of this war, the leader of this aggression,” Zelensky stated. “And they reach an agreement under which America allows Russia to export diesel.”
For Ukraine, the decision risks undermining one of the West’s most critical tools for pressuring Putin to end the war.
‘Additional money for this war against us’
Trump defended the arrangement in a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, announcing that Russia had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November and 1 million tons afterward.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote, adding that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons of diesel within a short period, depending on the operational condition of its refineries.
Combined with what Trump termed “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” the US president claimed the agreement would rapidly lower domestic fuel costs.
Shortly after Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department issued General License 135, officially authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading, and importation of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The sudden authorization came just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18 – legislation explicitly designed to choke off Russia’s energy revenues and financial networks. Bipartisan US lawmakers had strongly urged Washington to fully implement the law ahead of its mid-October deadlines, warning that the Kremlin was exploiting loopholes to keep bankrolling its front lines.
Zelensky warned that the financial windfall from lifting these sanctions is impossible to separate from the violence on the ground.
“This is additional money, additional money for this war against us, without question,” the Ukrainian president said. “It only fuels Putin and gives him the opportunity to wage even more war.”
“And at this very moment, when we are talking about peace, America is allowing Russia to export diesel,” Zelensky continued. “I don’t know whether we’re talking about millions or billions. In any case, all of it goes toward the war against people, against Ukraine, against all of us.”
US fuel prices prioritized over sanctions pressure
The White House has framed the deal as a pragmatic response to severe domestic economic pressures. US diesel prices have recently climbed to an average of approximately $6.28 per gallon, squeezing truck drivers, agricultural supply chains, and American consumers.
However, energy analysts and European allies note that the initial shipment of 300,000 tons is modest compared to total US daily consumption, raising doubts about whether the deal can deliver the sweeping price relief Trump promised.
Furthermore, the decision risks severely fracturing the unified Western sanctions strategy.
For nearly five years, the US and its allies have sought to starve Moscow of the energy revenues required to pay military salaries, manufacture missiles, and sustain its occupation.
Allowing Russian diesel back into Western-regulated markets effectively rewards the Kremlin without securing any corresponding concession, such as a halt to attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
‘Gifts to Putin will not bring peace’
Zelensky reinforced his criticism in a separate statement on X, describing the sudden easing of energy sanctions as an investment in prolonging the war rather than ending it.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world,” Zelensky wrote.
In an interview with Axios, Zelensky was even more direct, calling the arrangement “not fair and not honest,” likening it to a birthday present for Putin, who turned 74 earlier this week.
Zelensky concluded his remarks to journalists by returning to what he characterized as the fundamentally unfair treatment of Ukraine’s negotiating team.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” Zelensky said. “And that is definitely unfair. It is definitely not how partners should behave.”
“And it is a weak decision. Unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners. Glory to Ukraine!”

Donald Trump is on a fresh collision course with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies after his stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel upended years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.

While costs have risen for motorists – a gallon of regular fuel in the US is about $4.20 (£3.17) – it is the price of diesel, which last month hit a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most damage on Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm elections approach.
Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need it to operate machinery.
Democrats said the agreement undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.
“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Some Republicans also criticised the agreement.
“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”
Zelenskyy told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 this week.
In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.
“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Referring on Saturday to the attack on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 12 people, Zelenskyy wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia.
“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”
Separately, Russian media cited the defence ministry as saying its forces had captured the settlements of Lukashove and Lobanivka in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelenskyy previously said Putin had been playing games with Trump, and on Saturday, a Kremlin spokesperson said the Russian leader had responded with “understanding” to Trump’s proposals to de-escalate the conflict.
Trump announced the diesel deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.
Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.
“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.
Trump recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia stopped attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Tensions have been rising between Russia and European Nato members amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.
The latest development is likely to worsen Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”
But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment at his failure to reach a peace deal.
Trump’s willingness to reach a fuel agreement with Putin comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of US forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

Zelenskyy: US used meeting with us to strike deal with Putin behind our backs
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused US President Donald Trump's team of acting dishonestly by inviting a Ukrainian delegation to talks in the United States before striking a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin behind its back to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
Source: Zelenskyy in a telephone interview with Axios
Details: Zelenskyy said that a few days ago, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff proposed a meeting in Florida to discuss new American ideas for ending the war. However, during talks between the Ukrainian delegation and Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the US side did not once suggest that it was considering a deal with Russia to purchase millions of tonnes of diesel fuel.
It was only an hour before Trump's official announcement that the Ukrainian negotiators were informed that the US president planned to speak to Putin and lift sanctions. Zelenskyy stressed that this was unfair to Ukraine.
Quote: "Steve proposed to meet in Florida. And of course I accepted to go there and speak about the possibilities of negotiations. The Americans said they have some ideas and we agreed to come to discuss.
It's not honest, really, because we tried to build our relations in the best way. It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this."
Details: Zelenskyy stressed that he would support easing energy sanctions only in exchange for an energy ceasefire. Instead, he said, the current situation demonstrated US weakness, as Washington had secured no concessions in return.
Quote: "What did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world. It looks like Alaska No. 2.
You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible."
Details: Zelenskyy also suggested that Trump's representatives were trying to secure another visit to Moscow through the agreement.
Quote: "If you allow them to export diesel, and you think before that you have to go to Russia to negotiate, it looks that you are buying this meeting. Maybe I'm not right. But it looks this way. Otherwise, why do it?"
Details: Zelenskyy said he plans to obtain a full briefing from the Ukrainian negotiating team to establish whether the agreement is connected to the planned visit to Russia by Trump's envoys.
Despite his anger, Zelenskyy refrained from stating that Ukraine would reject US mediation. He stressed that "we need the Americans to try to stop this war".
Background:
- On the evening of 9 October, Trump said he had spoken by phone with Putin and agreed on supplies of millions of tonnes of Russian diesel to US and global markets.
- The US Department of the Treasury, through its Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued General Licence No. 135, authorising transactions involving the sale, delivery, unloading and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel into the US until 17 April 2027.
- Zelenskyy strongly criticised Trump's actions, describing the easing of sanctions as an "absolutely terrible" move. He stressed that this "happy birthday present for Putin" will provide Russia with billions more to continue the war.
- Zelenskyy said Ukraine's negotiating team in the US was being used as "cover" while Trump and Putin reached agreements on fuel supplies.
- Following his conversation with Trump, Putin confirmed that Russia is ready to supply petroleum products to the US and global markets. He also expressed hope for continued cooperation between the two countries.

'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:24:33 BST
08:24:33 KST

'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
- Published
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."
He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."
The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.
The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.
Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.
The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest.
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.
But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.
Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.
"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.
But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.
Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.
"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."
The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.
More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.
But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.
The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.
Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.
Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.
Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.
Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.
He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.
Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration.
"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.
Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.
She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.
The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.
The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.
This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.
Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.
And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.
What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.
The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.
Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.
She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.
For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.
But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition.
"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris.
"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."
As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.
But not for long.
A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street.
"The canteen is still open."
The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.
Additional reporting by Bruno Boelpaep and Manon Prat

10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday pledged Washington’s full support for Venezuela’s democratic transition following a meeting with Dinorah Figuera, president of the 2015 National Assembly, as political reconciliation talks prepare to enter a third round.
Rubio reaffirmed US support for efforts to secure political freedoms, electoral reforms, and lasting democratic institutions in Venezuela when he met Figuera in Washington.
“She has our 100% support,” Rubio told reporters, stressing that recovery must go beyond holding elections.
“This is a country that’s recovering from almost a quarter century of trauma,” he said, describing the process as Venezuela’s best opportunity in nearly a generation to establish an enduring democracy.
Rubio said achieving a peaceful transition would require participation from all sectors of society, patience, and sustained efforts to build institutions capable of ensuring stability, prosperity, and freedom.
The US State Department said the two discussed progress made during two rounds of reconciliation talks between representatives of the interim government and the 2015 National Assembly.
Achievements include the release of more than 1,200 political prisoners, restored access to over 70 previously blocked internet domains, and steps toward establishing an independent Supreme Court of Justice, it said.
Authorities have also launched efforts to reform the controversial 2017 Law Against Hatred, previously used to punish government critics, according to the US fact sheet.
The third round of talks is scheduled to begin on Oct. 14, with discussions expected to focus on judicial appointments and guarantees for political participation ahead of credible elections.
Rubio emphasized that elections alone would not be enough.
“More than just free and fair elections,” he said, Venezuela needs institutions that can sustain democracy for future generations.

71 killed in S.Sudan violence: government, witnesses

Breadcrumb
71 killed in South Sudan violence: government, witnesses
Inter-communal violence killed 71 people early Friday in South Sudan's central town of Rumbek, the interim government and witnesses said.
Several witnesses told AFP that ethnic and community conflict was behind the latest violence in the world's youngest country, which won independence from Sudan in 2011.
The country also suffers from endemic corruption.
Witnesses told AFP a group of young people from outside Rumbek had attempted to take control of the town and even succeeded briefly.
After police and military reinforcements arrived, the attackers withdrew, and two witnesses said the fighting had moved to outside the city limits.
"Armed civilians engaged in violent clashes in the city of Rumbek ... on Friday, October 9, around 4 am. resulting in significant loss of life," the South Sudanese interim ministry of information said in a statement.
Head of state Salva Kiir had dissolved the government ahead of elections in December leaving an interim administration.
"According to initial security reports, at least 71 people were reportedly killed," including four soldiers, the ministry added.
The statement noted the deployment of additional security forces to Rumbek, saying that they now "have the situation under control."
Four armed civilians were arrested, the statement revealed.
The caretaker government strongly condemned the violence and urged all communities to refrain from violent acts, exercise restraint and remain calm.
The statement added troops would seek to ensure civilians' safety.
In early March, intercommunal violence left at least 169 people dead in the north of the country, when young men from the Nuer ethnic group sought revenge for the killing of some of their own number at a market, according to information provided to AFP at the time.
At least 26 people were killed and 82 wounded in mid-September during inter-ethnic violence in Abyei, a region which Sudan and South Sudan both claim.

Will Zacharia follow Leavitt's combative approach?
Trump had announced that Leavitt would resign in August to spend more time with her young children and family.
Earlier this week, conservative-leaning broadcaster Fox News announced that Leavitt would provide commentary on the network starting from November 1.
Leavitt took a combative approach to questions from the White House press corps during her tenure as press secretary.
In January, she called a White House reporter a "left-wing hack" after a question regarding the fatal US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shooting of American citizen Renee Good in Minneapolis. She also had to defend Trump's controversial handling of the Epstein files and the ongoing Iran war.
Leavitt managed to stay in the role for over 18 months — a long tenure for a high-stress job under a demanding president. During Trump's first term from 2017 to 2021, he had four press secretaries: Sean Spicer, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany.
Zacharia's tenure comes as Trump faces low approval ratings due to high energy prices amid the Iran war and the looming midterms on November 3, where the opposition Democrats are expected to make major congressional gains.

Feature: 40 "phantastic" years: "The Phantom of the Opera" highlights enduring appeal of London's West End
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:10:12 CST
08:10:12 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 9, 2026 shows decorations for the 40th anniversary of the West End debut of the musical "The Phantom of the Opera" at His Majesty's Theatre in London, Britain. (Xinhua/Zhao Jiasong)
by Xinhua writer Zhao Jiasong
LONDON, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Thunderous cheers filled His Majesty's Theatre in London on Friday night as the audience rose to its feet for Sarah Brightman and Michael Crawford, the original stars of Andrew Lloyd Webber's "The Phantom of the Opera," when they performed on stage at the musical's 40th-anniversary gala.
The special performance marked exactly four decades since the musical opened at the same venue on Oct. 9, 1986, when it was known as Her Majesty's Theatre. Brightman and Crawford originated the roles of Christine Daae and the Phantom, respectively.
The gala brought together performers from different generations of the musical's history, including former cast members from productions around the world. During the special curtain call, they joined the current company in singing songs from the musical, with many gathering around Crawford in a tribute to composer Lloyd Webber. Some performers and audience members were visibly moved to tears.
PHANTOM AT 40
Speaking on stage, Lloyd Webber expressed his gratitude to those who had contributed to the musical over the past four decades. He gave special thanks to Brightman, recalling her role in the musical's early development and how she had helped bring him together with Crawford, who went on to become the original Phantom.
"It's one of those rare moments that any composer, any author would want, where every element of everything came together," Lloyd Webber said while addressing the audience.
Cameron Mackintosh, the musical's producer, also paid tribute to the performers and production teams around the world who have brought the show to audiences over the past 40 years.
"Phantom has always attracted wonderful, wonderful artists, but tonight's company is truly extraordinary," he said.
For some spectators, the anniversary gala was an opportunity they had long awaited. Clemence Delaunay, a French theatergoer who traveled from Paris especially for the occasion, told Xinhua that she had grown up watching recordings of the musical's 25th-anniversary performance.
"I'm thrilled to finally attend such a special performance in London. It feels like being part of theatre history, celebrating a musical that has touched audiences for generations," she said.
Based on the novel by French writer Gaston Leroux, the musical has become the third-longest-running production in West End history, behind "The Mousetrap" and "Les Miserables," according to the Society of London Theatre.
Over the past four decades, the musical has attracted around 160 million spectators across 229 cities and been performed in 23 languages. Its international tour is currently playing in Shanghai, where a 40th-anniversary season featuring 104 performances runs until Dec. 27 at the Shanghai Grand Theatre.
To mark the anniversary, the production team also announced plans to film the London production, including Friday's gala performance, for an international cinema release in 2027, allowing more audiences worldwide to experience the show from its original London home.
LONDON'S ENDURING THEATRICAL APPEAL
The longevity of "The Phantom of the Opera" reflects the strength of London's theater industry, which has developed a thriving market for live performances and continues to attract performers and audiences from around the world.
Earlier this year, international city guide Time Out named London the world's best city for culture in 2026. In a survey covering more than 24,000 residents across 150 cities, 99 percent of London respondents rated the city's cultural offerings positively. London scored 90 percent for theater, the highest rating among the cities surveyed, while 60 percent of respondents considered the city's arts and culture affordable.
The industry also makes a substantial contribution to Britain's economy. According to the Theatre in the UK 2026 report released in March by the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, the West End attracted a record 17.64 million audience visits in 2025, generating 1.08 billion pounds (about 1.43 billion U.S. dollars) in revenue.
The report estimated that every pound spent on a theater ticket generates a further 1.40 pounds in local economic activity, benefiting restaurants, hotels, transport and other businesses.
Nicholas Scrivens, Programme Leader of Master of Arts in Musical Theatre at the Guildford School of Acting, told Xinhua that the West End's international reputation has developed over centuries, supported by a highly skilled creative workforce. He said the rise of large-scale musicals in the 1980s, led by figures such as Lloyd Webber and Mackintosh, helped establish London as a global center for musical theater.
Beyond its major commercial productions, London has a network of smaller theaters that provide opportunities for new writing and experimental productions. The musical "Operation Mincemeat," for example, premiered at the New Diorama Theatre in 2019 before transferring to the West End in 2023 and Broadway in 2025.
Scrivens said the success of newer productions such as "SIX" and "Operation Mincemeat" showed growing opportunities for original works. He attributed the West End's appeal to its theatrical heritage, creative excellence and the community of artists and professionals sustaining the industry.
Affordable ticket schemes have also helped bring more people into London's theaters. According to the industry report, more than a quarter of West End tickets sold in 2025 cost less than 35 pounds, while most were priced at 56 pounds or below. Many theaters also offer discounted tickets for young audiences, students and families.
Chinese musical theater performer and creator Aimee Yue recalled that when she began studying in Britain at the age of 14, her teachers took students to see theater performances almost every two weeks, often benefiting from affordable school tickets.
She told Xinhua that these early experiences helped develop her lasting interest in theater and that giving young people greater access to live performances was essential to cultivating future audiences.
Friday's anniversary gala also raised funds for the training of young performers. According to the organizers, proceeds from ticket sales will be matched by contributions from the Andrew Lloyd Webber Foundation and the Mackintosh Foundation to establish a scholarship program supporting professional performing arts training in Britain.
Beatrice Penny-Toure, who played Christine Daae in Friday's anniversary performance, is herself a former recipient of an Andrew Lloyd Webber Foundation scholarship. ■
This photo taken on Oct. 9, 2026 shows a banner for the 40th anniversary of the musical "The Phantom of the Opera" in London, Britain. (Xinhua/Zhao Jiasong)

UNITED NATIONS/OTTAWA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and foreign ministers of eight countries on Friday criticized the U.S. announcement of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution.

Al-Masirah TV, however, gave a conflicting account, saying Houthi forces had repelled government troops advancing from the neighboring province of Lahj toward the southern approaches to Bab al-Mandab, claiming dozens of casualties among the advancing forces.
In Yemen's southern port city of Aden on Friday, a loud explosion was heard near the international airport. A local security official told Xinhua that preliminary information indicated that "the explosion was caused by a suspected Houthi attack targeting a military base close to Aden International Airport."
INTERNATIONAL CONDEMNATION
In a Friday briefing to the UN Security Council on Yemen, Hans Grundberg, UN Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen, said hostilities have intensified in recent weeks in Yemen, and he condemned Houthi attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
Ongoing instability in the Middle East continues to affect dynamics in Yemen, while developments there in turn reverberate across the region, noted the UN envoy, who urged a political settlement.
"Unless war is to become Yemen's permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now," said Grundberg.
Also on Friday, Türkiye strongly condemned the Houthis' attacks on Saudi airports, calling for an immediate halt to attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure.
"We condemn in the strongest terms the attacks," the Turkish Foreign Ministry said in a statement, reaffirming Türkiye's full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reiterated its call for resolving ongoing conflicts through dialogue and diplomacy.
Yemen has been embroiled in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of the north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, now based in the southern port city of Aden.
The renewed fighting marked a major escalation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities. ■

====================================================================================================

Falling off a cliff? What recurring nightmares mean and how to change their ending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
23:03:42 UTC
08:03:42 KST

You're falling off a cliff. Down and down you go, unable to stop. You're certain you're about to hit the ground when suddenly you wake up in a panic, your heart racing. It takes a few seconds to realize you're actually lying safely in bed. A few nights later, just when you've almost forgotten about it, the same nightmare returns. Once again, you're falling, only to wake up drenched in sweat.
"Falling from a great height, drowning, tsunamis and enormous waves are among the most common nightmares," says Ronit Jenny Nesher, a dream expert and wellness psychologist with a doctorate in psychology. "Among Israelis, dreams about wars, bomb shelters, explosions and airplanes are also common. Since October 7, the number of nightmares has increased, and their content has changed. Now we're seeing more dreams involving tunnels and terrorists."
But why does the brain create these terrifying scenarios? And what does it mean when a nightmare doesn't just happen once, but keeps coming back?
"Nightmares are what we call unprocessed material in psychology," Nesher explains. "They can involve fears, frustrations, anger and suppressed emotions that we haven't given enough attention to or fully processed during the day. They remain unfinished business, and at night they come back to haunt us."
According to Nesher, dreams should not always be interpreted literally. "Dreams speak to us in codes. I might dream about someone else, but really I'm dreaming about myself. The important thing is that there's something weighing on me that I haven't processed."
She believes that even the most frightening nightmare is not necessarily a bad thing.
"There's no such thing as a bad dream. Every dream is like someone tugging at your sleeve and saying, 'Hey, there's something here you haven't noticed.' If I keep suppressing those feelings, the fears won't disappear. But if a nightmare keeps repeating itself, I have an opportunity to work through it."
Don't go to bed watching the news
So what causes nightmares to appear on a particular night? Nesher suggests starting with what we take to bed with us, both mentally and physically.
"If I go to sleep after watching frightening news, it's going to find its way into my dreams," she says. "I tell my patients, half joking and half serious, that if they go to bed with the news, they shouldn't be surprised when it follows them into their dreams. And you know how people say you shouldn't go to bed angry? Well, arguments can increase nightmares too."
She also recommends paying attention to the bedroom environment.
"If the room is too hot, it can trigger nightmares. Synthetic bedding, particularly fleece blankets, can also have an effect," she says.
Nesher also believes that static electricity can influence what she describes as the body's energy field and contribute to disturbed sleep and nightmares, although this explanation is not an established scientific account of nightmares.
"That's why I recommend good sleep hygiene, less screen time before bed and cotton bedding," she says.
In her view, there is also an energetic dimension to sleep disturbances, even when nothing appears to be wrong with the sleeping environment.
"Imagine checking into a hotel room and feeling that something about it just isn't right. I'm sure plenty of people can relate to having a terrible night's sleep in a hotel. There was no noise, the room was clean, everything seemed fine, but you just kept tossing and turning."
Why does she think that happens?
"Sometimes sensitive people pick up on the energy of whoever stayed in the room before them. I travel a lot, and if I arrive at a hotel and the energy in the room feels unpleasant, I simply ask to change rooms."
She also suggests visualization exercises.
"You can imagine surrounding the room with a bubble or with sparkling lights, something I call the 'golden frequency.' Another option is to imagine yourself in bed surrounded by a bubble of red, orange, purple and blue. I sometimes use this in places where the energy doesn't feel right."
'A recurring nightmare is a friend'
When a nightmare keeps returning, Nesher believes the answer is not necessarily to try to get rid of it.
"A recurring nightmare is a friend. That's my slogan for children," she says. "The dream is telling us there's something valuable here, something we need to work on."
She gives the example of nightmares experienced before a wedding.
"Many brides dream that the groom runs away, that they arrive at the wedding naked, that they're driving around and can't find the venue, or that someone brings them a dress that doesn't fit. Those are all fears connected to getting married."
Rather than simply acknowledging that they had a nightmare, Nesher encourages people to examine what happened in the dream and how they might have responded differently.
"Explore the dream. Put yourself back into it and ask: How could I have acted differently? What does the feeling in the dream remind me of in real life? What am I afraid of? What can I do to feel more in control? Because a nightmare is about helplessness."
She recalls a student who repeatedly dreamed of falling.
"He was falling and falling, but at the bottom there was a trampoline, and he bounced straight back up. To me, that meant he had inner strength. He believed that even if he fell into a hole, he would have the resources to climb back out."
And what should you do when you wake up from a nightmare and the fear hasn't gone away?
"First, remind yourself that it was only a dream. Then get out of bed, wash your hands and face, have something to drink, tell someone about the dream or write it down. Get it out of your system and do something else."
Not every nightmare is a sign of a problem
Yakir Salem, a psychologist undergoing rehabilitation specialization training in the Dan-Petah Tikva district of Clalit Health Services, as well as a couples therapist and lecturer, offers another perspective.
For Salem, the important question is not necessarily what a nightmare means, but how much it affects someone's everyday life.
"In simple terms, a nightmare is a frightening dream that can also bring up feelings of guilt, disgust or shame," he explains. "Nightmares aren't a disorder in themselves. Having one doesn't mean I'm ill, that something is wrong with me, that something terrible has happened or that I've experienced trauma. They're part of our natural psychological activity."
There are many possible triggers, he says.
"Nightmares can be associated with anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress, but also with ordinary stress. Sometimes changes we consider positive, such as getting married, having a baby or moving house, can be extremely stressful and lead to more dreams and nightmares."
Certain medications, drug use and withdrawal from some sedative medications can also be associated with nightmares.
"I've even seen research linking very large meals just before bedtime, particularly spicy meals, to nightmares," he adds.
Salem also recognizes that dreams can reflect emotions and experiences that are not immediately obvious to us.
"I still think Freud's old observation about dream interpretation being the royal road to the unconscious holds value. But I take a much more individual approach."
He gives the example of two people dreaming that they have lost their wedding rings.
"For one person, it might represent a fear of losing the ring. For another, it could reflect a suppressed wish for that loss to happen, which creates anxiety. For a third, it might symbolize something entirely different that has taken the form of marriage or a relationship in the dream."
His approach is to explore what a particular dream means to the person having it, rather than assuming that a specific image carries the same meaning for everyone.
When should nightmares become a cause for concern?
According to Salem, the most important warning sign is whether nightmares begin interfering with sleep or daily functioning.
"What interests us more than how frightening the dream feels is whether the nightmares are affecting my ability to function," he says.
"Am I sleeping poorly because I wake up during the night and struggle to fall asleep again? Am I having trouble falling asleep in the first place because I'm afraid of what I might dream? Am I tired or irritable the next day? Do memories of the nightmare interfere with my concentration?"
If sleep remains restful and daily functioning is unaffected, he says, even strange or disturbing nightmares are generally less concerning.
He also pays attention to whether recurring nightmares change over time.
"If the nightmares keep coming back but look a little different each time, that worries me less. The more a dream resembles an exact replay of something that actually happened, repeating again and again without changing, the more we begin to consider whether it could be a post-traumatic symptom."
In those cases, Salem recommends seeking professional help.
How to rewrite your nightmares
One way to address recurring nightmares is to deliberately change the dream's storyline.
Salem points to a treatment known as Imagery Rehearsal Therapy, or IRT, which involves rewriting a nightmare and then mentally rehearsing the revised version while awake.
"I take the nightmare and rewrite it in the first person and present tense, making some kind of change," he explains.
"For example, suppose I dream that I'm walking along a cliff and there's a murderer waiting for me at the end. Every time I reach him, I wake up. I take that dream and rewrite it so that something different happens."
The new ending does not necessarily have to be a happy one, he says.
"It doesn't have to mean I kill the murderer or manage to escape. I might even jump off the cliff and die. The important thing is that I change something in the dream."
After rewriting it, the person practices imagining the new version at regular times during the day.
"It's an exercise in developing the ability to edit the dream, to make changes and to experience a sense of control over my mental activity, my memories and my dreams."
But does it actually work?
"Studies show that, on average, we begin to see improvement after about two weeks, whether in the frequency of nightmares, changes that start appearing in the dreams themselves or symptoms experienced while awake," Salem says.
"After two months, the improvements can be very significant."
He cautions, however, that not everyone will be able to use the technique successfully on their own.
"If someone tells me, 'I can't imagine a new dream. I can't change this memory even when I'm awake,' that's a red flag for me. In that situation, I recommend seeking help rather than trying to solve the problem through exercises at home."
Can we make sure we only have pleasant dreams?
There is no guaranteed way to prevent unpleasant dreams, but Salem believes certain habits may encourage more restful sleep.
"Things that support sleep, such as breathing exercises before bed, guided imagery, meditation or practicing gratitude, may also encourage more pleasant dreams," he says.
Still, he believes the goal should not simply be to eliminate bad dreams.
"I prefer being curious about what's happening inside us rather than just trying to have good dreams. Even bad and frightening dreams are worth approaching with curiosity, because they can tell us a great deal about what's going on beneath the surface."
What if your child or partner wakes up from a nightmare?
When someone close to us wakes up frightened, the instinct is often to reassure them immediately that nothing is wrong. But both experts suggest that listening and helping the person feel safe can be more useful than dismissing their fear.
"When a child is frightened, I don't tell them, 'There's nothing to be afraid of, I'm here,' because the child really is afraid," Nesher says.
Instead, she tries to help children recognize the things that can make them feel safe.
"If a child is afraid that someone might break into the house, for example, I'll ask: Is the door locked? Do Mom and Dad lock the door at night? If someone came in, would they wake up? That helps the child see what exists in reality that can give them a sense of security and control."
Salem emphasizes the distinction between ordinary nightmares and night terrors.
"If we're talking about night terrors, when someone screams, sits up or moves around in their sleep without being fully awake and sometimes doesn't remember anything the next morning, we can try to comfort and support them without forcing them awake."
When someone wakes from an ordinary nightmare, he says, the most important thing is to be emotionally present.
"In emotion-focused therapy, or EFT, we ask, 'Are you there for me?' In other words, are you accessible, responsive and emotionally engaged?"
He believes this is particularly important between partners.
"Put simply, be there for your partner. Curiosity in a relationship is a superpower. Try to understand what the person in front of you is experiencing and what they need before trying to persuade them, help them or cheer them up. Don't dismiss or minimize their feelings."
So the next time you dream about falling, drowning or someone breaking into your home, it may be worth doing more than simply trying to forget the experience. Consider what keeps returning, what triggers the fear or sense of helplessness, and whether you might be able to give the dream a different ending.

Trump Makes Deal With Putin On Diesel Exports. Ukraine Calls It A 'Gift'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
23:03:17 UTC
08:03:17 KST

WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump said he reached an agreement with President Vladimir Putin to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a move Ukraine immediately criticized as a "gift" to the Kremlin.
Seeking to contain soaring energy prices, Trump said in a social media post on October 9 that the two leaders agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that.
The move will see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote.
Diesel futures fell about 4 percent after the announcement but remained more than 110 percent higher than at the start of the year. Brent crude traded at around $104 a barrel, down just 0.3 percent on the day.
The decision came as Ukrainian, US, and European officials held talks in Miami aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. The discussions concluded without a breakthrough.
The waiver drew critical comments from Kyiv to lawmakers in Washington, who warned that easing restrictions could provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its war against Ukraine.
It also raised questions about US policy toward Russia following Trump’s recent signing of legislation intended to tighten sanctions against countries supporting Moscow’s energy trade.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media.
"Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis."
To enable the flow of diesel, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing the sale, delivery, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
Trump said that after the initial flows, Russia would supply a further 3 million tons “within a short period of time.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow was ready to increase supplies in October, with exports expected to rise in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance.
Diesel prices have climbed since the United States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran in February, sparking a conflict that is now in its eighth month.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing prices higher and urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian energy facilities.
“The problem I have with Ukraine and Russia is that, you know, a lot of the diesel comes … from Russia, and the Russia plants are being hit by Ukraine,” Trump told reporters recently.
Ukrainian officials have said they are prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Moscow halted its recent barrage of strikes on Ukraine’s energy and other civilian infrastructure installations.
As Ukraine’s negotiating team was in Florida, Zelenskyy also questioned the purpose of the Miami talks while Washington was allowing Russia to earn money from fuel exports.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” he said.
Earlier on October 9, Zelenskyy welcomed a bipartisan delegation of US senators to Kyiv and called for stronger pressure on Moscow.
Meanwhile, on Capitol Hill, the waiver for Russia drew the ire of several lawmakers.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia’s war economy is terrible,” Republican Representative Don Bacon told RFE/RL.
Democrat Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the bipartisan Russia sanctions legislation, called the decision an embarrassment, arguing that it would benefit Russia and China while undermining congressional efforts to pressure Moscow.
“This poorly concealed attempt to mitigate the havoc caused by Trump’s illegal war in Iran will only benefit the Chinese & Russian economies & lead to the slaughter of more innocents in Ukraine,” he wrote on social media.
Blumenthal called the agreement “a stain on our nation’s character” and said it ran counter to Congress’s intent in its recent passing of a sanctions bill.
He also warned US companies considering purchases of Russian fuel: “Congress is watching.”
Daniel Fried, a former US diplomat and sanctions expert, also criticized the timing of the waiver.
“General License allowing sale of Russian diesel, proceeds of which support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Not a promising start to the imminent talks on ending the war,” Fried said in a social media post.
Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior Treasury Department official who worked at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, said the move showed Trump was prioritizing the Iran conflict and its economic consequences over pressure on Russia.
“The Russia legislation put the onus, and the ability to act, in President Trump's hands,” Bitsoff told RFE/RL.
“Today's diesel license shows Trump is prioritizing the Iran conflict over pressure on Russia, and he likely doesn't intend to use a lot of the authorities in the bill,” she said.
Ukrainian sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said the waiver could also undermine Trump’s argument that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries were the main driver of rising diesel prices.
“If limiting diesel sanctions on Russia provides market relief then it’s clear the primary impact to the global diesel market was the Iran conflict and blockade, not Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, which would have had a secondary impact,” Vlasiuk told RFE/RL. “It lines up with price timelines.”
The decision also raises questions about the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has agreed to withdraw from Ukraine, recognized Ukrainian sovereignty, and poses no threat to NATO.
Supplied materials from officials on the decision does not establish how that provision applies to the new license.
The Miami discussions, initially expected to last two days, concluded on Friday, October 9, according to US envoy Steve Witkoff.
Representatives from the United States, the E3 group of European countries, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO held “constructive discussions” on ways to de-escalate and end the war before winter.
Witkoff said the agenda included winter preparedness, energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees, longer-term security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe, and support for Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction and eventual European Union accession.
“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on social media.
The Kremlin said Trump and Putin had also discussed prospects for resolving the war during their phone call, alongside the situation surrounding Iran and other bilateral issues.

Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in Ofsted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
23:01:40 UTC
08:01:40 KST

Tensions between England’s headteachers and Ofsted are developing into a crisis after school leadership unions said they had no confidence in the watchdog and would hold strike ballots unless “significant wellbeing issues” caused by Ofsted’s inspections regime were fixed.
The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL), which includes senior leaders in many secondary schools, described Ofsted’s inspection system as “an overbearing mess” and urged the government to pause inspections to stop teachers leaving the profession.
A spokesperson for ASCL said that “if change is not forthcoming” the union would seek to hold an indicative ballot on industrial action.
The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said it would also consider steps including strike action at a meeting of its leadership next week.
The combative moves come after a survey published by Ofsted showed 88% of schools reported that recent inspections had negatively affected staff wellbeing.
The Guardian reported last week that Lucy Powell, the education secretary, wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” and overhaul the framework introduced last year. The new framework was intended to lower the strain and workload caused by inspections, but many heads say the opposite has happened.
In response to ASCL’s announcement, a spokesperson for the Department for Education said: “Inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face.
“That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.”
An Ofsted spokesperson said: “We have worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge.
“We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do.”
Hostility towards Ofsted has been heightened since the death of Ruth Perry, a popular headteacher in Reading. In 2023 a coroner found that an Ofsted inspection contributed to Perry’s mental health deterioration and her death. Labour pledged to reform school inspections in its 2024 election manifesto.
But ASCL said it had “seen no meaningful progress on the part of Ofsted to address significant wellbeing issues caused by inspections, and that it is increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members”.
The motion of no confidence in Ofsted passed by ASCL’s executive stated: “We fear that the disproportionate stress and anxiety exerted by the inspection system will lead to school leaders deciding to leave their posts with a consequent impact on schools, children and young people.”
Pepe Di’Iasio, ASCL’s general secretary, said: “Our repeated attempts to resolve our concerns through discussion and negotiation have hit a brick wall … The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed.”
Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the NAHT, said: “Our deep concerns about this Ofsted framework and the impact it is having on professionals are longstanding. Our executive committee will be meeting at the end of next week and debating the next steps NAHT will take. We fully expect that debate to include the option of pursuing industrial action.”

Panama declares 'major disaster' after earthquake destroys buildings and roads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
23:00:36 UTC
08:00:36 KST

A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake has rocked Panama, causing buildings and roads to collapse in the centre of the Central American country but no immediate reports of casualties.
President Jose Raul Mulino labelled Friday’s earthquake a "major disaster" and said it destroyed roads near the epicentre. Mulino did not say whether the tremor caused any casualties.
The shallow tremor was felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System.
It lasted for around a minute.
In Panama City, about 200 kilometres from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city's emblematic skyscrapers.
"I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged. Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking," Salomon Andion, 46, told AFP news agency after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks.
A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building that's over 20 stories tall.
Another showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently but remaining upright as vehicles travelled across it.
"It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school," Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle province told AFP.
Tsunami warming
The US Geological Survey said the quake struck at 1756 GMT with an epicenter 10 kilometres from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in central Herrera province.
The USGS initially estimated it to be a magnitude-8.0 quake before revising it to 7.7.
A tsunami warming was issued for the eastern Pacific but later lifted.
The Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the channel, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, was unaffected and operating "as normal."
Mulino travelled to Penonome to coordinate the disaster response.
Health Minister Fernando Boyd said the most affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Cocle as well as Los Santos in the southeast.
He said the town of Tonosi in Los Santos was completely cut off.
"We are trying to figure out how to get there by air, because it's impossible by land," he said.
Panama City's international airport, a major hub for the region, was temporarily closed.
Several flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution, according to the Civil Aeronautics Authority.
The leaders of Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala all sent messages of solidarity and offers to send aid.
Over 80 aftershocks
Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in the western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica.
Former president Ricardo Martinelli posted pictures on Instagram of his house in the town of Sona in Veraguas province which collapsed.
A church and a hotel in Penonome also suffered extensive damage, images shared on local media showed.
Over 80 aftershocks, one above magnitude 6.0, were recorded by the local geosciences institute.
The education ministry announced the suspension of classes in schools nationwide.
The Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, meanwhile, made a credit line of up to $50 million available for Panama.
Additionally, the bank made a $250,000 donation to the country, it said in a post on X.
The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela's Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August.

Iran wants to join the CIS in a new format
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
02:00:10 EEST
08:00:10 KST

Iran wants to join the CIS in a new format
Kyiv • UNN
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian proposed a “CIS+1” format for political and economic cooperation. Tehran's full membership is not envisaged.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian proposed creating a new format of cooperation with the Commonwealth of Independent States called “CIS+1,” which would include Tehran’s participation. He announced the initiative during the CIS heads of state summit in Turkmenistan, The Moscow Times reports, citing the Iranian Fars news agency, UNN writes.
Details
Pezeshkian became the first Iranian president to attend such a summit as a special guest. According to him, the new format should become an effective mechanism for political dialogue and economic cooperation between the countries.
Regional diplomacy should not be limited to meetings but should help resolve crises, maintain contacts, prevent the escalation of conflicts, and develop practical cooperation
What Iran is offering the CIS countries
Pezeshkian paid particular attention to energy cooperation. He proposed creating a regional network for the production, transportation, and exchange of energy resources that would combine supplies of oil, gas, and electricity with the development of renewable energy.
The Iranian leader also urged the states to use the advantages of their geographic location to deepen economic ties and jointly develop infrastructure.
At the same time, the “CIS+1” initiative does not currently envisage Iran’s full membership in the organization. The proposal concerns the creation of a separate partnership mechanism between Tehran and the Commonwealth countries, which was founded in 1991 following the collapse of the USSR.
