Republican opposition widens to livestreamed execution; Trump still weighing it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:59:46 UTC
07:59:46 KST

Republican opposition widens to live-streamed execution; Trump still weighing the matter
WASHINGTON – Republican lawmakers joined religious leaders and international observers on Oct 9 in opposing a Pentagon plan to live-stream an execution by firing squad, while US President Donald Trump said he has not yet decided whether to allow the live feed.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance expressed scepticism over whether the Pentagon will proceed with live-streaming the scheduled Dec 3 execution of former US Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan, who was found guilty in a US military trial of fatally shooting 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
“I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters in Cincinnati, referring to the live-stream plan championed by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
If it is shown publicly, Vance said, “I’m not going to be watching it”.
Trump told reporters that Hasan deserves the death penalty by firing squad, calling him “totally nuts”. But when asked if he wants the execution live-streamed, the Republican President said he has yet to “make a determination about that”.
A senior US Catholic bishop and a US evangelical Christian leader voiced opposition to the plan, as did the UN human rights office.
Republicans voice concern
Several Republican US lawmakers argued against a live streaming.
Senator John Curtis wrote on social media that “a civilisation erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment”.
Senator Thom Tillis and Representative Austin Scott said live-streaming executions is what Islamist extremists would do. Representative Rob Bresnahan said the pain felt by victims and family members “deserves respect, not a public show”.
“This should be reconsidered,” Representative Michael Baumgartner wrote on social media.
Democrats were overwhelmingly opposed.
The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment.
A government execution has never been broadcast or live-streamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945.
Hasan, now 56, is believed to be confined to a wheelchair, having been shot by the police during his arrest.
A senior White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump does not oppose the idea of live-streaming the execution, but could change his mind.
The White House is hearing concerns from lawmakers, allies and religious leaders who are urging the administration not to live-stream it, the official said.
Hegseth, a Trump appointee, confirmed the plans for the live-streamed execution on Oct 8.
‘A culture of death’
Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, condemned the planned live streaming as a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death”.
Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, said on social media that a live-streamed execution by firing squad “risks turning one of the state’s most solemn responsibilities into a public spectacle, promoting a culture of death, rather than a culture that upholds the dignity of every human being”.
Hegseth, a member of a conservative evangelical denomination, has made his Christian faith a hallmark of his tenure as defence secretary and has led prayer services at the Pentagon. He also has brushed off Pope Leo’s criticism of the Iran war.
Hasan, an American-born Muslim, said during his 2013 trial that he carried out the shootings to try to stop what he called a US war on Islam.
“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance told reporters.
‘Free propaganda’
Joe Kent, who resigned in 2026 as Trump’s head of the National Counterterrorism Center, wrote on social media: “Streaming his execution is not just a stain on our morality – it also gives the terrorists free propaganda that they will use to radicalise and recruit more terrorists.”
Brendan Carr, chair of the Federal Communications Commission, told CNBC that it is his understanding that the execution would not air on broadcast TV. But he said he would defer to Hegseth on whether US networks could air it.
US law prohibits the recording or broadcasting of executions in the federal prison system.
Military regulations have not applied that same prohibition. Courts have rejected lawsuits brought by media organisations seeking broader public access to executions.
The UN human rights office said public executions violate prohibitions against torture.
“Public executions constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment,” Shabia Mantoo, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, told a news briefing in Geneva.
Amnesty International called the use of a firing squad “reprehensible”.
Mental health experts said it also could traumatise children.
The execution is scheduled to be held at the same sprawling military base where Hasan opened fire with a handgun in a medical facility.
The Pentagon on Oct 9 declined to say whether families of those killed in Hasan’s attack would be invited to attend the execution, as is common practice in US civilian executions.
It remains unclear how the US Army would select the shooters and what protocols might be followed during the execution itself.
The Pentagon said it would release details later.
The plan to live-stream the execution comes at a time of heightened debate in the US over the death penalty. It follows the botched lethal injection last week of a Tennessee woman who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder.
The controversy has flared in the run-up to the Nov 3 US midterm elections, in which Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. REUTERS

SC: Nothing wrong in deleting dead or those who've shifted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:59:21 UTC
07:59:21 KST

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Friday said there is nothing wrong in deletion of names of the dead, and those who have either shifted out from the ward or duplicate names during Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls but said that on the date of notification of elections, the voter list which is final - either the post-SIR list or the one on Jan 1, 2026, would be used for local body polls in Andhra Pradesh.A bench of chief justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana refused to entertain YSR Congress Party's appeal against Andhra Pradesh high court's decision rejecting its plea for deferment of local body elections till finalisation of SIR of electoral rolls.
The bench said SIR is a necessity as those who have passed away or shifted cannot be allowed to vote in the wards. The duplicate voters' names also are required to be struck down, and these are the anomalies that are taken care of through SIR, it said.On the plea that HC has directed finalisation of post-SIR voter list by Oct 16, the bench said as per the legislations governing the panchayat, municipalities and municipal corporations, the elections would be held based on the final voter list available on the date when the EC notifies the elections.When the SEC said that the election dates have not been notified and that it would be bound to take the final voter list available on the election notification date, the bench agreed and said if for some reason the post-SIR final electoral rolls are not published prior to the election notification, then the EC would consider holding polls based on the voter list as finalised on Jan 1, 2026.

No correlation between SIR deletions &amp; assembly poll results: Bengal CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:57:32 UTC
07:57:32 KST

NEW DELHI: The chief electoral officer of West Bengal Friday dismissed as "misleading and speculative" claims made in an "analysis" posted on YouTube that deletions made during special intensive revision in the state had a direct bearing on the outcome of the recent assembly elections.In a post on X, the CEO quoted the analysis by DeKoder and countered it with electoral data from five West Bengal seats that saw the highest SIR deletions - four of them were won by Trinamool Congress and one went to BJP. As for the five constituencies with the lowest SIR deletions, BJP ended up winning in all.
Refuting the claims made in the YouTube video - which relied on electoral data from 25 seats with the highest and lowest SIR deletions, and pointed to -10.5% and -5.3% swings respectively, for TMC - West Bengal's top electoral officer said "the electoral data... does not support the political narrative".The officer also dismissed the claim that women accounted for 62% of the electors deleted through SIR in West Bengal. "The claim... is unverified. As per the total data on deletion of invalid entries (excluding adjudication), around 50% or half of the deletions related to women," he posted on X.
Regarding the DeKoder claim that deletions of Muslim electors were 52% more than those of non-Muslim electors, the CEO pointed out there was no data based on religious identity of the voters.
"Hence the analysis claimed is based on mere unverified assumptions," he posted."...The facts do not support the allegations," the officer stated and asserted that no voter could be deleted without due process. "Issuance of notice, an opportunity for hearing and a speaking order by the ERO (electoral registration officer) are part of the safeguards. Appeals are available at two levels," he added.The CEO said SIR was not about deleting genuine voters but about protecting the integrity of the electoral roll and was being conducted in accordance with Article 324 of Constitution and Section 21 of R P Act 1950, with due process and safeguards. "SIR is a lawful, transparent and ongoing exercise to ensure that every eligible elector is on the roll and that ineligible entries are removed. Electoral rolls must be based on facts - not speculation," he noted.

Serial killer could be on the loose in US state – police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:54:28 UTC
07:54:28 KST

Serial killer could be on the loose in US state – police
Police in Lansing, Michigan, are investigating whether a serial killer is responsible for the deaths of five men found along a short stretch of a river trail in the city over the past year.
The victims, aged between 22 and 70, were all believed to be homeless. Their bodies were discovered along a 1.5-mile (2.4-km) section of the trail near downtown Lansing between October 2025 and August 2026.
”One question that we are being asked is ‘Do we have a serial killer in Lansing?’” Police Chief Robert Backus told reporters at a recent briefing.
”What we need the public to know is that we are investigating all of these cases. They are all active investigations, and we are looking at the idea or the possibility that these may be related cases.”
Four victims suffered apparent blunt-force injuries to the face, while the fifth was stabbed. Three deaths have been ruled homicides, one remains undetermined, and the cause of the fifth has yet to be established.
Edward Smith has been charged with murder in connection with the August 20 stabbing of Daniel Lusk, 22, but police have not linked him to the other deaths. Another victim, Louis Woodruff, 57, was found injured on August 30, after Smith’s arrest, and died on September 1.
Investigators suspect some of the men may have been attacked overnight while lying down or sleeping, although police stress that this theory remains unconfirmed.
A lack of witnesses and limited surveillance footage have hampered the investigation. Police have stepped up patrols and deployed mobile surveillance cameras along the trail, while social workers are reaching out to homeless residents to help them secure housing.
Serial killings are rare in the US, accounting for less than 1% of all murders according to the FBI. One of the country’s most high-profile recent cases involved Rex Heuermann, arrested in July 2023 in connection with the Gilgo Beach murders in New York. He was sentenced to life in prison this June after admitting to killing eight women.

Amid Form 7 bulk filing row, Election Commission limits it to 10 per elector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:44:17 UTC
07:44:17 KST

NEW DELHI: Election Commission Friday, to discourage bulk submissions of Form 7 (objection to inclusion of an elector in the electoral roll), capped the maximum number of these applications that may be filed by an individual elector during the claims and objections period of special and summary revisions to 10.For Form 7 applications filed by an individual elector during the period of continuous update of the electoral roll, the upper limit shall be five per month.
The ceilings - which follow Congress flagging bulk filings across many constituencies in Karnataka, including Ballari where a single BJP worker allegedly submitted 7,561 Form 7 applications - will apply to filings by individual electors both in online and offline modes.In a letter to chief electoral officers of states and UTs, EC explained that while the number of applications to be filed online by an individual elector had been fixed as six at a time, subject to disposal, the number of physical forms presented in bulk had not been defined and was left to the judgement of electoral registration officers (ERO). The new limits seek to remove any scope for ambiguity, an EC officer told TOI.
According to Rule 13(2) of Registration of Electors Rules (RER) 1960, every objection to the proposed inclusion of name or application for deletion of name in the electoral roll of a constituency is to be referred only by a person whose name figures in the roll of that constituency.
For the SIR period, EC has allowed booth-level agents of political parties to submit to a booth level officer Form 7 applications in bulk, with a limit of 50 forms per day before the draft publication and 10 forms per day thereafter.The poll panel Friday said any claim or objection not lodged within the specified period or in the form and manner specified in the rules, shall be rejected by ERO, who will also verify the applicant's name in the electors' list.Once a Form 7 application is found in line with norms, the ERO shall first issue a notice to the objector, hear him personally, record his statem-ents separately for each Form 7 and satisfy himself about the validity of the objections.EC directed EROs to take action against false and fabricated Form 7s, including prosecution of the applicant under R P Act 1950 for knowingly making a false statement or declaration in writing.

In Norway, archaeologists discovered mysterious stone circles dating back about 2,000 years
Kyiv • UNN
At the Gunn burial site, ground-penetrating radar revealed ring ditches, burial mounds, and possible graves. The purpose of the stone structures remains unknown.
At the ancient Gถunn burial ground in eastern Norway, archaeologists discovered traces of previously unknown stone circles that may have been used during burial rituals around 2,000 years ago. Science Norway reports this, writes UNN.
Details
The discovery was made using ground-penetrating radar, which allowed researchers to examine underground structures without carrying out excavations.
In the western section of the burial ground, scientists recorded ring-shaped ditches and the remains of large burial mounds. Previously, similar stone structures had been found only in the southern section.
What the stone circles were created for
Archaeologists suggest that the ring-shaped ditches may have served as markers for the construction of burial monuments.
Another theory is that they were formed as a result of ritual processions around the burials.
The researchers also discovered several possible graves. Scientists are convinced that vertically positioned stones once stood in this area, but the exact purpose of the structures remains unknown.

Scientists have linked the ratio of T cells to the risk of diabetes, hypertension, and organ diseases. The blood analysis method is still experimental.
American scientists have identified features of immune cells that may help predict the risk of developing chronic diseases long before symptoms appear. The study's results were published in the scientific journal Immunity, Medical Xpress reports, writes UNN.
Details
Researchers at the University of Washington analyzed around 12.4 million immune cells from 2,609 people of different ages.
They found that the ratio of two types of T cells is associated with the rate of immune system aging and health risks.
Which diseases may be predicted
Additional analysis of data from 50,000 people showed that a particular immune profile is associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, liver disease, and kidney failure in the following years.
Scientists are working to develop a simple blood test that would make it possible to detect such risks at an early stage.
For now, the method remains experimental and requires further validation before it can be used in hospitals.

Hoods, Palestinian flag and samurai sword: Student unrest spreads to Belgium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:33:12 UTC
07:33:12 KST

The wave of student protests sweeping France has spread to neighboring Belgium, where tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Brussels on Friday to protest government spending cuts, as separate groups of masked rioters clashed with police, set fires and hurled objects at officers.
Police estimated that around 30,000 people joined the demonstrations in the Belgian capital, including students from the country's French-speaking community who have been protesting education budget cuts, inspired in part by the unrest across the border in France.
Violence erupted near Brussels Central Station, where masked youths dressed in black confronted riot police. Groups of rioters threw bricks, glass bottles, barriers, road signs and fireworks at officers, while videos circulating online appeared to show smoke canisters and other explosive devices being hurled toward police lines.
In one video, an officer was seen confiscating a samurai-style sword from a demonstrator. Other footage showed hooded protesters throwing objects into fires as police stood nearby. A Palestinian flag was also visible at the demonstrations.
Riot police responded to the disturbances with tear gas, water cannons and baton charges. Authorities stressed that the main trade union demonstration had remained peaceful and said the groups responsible for the violence were not affiliated with the organized march.
The student protesters joined a broader wave of industrial action organized by Belgian trade unions, which are demanding that the government raise taxes on the country's highest earners rather than increase value-added tax or impose cuts to public services, including education and healthcare.
"Things are getting worse at an ever-faster rate; people have had enough. Like the teachers, the pupils can also see that conditions are deteriorating," union representative Luc Toussaint said.
Rising living costs fuel anger
Belgium has experienced repeated strikes in recent months over Prime Minister Bart De Wever's efforts to save 10 billion euros in the coming years to reduce the country's substantial budget deficit.
The proposed austerity measures have intensified public frustration over rising living costs, with demonstrators accusing the government of placing the greatest burden on households already struggling financially.
"Everything just keeps getting more expensive. I don't even dare look at the pump anymore when I fill up my car," one protester told local media.
"Take the money from where it is. I support a tax on billionaires. They always demand more money from people who barely have anything left."
Friday's strike disrupted services across Belgium, including public transportation, schools and air travel. Brussels Airport was forced to cancel around 140 arriving and departing flights after employees of a ground-handling and baggage services company joined the industrial action.
The unrest in Brussels followed days of student demonstrations in the Belgian city of Liège, where clashes with police and incidents of vandalism prompted authorities to restrict public gatherings. More than 200 people were arrested there, and dozens of officers were injured.
France reports nearly 6,900 people detained, most of them minors
Meanwhile, in France, where student protests have shaken cities and towns for nearly two weeks, most students returned to classrooms on Friday, although tensions remained high.
Tens of thousands of demonstrators have taken to the streets across the country since late September, when high school students began blocking entrances to schools in protest against deteriorating conditions in the education system.
The protesters, most of them between 15 and 18 years old, have complained about chronic teacher shortages, overloaded timetables, poorly maintained classrooms and school buildings unable to cope with increasingly high temperatures.
France's Justice Ministry reported Friday that 6,877 people had been taken into police custody since the unrest began, with minors accounting for 86% of the total.
Although most demonstrations have remained peaceful, some have escalated into violence, with protesters setting fires and vandalizing bus shelters and other public property.
Police have responded with tear gas, batons and stun grenades, prompting human rights organizations to accuse authorities of using excessive force against young demonstrators.
The controversy intensified on Monday when a 15-year-old boy lost his hand after a police-fired stun grenade exploded during a confrontation in the northern city of Lens. The government subsequently suspended the use of the weapon at student protests pending an investigation.
The incident further inflamed anger over police tactics and added pressure on the government to address the students' demands.
French government promises thousands of substitute teachers
In an effort to ease the crisis, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced that approximately 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to cover staff shortages at 114 high schools affected by the protests.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also pledged to present a comprehensive plan to address the education crisis by the end of October.
Economy Minister Roland Lescure said there was room to accommodate demands for additional school funding in next year's budget, despite the country's financial constraints.
The promises come as France's government faces growing pressure to improve conditions in public schools and address allegations of excessive police force against teenage protesters, while the unrest that began in French classrooms continues to inspire demonstrations beyond the country's borders.

Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
- Published
Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.
The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.
As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.
He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.
His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.
With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.
But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.
Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

October 8: The war Israel still has not learned to fight - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:29:40 UTC
07:29:40 KST

On Wednesday, October 7, like many Israelis, my wife and I made the long drive from Jerusalem to the Nova music festival memorial. We wanted to offer support to families whose tears, understandably, have not dried up three years later.
We met the ZAKA commander who led teams recovering human remains from the devastated festival grounds. With extraordinary dignity, he described what his teams encountered and carefully showed us what was appropriate to see.
A crowd gathered. Fighting back tears, he asked everyone to stand together, united as one nation.
On our drive home, his words stayed with me.
Because as Israel approaches another election, we are doing something we do extraordinarily well.
We are fighting among ourselves.
Who knew what exactly, before October 7? What did Netanyahu know? Which agencies and/or intelligence officers failed? Who ignored the warnings? Why are these accusations only appearing now before the elections? Why, three years later, are we still fighting over a credible commission of inquiry?
These questions demand answers. Accountability is essential. But instead of allowing October 7 to strengthen our common purpose, we risk turning its memory into another political battlefield.
Meanwhile, we are overlooking something potentially more consequential.
October 8.
Two dates. Two different wars.
October 7 was a catastrophic failure within a world Israel understands.
Israel knows armies, terrorism, intelligence, deterrence, and military technology. We built an extraordinary defense ecosystem: the IDF, Mossad, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), defense industries, reserves, intelligence organizations, and alliances.
That ecosystem failed catastrophically. But we understand how to repair it.
October 7 revealed the failure of an ecosystem Israel already knew it needed since its inception.
October 8 revealed something entirely different.
An ecosystem we had never adequately built.
Before Israel’s military response in Gaza could explain the international reaction, anti-Israel demonstrations and narratives were already spreading.
The vocabulary of colonialism, apartheid and resistance was ready. Campus organizations, activists, influencers and digital networks were prepared to mobilize.
This did not require one giant conspiracy.
It required an ecosystem.
Foreign governments fund academics who produce ideas. Activists translate them. Organizations create campaigns. Influencers generate content. Algorithms amplify it. Demonstrations produce images. Media broadcast them. Politicians respond.
And the cycle accelerates.
Sinwar’s victory beyond the battlefield
Yahya Sinwar did not launch October 7 expecting Israel to remain passive.
He knew Israel would retaliate. He accepted the prospect of devastating consequences for Gaza while seeking a confrontation that could ignite additional fronts.
In effect, he launched a suicidal strategic gamble, sacrificing Hamas’s military position and exposing Gaza’s population to catastrophic consequences in pursuit of a larger objective.
Sinwar and his colleagues were killed. Hamas suffered enormous military losses. But we should not confuse military defeat with defeat on every battlefield.
Sinwar achieved a consequential victory in the battle for international perception.
Whether he anticipated every dimension of the international response is debatable. What is undeniable is that a preexisting pro-Palestinian ecosystem was capable of exploiting the war at extraordinary speed.
And where were we?
Still explaining. Still correcting. Still reacting.
A September 2026 Marquette Law School national poll found that 59% of Americans now view Israel unfavorably, compared with just 29% favorably. Only 18 months earlier, Americans were evenly divided, 43% to 43%.
It is a dramatic deterioration in Israel’s standing among the American public. The consequences are for the political and social environment in which American Jews must live, and for Israel’s ability to manage current American government support.
Not all this change can be attributed to propaganda. Israel’s decisions, the war’s humanitarian consequences, and changing American attitudes matter. But that makes our strategic failure more urgent, not less.
We failed to build a sufficiently competitive ecosystem before the crisis arrived.
Israel’s decisions do not stop at Israel’s borders
There is another dimension Israelis cannot afford to ignore.
When Israel acts, Jews in New York, London, Paris, Toronto and Sydney often experience the consequences.
Israel’s policies and military decisions become subjects of international debate. But increasingly, anger directed at Israel spills into a cover for antisemitic hostility toward Jewish students, synagogues, businesses and communities with no responsibility for those decisions.
Our adversaries exploit that vulnerability.
Their opportunity is to transform opposition to Israeli policies into opposition to Zionism, and opposition to Zionism into hostility toward Jews who identify with Israel.
The result can drive a wedge between Israel and Diaspora Jewry.
Some Diaspora Jews become increasingly uncomfortable defending Israel. Others fear that distancing themselves from Israel means abandoning a fundamental part of Jewish identity.
This is precisely the fragmentation our adversaries planned to exploit.
We cannot expect Diaspora Jews to defend every Israeli government decision.
But we must recognize that Israel’s security, Jewish identity, and the safety of Jewish communities worldwide are increasingly interconnected.
The battlefield of October 8 has no geographic borders.
Stop fighting fire with water
For decades, our preferred response has been hasbara (public diplomacy).
A lie? Correct it.
A hostile documentary? Challenge it.
A viral accusation? Provide the facts.
I call this fighting fire with the purity of water.
Water is necessary. Truth matters.
But what happens when the fire is a wildfire? Worse, what happens when it sits above a gas field, continuously replenishing the fuel?
Governments like Qatar, ideological movements, donors, media networks, and digital platforms continue supplying energy.
We extinguish one flame. Another appears.
We need to stop asking only where the fire is and start asking where the valves are.
The lesson from Bill Gates
Bill Gates and the global vaccine initiative Gavi (originally the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization) provide an unexpected example.
They did not simply purchase more vaccines. They examined why the entire system wasn’t delivering the desired results.
Then they identified catalytic leverage points: financing, procurement, market incentives, manufacturing, and distribution.
They didn’t need to own the ecosystem.
They needed to change how it functioned.
The Jewish world should be asking the same question.
We don’t lack money, leadership, institutions, intelligence, or talent.
We lack persistent interoperability.
Religious and secular. Left and Right. Israeli and Diaspora. Jews supporting Palestinian statehood and Jews convinced it threatens Israel’s existence.
We are, as the Bible observed, a stiff-necked people.
Perhaps our mistake has been pursuing unity where interoperability is what we need.
Unity says: We agree.
Coordination says: We will work together.
Interoperability says: We can disagree and still make one another stronger.
NATO demonstrates the principle. Its members disagree politically but maintain common standards, intelligence relationships, operational capabilities, and mission-critical responsibilities.
Why shouldn’t Israel and Diaspora Jewish institutions develop a similar hybrid approach?
Shared threat intelligence. Early-warning networks. Coordinated research. Trusted non-Jewish partners. Cultural engagement. Digital capabilities. Investment in approaches that demonstrate results.
Not another organization competing for the same donors.
An architecture that makes existing organizations more effective together.
And one minimum common mission:
Whatever else divides us, we will cooperate to protect Jewish lives, Jewish identity, and Israel’s right to exist securely.
Preventing the next October 7
The danger is not confined to Israel.
The next October 7 may not resemble the last. Its perpetrators, weapons, and targets may be different.
A mass-casualty antisemitic attack could occur in Israel, New York, London, Paris, or elsewhere. We cannot predict where. We can recognize why preparedness must be global; the recent Fly Dubai hijacking is a case in point.
Our enemies are adapting. Are we?
October 7 demonstrated that Jews can overcome extraordinary divisions when catastrophe strikes.
But why must we wait for catastrophe?
The ZAKA commander’s appeal for unity should not fade when the memorial ceremonies end.
We owe the victims remembrance. We owe ourselves accountability.
And we owe future generations something more.
October 7 showed us what happens when an ecosystem we built fails.
October 8 warns us what happens when the ecosystem we need has not yet been built.
If we truly want to prevent the next October 7, perhaps it is time we finally learned how to fight October 8, by building our ecosystem.
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn2020

22:29:33 UTC
07:29:33 KST

Analysis of animal DNA extracted from medieval manuscripts has allowed researchers to trace the nearly 4,000-year history of the sheeppox virus, according to a recently study published in Science Advances.
Sheeppox is a highly contagious disease that can spread rapidly throughout a flock, causing high mortality rates, as well as damaging wool, meat, and milk yields.
Among the works analyzed were the York Gospels, from the early Anglo-Saxon period, and the Corpus Glossary of Corpus Christi College Cambridge, one of the earliest English dictionaries.
In several cases, multiple pages from the same manuscript were found to contain sheeppox virus DNA, indicating that infected animals were used in their production.
“The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA,” explained Louis L’Hôte, PhD candidate at University College Dublin (UCD) and lead author of the study. “It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past.”
“These genomes help us understand how these pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies - such as sheeppox virus, which we show has been affecting Eurasian sheep herds for at least three and a half millennia.”
Cross-species infection or parchment contamination?
One of the most unexpected findings was the detection of sheeppox on parchment made from calfskin and goatskin, according to the study, suggesting that either a rare example of cross-species infection or contamination during the parchment-making process.
“Parchment making has been considered a vanishing craft, but we are beginning to understand just how much of the past it has retained,” said UCD School of Agriculture and Food Science Associate Professor Kevin G. Daly, who also serves as the study’s supervising author. This project shows that parchments not only preserve our cultural history for hundreds of years, but also the landscape of disease in our livestock in the medieval period.”
“This kind of exciting, surprising discovery is only possible when researchers from a range of disciplines come together to share their expertise and data - a generosity and trust that collaborative science depends on.”
Sheeppox around for over 3,700 years
Additionally, by combining the analysis of these medievial manuscripts alongside Bronze Age sheep teeth samples, researchers found that sheepox has been around for over 3,700 years.
By combining the study of manuscripts with even older samples from Bronze Age sheep teeth, the study reveals that Sheeppox has threatened livestock for over 3,700 years.
Unlike other skeletal material, teeth can preserve genetic evidence of infection over thousands of years, explained the study, in turn providing a valuable record of ancient outbreaks.
The earliest known detections of sheeppox virus came from livestock dental remains unearthed at ancient pastoralist settlements in the Eurasian steppe.
By comparing ancient and modern virus sequences, researchers were able to estimate that the sheeppox virus, goatpox virus, and lumpy skin disease virus, which all come from the same virus lineage, diverged between 11,500 and 3,700 years ago.
“People around the world are still fighting against this pathogen, there is currently an outbreak of sheeppox in Greece, causing much economic damage,” said L’Hôte.
“Ancient genomes can help us understand how these pathogens affecting us today evolved. We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia.”
L’Hôte added that the discovery may prove the importance of genetic changes before this point were crucial to how sheepox infects its hosts, “which may help us fight the pathogen in the future.”
The study was funded by Taighde Éireann-Research Ireland and the European Research Council, and led by University College Dublin, in collaboration with over 30 Irish and international institutions including Trinity College Dublin, the Helmholtz Institute for One Health, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, the University of Leicester, Cambridge University, and the University of Copenhagen.

‘History will judge’: ICC defies sweeping US sanctions as allies rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:23:42 UTC
07:23:42 KST

Countries around the world condemned the United States on Friday over its decision to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, expressing concern about the consequences while reaffirming their support for the tribunal and pledging to ensure it can continue operating despite the restrictions imposed by Washington.
The ICC itself strongly condemned the move, rejecting the sanctions and urging its member states to take steps to safeguard its operations. In a statement, the court described the measures as an attempt to obstruct justice and prevent it from fulfilling its mandate.
"This is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do," the statement said. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order."
The court stressed that it would continue fulfilling its mandate to prosecute individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression when national authorities are unwilling or unable to do so.
"The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the States that created it," the statement said, warning that the dispute extended far beyond the future of a single institution.
The ICC said the international community now faced a test of its commitment to the legal order it had established. "History will judge this moment," it warned.
The American sanctions target the court, which was established under the Rome Statute, as an institution. They include freezing its assets and property interests under U.S. jurisdiction and restricting transactions involving those assets by American individuals and companies or through the U.S. financial system.
Although the designation was announced Friday, a series of licenses issued by the U.S. Treasury Department will allow certain transactions and routine operations to continue for 180 days, delaying much of the practical impact of the restrictions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who sharply criticized the court and threatened to dismantle it, also signaled that Washington was leaving room for negotiations.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio warned, accusing the tribunal of exceeding its authority and threatening American sovereignty.
At the same time, Rubio said Washington remained hopeful that a diplomatic solution could be reached. He explained that the measures had been structured to give the court's member states an opportunity to negotiate and propose a solution addressing American concerns.
"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns," he said, warning that Washington would continue adjusting its measures if those efforts failed.
Global condemnation, deep concern and calls to protect the court
Among the strongest diplomatic responses was a joint statement issued by the foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.
The eight countries reaffirmed their unwavering support for the court's independence, impartiality and integrity, while warning that the American measures could have far-reaching consequences.
"If put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families," the ministers said.
They emphasized that ICC employees work every day to bring people accused of the world's most serious international crimes to justice and provide support to victims.
The ministers also pledged to remain united in defending the court and to engage in constructive dialogue with countries that are not parties to the Rome Statute.
The European Union issued its own condemnation, describing the American decision as deeply regrettable and promising to work closely with the ICC to ensure it could continue operating effectively.
The European Commission said the bloc remained committed to protecting the court's independence and was prepared to take whatever measures were necessary to allow it to fulfill its mission.
Brussels also pointed to the six-month transition period as an opportunity to pursue negotiations with Washington.
"As there is a six-month delay before the measures are applicable, there is room for dialogue," the commission said.
It added that the EU was ready to take necessary steps to enable the ICC to continue investigating and prosecuting war crimes and crimes against humanity, while also protecting European businesses and other entities from the effects of the sanctions.
Belgium adopted a particularly forceful position.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot strongly condemned the new sanctions and urged the European Union to activate its Blocking Statute, a legal mechanism designed to protect European individuals and businesses from the extraterritorial application of certain foreign laws.
The mechanism could potentially help shield European entities from the American restrictions, allowing financial and other support for the court to continue despite Washington's measures.
If activated to cover the new sanctions, the mechanism could provide a legal basis for European entities to resist complying with specified U.S. restrictions, although its effectiveness would depend on how the protections were applied.
Prévot called for concrete European action to defend the institution and those supporting its work.
"The Court's independence cannot depend on whom it investigates," he said.
"Europe must act," he added, urging the activation of the EU Blocking Statute.
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres also condemned the American move, expressing deep concern about its expected consequences for the ICC and its ability to carry out its responsibilities.
Guterres, whose term as UN secretary-general ends in December, warned that the sanctions could undermine the court's work, including cases referred to it by the UN Security Council and countries that are parties to the Rome Statute.
"Today's decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar," he said in a statement issued through his spokesperson.
Guterres emphasized that accountability for international crimes and justice for victims were essential elements of the international community's commitment to peace, security, human rights and fundamental freedoms.
He reiterated his unwavering support for the independence of the court and its officials, calling on all countries to uphold their obligations under international law and support efforts to ensure accountability for the gravest crimes.
The UN, he added, remained committed to cooperating with the ICC under the relationship agreement approved by the General Assembly on September 13, 2004.
Meanwhile, the Palestinian Authority welcomed the decision to award the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay, who led a UN commission that concluded in a report last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry praised what it described as the well-deserved recognition of Pillay, commending her work defending oppressed communities.
"Throughout her distinguished career, she has sought truth and defended the rights of the oppressed in South Africa and around the world, including in Palestine, with integrity, courage and dignity," the ministry said in a statement.

Canada's employment declines in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:14:12 CST
07:14:12 KST

OTTAWA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Canada's employment declined by 68,000, or 0.3 percent, in September and the employment rate fell by 0.2 percentage points to 60.6 percent, Statistics Canada said Friday.
According to the national statistical agency, the employment decline was concentrated among youth aged 15 to 24 as well as women aged 25 to 54. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate edged up by 0.1 percentage points to 6.5 percent.
The labor force participation rate -- the proportion of the population aged 15 and older who were employed or looking for work -- fell by 0.2 percentage points to 64.8 percent in September, the lowest level since December 1997, excluding 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, said the agency.
Year on year, the participation rate was down 0.4 percentage points in September, largely reflecting population aging, the agency added.
In September, people aged 65 and older accounted for 23.2 percent of Canada's working-age population, up from 20.5 percent in September 2019.
Population aging is expected to continue to exert downward pressure on labor supply in the coming years, said Statistics Canada. ■

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10

BELGRADE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The Confucius Institute in Belgrade celebrated its 20th anniversary on Friday, bringing together Chinese and Serbian representatives from the education and cultural sectors, along with teachers and students, to mark two decades of Chinese language education and cultural exchanges.
Han Dianxiu, education counselor at the Chinese Embassy in Serbia, said at the ceremony that the institute, the first Confucius Institute established in the Balkans, had opened a new chapter in language and cultural exchanges between China and Serbia.
Over the past two decades, the institute has trained numerous Chinese-speaking professionals who have gone on to work in the fields of diplomacy, education, culture and in Chinese companies, becoming an important force in promoting cooperation and exchanges between the two countries, Han said.
Li Xinren, Chinese director of the institute, said that more and more Serbian people have come to know China through learning the Chinese language, gaining a deeper understanding of Chinese culture through study and exchanges. He said Shandong University was ready to take the anniversary as an opportunity to further strengthen exchanges among teachers and students and expand practical cooperation with the University of Belgrade and other Serbian partners.
Radosav Pusic, Serbian director of the institute, said the institute currently operates 16 teaching sites across three Serbian cities, covering one university, four secondary schools and 11 primary schools, in addition to its main center at Faculty of Philology of Belgrade University and a Confucius Classroom at the Philological High School in Belgrade.
Over the past 20 years, the institute has recorded 17,130 student enrollments and organized more than 600 cultural events, offering local residents opportunities to learn Chinese and explore Chinese culture, Pusic said.
The anniversary celebration, held at the historic Manak's House in Belgrade, featured an art exhibition titled "Encounter with China," showcasing calligraphy, paintings, photographs and handicrafts created by students of the institute. An award ceremony and cultural performances were also held.
Pavle Maksimovic, a 26-year-old Serbian painter who visited the exhibition, told Xinhua that the artworks on display had left a deep impression on him. He said seeing Serbian people learn Chinese calligraphy and express their understanding of Chinese culture through art gave him a greater appreciation of cultural exchanges between China and Serbia. ■

China
Unknown Publisher

06:13:32 CST
07:13:32 KST

PANAMA CITY, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- A 7.2-magnitude earthquake struck Panama on Friday, with its epicenter 39 kilometers northwest of Tonosi, a town in Los Santos province, according to a revised report from the University of Panama's Institute of Geosciences.
Strong shaking was felt locally. Videos shared on social media showed the roof of the Albrook bus terminal swaying and windows shaking violently in several buildings.
Tremors were felt in the capital, Panama City, a Xinhua correspondent in the city reported, with strong side-to-side jolts while sitting and a hanging light in a room swaying intensely.
The United States Geological Survey, which initially reported a magnitude of 8.0, later revised its estimate to 7.7.
The U.S. Tsunami Warning System issued a tsunami threat following the earthquake, warning that hazardous tsunami waves were possible along parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico within the next three hours. The U.S. tsunami warning was later revoked.
The tsunami warning department of the Chilean Navy's Hydrographic and Oceanographic Service issued an alert, saying the earthquake could trigger a tsunami affecting the country's Easter Island.
The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally after the earthquake struck. Emergency protocols had been activated, and technical teams were inspecting canal facilities for possible damage, it said in a statement.
Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino urged the public to remain calm in a post on X.
"What happened must not be used to spread alarm and disorder," he wrote.
Mulino added that he had asked Government Minister Dinoska Montalvo for a report on the earthquake's impact.
The Education Ministry suspended afternoon classes at all schools nationwide. Its administrative offices would also remain closed. ■

Chemists, wholesalers may need government nod to advertise prescription drugs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:05:43 UTC
07:05:43 KST

NEW DELHI: Chemists, wholesalers and drug distributors may soon have to seek Centre's approval before advertising certain prescription medicines, with health ministry proposing to extend existing curbs on advertisements of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs to those involved in their sale and distribution.
The proposal assumes significance as regulators have raised concerns over promotion of potent prescription medicines, including antibiotics, hormonal preparations, psychotropic drugs, anti-cancer medicines, narcotic drugs and life-saving injectables.
The ministry has now proposed inserting a new sub-rule under Rule 65 of Drugs Rules, 1945, stating no advertisement of drugs specified in Schedule H, H1 or X shall be made without previous sanction of central govt. The provision would apply to those holding licences to sell, stock, exhibit, offer for sale or distribute such drugs.
Importantly, the proposal does not mean that advertisements of these medicines are currently freely permitted. Drugs and Cosmetics Rules already require prior govt sanction for advertisements of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs.

CubaFruta: A Cooperative Initiative Strengthening Production on the Island
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
00:02:23 CEST
07:02:23 KST

Producers, municipal governments, scientific institutions, universities, cooperatives, and decision-makers gathered in Havana to share the results of CubaFruta, an initiative of Italian Cooperation that has worked for several years to strengthen the pineapple and avocado supply chains in four municipalities of Matanzas (Los Arabos, Colón, Calimete, and Jagüey Grande).
                                    
The project, with a budget of 2,500,000 euros—according to a statement from the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation —has contributed to strengthening fruit production, processing, and marketing, benefiting over 1,400 members of cooperatives and production entities in the involved territories.
                                    
During the opening of the final workshop, the Italian Ambassador to Cuba, Simona De Martino, emphasized that “CubaFruta has promoted solutions to strengthen environmental sustainability and energy resilience. In a complex context, focusing on models less dependent on conventional sources is not merely a technological investment, but a choice that supports the continuity and adaptability of these regions.”
      From the fields where food is produced daily for Cuban families to forums for technical and institutional exchange, the project has promoted a development model based on a network of collaboration among municipalities, which has enabled the creation of shared strategies to address production, commercial, and technological challenges.
                                    
As Heberto Soto Ravelo, production manager at the UBPC Gispert in Colón, stated: “Without the project, we probably wouldn’t have established any alliances at the local level. We’ve remained constantly connected, we continue to work together, and we owe this to CubaFruta.”
     From its launch—marked by restrictions on mobility and operational activities due to COVID-19—through to its conclusion in a context characterized by significant challenges, CubaFruta has maintained its commitment to strengthening local production chains. In this particularly complex scenario —the statement concludes—pineapple production in the target municipalities rose from 5,600 metric tons in 2020 to over 6,000 metric tons in 2025, while the cultivated area increased from 990 to over 1,100 hectares.

Lockheed Martin unveils PAC-3 Edge interceptor to counter hypersonic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:00:45 UTC
07:00:45 KST

Lockheed Martin has unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a missile interceptor designed to defend against hypersonic and advanced missile threats, as the US military looks to strengthen its capabilities to counter emerging aerial threats.
Growing demand for air and missile defence systems amid conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East has strained US weapons stockpiles, prompting the US Army to award Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $58.6 billion in July to ramp up production of PAC-3 interceptors.
Lockheed Martin said PAC-3 Edge incorporates a new seeker, upgraded flight controls and a multi-pulse rocket motor supplied by Northrop Grumman, enhancing the interceptor's ability to counter advanced threats, including hypersonic missiles, at longer ranges and higher altitudes.
"The cost of this would be about that of the existing PAC-3 MSE," Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control at Lockheed Martin, told Reuters news agency.
"At full production, the annual rate would be about 2,000 units a year, comparable with PAC-3 MSE."
"Lockheed Martin's PAC-3 Edge interceptor leverages the combat-proven PAC-3 MSE, delivering even greater maneuverability, power and velocity to ensure the Army's layered defensive architecture remains the most advanced in the world," added Cahill.
In January, Lockheed Martin signed a seven-year framework agreement with the US Department of Defense to expand production of its PAC-3 missile interceptors, aiming to increase annual manufacturing capacity to 2,000 units from about 600.
Lockheed Martin said it will advance development and begin testing PAC-3 Edge in 2027 to prepare for rapid deployment by 2031.

Mexican court finds three men guilty of 2024 killing of Australian, US surfers
MEXICO CITY, Oct 9 - A Mexican judge on Friday found three men guilty of the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend during a surf trip to the state of Baja California, a source at the court told Reuters.
Jesus Gerardo Garcia, known as "El Kekas," and the co-defendants identified simply as Irineo Francisco "N" and Angel Jesus "N," were found guilty of aggravated homicide, violent robbery and vehicle theft by a Baja California court.
The prosecution had sought sentences of up to 150 years against the suspects. According to the same source at the state court, the sentence will be announced on October 16.
Brothers Callum, 33, and Jake Robinson, 30, and American Jack Carter Rhoad, 30, were camping and surfing near Punta San Jose, about 80 km (50 miles) south of Ensenada, when they were reported missing in late April 2024.
After a days-long search, aided by the FBI, their bodies were found on May 3 at the bottom of a well. The victims were each found with gunshot wounds in the head, authorities said.
Prosecutors said the accused had attempted to carjack the tourists, who were shot when they tried to resist. Their truck was later found burned nearby.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the Robinsons' parents, traveled from their hometown of Perth to attend the four-week trial. Rhoad's widowed fiancee, Natalie Weirtz, spoke via video call from the United States.
In November 2025 Gisell Silva, Garcia's then-girlfriend, was sentenced to 20 years in prison for her involvement in the case. The woman, who was 23 at the time, was arrested a few days after the bodies of the victims were found.
While the Ensenada area is considered relatively safe, Baja California ranks among Mexico’s most violent states. Following the killings, the US State Department urged Americans to reconsider travel to the state due to crime and kidnapping risks. REUTERS

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday criticized New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over the city’s sanctuary policies following a shooting involving an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer that left a 28-year-old immigrant wounded.
The incident took place Thursday when an ICE officer shot Oscar Belgal, a Dominican Republic national, in the neck while he was driving with a 5-year-old child in the vehicle. Belgal was taken to a nearby hospital, while the child was unharmed and remained with a family member, according to information provided by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Speaking at a news conference with ICE officials, Mullin defended the federal government’s immigration enforcement policies and accused Mamdani of using political rhetoric that could increase hostility toward federal officers.
"I am speaking facts; the mayor speaks with political tone,” Mullin said. “His words are dangerous and incite hostility; it doesn’t help."
Mullin argued that sanctuary policies undermine public safety by limiting cooperation between local authorities and federal immigration officials.
“I want to make it very clear: sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe,” he said.
“If you actually want justice, you should want justice for actually everyone,” Mullin added. “It's shameful that you have a mayor that goes out there and puts criminals over law-abiding citizens.”
 
‘Incredibly serious situation,’ says Mayor Mamdani
Mullin said he spoke with Mamdani several times Thursday night about Belgal, alleging that the mayor wanted federal authorities to release the man without ensuring he remained in custody.
According to Mullin, President Donald Trump intervened and indicated that Belgal could be transferred to the New York Police Department if local authorities are willing to pursue charges against him.
“If sanctuary politicians refuse to take care of their own streets, President Trump has made it very clear we will,” Mullin said. “This individual is a threat to our community.”
Mamdani condemned the shooting on Thursday and called for an end to ICE enforcement operations in New York City.
“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” the mayor said.
He added that he planned to speak with Trump and demand that the administration end federal immigration enforcement actions in the city.
“I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities,” Mamdani said.
Since the start of US President Trump’s second term, ICE has expanded and stepped up its enforcement operations, including a number of incidents with casualties, drawing criticism from Democrats and some local leaders.
The Trump administration says it is targeting illegal immigrants who have broken the law, arguing they constitute a threat to law and order.

Zacharia was a frequent join Fox News commentator, often promoting or defending the US president’s policies while harshly criticizing Democrats.

UK bans Protestant march from Catholic area in Northern Ireland

UK bans Protestant march from Catholic area in Northern Ireland
After a 13-day standoff in Portadown, the reversal thrills Irish republicans and enrages Northern Ireland’s unionists, who had hoped to complete a parade blocked since 1998.
DUBLIN — The U.K. government has reversed a decision to permit a parade by Protestant hard-liners through a Catholic district in Northern Ireland, a U-turn that overjoyed Irish republicans and infuriated the region’s British unionists.
After a nearly two-week standoff in the predominantly Protestant town of Portadown, Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant announced late Friday that the Orange Order would not be allowed to parade through the town’s main Catholic district for the first time in 28 years.
The Orange Order, a Protestant fraternal group reviled by many Catholics, had been barred from the route since 1998 following years of widespread violence triggered by the annual sectarian showdown.
Advertisement
“I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions,” Bryant appealed in a statement explaining why he was reversing the original decision by the Parades Commission, Northern Ireland’s independent body for managing the region’s chronic conflicts over Orange Order demonstrations.
Street fighting over those traditional marches helped to trigger the onset of Northern Ireland’s three-decade conflict, known as “The Troubles,” which left nearly 3,700 dead before a 1998 peace accord.
Hundreds of Catholic locals backed by Sinn Féin, the Irish republican party that leads Northern Ireland’s fraying cross-community government, gathered along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown to cheer the reversal.
First Minister Michelle O’Neill, who has been accused of breaking the law while helping locals block the Orangemen’s intended path since Sept. 27, went on Ireland’s flagship TV talk show, the Late Late Show, to express relief on behalf of the residents of Garvaghy Road.
“For the last 13 days they’ve been living with this constant fear and a cloud hanging over them that this unwanted sectarian march was going to be forced down that road,” she said.
But the main pro-British party in the coalition, the Democratic Unionists, denounced Bryant’s move as a capitulation to mob rule. Some DUP lawmakers called for Northern Ireland’s police chief, who had recommended the policy reversal, to be fired.
Democratic Unionist leader Gavin Robinson said the U.K. government had sent a dangerous message that Northern Ireland “should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest.”
Northern Ireland’s nearly three-decade system for managing conflict over parades “now lies in tatters,” he said, “and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.”

====================================================================================================

Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:36:18 UTC
06:36:18 KST

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.
At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”
Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”
Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.
An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.
Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.
“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.
The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.
In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.
Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.
The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.
“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.
Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.
Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.
The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.
Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.
This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”
When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.
Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”
