Strong earthquake shakes Panama, prompting tsunami alert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:03:00 UTC
04:03:00 KST

Strong earthquakes, aftershocks shake Panama
October 9, 2026
A powerful magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck Panama on Friday morning.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the quake's epicenter was located approximately 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama's southern tip.
The quake struck at a depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.
The USGS later reported that a second powerful earthquake, measuring 6.6 in magnitude, struck the country following a series of aftershocks.
The tremors were strongly felt in the capital Panama City, causing buildings to shake and sending people rushing into the streets.
"We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're okay, though we're very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared."
Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino described the earthquake as a "major disaster" which had destroyed roads near the epicenter.
What do we know about damage?
Mulino did not say whether there were any casualties.
According to Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service, damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.
Smith reported several injuries, as well as partial collapses and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage to the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.
Meanwhile, local news outlets reported that the colonial-style Church of San Atanasio in Panama’s Los Santos province collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.
Tsunami warning lifted
The US Tsunami Warning System issued an alert stating that hazardous tsunami waves were possible along parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico within the next three hours.
The system also reported a tsunami threat to Hawaii. The warning was lifted later on Friday afternoon.
Initially, there were no reports of damage to the Panama Canal. The Panama Canal Authority stated that the waterway was operating as usual.
Tocumen International Airport in Panama City briefly suspended operations and activated evacuation protocols before reopening later on Friday afternoon.
Panama is located along the so-called "Ring of Fire," a line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

Russia Keeps Striking Ukraine’s Energy Grid—Now It Wants Sanctions Relief to Stop, Report Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:01:17 UTC
04:01:17 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Keeps Striking Ukraine’s Energy Grid—Now It Wants Sanctions Relief to Stop, Report Says
Russia is seeking sanctions relief from the United States in exchange for a possible agreement to suspend attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, while also pushing to include a ceasefire in the Black Sea as part of a wider arrangement.
According to The Kyiv Independent report on October 9, citing American and Ukrainian officials familiar with the discussions, Moscow has privately signaled that it could consider an energy ceasefire but is seeking additional concessions before agreeing to the proposal.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s demands emerge amid an escalation of strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities, which have left communities across the country facing significant electricity disruptions.
A senior Ukrainian defense official told the publication that Moscow is attempting to cause as much damage as possible to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure to improve its bargaining position ahead of potential negotiations.
While discussions over a possible agreement continue behind closed doors, Russian officials have publicly expressed little interest in suspending attacks on energy infrastructure.
According to The Kyiv Independent, on October 8, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed the prospect of negotiating a ceasefire limited to the energy sector.
“Kyiv is not currently proposing a long-term settlement, but rather a ceasefire in an area that is its Achilles' heel—the energy sector,” Peskov said.
Nevertheless, two Ukrainian officials and one American official told The Kyiv Independent that Moscow had privately indicated a willingness to consider the initiative, although it was linking any potential agreement to further demands.
Washington has been urging both Kyiv and Moscow to stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure, with the proposal emerging as a key element of US-led efforts to advance negotiations.
Several Ukrainian officials also indicated that US President Donald Trump is seeking tangible diplomatic progress on Ukraine ahead of the upcoming American midterm elections.
Following their most recent trip to Russia, Trump’s representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly concluded that an agreement to suspend strikes on energy facilities remained possible.
The proposal was also raised during two visits to the United States in September by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who held discussions with Witkoff and Kushner. According to US and Ukrainian officials briefed on those meetings, Dmitriev made clear that Moscow wanted sanctions restrictions eased as part of any potential deal.
However, the precise measures Russia is seeking to have lifted have not been identified. Ukrainian officials familiar with the negotiations acknowledged that sanctions relief had been raised but said they remained unaware of which specific restrictions Moscow wanted removed.
One European diplomat informed about the discussions suggested that Russia might be seeking the release of frozen Russian assets as part of the arrangement.
“If they get sanctioned funds released… the likelihood that these will be used to escalate (war) is almost guaranteed,” the diplomat told The Kyiv Independent. “No one really thinks they are genuinely seeking to adhere to a ceasefire.”
Moscow’s demands are expected to become a subject of further discussions between Ukraine and the United States as diplomatic efforts continue.
A Ukrainian delegation is due to meet with Trump’s representatives in the United States on October 9 to examine proposals for suspending attacks on energy infrastructure and establishing a ceasefire in the Black Sea, the outlet reported.
The Ukrainian officials are also expected to be briefed on Washington’s recent contacts with Moscow and request further details about the sanctions relief Russia is seeking in exchange for a potential agreement.
The discussions come amid a separate diplomatic initiative by the Trump administration that could also involve easing sanctions against Russia. The Atlantic reported on September 29 that Washington was considering offering Moscow sanctions relief in exchange for the release of political prisoners, potentially creating an opportunity to restore economic ties between the two countries despite Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
The proposal was developed by Trump’s envoy to Eastern Europe, John Coale, who reportedly presented the initiative to the US president several months earlier. Trump is said to have approved the proposal, although the initiative remains in its preliminary stages.

Germany Concerned About Threat Russian Satellites Pose to Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:57:52 UTC
03:57:52 KST

The ability of Russian satellites to perform coordinated active maneuvers raises concerns about a potential attack on Starlink satellites.
Major General Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, spoke about this in an interview with Reuters.
According to him, in May 2026, a group of Russian military satellites tracked a Western satellite assisting Ukraine, demonstrating capabilities that could threaten commercial satellite constellations.
General Traut stated that a direct attack on a Starlink satellite would constitute a significant escalation, but Moscow could employ gray zone tactics.
He described a hypothetical scenario in which a Russian satellite would shift into Starlink’s orbital path and then break up into debris. This would force the satellites to perform evasive maneuvers, consuming fuel and potentially shortening their operational lifespan.
According to the U.S. Space Force, in May, Russia maneuvered four military satellites — Cosmos 2610–2613 — bringing them closer to a commercial radar imaging satellite operated by the Finnish company ICEYE.
ICEYE CEO Rafal Modzewski told Reuters that the company subsequently changed the position of its satellite, after which the Russian satellites performed additional maneuvers.
According to him, this incident demonstrated that satellites are increasingly likely to maneuver close to one another to observe or potentially cause damage. Modzewski noted that this incident underscores the need to monitor activity in orbit and raises questions about the need for protection.
According to Western military officials, Russia’s interference with Western space systems has significantly intensified since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
They note that this includes jamming via ground-based assets and in-orbit surveillance to gather intelligence and test the West’s limits of tolerance.
In early September, the U.S. simulated a Russian nuclear explosion in space and its impact on satellites. The simulation shows that the radiation belt created by the explosion could cause 11,000 satellites to fail within a week.
Separately, the authors suggest that Moscow could use a space-based nuclear threat against Starlink to force Washington or SpaceX to limit their support for Ukraine.

18:57:10 UTC
03:57:10 KST

The Fourth Law and Odd Systems have unveiled Project Foundation, a semiconductor initiative to mass-produce uncooled thermal sensors in Europe and the United States.
The companies say the project aims to quadruple European thermal sensor output and double US output within three years, expanding production capacity for defense and civilian applications.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The initiative plans to develop proprietary uncooled long-wave infrared (LWIR) sensors, also known as microbolometers, and manufacture them at scale. The companies say the goal is to strengthen European and US control over thermal sensor supply.
The sensors are intended for drones, cars, factories and robots, with production planned through partner semiconductor foundries and dedicated facilities.
The first two planned fabrication facilities, First Foundation and Second Foundation, would be located in Europe and the United States, respectively. They would share a common technology base and proprietary sensor designs.
Odd Systems develops and manufactures thermal and daytime cameras for drones and other robotic systems. Its flagship product, the Kurbas thermal camera, is supplied to more than 70 Ukrainian drone manufacturers, according to the companies. The Fourth Law builds technologies that enable drones to continue their missions when communications are disrupted, with an initial focus on defense.
Drawing on Isaac Asimov
Both companies were founded by Yaroslav Azhnyuk, whose earlier ventures include Petcube, Fuel Finance and Ozero Design. Petcube has featured in Kyiv Post’s coverage of Ukrainian startups.
Russian Refinery Seeks Air Defense Operators Amid Escalating Drone Strikes
The two companies were established in Kyiv in 2023 with a team of engineers, operators and veterans. They operate across Ukraine, the rest of Europe and the United States.
According to the companies, the founding team has 14 years of camera development experience, including work on more than one million consumer smart cameras.
Project Foundation is headquartered in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, which the companies described as a major European semiconductor technology hub.
“Building thermal cameras has shown us what manufacturers need from the sensor inside: performance, a reliable supply and a price that works at scale,” Project Foundation CEO Igor Nakonechnyi said in the press release.
The companies said the project had attracted interest from investors and partners, with financing arrangements to be announced once confirmed. They did not disclose an investment amount.
The project’s name follows the group’s practice of drawing on Isaac Asimov. The Fourth Law refers to his Laws of Robotics, while Project Foundation draws on the Foundation series and its theme of preserving knowledge through periods of upheaval.

Strong 7.7 magnitude earthquake felt in Panama, Costa Rica, tsunami waves possible, USGS says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:56:03 UTC
03:56:03 KST

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
The US Geological Survey said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 km (7.8 miles), with an epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200 km (124 miles) from the capital, and that some casualties were possible.
In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations, and the Tocumen International Airport lifted a suspension on flights.
Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about getting home in the snarl of traffic after the quake sent thousands into the streets.
Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old employee of the Ministry of Economy, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive.
"They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?"
President Raul Mulino traveled to Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicenter and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged.
Prolonged termors
Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive buildup of pressure that is occasionally released.
"The seismic signals have traveled throughout the national territory, and that is why it could be felt everywhere."
In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors.
Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old US military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged.
"The quake felt strong and lasted a long time, the longest I’ve felt in years,” Rios said.
Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. “It’s a miracle they didn’t get killed,” he said. “They looked like they were swinging in a hammock.”
Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets.
“We’re scared. It’s just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it could fall on us,” said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes.
Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told news outlet Telemetro Reporta that impacts had also been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province.
The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1% to 10% of Panama's gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces.
Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday of next week to test the country's emergency response.
Shipping through the Panama Canal remains uninterrupted
The Panama Canal Authority said the canal was operating normally and that staff were inspecting for earthquake-related damage, later adding that ships are passing through the canal without interruption.
Panama is set to hold a national evacuation drill next Monday to test the country's earthquake response.
Vessel passage at the Panama Canal was not interrupted on Friday after a strong earthquake caused infrastructure damage in the Central American country, the waterway's authority said.
Operations at the canal were normal while technical teams inspected facilities, the authority said in a release, adding that an emergency protocol had been activated.
The quake prompted tsunami warnings for parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico.
About 90 vessels, including bulk carriers, tankers, and container ships, were on Friday at both ends of the canal waiting to pass or to dock at any of the berths serving storage terminals and trans-shipment services, according to monitoring data from LSEG's Workspace.

A third Il-96, with registration number RA-96025, departed Turkmenbashi at 3:52 p.m. and flew over Moscow even though it was scheduled to land at Vnukovo. It was eventually diverted to St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport and later departed for Moscow.
Restrictions were imposed at all Moscow airports around 3:40 p.m. and fully lifted by 6:40 p.m. According to estimates from Ostorozhno, Novosti, more than 200 flights were delayed and more than 100 canceled amid the restrictions.
It is unclear which aircraft Putin was aboard. At 1:52 p.m., TASS reported that the president had ended his visit to Turkmenistan and boarded one of the Rossiya detachment’s aircraft, which was preparing to depart Turkmenbashi. Agentstvo suggested that Putin may have been aboard RA-96025. He had flown to Turkmenistan on that aircraft on October 8.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had threatened to “close the skies” over Russia in early September. 03:55:22 KST

Islamism is a “systemic” and “deep-rooted” problem in the UK, while antisemitism is “not going to get any better,” former British home secretary Suella Braverman told The Jerusalem Post.
The Post spoke to Braverman, 46, ahead of the publication of her first book, the memoir Patriot: Empire, Betrayal and Hope. Released on October 1, it explores Braverman’s time as a barrister-turned-MP-turned cabinet minister, and her wider views on the issues in the UK, such as Islamism and political weakness. She served as home secretary under the Conservative government, before leaving the party for Reform UK in 2026.
Braverman noted that there are “systemic, profound, deep-rooted, social and cultural and institutional problems with Islamism in the United Kingdom.”
“Whether it’s in our schools, our police force, our political parties, our broader institutions – there’s a crisis. And it’s been caused by cowardice and appeasement by political leaders, most recently conservative political leaders who actually – instead of just failing to stand up to Islamism and extremism – actively engaged with it.”
She cited an example from her book of how former prime minister David Cameron invited the Muslim Brotherhood’s spokesman to lunch at Chequers, the prime minister’s official country residence.
“That’s a group that should be prescribed, not embraced by governments,” she continued.
Braverman says political courage, strong leadership can counter Islamist extremism
Despite the pervasiveness of the problem, Braverman said she does believe it can be fixed.
“We don’t need to surrender to the fate of our country being taken over by Islamists and extremists. It’s not going to be easy. It does require a high level of courage and political leadership. But I do think it is possible with a clear formula,” she said.
In fact, in Braverman’s view, the solution to Islamism in the UK is “not complex” but simply requires “a high level of political determination.” And that’s not something that can be found under a conservative leadership, she opined.
“They had 14 years, and it got worse under the conservatives during that time,” she noted.
The Conservative Party’s failure to address the worsening issues of radicalization and Islamism was the reason Braverman left the cabinet.
“There were Islamists demonstrating in our streets in marches day in, day out. I wanted to ban them and actually stop antisemitism. The prime minister of the day didn’t agree with me, and he sacked me instead,” she recalled.
“I blame the Conservative Party and many of the people still in the party for the problems that we are enduring today.”
But is there enough public concern about these issues that it could sway a future election?
Braverman claims Islamist extremism accounts for 75% of MI5's caseload
Braverman acknowledged that her views are derived from running the Home Office, dealing with counter-terrorism, working with MI5 – in fact, she revealed that Islamism makes up 75% of MI5’s caseload – which does not mirror the everyday experience of most people, and most voters.
“I am beginning to see that with the crisis of illegal migration and the insecure borders that the UK has had now, coming up to a decade – the consequences of that are making people more alert to the issues of Islamism, because the two are connected,” she said.
She pointed out that a large proportion of the people entering the UK illegally have “Islamist tendencies and intentions.”
“There’s no doubt that among them will be Iranian hostile actors coming illegally into our country who want to terrorize British citizens.”
The boat issue has made Islamism in the UK a more pressing issue, she said, because it’s on television every day.
“When people start considering that crisis in more detail, they can join the dots and see that our illegal migration crisis is a cause that will exacerbate our security threat.”
If she were here, home secretary again now, Braverman is very clear on what her first steps would be.
“First of all, we’d have to secure our borders and take a robust approach to who is coming into the country, and stop illegal migration. That would very quickly reduce the national security threat that we’re facing.
“When it comes to the existing threat of Islamism in our country, we need to make the law clear that the damaging aspects of Islamist culture are unlawful.”
Braverman calls for UK bans on burkas, polygamy, and first-cousin marriage
She cited banning the burka, polygamy, and first-cousin marriage as priorities.
“Banning the burka would be unequivocal. It’s clear in law that it’s unlawful, and there would be police powers to enforce against it. It is an obstacle to communication and integration, and is a simple symbol of female oppression. It has no place in 21st century Britain,” she said, adding that people who wanted to wear the burka and their families “would leave the country.”
“Polygamy; first-cousin marriage, which has led to a high level of severe deformities among children born of these unions, should be made illegal. Sharia courts – all of that must go.”
Braverman also said that Islamist preachers who are routinely invited and platformed at mosques and public events in the UK must be put behind bars and be deported “if they’re not British,” and that the Muslim Brotherhood needs to be proscribed.
She also believes the Muslim call to prayer should not be permitted in large public spaces.
“This is a Christian country, not a Muslim one,” said Braverman. “People need to speak English in the country.
“Constitutionally, we are not actually a secular country. We are constitutionally and institutionally a Christian country. And our head of state is the head of the Church of England,” she continued.
Braverman nevertheless stressed that she is not calling for other religions to be banned. She is a Buddist, and her husband, Rael, is Jewish.
“We are a Christian country, and I’m trying to encourage people to have that confidence in their Christian faith and the Christian heritage of this country.
“However, having said that, we are not banning non-Christians. And we are in many ways de facto a secular society. So people of other faiths are free to practice their faith. They’re free to participate in their religion’s customs and rituals. But there has to be a line whereby they do that in a way that’s consistent with British values and the Judeo-Christian values of Britain.”
Braverman says fear of Islamophobia accusations prevents politicians from confronting Islamism
While she said there is a desire by many to return to these values in Britain, Braverman said that many in politics are afraid of cracking down on Islamism for fear of being labeled Islamophobic.
“On the Right, my Conservative colleagues were terrified of being called Islamophobic,” she said. “They wanted to do everything they could to avoid that accusation, from inviting the Muslim Brotherhood to lunch at Chequers, to biting their lips when it came to calling out grooming gangs.
“On the Left, it’s slightly different. For example, we’re seeing the Labour government do appalling things right now. They have basically come out against Israel, opened a refugee route for Palestinians and people from Gaza, recognized Palestine, and put an arms embargo on Israel. All of that – that’s not because they don’t want to look Islamophobic. That’s because they want to shore up the Muslim vote.
“It’s all about cynical politics,” she continued, arguing that Labour’s policy is more about suppressing the Greens by pivoting against Israel and securing a Muslim vote.
All of this – the cynical anti-Israel politics, the permissibility around Islamism, and the decrease in Christian values – have led to a situation where the UK is arguably not safe for Jews, Braverman said.
“Almost every week, there are more Jewish people who seriously question whether they have a place in the United Kingdom. The Labour Party has now nailed its colors to the mask, which is that they are anti-Israel, anti-Zionist, and have joined the hate movement calling for Intifada.
“They don’t see Israel as an ally anymore; they see Israel as the aggressor in the wrong. I think that is morally devoid and heartbreaking.”
Because of this, Braverman believes that antisemitism in the UK, “which is already at unprecedented levels,” is not going to get any better.
“I think if we don’t turn it around at the next election, there’s no hope,” she said, adding that the next general election will be the most consequential of her lifetime.
“I think the choice will be very, very clear and binary. And it will either be four more years of socialism, and more immigration, higher taxes, more poverty, more humiliation on the world stage, more antisemitism.
“Or we can begin the fight back and the recovery. I’m with Reform because I genuinely believe that the only vehicle that can stop Labour and stop socialism is Reform.
“The Conservative Party isn’t viable as a serious proposition to win. So to anyone on the Right, to anyone who wants to bring an end to this kind of madness and chaos and nonsense that’s going on in the UK, there is only one way.”
Braverman rejects antisemitism allegations against Reform UK and Nigel Farage
When asked for her response to accusations of antisemitism in the Reform party, including those against its leader, Nigel Farage, she replied: “I would never join ranks with people who are antisemitic. I’ve taken a political stand over antisemitism. I was sacked as home secretary over antisemitism. I’m not going to join a party, or try and make someone prime minister, who I thought had a gram of antisemitism in them.”
She also noted that many leading figures in the party are outspoken friends of Israel.
Deputy leader Richard Tice, for example, has traveled to Israel to show support, and is a strong advocate against antisemitism, against Islamism, and for the Jewish community.
“And the same with Nigel and obviously Robert Jenrick [elected as a Conservative Party MP who joined Reform in January 2026], and myself,” she said.
In fact, Braverman wanted to stress that she has “always been a friend of Israel and will always continue to be a friend of Israel.”
She visited Israel after the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led massacres, showing her solidarity with the country, and meeting with survivors, heroes, and families.
“I was incredibly inspired, frankly, by the resilience of the people in Israel. and Israel as a whole, and particularly the young people who were fighting to defend their nation.
“If there is a Reform government, which I hope there will be soon, we will reestablish diplomatic relations with Israel.”
Braverman backs recognizing Jerusalem as Israel's capital, moving UK embassy
While Braverman said she could not speak about Reform’s official stance on recognizing Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and moving the embassy there, she noted that she has personally supported this in the past.
Regarding recognition of a Palestinian state, Braverman said it is “an ideal,” but currently not realistic.
“Hamas needs to be totally degraded, disarmed, and disabled. There must be no authority in Palestine that has access to arms or the ability to attack Israel. There must be zero tolerance of extremism, antisemitism, and Islamism in a potential future Palestinian state. There needs to be authority with whom neighbors, whether it’s Israel or Jordan or Egypt or any other country, can do business.
“We need to know they’re honest brokers, that they’re legitimate, that they have free and fair elections, that they’re not going to distort figures and statistics and elections and stop aid. And they’re not going to divert aid to the construction of tunnels. If those conditions can be met, then I think Israelis would support living side by side with a peaceful neighbor.
“But if those conditions are nowhere near being satisfied, then I’m afraid no, we cannot allow Palestine to be an independent state; we cannot recognize it. And right now, it seems that we’re very, very far away from that.”

Moldova to change laws to produce arms for itself, parliament head says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Moldova to change laws to produce arms for itself, parliament head says
CHISINAU, Oct 9 - Moldova's pro-European government intends to press for changes in legislation to allow for the production of weapons, but needs them for its own defence and has no intention of providing them to neighbouring Ukraine, the head of parliament said on Friday.
Parliament Chairman Igor Grosu, the No. 2 official in Moldova's state hierarchy, said the changes were needed to proceed with the manufacture of dual-purpose weapons, like drones.
"I would very much like for us to produce them for ourselves. We need them, particularly for dual-use purposes," Grosu told a two-day international security forum, citing drone use for national security, emergencies and agriculture.
Grosu, head of President Maia Sandu's Action and Solidarity Party, which holds a majority in parliament, dismissed any suggestion that they might be meant for use by Ukraine in its 4-1/2-year-old war with Russia.
"Of course not! Why would we?" he told reporters. "We would produce them for ourselves."
Sandu's administration, which wants Moldova to join the European Union by 2030, has been fiercely critical of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
Moldova, lying between Ukraine and EU member Romania, has been buffeted by the war. Increasing numbers of drones and missiles, believed by authorities to be Russian, have intruded into the country's airspace in recent weeks, with debris crashing on its territory.
Grosu told the forum that 88 such violations of Moldova's airspace had been recorded since Russia's February 2022 invasion.
"With such figures, people are asking a simple question: Can our state defend us?" he said.
"We cannot provide this defence overnight. And we cannot in four years make up for 30 years of failing to finance our defence. To protect our airspace we need radar, equipment, trained personnel, communications, infrastructure and procedures."
Sandu told the forum on Thursday that Moldova's position in the region was "vulnerable". She said domestic defence production was a key part of future defence planning and changes to legislation would soon be submitted to parliament. REUTERS

Trump allows Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel to US, global markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:53:55 UTC
03:53:55 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 9 that Russia had agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" he added.
The U.S. Treasury Department said that, following Trump’s direction, "the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
"We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we are happy to get it," Trump told reporters.
"I want to thank President Putin, to be honest with you," he added, but nonetheless called Washington Ukraine's "strong partner."
Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chuck Schumer, and Elizabeth Warren condemned the six-month authorization for global purchases of Russian diesel, calling it "a total betrayal of Ukraine, our European allies and American national security."
In a joint statement, they accused Trump of funding Russia’s war effort to offset fuel price increases caused by the U.S. war with Iran. They also said the decision undermined bipartisan legislation passed weeks earlier to curb Russian energy revenues.
"Putin only responds to strength, which means cracking down on Russia and the enablers of its war against Ukraine," they said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also criticized the decision, saying it would provide Russia with additional revenue to finance its war against Ukraine.

"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the very moment when we are talking about peace, America is allowing Russia to export diesel."
Zelensky said Ukraine’s negotiating team is currently in Florida for two days of talks with U.S. officials on ending the war, or at least securing a ceasefire that could begin with a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. This is certainly not honest, and it is certainly not how partners should act," he told reporters, calling the move "a weak decision by our strong partners."
Zelensky added that Ukraine was ready to reciprocate any Russian steps toward de-escalation, a position already known to U.S. negotiators. He said Ukraine would halt strikes on Russian refineries and other oil facilities if Moscow stopped attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, describing Ukraine’s strikes as a response to years of Russian attacks on its power system. Kyiv has proposed such an agreement to Washington, he added, and believes the U.S. has enough influence to secure it.
A European diplomat questioned whether the deal would lower diesel prices, telling the Kyiv Independent: "This is very unlikely to have a real impact on prices but the symbolism will have a real impact."
European Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho told the Kyiv Independent that "the EU is reducing its dependence on Russian fossil fuels and will resolutely continue to do so."
"Europe knows too well the hidden costs linked to over reliance on Russian hydrocarbons — and Europe does not wish to fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine," Pinho said.
Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, also responded to the deal by saying "EU Foreign Ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war," she wrote on X.
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t," she added.
Ukrainian sanctions official Vladyslav Vlasiuk called the deal "economically pointless" in his social media post.
"The U.S. consumes 3.5 million tons of diesel weekly and produces 4.9 million. Russia’s proposed 300,000 tons cover just 15 hours of U.S. demand, or 1.5 days of U.S. diesel exports. Economically pointless," Vlasiuk wrote.
The Kremlin said Russia had confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to U.S. and global markets during the call.
The move comes as Russia is seeking relief from U.S. sanctions in talks over a potential halt to attacks on energy infrastructure in its war with Ukraine, the Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 9, citing American and Ukrainian officials with knowledge of the negotiations. Moscow also wants to link the proposed energy truce to ceasefire arrangements in the Black Sea.
Those talks follow intensified Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. A senior Ukrainian defense official told reporters that Moscow aims to strengthen its negotiating position by causing as much damage as possible to the country’s power system.
Russia may also seek the release of frozen Russian assets, a European diplomat familiar with the discussions told the Kyiv Independent.
Russia’s government on Sept. 30 extended a ban on diesel exports by fuel producers through Oct. 31 amid problems in the domestic fuel market. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct. 2 that domestic diesel supplies were sufficient and that Moscow could partially reopen exports if production exceeded demand, according to state media.
Putin said on Oct. 1 that Russia had enough diesel but that sanctions prevented it from supplying global markets. Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club, he dismissed as "absurd" a proposal to halt Russian strikes on Ukrainian ships in exchange for Ukraine stopping attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that sanctions would still prevent additional Russian diesel from reaching international buyers.

Tanker attacks in Strait of Hormuz surge to wartime high as Iran tries to choke off oil exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:52:49 UTC
03:52:49 KST

Oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz are coming under fire almost daily, as Iran escalates its attacks in an effort to choke off a rebound in crude exports.
Eleven tankers came under attack while transiting Hormuz during the week that ended Oct. 4, the most strikes on commercial ships since the war began in late February, according to data from the International Maritime Organization, or IMO, a United Nations agency.
Another five tankers have come under attack this week. Twelve sailors were injured Monday when a projectile struck their tanker as it transited Hormuz. The sailors were Indian nationals and the ship, On Peace, is owned by the United Arab Emirates, according to the maritime security firm Marisks.
"These actions continue to demonstrate Iran's intent to assert [its] presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels," the Joint Maritime Information Center warned commercial ships in a Thursday notice. The center is a coalition of U.S. allied militaries headquartered in Bahrain that monitors maritime security in the region.
A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard official said Wednesday that Iran will block all "illicit routes" through Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency, an outlet considered close to the Guard.
The surge of attacks on tankers comes as crude oil exports from the Middle East rebounded in September to prewar levels, due in large part to the U.S. military escorting ships through Hormuz using a route along Oman's coast.
"Volumes are getting through but they're getting through at a time of extremely high maritime risk," said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, a provider of risk management and surveillance.
At least nine sailors have died in ship attacks since July, according to the IMO.
"This is not a sustainable new normal," said Richard Meade, editor in chief of the shipping industry trade journal Lloyd's List, in a Thursday briefing.
U.S. Central Command briefed shippers Thursday on conditions in Hormuz. On Wednesday, Centcom said that 20 million barrels of crude had transited the strait, rejecting Iranian claims that the waterway was closed.
Crude flows have recently pulled back as the attacks have increased. Exports through Hormuz stood at 8.5 million barrels a day (bpd) for the week ended Wednesday, about 40% below normal before the war, according to Kpler data published Friday. Shipments from the Middle East as a whole stood at 15.3 million bpd, 10% below prewar levels, the data showed.
Iran, meanwhile, has not loaded any crude oil for export since late August due to the U.S. naval blockade of the Islamic Republic, according to Kpler.
Tehran has struck deeper into the Persian Gulf as the Revolutionary Guard warned it will not confine its attacks to Hormuz. The Guard said it will pursue ships throughout the region that violate Iran's transit rules, according to the state media outlet Tasnim.
A tanker was hit by multiple projectiles off the coast of Qatar on Wednesday resulting in casualties, according to a British maritime security agency that monitors conditions in the Gulf.
Another tanker, Gem No. 2, was hit by a projectile Friday off the coast of the UAE resulting in a fire onboard. The ship departed Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia, in March and has remained in the Persian Gulf since the war began, according to Marisks.
Since the Iran war began in late February, at least 24 sailors have died in attacks on 100 commercial ships in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, according to the IMO.

Shams Tabrizi mausoleum opens in Khoy after 20-year wait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:52:34 UTC
03:52:34 KST

Shams Tabrizi mausoleum opens in Khoy after 20-year wait
TEHRAN- The mausoleum of Shams Tabrizi in Khoy, West Azarbaijan province, has officially opened after two decades of anticipation, marking a new step in efforts to promote Iran’s Sufi heritage and cultural tourism.
The inauguration ceremony was attended by Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri, West Azarbaijan Governor Reza Rahmani, and a number of national, provincial and foreign dignitaries on Wednesday, October 7, ISNA reported.
A statue of Shams Tabrizi was also unveiled at one of Khoy’s main squares during the ceremony. The square was named after the celebrated mystic, further highlighting his longstanding connection with the city’s cultural identity.
The shrine complex, covering an area of 7,000 square meters, includes a domed chamber, an 8,000-volume library and research facilities. The site was inscribed on Iran’s National Heritage List on October 3, 2026.
The opening is expected to strengthen Khoy’s position as a destination for cultural and spiritual tourism, building on the city’s historical association with Shams Tabrizi, the 13th-century Persian mystic and spiritual mentor of the renowned poet Jalal al-Din Rumi.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the inauguration, Salehi-Amiri announced plans to develop a nationwide Sufi tourism route connecting sites associated with prominent Iranian mystics.
The proposed route would extend from Shahroud, home to the mausoleums of figures such as Sheikh Kharaqani and Bayazid Bastami, to Khoy and the shrine of Shams Tabrizi. Other sites associated with mystics and philosophers, including Suhrawardi and Sohrevard, would also be incorporated into the broader itinerary.
The minister also announced plans for a cultural and spiritual corridor linking Khoy with Konya in Türkiye, where Rumi’s mausoleum is located. He said discussions and follow-up work on the cross-border initiative would resume when conditions in the country had stabilized.
Salehi-Amiri described the shrine’s inauguration as a starting point for further cultural projects centered on mysticism, acknowledging the efforts of officials involved in bringing the project to completion, particularly the provincial governor.
He also said the government intended to inaugurate one heritage structure each month, emphasizing Iran’s wealth of historical and civilizational landmarks.
The shrine’s opening and the unveiling of the statue represent efforts to integrate the legacy of Shams Tabrizi more visibly into Khoy’s urban landscape while developing the infrastructure needed to introduce his spiritual and literary heritage to a wider audience.
The proposed route to Konya could also provide a framework for closer cultural cooperation between Iran and Türkiye, connecting places associated with the enduring spiritual relationship between Shams and Rumi.
Shams Tabrizi (c. 1185–1248) was a Persian mystic and spiritual teacher whose encounter with Jalal al-Din Rumi profoundly transformed the renowned poet’s life and literary outlook. Their relationship is regarded as one of the most influential spiritual partnerships in Persian literature and Sufi tradition.
Shams’s teachings emphasized spiritual love, self-knowledge and a direct, personal experience of the divine, inspiring Rumi to develop the mystical poetry for which he became internationally celebrated. Rumi’s Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi, one of the major works of Persian mystical literature, bears Shams’s name and reflects the depth of their spiritual connection.
Although historical accounts of Shams’s life and final years vary, his legacy remains closely intertwined with Rumi’s poetry and the broader development of Sufism.
Khoy, in Iran’s northwestern West Azarbaijan province, is traditionally associated with Shams and has long occupied a strategic position along routes connecting Iran with Anatolia and the Caucasus. Its historical role as a crossroads of culture, commerce and intellectual exchange makes the city a significant setting for efforts to preserve and promote the heritage of the celebrated mystic. The development of Shams’s shrine and related cultural facilities is expected to further strengthen Khoy’s profile as a destination for spiritual and cultural tourism, while drawing greater attention to the historical connections between Iranian mysticism and the wider Persianate world.

Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has urged World Trade Organization (WTO) Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala to support international efforts to restore safe shipping in the Black Sea, amid ongoing Russian attacks on civilian vessels and ports that have already begun disrupting global food supplies due to a sharp rise in prices.
The two spoke via telephone, according to a statement released by the Foreign Ministry on Friday. The WTO chief was also briefed on Russia’s escalating strikes on civilians across Ukraine, including the deadly strike on a residential building in Pryluky on Wednesday, that left 22 people dead.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russian attacks on civilian vessels, sailors, and Ukrainian ports in the Black Sea pose a threat to global food supply chains. The security of shipping must be restored without delay,” Sybiha said, adding that Kyiv is counting on WTO’s support to achieve a just peace.
Ports under constant pressure
While the Black Sea ports and their maritime corridor technically remain open, reciprocal strikes between Russia and Ukraine have increased in recent months, making food shipping severely dangerous and effectively functioning as a blockade.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, at least 274 civilian vessels and 1,173 port infrastructure facilities have been damaged or partially destroyed, Ukraine’s Ministry for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport reported on Sept. 14.
US Congress Delegation Backs Expanded Starlink Access for Ukraine
Since then, the escalation has continued and increased, with Russia consistently targeting foreign-flagged civilian vessels heading towards Ukrainian ports. Drone incursions and violation of EU members have also increased, particularly in Romania and Turkey.
The latest strike on a civilian vessel was recorded on Monday, Oct. 5, when a Russian drone strike on a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn. The Royad Mammadov sank in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, killing its captain and leaving other crew members displaced.
“Freedom of navigation cannot depend on whether Moscow decides to observe it on one day or another,” Sybiha said, adding that the strike proves particularly cynical given Turkey’s ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions, advance peace initiatives and ensure security in the region.
Since late June, at least 25 Turkish-owned or Turkish-operated merchant vessels have been caught in the crossfire in the Black Sea.
The Kremlin has previously responded to international criticism by asserting that commercial vessels were being used to transport weapons, ammunition, and fuel for the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), announcing that Moscow would continue destroying such shipping.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov similarly claimed that Russian attacks on transport arteries were retaliatory measures following Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian economic and refining assets.
So far, Russia has also rejected all peace proposals from the US and Turkey, claiming it would only benefit Ukraine.
Kyiv’s push for remote audits
With sea routes under attack, Sybiha said, opening new markets for Ukrainian agricultural products has become especially important, and remote audits could be key to that effort.
According to the Foreign Minister, Ukraine had developed unique experience with the tool during the war and has agreed with the EU, UK and Canada to apply it in practice.
This could “make global agricultural trade more resilient,” he said. In remote audits, foreign regulators can review a country’s food safety controls without having to travel there for an on-site inspection.
Sybiha reiterated that Ukraine is ready to advance and promote, within the WTO, “an international standard for conducting remote audits and inspections and for recognizing their results.”
He appealed to Okonjo-Iweala for help towards building support for the initiative among other WTO members, subsequently expressing gratitude to the WTO chief for “an open and constructive exchange of views.”

Training workshop helps Kermanshah artisans explore Iraq’s handicrafts market

Training workshop helps Kermanshah artisans explore Iraq’s handicrafts market
TEHRAN- Nearly 50 handicraft artists and practitioners in Iran’s western Kermanshah province have attended a training session on exporting their products to Iraq, as part of efforts to expand international markets for locally made traditional crafts.
The workshop, titled “Handicraft Exports to Iraq,” was organized by the Handicrafts Department of the Kermanshah Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Office in cooperation with Madaen International, an export accelerator company, CHTN reported on Friday.
Amin Kogani, deputy head of handicrafts in Kermanshah province, said the development of new markets and sales channels for handicrafts was among the department’s main priorities.
He noted that Iraq, due to its geographical proximity and existing market potential, offers promising opportunities for Kermanshah’s artisans to introduce their products to international customers.
During the session, participants learned about the characteristics and potential of Iraq’s handicrafts market, marketing and sales strategies, requirements for entering foreign markets, and practical procedures for exporting their products to the neighboring country.
Kogani emphasized that producing high-quality handicrafts alone was not sufficient to ensure success in international markets. Artisans also need to understand their target markets, consumer preferences, marketing techniques, packaging standards, sales channels and export regulations.
He added that specialized training sessions could strengthen the commercial knowledge of artisans and producers while helping bridge the gap between production and access to markets.
The provincial handicrafts official said the department sought to support both the production of traditional crafts and the preservation of their authenticity, while creating more opportunities for local artisans to promote and sell their work in domestic and international markets.
He described Iraq not merely as a nearby destination for Kermanshah’s handicrafts, but also as a potential gateway for expanding exports and introducing the province’s artistic and cultural capabilities to a wider audience.
The workshop also focused on practical ways for artisans to enter the Iraqi market, enabling participants to pursue marketing, sales and export opportunities with a better understanding of the requirements involved.
The initiative reflects broader efforts to strengthen the commercial capacity of Iran’s handicrafts sector by combining traditional production skills with professional marketing and export training.
Iran is home to a rich variety of handicrafts shaped by its diverse regional cultures, centuries-old artistic traditions and locally available materials. Persian carpets and kilims, pottery and ceramics, metalwork, woodcarving, traditional textiles, enamelwork, miniature painting and inlaid woodwork are among the country’s best-known crafts. These products represent not only artistic skills passed down through generations but also an important part of Iran’s cultural heritage and creative economy.
The handicrafts sector has considerable potential to generate employment, support small businesses and create income opportunities, particularly for women and rural communities. Unlike many industrial products, traditional crafts often rely on specialized skills and distinctive regional designs, giving them cultural and artistic value in international markets. Expanding their commercial reach can therefore contribute both to economic development and to the preservation of traditional knowledge.
Export development, however, requires more than producing distinctive and high-quality goods. Access to international markets depends on identifying customer preferences, adapting product presentation to different markets, ensuring suitable packaging and shipping, developing recognizable brands and establishing reliable distribution channels. Digital marketing and e-commerce can also help artisans reach overseas customers directly, reducing their dependence on traditional intermediaries.
Neighboring countries, including Iraq, offer potential opportunities for Iranian handicrafts because of geographical proximity and longstanding cultural and commercial connections. For provinces such as Kermanshah, these links can provide a starting point for developing cross-border trade, establishing business partnerships and introducing local products to new customers. Training artisans in export procedures, pricing, market research and international sales can help turn this potential into sustainable business opportunities.
Strengthening cooperation between handicraft producers, export companies, trade organizations and cultural institutions could further improve the sector’s competitiveness. By combining the authenticity of traditional Iranian craftsmanship with modern business practices, Iran can broaden the international reach of its handicrafts while supporting artisans, preserving cultural heritage and creating new sources of income.

The illusion of control in Washington’s Iran gamble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:50:03 UTC
03:50:03 KST

The illusion of control in Washington’s Iran gamble
TEHRAN — Gore Vidal’s famous observation that the United States is a nation of amnesia, learning nothing because it remembers nothing, was never merely a witty aside. It was a prophecy dressed as satire. Washington has spent decades proving him right.
Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya each arrived with their own vocabulary of justification, carefully packaged as liberation, security or necessity. Now American power may move toward Iran again, while Yemen may become another front in a conflict Washington claims it can manage.
The pattern is familiar: military superiority creates confidence at the beginning, while political control proves far more elusive afterward.
The same script, a different stage
Washington speaks of “pressure” and “diplomacy” in the same breath, as though sanctions, military threats and economic coercion constitute genuine negotiation.
Iran, however, is not Iraq. After decades of sanctions, pressure and confrontation, Tehran has built a strategy designed for endurance rather than surrender.
Its military capabilities are dispersed and hardened, while its geography is vast, mountainous, and strategically difficult.
Yemen: The warning Washington should not ignore
Yemen provides a powerful warning. Saudi Arabia, supported by Western arms and assistance, entered the war in 2015 expecting military pressure to produce a decisive outcome.
Years later, the conflict had become a prolonged catastrophe, while Ansarallah demonstrated resilience and retained the ability to challenge their opponents.
For Washington, the lesson should be obvious. Opening another front against an adversary such as Iran would create consequences that cannot be neatly contained.
Where regional war becomes global crisis
The Strait of Hormuz turns the confrontation into an international economic problem. Any serious disruption immediately affects oil markets, shipping costs, insurance rates, and supply chains far beyond the Persian Gulf.
Recent reductions in commercial traffic demonstrate how quickly geopolitical confrontation can become an economic shock. Iran’s ability to influence access to Hormuz gives Tehran leverage that cannot simply be neutralized by deploying more military hardware.
This is the contradiction Washington repeatedly overlooks. Governments make strategic decisions inside secure rooms, but the economic consequences escape those rooms almost immediately.
A military confrontation in Iran means higher fuel prices in America, rising transport costs in Europe, and increased inflation across Asian markets.
The trap of coercive pressure
Washington’s strategy appears to rest on the belief that enough pressure will eventually force Iran to abandon its strategic position and accept terms dictated by its adversaries. Yet decades of sanctions have produced a different response: adaptation.
Iran has expanded alternative trade relationships and strengthened its position within emerging Eurasian transport and economic networks. The International North-South Transport Corridor, connecting India, Iran and Russia, has gained greater strategic importance as states seek alternatives to Western-dominated routes.
Iran’s geography, energy resources and transport infrastructure also make it significant to China’s wider Eurasian connectivity.
This does not mean Beijing, Moscow and Tehran constitute a formal military alliance. They do not. But sustained pressure has encouraged greater cooperation among countries seeking to reduce dependence on Western systems.
That is the paradox of coercion. Pressure intended to isolate an adversary can encourage it to build new partnerships, new routes and new forms of resilience.
Diplomacy is not surrender
The most dangerous assumption is that another application of military force will somehow produce a different political result from previous wars.
A wider confrontation with Iran would be difficult to contain. Strikes on Iranian military facilities provoke retaliation against American and allied interests across the region.
Attacks affecting energy infrastructure damage the very economic networks on which global markets depend.
Disruption in Hormuz, combined with instability around the Red Sea, intensifies pressure on energy and shipping markets and deepens an already fragile global economy.
Diplomacy is not weakness. Negotiation is not surrender. They are recognition that some conflicts cannot be solved by destroying enough infrastructure, and that military superiority does not guarantee political control.
The human cost of the gamble
Behind every military calculation are people who never made the decisions that put them at risk. Families in Tehran and Sanaa do not write speeches in Washington, yet they absorb the consequences.
Washington can launch the first missile, but it cannot dictate everything that follows. It cannot guarantee that escalation will remain limited, that retaliation will stop at a chosen point, or that economic blowback will stay overseas.
That is the illusion at the heart of modern interventionism: believing that superior firepower is equivalent to control. It is not.
Iran is not Iraq, and the Persian Gulf is not a battlefield that can be entered, dominated, and forgotten.
Washington may think it is gambling with Iran, but Iran is not a wager that can be settled by overwhelming firepower. Tehran has spent decades preparing to endure pressure, adapt to isolation, and resist attempts at coercion.
The real danger is not simply what America can destroy. It is what America cannot control once the destruction begins.
The choice is not between war and surrender. It is between diplomacy and hubris. Washington should understand the difference before another gamble turns into a catastrophe no power can contain.
Washington may think it is gambling with Iran, but Iran is not the kind of opponent a superpower can threaten into submission; it is the kind that can turn America’s gamble into its greatest strategic reckoning.
The article does not necessarily represent the views of the Tehran Times.

Air-raid sirens cost Kyiv’s weapons makers 61.8 working hours in month, nearly eight days, yet their contract deadlines stay fixed, two groups say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:49:16 UTC
03:49:16 KST

Air-raid sirens are quietly stealing the hours Ukraine needs to build its weapons. The alerts ate up 61.8 hours of the standard work schedule in Kyiv between 27 August and 29 September, almost eight working days in a little over a month, yet weapons makers still face unchanged contract deadlines, the Ukrainian Gunmakers Council and the League of Defense Enterprises of Ukraine say.
In September 2026, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said that every hour of air-raid alerts costs Ukraine’s economy about $45 million as businesses halt and workers shelter. For arms makers, those lost hours collide with fixed delivery dates and the penalties that follow if they slip.
The council’s figure covers Kyiv alone, and each plant loses more depending on its location, schedule, and processes, the groups said. On top of the siren time comes the wait to shut equipment down safely, move workers to shelter, and restart once the all-clear sounds.
A missed deadline carries a daily fine, and after 30 days, an extra 7 percent penalty. Money meant for components and the next orders goes instead to penalties and court disputes.
A rule that ignores the sirens
The contract date stays fixed unless the customer agrees to move it, the groups said. That leaves producers paying for stoppages they do not control, while the weapons still have to ship.
The Gunmakers Council has drafted changes to Cabinet Resolution No. 1275 to establish a single method for confirming real downtime from alerts and its effect on each contract’s deadline, it said. A customer could check alert times against official data and verify stoppages and restarts against a plant’s own production records, with each request judged on a case-by-case basis.
Waiting on the ministry
The groups say they have repeatedly raised the issue with the Defense Ministry and sent official letters proposing changes, and they are urging the ministry and the Defense Procurement Agency to act without delay.
They want a defined list of supporting documents, a deadline for reviewing requests, and rules for applying the mechanism to contracts that have already been signed. Until a decision comes, enterprises keep losing production time, and the risk of delay grows, the groups say.

Why Afghanistan’s Neighbors Have Not Backed Pakistan’s Strikes on the Taliban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:48:00 UTC
03:48:00 KST

On October 5, Moscow hosted the eighth meeting of the special representatives and senior officials from regional countries for the Moscow Format to discuss political and economic relations with Afghanistan and counterterrorism and counter-narcotics cooperation. The Moscow Format includes Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan.
But the meeting failed to adopt a joint statement because the Pakistani and Afghan delegates disagreed over the language on terrorism. The Taliban objected to the frequent mention of terrorism in reference to Afghanistan.
Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, said the Afghan delegates accepted similar language last year. He believed that the changed relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan might have caused Kabul’s objection this time.
The meeting was held only a week after the most recent confrontation between Islamabad and Kabul. On September 18 and 26, Pakistan suffered deadly terrorist attacks in its northwestern province, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, that together killed about 44 people and injured about 138. Pakistan responded with airstrikes on different targets in Afghanistan that it believes were the training camps and hideouts of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and its associated factions responsible for the cross-border attacks.
At the Moscow summit, Pakistan’s delegation said the Taliban were complicit in those attacks in Pakistan because the terrorist groups were operating on Afghan soil with impunity. The Taliban said Pakistan was using military aggression in violation of international law for an issue that could be resolved through political negotiations.
The Moscow Format meeting failed to bridge these differences enough to allow for a joint communique. What’s noteworthy is that other countries that share borders with Afghanistan – such as China, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – did not use their diplomatic capital to reach an understanding on language that included everyone’s concerns.
Afghanistan’s neighbors have different levels of concern about militancy there. Their strategies, especially on counterterrorism, are a function of the nature of their border with Afghanistan, the extent of the threat from militant groups on Afghan soil, and the Taliban’s scale of cooperation regarding those groups. From their perspective, military force is not the most effective solution to address the issue.
China shares a border of only about 92 kilometers with Afghanistan, high in the Wakhan Corridor, marked by rough terrain and the nearly 5,000-meter high Wakhjir Pass. In terms of a terrorist presence in Afghanistan, Beijing considers the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) its main concern and has pressed the Taliban to act against the group. The Taliban have reportedly relocated ETIM fighters away from the border, and they now have a dispersed presence. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat to China is smaller, and any movement across the pass is easy to detect.
Uzbekistan similarly shares a short border of 144 kilometers with Afghanistan, almost entirely along the Amu Darya. Regular cross-border movement is concentrated at the closely guarded Termez-Hairatan road and rail crossing. But the militant groups in Afghanistan that concern Tashkent have shown only a limited capacity for cross-border attacks. There was one incident in 2022 of rockets being fired toward Termez, which didn’t cause any casualties. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat is relatively small and easier to contain.
Tajikistan’s case is closer to Pakistan’s in terms of the long border and threat. Dushanbe shares about 1,374 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, much of which runs along the Panj River and passes through remote and mountainous territory and is difficult to monitor consistently. The cross-border threat therefore needs more immediate attention. In November 2025, two cross-border attacks from Afghanistan’s Badakhshan province killed five Chinese workers in Tajikistan.
As for Taliban cooperation, Kabul has offered these countries help in investigations and has arrested suspects after cross-border attacks.
Pakistan’s case is of a different magnitude on all these counts.
Pakistan shares 2,640 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, where Pashtun and Baloch communities live on both sides. Afghanistan has never recognized the border since Pakistan’s founding. Islamabad has been fencing it since 2017, but militants continue to cross it. A disputed frontier with kinship networks on both sides gives militants far more routes and tricks to enter Pakistan than Afghanistan’s northern borders offer.
Pakistan also faces a much larger threat. Its key concerns are the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), and the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). Islamabad charges that all three groups have a presence in Afghanistan, especially the TTP. U.N. monitors estimate the TTP, which has carried out the most frequent and lethal attacks in Pakistan, has about 6,000 fighters in Afghanistan.
By September 2026, Pakistan’s terrorism situation had worsened sharply, with 1,232 militant attacks in nine months, already 169 attacks above those recorded in all of 2025. Consistent attacks on this scale raise domestic pressure to take firm action.
Moreover, the Taliban have shown limited willingness to cooperate with Pakistan on the issue of militant groups. The Taliban leadership describes TTP members as Pakistani refugees and refuses to classify them as militants. U.N. monitors report that the group enjoys greater liberty and support from Taliban authorities. Kabul has offered to relocate the TTP fighters away from the Pakistani border, but that step cannot stop the militant movement through the long and porous border with Pakistan.
Pakistan has, therefore, asked for written guarantees that the militants would not use Afghan soil as a base for attacks in Pakistan. The Taliban have rejected this demand, which was why the Istanbul talks failed in November 2025.
Pakistan has said its operations will continue until the Taliban take verifiable action against militant groups on Afghan soil. Yet none of Afghanistan’s neighbors has publicly supported Pakistan’s airstrikes. China, Russia, and Iran have called for restraint and offered to mediate, and Uzbekistan urged a diplomatic resolution. China hosted informal talks in Urumqi in April but those ended without agreement.
Whether in Urumqi or more recently in Moscow, repeated efforts at finding common ground have fallen flat. While none of Afghanistan’s neighbors is comfortable with the idea of cross-border terrorism, none of them has sanctioned Pakistan’s military retaliation, either.

"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," Republican Sen. Thom Tillis wrote on X. "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America."
History of public executions in U.S.
Two public executions in the mid-1930s are considered to be the last public uses of the death penalty in the United States.
The last large-scale example of a public execution in the United States was Rainey Bethea in 1936. The crowd on hand to watch the hanging was estimated at 20,000 people, according to a local newspaper at the time.
Bethea was accused of raping and murdering a 70-year-old woman in her home in Owensboro, Kentucky, in June 1936. He accidentally left his recognizable prison ring at the scene, and confessed to the crime several times, though he did recant during a failed appeal.
He was never convicted of murder, only rape, which still carried the death penalty. Bethea, who was 26 years old, was hanged on Aug. 14, 1936.
A year later, Roscoe "Red" Jackson was executed in Galena, Missouri, also by hanging. He was convicted of killing a traveling salesman and stealing his car after being picked up by the victim as a hitchhiker.
The crowd for Jackson's execution was much smaller, since it was not held in the public streets of the city like Bethea's hanging.
"Just how many were inside is not known, though it is thought the space would accommodate at least 400 people," wrote the authors of an article on the execution from the local Stone County News-Oracle.
"Executions shouldn't be public spectacle," Human Rights Watch interim U.S. Program Director Michael Bochenek told CBS News in a statement. "The death penalty is a relic of an inhumane past and should be abolished once and for all."
Public executions in Iran
Iran, which the United States has accused of gross human rights violations, is one of the most prolific users of public executions in the world currently. The U.S. and Iran are also locked in a war, and President Trump has routinely cited Iran's executions of protesters as a reason the regime deserved to be deposed.
At least 24 people were publicly executed in Iran from 2022 to 2025, according to Amnesty International.
Fifty-nine people were executed this year in Iran between March 18 and Aug. 31, including dozens who took part in anti-government protests earlier this year, according to Human Rights Watch. Five of those executions have been public, the organization said.
While not capital punishment, thousands of protesters were also killed by government troops opening fire on those demonstrations.
In late February, eight days before launching strikes against Iran, Mr. Trump said he had threatened military action against Iran if they publicly executed hundreds of people.
"They were going to hang 837 people, and I gave them the word, if you hang one person, even one person, that you're going to be hit right then and there," Mr. Trump said. "I wasn't waiting two weeks and negotiating. And they gave up the hanging. They didn't hang 837, supposedly they didn't hang anybody."
Public executions in Afghanistan
Afghanistan has publicly executed at least 12 people since 2022, according to Amnesty International, though its reports note there were possibly more.
Public executions in Afghanistan have spiked since the Taliban swept back into power in August 2021. Executions have even been carried out in front of thousands of onlookers in sports stadiums, including one in November 2024 that earned worldwide condemnation.
"I condemn today's horrific public execution," Richard Bennett, who monitors human rights violations in Afghanistan for the United Nations, said in a statement at the time. "These atrocious punishments are clear violations of human rights and must be immediately halted."
Another person, reportedly convicted of murder, was publicly executed in a sports stadium in October 2025, according to the U.N.
The Taliban regularly carried out public executions during their first period of rule in the 1990s, until the U.S. invasion in 2001 forced them out of power.
Public executions elsewhere in the world
North Korea is also believed to carry out public executions, though reporting is difficult from the extremely isolated country.
In February, Amnesty International put out a report that included interviews with North Korean defectors who said they had been forced to watch public executions as a way of warning them against committing similar supposed crimes — sometimes for as little as watching foreign television programs.
"Authorities told everyone to go, and tens of thousands of people from Sinuiju city gathered to watch," one female defector interviewed by the human rights group said. "They execute people to brainwash and educate us."
Saudi Arabia, which was widely criticized for its public executions for decades, has apparently ended its use entirely in recent years. The infamous Deera Square, where many beheadings took place in the capital, Riyadh, has not hosted an execution since 2019, according to Reuters.
The death penalty is still used frequently in Saudi Arabia, even if not public. There were a record 347 people executed in 2025, according to the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights. The year prior 345 people were executed. By comparison, 47 people were executed in the United States last year.
The Iran-backed Houthi militant group, which controls large areas of western Yemen, also sometimes carries out public executions. Though not recognized as the controlling government, they do hold enormous power in the country. Nine people were executed at once in public in 2021 for the killing of a Houthi general, according to the Geneva International Centre for Justice.
"International human rights bodies have long found public executions as incompatible with the prohibition on cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement to CBS News. "The claim that the death penalty serves as a greater deterrent is simply unfounded: there is no evidence that it has a unique deterrent effect. The death penalty does not make us safer."
"Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end," he added.

U.S. plan to livestream execution by firing squad draws bipartisan, international outrage
