Pakistan has 'substantial' number of forces in Saudi Arabia: Foreign Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:20:06 UTC
02:20:06 KST

Faisal Mahmud, Riyaz Khaliq
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Pakistan has deployed “substantial” number of military forces and resources in Saudi Arabia, the Foreign Ministry said Friday.
“Pakistan already has a substantial number of forces, as well as resources, in Riyadh,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told reporters in Islamabad, according to an official transcript of his news conference.
Khan stressed the Mecca pact between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia “is a defensive organisation… an alliance intended to defend the three countries against aggression.”
“Therefore, these forces would not cross the border into Yemen to launch attacks against the Houthis. However, they would, of course, be utilised to defend the country’s territory and safeguard its sovereignty,” he explained.
The new Mecca Alliance was formed on Aug. 7 by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, followed by a series of steps by its three member states to institutionalize the agreement.
However, Khan said it was up to the alliance organization “to assess the threat perception and operate in accordance with its own mandate.”
Before the trilateral Mecca pact was signed, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had signed a bilateral defense agreement last September, following which “there has again been some deployment,” said Khan, the ministry spokesman.
Earlier Wednesday, Pakistani military spokesperson Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told CNN: “The Pakistani troops have been there for decades in multiple capabilities.”
Chaudhry said Pakistani forces were already present in Saudi Arabia across multiple domains but declined to disclose troop numbers or operational capabilities, citing their sensitive nature.
The Foreign Ministry spokesman Khan added: “Since 1982, the Pakistan armed forces have been present in Saudi Arabia in one capacity or another, sometimes under logistical arrangements and sometimes as part of training missions.”
The remarks came after Islamabad rejected a New York Times report claiming Pakistani fighter jets were conducting strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.
“We have been a very honest broker. The neutrality comes from honesty,” the Pakistani army spokesman said.
After the US and Israel launched war on Iran early this year, Pakistan mediated a ceasefire in April and later hosted high-level talks and secured June 18 Islamabad MoU between Washington and Tehran.

Netanyahu's Oct. 7 records probe: What was allegedly altered, and why is it stalled? | Explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:19:48 UTC
02:19:48 KST

Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, who served as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's military secretary before, during and after the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, publicly alleged Thursday for the first time that at least one official record from the morning of the attack had been altered inside the Prime Minister's Office. He identified former chief of staff Tzachi Braverman as the person allegedly responsible.
The allegations prompted calls across the political spectrum for an investigation. But the matter has already been investigated, and the case has been awaiting a decision by prosecutors for more than a year. With Israel approaching elections, no decision is expected for at least another month.
What exactly is Braverman suspected of doing, what did Gil reveal, and why has the investigation yet to produce a decision? Here is what we know.
Has an investigation been opened?
Yes. Police opened an investigation into Tzachi Braverman over suspicions that official records from the Prime Minister's Office had been falsified.
Braverman was questioned under caution in November 2024 and denied the allegations. His attorney, Jacques Chen, maintained that Braverman had acted within his authority to correct a clerical error in the records.
Although the investigation has been completed and the case transferred to the prosecution, no decision has been made on whether to file charges.
What exactly was investigated?
The investigation centered on suspicions that Braverman personally altered the recorded time of a telephone conversation between Netanyahu and his then-military secretary, Avi Gil, on the morning of October 7, 2023.
According to the allegations, the time of the call was changed from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m., an 11-minute difference during the critical opening moments of the Hamas attack.
Investigators examined claims that Braverman initially instructed a stenographer in the Prime Minister's Office to change the time recorded in the transcript. When she refused, he allegedly made the alteration himself.
The dispute concerns the official documentation of Netanyahu's communications that morning and the chronology of the information he received as the attack unfolded.
What is the status of the investigation?
The case was transferred to the prosecution for a decision approximately one year and three months ago. Since then, prosecutors have not announced whether Braverman will face criminal charges.
Despite renewed public attention following Gil's interview, a decision is not expected within the coming month because of the election period.
The central question is therefore no longer whether authorities will investigate the allegations, but whether the existing evidence is sufficient to justify an indictment.
What did Avi Gil reveal Thursday night?
In an interview with Channel 12 News, Gil confirmed two reports previously published by journalist Nadav Eyal in Yedioth Ahronoth: the alleged alteration of records at the Prime Minister's Office and a warning about the possibility of war delivered by former Shin Bet director Ronen Bar.
Gil said he first became concerned during the war, when he learned that records and transcripts were being collected inside the Prime Minister's Office in violation of established procedures.
"During the war, while we were preparing the ground maneuver, I was approached and told that records were being collected in the Prime Minister's Office, contrary to regulations," he said. "I contacted the attorney general. At the height of the war, stenographic transcripts and protocols were being collected. I didn't want to accuse anyone. I wanted to stop it."
Gil said he asked the attorney general to formally clarify the rules governing access to the records.
He described a subsequent incident in January 2024, when a stenographer approached him privately and said she had been instructed by the chief of staff to change the recorded time of Netanyahu's 6:40 a.m. conversation.
"She came into my office, closed the door and told me," Gil said. "That says everything. She understood that it was unusual. I believe she was distressed."
According to Gil, the stenographer refused to make the change because the original computer record documented the conversation as having taken place between 6:40 a.m. and 6:44 a.m.
"She said, 'I'm not allowed to change it. The computer shows 6:40 to 6:44.' Those are facts, and they are not in dispute," he said.
Gil questioned why anyone would seek to alter the documentation of a four-minute conversation from the morning of October 7, particularly months after the attack.
"The first thing I ask myself is why anyone is dealing with the stenographic record of a four-minute conversation on the morning of October 7," he said. "Who cares about it, and what was said in that conversation that made it so important?"
Gil said he had shared his assessments with the appropriate authorities but distinguished those assessments from what he described as an established fact.
"Someone was dealing with certain narratives. It was important to them to examine something that happened on October 7, sometime in mid-January 2024," he said. "This is changing a stenographic record, changing the truth."
He said he immediately documented the incident in a handwritten note to the attorney general.
"I didn't wait. We were between two meetings, and I sat down and wrote a note to the attorney general in my own handwriting, updating her on the matter," he said.
Gil described the alleged alteration in unequivocal terms.
"This is forgery. Factually, an instruction was given to change the time of a conversation," he said.
He also urged any future commission of inquiry, as well as the state comptroller, not to rely solely on written transcripts when reconstructing the events of October 7.
"I have one recommendation for the commission of inquiry that will be established, and for the comptroller: Don't settle for transcripts. Demand the original recordings."
How did Netanyahu respond, and how did his account change?
Netanyahu responded Thursday by accusing Gil of knowing about indications of an impending attack on October 7 and failing to wake the prime minister in time.
The accusation echoed similar claims Netanyahu has directed at former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, who has said he intends to sue the prime minister, and former IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi.
In a statement issued through Likud, Netanyahu's party accused Gil of attempting to divert attention from his own failures.
"Tonight, Channel 14 revealed that Avi Gil is trying to divert attention from his personal failures that night with lies," the statement said. "Like others, Avi Gil knew about the impending attack and chose not to wake the prime minister in time."
According to Likud, at 3:55 a.m. on October 7, Gil received a text message from an intelligence officer in the Prime Minister's Military Secretariat describing several warning signs.
These included the activation of SIM cards in Hamas facilities in central Gaza and Khan Younis, the activation of Hamas emergency communications systems and unusual activity involving Hamas military commander Mohammed Deif.
"Avi Gil did nothing with the information," Likud said. "Gil's interviews are attempts to obscure the simple and painful truth about his failure to perform his duties."
However, Netanyahu's latest accusation contrasts with a statement he issued in March 2025, when he defended the conduct of his military secretariat.
At that time, Netanyahu said an intelligence officer in the secretariat had received a message during the night of October 7 describing several warning signs, but also indicating that Hamas was operating normally and that the head of the IDF Southern Command would discuss the situation only the following morning.
"The intelligence officer immediately forwarded the message, word for word, to the military secretary," Netanyahu said in March 2025. "However, in light of the message's assessment that this was not an urgent event, he chose not to wake him."
The statement concluded: "Prime Minister Netanyahu has full confidence in the military secretariat of his office."
The difference between the two statements has become a central point of contention, with Netanyahu's critics accusing him of changing his account of the intelligence warnings and the actions taken by his staff before the massacre.
How have political leaders responded?
Opposition leader Yair Lapid accused Netanyahu of attempting to rewrite the history of October 7 rather than accept responsibility for the failures that preceded the attack.
"The truth that emerged from Maj. Gen. Avi Gil's testimony is simple and indisputable: Netanyahu was warned and ignored it, and since then he has evaded responsibility, whined that no one woke him up and done everything possible to rewrite history," Lapid said.
"If he remains in office, there will be more October 7s, and our children will not be safe," he added.
Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman called for an immediate criminal investigation into Netanyahu and members of his office.
"I call on the attorney general to order an immediate investigation against the prime minister and his associates on suspicion of treason and conspiracy," Liberman said.
He also urged the IDF chief of staff to prevent any attempt to use the military for political purposes, accusing Netanyahu's camp of trying to change the public agenda immediately before the elections.
Democrats chairman Yair Golan described Gil's allegations as an extraordinary development.
"This is an earthquake. Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil's testimony is among the most serious ever heard in Israel," Golan said.
"The blame and responsibility of Netanyahu for the massacre of 1,200 people and the abduction of 251 have never been clearer," he added, accusing the prime minister of committing a grave offense against Gaza border communities, former hostages and the Israeli public.
For now, the investigation into the alleged alteration of official records remains unresolved. Braverman has denied wrongdoing, prosecutors have yet to decide whether to file charges, and Gil's public account has renewed scrutiny of how Netanyahu's office documented the crucial first minutes of October 7.

Drone strike kills 30 people in Sudan’s Blue Nile region

At least 30 displaced people, including women and children, have been killed and dozens of others have been wounded following a drone attack in southeastern Sudan.
The governor of Wad al-Mahi province told Al Jazeera on Friday that a drone belonging to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted the centre of the province, killing 26 women and four children.
Governor Mahjoub Al-Sheikh described the attack as “cowardly”. He said the drone was launched from “inside Ethiopia”, according to the AFP news agency.
Al Jazeera Arabic’s Sudan correspondent, Wadah Al-Tahir, explained that the attack was the latest in a wave of drone strikes targeting the Blue Nile region and this time Wad al-Mahi province near the city of Damazin was struck.
Friday’s attack was just outside a displacement camp, near an informal gold mining site, where women earn a daily wage using chemicals and their bare hands to clear gold nuggets from the earth extracted by men.
The latest frontline in the war between the Sudanese army and the RSF is the border region with Ethiopia, which is facing its own internal conflict that threatens to escalate.
Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of harbouring RSF fighters and bases – Ethiopia has denied the allegations.
Local sources say the porous border between the two countries is a key supply line for the paramilitary and its allies, AFP reported.
The RSF launched its offensive towards Damazin but the advance could put the army in a bind, forcing it to defend territory on both the Blue Nile front and in the Kordofan region, where a year of deadly drone strikes has left the two sides deadlocked.
Aid workers estimate that Sudan’s civil war has killed more than 200,000 people since it started in April 2023, creating one of the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises.
Nearly 100,000 people have been displaced in Blue Nile state this year alone, according to United Nations figures.

Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:14:44 BST
02:14:44 KST

Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
- Published
Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.
Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.
The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".
Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.
But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

UN envoy warns Yemen has returned to 'full-scale war,' urges political settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:14:28 UTC
02:14:28 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Yemen has returned to "full-scale war" as fighting spreads across multiple fronts, with civilians bearing the brunt of escalating violence, UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg warned Friday.
Briefing the UN Security Council, Grundberg said hostilities have intensified in recent weeks following advances by Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, toward Mokha and the coast along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
He condemned Houthi attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including recent strikes on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed and injured civilians.
"I echo the Secretary-General's condemnation, and repeat my call on Ansar Allah to cease these attacks," Grundberg told the council. 
Civilians 'bearing the brunt of escalating violence'
Grundberg warned that civilians, particularly women and children, were again suffering the consequences of intensifying conflict amid severe economic hardship.
"While the situation in Yemen remains highly fluid, one fact is clear: civilians, especially women and children, are once again bearing the brunt of escalating violence," he said.
Grundberg cited the International Monetary Fund's ranking of Yemen as the world's poorest country.
He urged all parties to comply with international humanitarian law, including requirements to distinguish between civilians and combatants, avoid disproportionate harm and take all feasible precautions to protect civilians.
He stressed that children were entitled to special protection and that their recruitment and use in armed conflict were prohibited.
Grundberg also called for the protection of medical facilities, humanitarian personnel and operations, and people no longer participating in hostilities.
The envoy warned that Houthi threats against Saudi-linked commercial vessels in the Red Sea undermined freedom of navigation.
He said the threats were becoming increasingly intertwined with disputes over maritime trade routes and pressures on international energy markets.
Grundberg acknowledged that regional security, freedom of navigation and international trade were legitimate concerns.
However, he stressed that international efforts must also reflect conditions inside Yemen and the needs and aspirations of its people.
He warned that shifting military calculations were influencing the parties' assessments of when and how to pursue negotiations.
Call for political process
Grundberg said military pressure could strengthen negotiating leverage but stressed that military action and diplomacy were not mutually exclusive.
"Ultimately, gains on the battlefield cannot substitute for the negotiations that will be required to settle the conflict," he said.
As mediator, Grundberg said his responsibility was to create space for a Yemeni-led political settlement.
He stressed that the parties owed a political solution to approximately 40 million Yemenis who had endured more than a decade of conflict.
"Unless war is to become Yemen's permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now," he said.
The envoy also expressed concern about the continued detention of UN personnel and staff from nongovernmental organizations, civil society groups and diplomatic missions.
He called for urgent action and continued Security Council support.
"Without a credible political process that sustainably resolves the conflict, it will continue to resurface, deepen regional tensions, and threaten broader stability," Grundberg warned.
He urged Security Council members to maintain unity, sustain their attention on Yemen and collectively support mediation efforts to end the conflict.

Tesla drops 'Full Self-Driving' brand name in Europe after regulator pushback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:12:32 UTC
02:12:32 KST

Elon Musk's automaker Tesla has changed the brand name of its "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)," or FSD, system in Europe to "Assisted Driving" after German regulators called the branding "somewhat misleading."
The package is still sold under the Full Self-Driving (Supervised) branding in the U.S. as a $99 per month subscription for Tesla owners.
Tesla is gunning for approvals across Europe, where EV sales have been on the rise this year amid soaring fuel costs caused by the war in Iran, and where Tesla sales have shown signs of recovery from a sales slump last year.
On Tuesday, the German Federal Ministry of Transport, known as the BMV, said in a statement that Tesla's brand name "FSD" was "somewhat misleading," adding that "It is not a system that takes over the entire driving task. Rather, it is a driver assistance system that can support certain driving tasks such as accelerating, braking, and steering. The driver must remain attentive at all times."
Tesla has been pressuring automotive regulators in Europe, especially in the Netherlands, for rapid approval of their system. Reuters reported that in some cases, Tesla's "browbeating" pushed regulators to reduce the intensity of their safety tests and reviews of the company's technology.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the U.S. automotive safety regulator, is also investigating Tesla's FSD to determine if it is safe for drivers to use in fog, glaring sun or other reduced visibility conditions, and is investigating Tesla to determine whether FSD caused Tesla drivers to commit traffic violations — some that resulted in collisions.
In December 2025, a judge in California determined that Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing around its Autopilot and FSD systems, falsely implying they were fully automated driving systems. Tesla has countersued the California DMV to try to shed that "false advertiser" label in a Los Angeles superior court. That litigation is ongoing.
Autonomous systems expert Missy Cummings, an engineering professor at George Mason University and outspoken critic of Tesla and other autonomous vehicle developers, said renaming FSD isn't a strong enough measure to ensure the systems are safe for broad release in Europe.
In an email to CNBC, Cummings said European agencies are "ignoring both past and ongoing NHTSA investigations" into safety defects with Tesla's FSD.
"The EU is struggling to keep up in the AI marketplace," she said. "Musk sees this and is definitely bullying them as a result."
She criticized the Dutch regulator, known as RDW, for approving Tesla FSD for release in Europe, "based on secretive data," adding that, "The public should demand transparency in any approval of a transportation system with embedded AI."
Tesla and RDW did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million "active" FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were activated from free trials or other incentives.

Colombia: Italy Supports the Restoration of Cartagena’s Historic City Walls
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:11:31 CEST
02:11:31 KST

Italy is supporting a project for the conservation of the historic city walls of Cartagena de Indias, in northern Colombia. The Italian Embassy, the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS), and the city government are finalizing the guidelines for the national ideas competition “Imagine the Future of Cartagena’s Walls,” open to architecture students and architects up to age 30. The initiative aims to gather proposals to improve the connection between the San Ignacio and San Francisco Javier ramparts, two key points of the city’s fortified system, which is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Entries may be submitted through November 5. The competition is part of an international cooperation project funded by the Italian government with a grant of 3 million euros, earmarked for heritage preservation, the promotion of sustainable tourism, and the strengthening of the local economy. The planned interventions include the restoration of several sections of the walls, such as the La Tenaza spur and the Murallita del Diablo, as well as the construction of an elevated walkway connecting the two bastions. The project also includes work on the Cathedral of Santa Catalina de Alejandría and the Santo Domingo bastion. Proposals must consider not only architectural aspects but also the relationship between the city walls and public spaces, the landscape, local culture, and the city’s residents and visitors. Participation is open to individuals or groups of up to three people, with at least one member from Cartagena. Ten projects will be selected, from which the three best will be chosen. The selected ideas will be exhibited and may contribute to the subsequent phases of the project.

FlyDubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Tel Aviv airport inspired by 9/11, prosecutor says
The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of FlyDubai flight 1073 had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport in a suicide attack, the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor said Friday. The Israel-bound flight carrying 182 people made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of its rudder was torn away.
The co-pilot who attacked the captain of a FlyDubai jet last week had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport, the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor said on Friday.
In the aftermath of the incident, people on board – the majority of whom were Israeli – described a sudden plunge in altitude and a fight for control of the aircraft, which was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The passengers were repatriated on a second flydubai flight hours later.
The unnamed Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from al Qaeda's September 11, 2001 suicide attacks on the United States, and carried out his attempt "with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life", according to the Emirati prosecutor's findings published by state media.
The prosecutor found that the co-pilot had first begun to be radicalised while studying in Australia "through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks".
He said last week's flight had been the co-pilot's third to Tel Aviv, and that he had used the two earlier trips to plan the attack.
Read moreWho are the mystery pilots who successfully landed endangered FlyDubai flight 1073?
During the flight, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane's Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help.
Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board "noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner", according to the findings.
After gaining entry, he "intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect".
The return flight captain and his co-pilot then landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
No sign of intentions
Israel and the UAE have become close partners since normalising ties under the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020, and Israel carries out stringent security checks on those travelling to the country.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu previously said that the co-pilot – identified in reports as Hamam al-Hammami – must have got around restrictions preventing individuals from nations that do not recognise Israel operating flights to the country.
The UAE prosecutor's "findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot's licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks".
"However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot."
The co-pilot had previously worked for Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, but media outlets reported after the incident that he had been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views.
After the incident, Netanyahu had hailed the passengers and the plane's captain for their bravery in averting what would have otherwise been a catastrophe.
He later ordered a "thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel" in response to the incident.

China, EU reach deal to 'moderate' China's car exports to EU
October 9, 2026
European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic announced on Friday that China and the European Union had reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the EU by more than half.
This announcement followed two-day talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU's growing trade deficit with China.
Earlier, Sefcovic said this week's talks were the culmination of three months of intensive work.
What do we know about the EV deal?
According to Sefcovic, the deal would "moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU."
He added that this opens the prospect of cutting China's exports by more than half, based on projections over a four-year period.
"By this step, we're actually preventing several millions of cars exports from China to the European Union," Sefcovic said.
Although he did not offer details on how the agreement will be implemented, Sefcovic said he believed the two sides had achieved a very good result.
What else was decided?
Sevcovic added the two sides also reached an agreement to reduce Chinese import duties on €4 billion ($4.5 billion) worth of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil and footwear.
They also agreed to simplify China's process for granting export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets.
The agreement will require approval from the leaders of all 27 EU nations, who will discuss the outcome at the start of their summit in Brussels on Thursday.
Rebalancing EU-China trade
According to UN Comtrade data, Chinese exports to the EU totaled $560 billion (€500 billion) last year, up from $517 billion in 2023. Exports to major economies, including Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland, each rose approximately 10% from a year earlier. Shipments to Hungary increased by 43%.
Meanwhile, China imported $268.3 billion (€240 billion) worth of European goods last year, down from $269.4 billion the previous year. Purchases from Denmark, Ireland, and France led the way.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned lawmakers at the European Parliament that the trade gap had reached a tipping point. She said the EU would use all available tools to rebalance the relationship.

Both Mikhail and Valeriya Zvinchuk have been blacklisted by Western governments as key figures in malign hybrid activities and foreign information influence operations.
Police said the group had entered Montenegro less than two days prior and was staying at a hotel in Risan. Following a joint intelligence operation, authorities revoked their residency and issued formal expulsion orders under the Law on Foreigners, citing direct threats to "national and internal security."
During the raid, officers confiscated what they described as "sophisticated digital equipment," including a drone, high-resolution cameras, GoPros, and multiple mobile phones. The seized gear has been handed over to state prosecutors in Podgorica and Kotor for forensic analysis to determine its intended use.
Responding to the raid, Rybar confirmed on Telegram that Zvinchuk and his team had been detained but rejected any allegations of wrongdoing. The group stated its team was residing in Montenegro legally to film content at the historic Cetinje Monastery after submitting an official request to local authorities—a claim that aligns with the confiscated camera equipment but which authorities view as a cover for malign operations.
However, despite claims that the visit was strictly focused on documentary production, Rybar's own recent activity demonstrated active engagement with the region's geopolitical shifts from inside the country. On September 28, the channel published a post from Montenegro addressing Podgorica's decision to introduce a visa regime for Russian and Belarusian citizens to align with EU policies. The post also wove in regional and international commentary, including domestic political shifts in Serbia, defense cooperation between Turkey and Kosovo, and military developments in Ukraine.
This mirrors an operational pattern previously utilized by the network across the region. According to a December 2025 investigation by the Balkan outlet Detektor, Zvinchuk similarly traveled unannounced to Banja Luka, Bosnia and Herzegovina, during the extraordinary elections for the presidency of Republika Srpska. The following day, Rybar published a video analysis featuring Zvinchuk standing in front of the local government building, broadcasting political commentary that the elections had been "imposed from outside."
The detentions drew a sharp reaction from Moscow. Rybar noted that Russian diplomats, backed by statements from presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov and Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova, are working to protect the detainees' rights. Meanwhile, Dmitry Medvedev, Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council, warned Russians against traveling to European countries, claiming on Telegram that a "hunt" has been declared against citizens who speak the truth. Medvedev suggested that Russia may need to replenish its "exchange fund" with "European and American idiots" to secure the release of its citizens.
Founded in 2018, Rybar initially focused on military analysis before expanding into one of the most influential pro-war Telegram channels during the invasion of Ukraine.
The United Kingdom sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar LLC, alongside Russian ideologue Aleksandr Dugin and the Kremlin-backed foundation Pravfond. OCCRP and its partners previously revealed that Pravfond—created by Russia’s Foreign Ministry to ostensibly provide legal aid for "compatriots" abroad—has quietly funneled money to spies, propagandists, and a network of affiliated entities, which includes Rybar.
The network has also been heavily targeted by the United States. The U.S. State Department’s "Rewards for Justice" program is offering up to $10 million for information on foreign interference in U.S. elections, publicly identifying Rybar LLC and 19 individuals—including Rybar Director Mikhail Zvinchuk and Creative Director Valeriya Zvinchuk—who have carried out malign influence operations.
According to the official State Department notice, Rybar was previously funded by the late Russian mogul Yevgeny Prigozhin and currently receives funding from the sanctioned Russian state-owned defense corporation Rostec. The U.S. government noted that Rybar relies on Rostec funding to bolster Russia’s military capabilities and advance anti-Western narratives.
Ahead of the 2024 U.S. presidential election, Rybar specifically established the "TEXASvsUSA" channel on X alongside other propaganda channels like #HOLDTHELINE and #STANDWTHTEXAS. Through these platforms, the State Department states that Rybar exploited the politically sensitive issue of undocumented immigrants at the Texas border to "sow discord, promote social division, stoke partisan and racial discord, and encourage hate and violence in the United States."
The regional presence of Zvinchuk aligns with a November 2024 analysis by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), which highlighted his public claims that Rybar oversaw a global network of over 250 channels operating in 28 languages, alongside plans to establish "media schools" in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kyrgyzstan to project influence.

Labour byelection win shows party starting to win back voters on left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:08:19 UTC
02:08:19 KST

Labour is starting to win back voters on the left who became disillusioned under Keir Starmer’s leadership, the party’s deputy leader has claimed after it saw off Zack Polanski and the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.
Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% of a relatively low turnout to keep Starmer’s old north London seat for the party, pushing Polanski, who had stood for the party he leads, into second place on 33%.
While the result was broadly as predicted, Labour strategists were buoyed up by the party’s relatively straightforward route to victory in a diverse inner-city area of the sort the Greens have been targeting with recent success.
The result “sends a clear message to those voters who lost faith in Labour in recent years”, said Lucy Powell, who called last month for the party to unite progressive voters under Andy Burnham if it wants to win the next election.
After the byelection win, she told the Guardian: “We hear you, we’ve listened and we know we needed to be clearer about what we stand for and what type of country we want to see, proudly putting our values centre stage. We’re delighted so many of you are backing us once again.”
The byelection came after the Green party voted at their conference last weekend to adopt a hugely controversial policy equating Zionism with racism, and saying Israel should be replaced with a single Palestinian state.
Polanski has been criticised for showing minimal leadership on the most toxic internal debate the Greens have faced in living memory, with the chair of Jewish Greens saying he should resign.
The byelection, called after Starmer resigned his Commons seat shortly after he was ousted by Burnham, saw a low turnout of 38.7%, possibly due to the widespread predictions that Labour was set to win, despite a major campaigning effort from the Greens.
The turnout also suggests Burnham could still face a battle to engage some voters in urban areas, particularly London, where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.
In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.
“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain.”
Responding to the defeat, Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, said that while the result showed his party remained a major threat to Labour, many voters had told him they wanted to “give Andy Burnham a chance”.
It was the Greens’ second best-ever byelection result, more evidence of the party’s increased prominence and campaigning power since Polanski became leader 13 months ago.
The best came in February, when the Greens took an equally safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton in Greater Manchester, in a major upset that weakened Starmer’s position. Around the same time, the Greens peaked at 21% in national polling, above Labour. They are now about 11%, more than 15 points behind Burnham’s party.
Polanski’s position has come under scrutiny since the Zionism motion was passed, with critics accusing him of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate to campaign in the byelection, giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.
In interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.
On Friday, Vivien Lichtenstein, chair of Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.”
However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.
Speaking shortly before the byelection result was announced, Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, said Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”.
Speaking to Newsnight, she said: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.”
Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the … coming days and weeks.”
There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year.

The U.S. Treasury Secretary will skip the IMF and World Bank meetings — why this is unusual and what the reasons are

The U.S. Treasury Secretary will skip the IMF and World Bank meetings — why this is unusual and what the reasons are
Kyiv • UNN
Scott Bessent will not travel to the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok due to domestic affairs. The U.S. delegation will be led by his deputies.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will miss the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank, which will take place next week in Bangkok, Thailand, due to domestic matters. A U.S. official said this on Friday, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The Treasury Department confirmed that the U.S. delegation from the department will be led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke and Deputy Secretary for International Affairs Erin Brown, with a number of urgent economic issues on the agenda.
The Treasury Department said that during the meetings, U.S. representatives would work with partners to address policy issues and structural imbalances holding back economic growth, while also insisting on "greater transparency and more effective approaches to managing sovereign debt."
Bessent's absence from this important financial event comes at a critical moment: yields on benchmark U.S. Treasury bonds have reached their highest level in nearly 25 years, while a prolonged energy shock caused by the war in the Middle East has slowed the pace of global economic growth.
Trump announced an important statement amid record diesel prices09.10.26, 19:37 • 1104 views
It is not yet known for certain exactly what domestic matters are forcing Bessent to remain in the country, but he plays a key role in promoting domestic economic policy ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
In addition, the United States is chairing the "Group of Twenty" (G20) this year, and normally the Treasury secretary would chair the meeting of finance ministers and central bank heads from around the world. Bessent is expected to attend the G20 leaders' summit, which will take place in December in Miami, Florida.
The publication adds that it is not unusual for senior officials to miss individual meetings due to scheduling conflicts or other circumstances; however, Bessent's decision may displease representatives of other countries, who typically use such events to hold official and unofficial bilateral meetings with their American counterparts.
Last year, Bessent missed the G20 meetings in South Africa due to the Trump administration's objections to land reform in that country and other issues.
The Treasury Department said that the U.S. delegation would focus on debt problems so that countries facing difficult debt situations could restore stability and return to economic growth, while "clear and consistent standards" would be applied to creditors and borrowers. The United States will also continue to insist that the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank — in which the United States is the largest shareholder — focus on carrying out their core missions, operate effectively, and support policies that promote economic stability, productivity, and growth.
"Our participation in the events in Bangkok will be guided by a clear objective: to ensure that international financial institutions and the broader international economic system help advance U.S. economic interests and national security interests," the Treasury Department said in a statement.

The police said the organisers were proceeding without permission and stressed that the temporary curbs were necessary to prevent overcrowding and keep the capital functioning.In a statement posted on X, the force said, "The right to protest must be protected, but so must the right of a city to function safely. Responsible policing is about balancing both."
The police cited violence during a protest in July to explain its concerns.According to the statement, permission had been granted for a one-day demonstration, but it continued for a month. More than 200 police personnel were injured, while over 2,000 people with criminal antecedents joined the protest, contributing to the violence.The police said the situation eventually spiralled out of control, leading to clashes in which students were also injured. It added that women constables had been molested and assaulted by protesters at Jantar Mantar in the past week.
Crowd management and public safety
The police also pointed to the limited capacity of Jantar Mantar, saying the site could accommodate only 1,000 people at a time. It said restrictions were needed to prevent overcrowding and protect protesters, residents, shopkeepers and others in the area.The force said Delhi Police had to balance the right to protest with the safety of residents and the capital's economic interests. It added that the city could not be brought to a halt every time a demonstration took place.According to the statement, seeking permission allows authorities to estimate crowd numbers and plan traffic diversions, emergency access and safe movement around the protest site. The police said this would help demonstrators raise their concerns while allowing residents, workers and businesses to continue with their daily activities.
Police cite legal position on unauthorised protests
The police said the Cockroach Janta Party was proceeding with its planned gathering without permission. Citing the Supreme Court's position, the statement said a protest held without permission was unlawful and participants could face prosecution.It added that organisers were responsible for explaining the legal position to those they invited to attend."The restrictions being put in place today are temporary. They are intended to regulate the flow of people, prevent overcrowding and keep protesters, residents, shopkeepers and others in the area safe," the statement read.The police said the precautions were intended to ensure that people could raise their concerns peacefully without compromising public safety or disrupting the functioning of the city.

Local human rights activists, however, insist the real number of recruits could be as high as 841 Kenyans who ended up in the combat zone.

====================================================================================================

Andy Burnham is lucky – Polanski, Farage and Badenoch all seem determined to help him | Jonathan Freedland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:05:50 UTC
02:05:50 KST

I don’t know where Andy Burnham found his magic lamp, but I hope he’s taking good care of it. In the early hours of Friday morning, the genie that’s looked so kindly on him these past few months granted him yet another wish, with a byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. It was just the latest gift for a prime minister for whom things keep going right – and who is especially blessed in his choice of opponents.
Let’s start with that win in London, where Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali defeated the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. It’s easy to miss how rare such a victory is. As the veteran psephologist Peter Kellner pointed out, this was a win that “defied history”. If the past half-century were any guide, Labour should have lost, thanks to a “truly dreadful record” defending its own seats when in government and facing a byelection challenge from the left or centre-left, the likes of the Greens or the Lib Dems. The average swing against Labour in such contests had been 24%. “On those figures,” wrote Kellner, “Polanski should have won at a canter.” But he lost.
That reinforces the case Burnham made for why he should replace the previous Holborn and St Pancras MP, one Keir Starmer, as Labour leader: namely, that he was uniquely placed to defeat challenges from both left and right. This latest win over the Greens, coupled with his own success in Makerfield in June, is early vindication of that argument.
Burnham can claim much credit for the London result: it’s his leftward shift that has persuaded many progressive voters that they don’t need to vote Green to get what they want and that they should give Labour another chance. But Burnham really ought to share the credit with Polanski himself, who has proved a most generous adversary.
Yes, Polanski brought an initial surge in energy, enthusiasm and membership to the Greens. But under him the party has steadily dismantled the moral halo it once enjoyed as the UK’s foremost advocate for the planet, reshaping itself into something darker. Thanks to Sunday’s conference vote branding Zionism as racism, which Polanski ducked, the party now demands the destruction of a state founded, and still regarded by most Jews, as an essential refuge, one whose creation was approved by a UN vote. “Destruction” is not metaphorical, by the way. The motion passed says that the change it seeks – a Palestinian state replacing, rather than existing alongside, Israel – must be secured “by all available means”, a phrase clarified in an accompanying booklet produced by the motion’s proposers to include “armed struggle”. Meaning, violence.
Thus have the Greens allowed themselves to become toxified by the kind of cranks and bigots whose manias crowd out anyone who dares hold a moderate or nuanced view, including many longtime, dedicated local activists. A moment like this calls for leadership, but all the Greens have is a quack hypnotherapist who once earned a living promising to make women’s breasts larger and who, when faced with a difficult decision, ran away. (Now, after the event, Polanski says he would not have voted for the Zionism resolution.) Instead of a leader, the Greens are stuck with a charlatan and a coward.
No wonder former leader Caroline Lucas could not say yes, when asked by Newsnight, whether Polanski should stay in his post. Burnham himself would have no such hesitation: the PM might even be quietly pleased that Polanski performed just well enough in Thursday’s byelection to fend off an immediate challenge. The longer Polanski leads the Greens, the better for Labour.
Meanwhile, Burnham’s other opponents seem similarly determined to do him a favour. Of course, there will be stormier times ahead, but the party conference season now concluded was like a warm, extended summer for the prime minister.
Reform UK, for so long Labour’s strongest challenger in the polls, saw its moment in the sun clouded by eve-of-conference revelations that two senior aides to Nigel Farage had been caught on film apparently discussing how they might get around UK electoral law to take a £500,000 donation from a US benefactor. In politics, the scandals that bite hardest are those that confirm suspicions the voters already harbour. In this case, three in four Britons told YouGov back in July that they regarded Farage as sleazy, with 56% describing him as “very sleazy”.
The party’s leading lights tried to make assorted policy announcements, but the only debate that really cut through was the one started by Suella Braverman, with her eccentric and exclusivist insistence that certain minorities, even those born in England into families rooted in the country for several generations, are not truly English – a definition that would exclude Rishi Sunak and a good portion of the England football team. Farage’s army of would-be mavericks and rebels looks increasingly like a rabble of crooks and spivs and – as if to prove the Greens have no monopoly on the demographic – cranks and bigots.
All this has created an opening for the Conservatives to reclaim their place as the dominant party of the right – but here, too, the genie has smiled on Burnham. True, Kemi Badenoch continues to enjoy higher ratings than her party, but that isn’t saying much. True, too, that she has, belatedly, woken up to the fact that victory will not come solely from trying to out-Reform Reform – people will always vote for the real thing – and that she has to appeal to that vast swathe of Middle England seats lost in 2024 to the Lib Dems.
Her conference pitch – promising to abolish inheritance tax on even the most expensive homes, and to extend free childcare to those earning over £100,000 – might conceivably appeal to some of those high earners. But it draws a dividing line with Labour that Burnham could only have dreamed of. Now the Tories have made plain that, in an age of stretched resources, their priority is to help some of the richest people in the land. That is a battle Burnham will be itching to fight.
As for the Lib Dems, the PM will be only too happy to see them muddling along, an inoffensive receptacle for Tory-sceptic voters in parts of the country that would never go to Labour. Though Burnham wants to eat into their vote too, promising that he will, in the next term, deliver on two of their signature issues: Europe and electoral reform.
He did that in a speech that was the highlight of the conference season, one that showed a politician who understands the importance of making arguments – and is comfortable making them. After Starmer, who was the opposite in both respects, listening to Burnham was like “gulping down oxygen”, one cabinet minister told me.
And yet, everyone at Labour’s top table knows that the weather will change soon enough. The government, and everyone else, is paying too much to borrow money. At some point, the welfare budget will have to be cut: Labour MPs may be applauding now, but they will be less cheerful when asked to vote for reduced benefits, especially as they face re-selection contests in their local parties, a process that gets under way as soon as January.
There’s a hole in defence spending to fill, the full sweep of public services crying out for cash, a US president apparently bent on driving up global oil prices and therefore inflation, and a civil service machine that ministers privately curse as bloated and ineffective. What’s more, the period we’re in right now – the middle of the parliament – is when governments should be focused entirely on delivery, driving through their agenda. Instead, vital time has been spent on the transition from one PM to another – time Labour will not get back.
For now, Burnham is lucky in his opponents, whose choices hurt them and help him. But the skies will eventually darken and, when they do, the prime minister will reach once again for that magic lamp – hoping against hope that it still works.
- Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Forum in Paris discusses Ukraine’s future in EU and NATO, conditions for lasting peace
The event was organized by the New Europe Center and the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI), according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
French Minister Delegate for Europe Benjamin Haddad and Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration Vsevolod Chentsov addressed the participants remotely.
“For us, dialogue with Paris is always about seeking strategic clarity regarding our shared European future,” Chentsov said.
He recalled France’s support during its presidency of the Council of the EU in 2022, when Ukraine was granted EU candidate status. The membership talks, the official said, have now moved to substantive work.
“We have opened two negotiating clusters. We hope to open the second and third next week, and the fourth and fifth by the end of the year. At the same time, our country is already aligning its legislation with European law and deepening cooperation with the European Union in energy, transport, digitalization and defense. We are not waiting for the final point. We are already integrating and deepening our interaction. For Ukraine, amid the war, it is very important to feel the results of closer ties with the European Union already today,” Chentsov said.
During a discussion on European integration, Vincent Guérend, Director of the European Union Department at the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, noted that the EU itself must also prepare for the admission of new members. France, he said, supports Ukraine’s accession “without any ambiguity.”
“In all the negotiations, we are making every effort to advance the issue of Ukraine’s membership,” the diplomat assured.
Ukraine’s Ambassador to NATO Alyona Getmanchuk stressed that membership in the Alliance remains Ukraine’s strategic course.
“NATO has a lot to offer Ukraine and helps it defend itself. But Ukraine also has a lot to offer NATO. It is helping the Alliance prepare to defend itself in the future,” Getmanchuk said.
She also highlighted the PURL program, through which Ukraine receives U.S. weapons, including interceptor missiles for Patriot systems, and thanked France for its assistance in protecting Ukrainian airspace, in particular through SAMP/T systems and Aster 30 missiles.
Speaking about the future security architecture of Europe, Getmanchuk called for NATO to be renewed and for the role of its European members to be strengthened. “Without Ukraine, NATO will be much less effective than it would be with Ukraine,” she stressed.
A separate discussion focused on the possibility of a diplomatic settlement to the war and the conditions for lasting peace. The forum participants also discussed changes in Ukrainian society and prospects for the country’s post-war reconstruction.
As reported by Ukrinform, Arnaud Guillois, Director of the Continental Europe Department at the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, said during the France-Ukraine Forum in Paris that collective assistance should match the scale of the Ukrainians’ resistance, which Russia has failed to break.

Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi foils Russia’s plan to encircle the Donbas, ISW analysis shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:04:36 UTC
02:04:36 KST

Ukraine’s counter-offensive on the Lyman axis collapsed the northern arm of a Russian pincer movement aimed at surrounding Ukrainian-held Donetsk, liberating up to 176 square kilometres and forcing Russian units onto the defensive, the Washington-based think tank said.
Ukrainian forces have derailed Russia’s plan to encircle and occupy the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory of the Donetsk region this year, the Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War (ISW) concluded in an assessment based primarily on open-source intelligence.
The Russian campaign centred on a deep pincer movement targeting what the report calls the “fortress belt” — a defensive and logistical network protecting the Ukrainian-held portion of the Donbas — advancing from Lyman in the north and Dobropillia in the south-west, with both arms intended to link up near Barvinkove in the Kharkiv region.
Completing such an encirclement would have gone a long way towards Moscow’s longstanding objective of occupying all of Donetsk region and would have given the Kremlin something to show Russian society for the costs of the war.
Ukraine’s counter-offensive on the Lyman axis, dubbed Operation Vivaldi, dismantled the northern arm of that pincer.
Ukrainian forces advanced along the Ridkodub–Nove–Novomykhailivka line in the north and the Yarova–Drobysheve–Stavky line in the south, collapsing the salient Russia had built to threaten Sloviansk from the north-east and forcing Russian units onto the defensive.
Commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps Andrii Biletskyi said the first three phases of the operation in mid- to late September liberated 176 square kilometres of territory.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy put the figure at between 125 and 140 square kilometres as of 3 October, adding that Russian losses had risen sharply over the preceding two to three months.
ISW suggested the operation may have been more successful than Kyiv’s official figures reflect.
The defeat of the northern pincer forced Russia to abandon its plans to advance on Sloviansk from the north-east and deprived it of positions intended to threaten northern approaches to the fortress belt.
Ukraine’s retained control over the Lyman area also preserved key supply routes. Russian units on other parts of the front may have been redeployed to reinforce the northern sector.
Russia’s south-western advance from the Pokrovsk–Dobropillia area — the surviving arm of the original encirclement — now faces far more ambitious objectives on its own.
ISW regards the collapse of the northern pincer as an operational failure, as Russia has not just lost ground around Lyman but also a key component of the campaign plan for the fortress belt.
Russian forces retain limited gains around Kostyantynivka and east of Sloviansk but have struggled to sustain the pace of advance in both areas.
ISW argued that their reliance on infantry infiltration, drones and bombardment can produce gradual attrition but cannot generate the fast mechanised manoeuvres required to collapse Ukraine’s defences at the scale Moscow needs.
The situation remains fluid, the institute added, and Russian forces will probably adapt over time, but for now, Ukraine appears to have halted the advance.
A further Russian mobilisation and technological adaptation could alter the balance, although neither would necessarily enable a breakthrough.
Putin’s September figures challenged
ISW also challenged claims, widely circulated in pro-government Russian media, that Russian forces occupied further 1,301 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory in September alone, roughly two and a half times the figure reported in previous months.
Based on geolocated photo and video footage, satellite imagery and visually confirmed data, the institute calculated that Russian assault units had in reality been pushed out of at least 80 square kilometres in September.
Russia's net retreat in September rose to 175.18 square kilometres, including areas it temporarily penetrated but did not hold.
Putin told the Valdai Club last week that Russia now occupies 89% of Donetsk region. ISW puts the figure of Russian-occupied territory in the Ukrainian region at no more than 81%.
The institute assessed that Putin’s claims of Russian breakthroughs in September were “so far removed from reality that they resemble hallucinations.”
It could not determine whether Putin knows the figures he cites are false or has come to believe the fabricated frontline data he receives, a product of what ISW describes as a deeply embedded culture of dishonesty in the Russian military command.

FlyDubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Tel Aviv airport inspired by 9/11, prosecutor says
The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of FlyDubai flight 1073 had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport in a suicide attack, the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor said Friday. The Israel-bound flight carrying 182 people made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of its rudder was torn away.
The co-pilot who attacked the captain of a FlyDubai jet last week had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport, the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor said on Friday.
In the aftermath of the incident, people on board – the majority of whom were Israeli – described a sudden plunge in altitude and a fight for control of the aircraft, which was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The passengers were repatriated on a second flydubai flight hours later.
The unnamed Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from al Qaeda's September 11, 2001 suicide attacks on the United States, and carried out his attempt "with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life", according to the Emirati prosecutor's findings published by state media.
The prosecutor found that the co-pilot had first begun to be radicalised while studying in Australia "through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks".
He said last week's flight had been the co-pilot's third to Tel Aviv, and that he had used the two earlier trips to plan the attack.
Read moreWho are the mystery pilots who successfully landed endangered FlyDubai flight 1073?
During the flight, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane's Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help.
Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board "noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner", according to the findings.
After gaining entry, he "intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect".
The return flight captain and his co-pilot then landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
No sign of intentions
Israel and the UAE have become close partners since normalising ties under the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020, and Israel carries out stringent security checks on those travelling to the country.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu previously said that the co-pilot – identified in reports as Hamam al-Hammami – must have got around restrictions preventing individuals from nations that do not recognise Israel operating flights to the country.
The UAE prosecutor's "findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot's licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks".
"However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot."
The co-pilot had previously worked for Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, but media outlets reported after the incident that he had been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views.
After the incident, Netanyahu had hailed the passengers and the plane's captain for their bravery in averting what would have otherwise been a catastrophe.
He later ordered a "thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel" in response to the incident.

US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court, hours after former judge wins Nobel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:04:05 UTC
02:04:05 KST

US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The ICC's deputy prosecutor, Nazhat Shameem Khan, condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal's work.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday's move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement, first published by Reuters.
"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off its resources and crippling its ability to operate."
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Khan told Reuters the sanctions "must be condemned."
"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," Khan said. "Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions."
The sanctions are "an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law," the ICC said in a statement.
"The designation is aimed at disrupting the Court’s operations and at intimidating those who work for or cooperate with the Court. The Court, for its part, will not be deterred. ... Yet the Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the States that created it," it continued.
Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.
The court counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey. It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries including major US allies, and is based in the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member.
Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize earlier on Friday, had served as a judge on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003-2008. The prize committee said in its citation that in naming her it had sought to "issue a reminder" at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack."
"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account, and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the prize committee said.
Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns.
Washington immediately allowed some exemptions. Shortly after the sanctions were announced, the US Treasury issued four general licenses, which would allow some transactions for ICC telecommunications, software and pension payments, and transactions linked to ICC detainees.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu commended Trump and Rubio for taking the "critical decision" to impose the sanctions in a post on X/Twitter on Friday.
"The ICC is not a court," he said. "It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty. Thank you for your leadership."
US expects allies to 'rein in the court'
US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organization, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.
The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.
Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
The court's registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler called earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called "blocking mechanism" that lets it shield European countries from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions.
In his statement, Rubio said the United States had delayed its sanctions, hoping that the ICC and the countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address US concerns, but they had failed to do so.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and who rely on American service members for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said.
"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly," Rubio said.
UN rights chief Turk urges immediate safeguards for ICC after 'unacceptable' US sanctions
UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday called for immediate measures to protect the International Criminal Court (ICC) after the United States imposed "unacceptable" sanctions upon it.
"These sanctions – the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel for the work they do every day to advance accountability for the very worst violations of human rights – are unacceptable," Turk said.
Netherlands and EU willing to take steps to protect ICC, Jetten says
EU countries, including the host country, the Netherlands, will take measures to keep the International Criminal Court functioning after the United States impose sanctions on it, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and EU Council President Antonio Costa said at a joint press conference on Friday.
Jetten said it was "crucial" that there is still time to continue talks with the US during the six-month period before the sanctions take effect.
UN SECRETARY-GENERAL ANTONIO GUTERRES:
Officials condemn sanctions
"The Secretary-General condemns the announcement of the imposition by the United States of sanctions against the International Criminal Court as an institution," according to a statement read by UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric during a press briefing. "Today's decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar," he added.
Executive Director of Human Rights Watch Philippe Bolopion also responded to the sanctions, saying, "The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court. The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, is above the law."
"Governments that value human rights and accountability should condemn this outrageous move and take swift action to protect the ICC, its staff, and all those who cooperate with it, starting with the European Union using its laws to mitigate the sanctions’ impact in the region."
German Justice Minister recalls WWII
"Historically, hardly any country has done more for international criminal law than the USA. For it was the United States that, after the Second World War, championed the cause of bringing the principal perpetrators of the Nazi regime to trial in Nuremberg – and thereby laid the foundations for international criminal law. It is utterly staggering that the US, of all countries, is now setting out to destroy this idea once and for all."

Segev said that readiness for such operations doesn’t entail “putting the operational orders in a drawer and waiting for someone to tell us to carry them out.”
"It means keeping entire teams working and active, the technology division, explosives, a thousand and one other things,” he said. “But every time we came back and said, 'We're ready,' we received the same response: 'Maintain readiness.'"
