====================================================================================================

Café Basimta: The Jerusalem café where Shabbat, religious freedom, and evangelism collide - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:03:17 UTC
02:03:17 KST

When it opened, Café Basimta, operated by an Israeli associated with Jews for Jesus, opened its doors on Shabbat and began serving espresso in the heart of Jerusalem.
Unsurprisingly, an ultra-Orthodox group began showing up, holding regular protests on Shabbat to demonstrate against the public desecration of Shabbat. Its position was about the desecration of Shabbat, not about the café’s apparent Jews-for-Jesus ownership, even after that became clear.
Basimta was not the first establishment in Jerusalem to serve customers on Shabbat, but it became the focal point of a very public battle over what Shabbat should look like in Israel’s public square.
Then, also unsurprisingly, came the counterprotest. Secular Israelis began showing up, buying coffee not because they wanted to hear about Jesus, but because they wanted to make a point about religious coercion. Their message was clear, too: Keep your Shabbat observance out of my cup of coffee.
And in an Israel already simmering over military exemptions, economic disparities, and the perceived unequal sharing of national responsibilities, the controversy tapped into something much deeper. For many secular Israelis, this wasn’t really about a latte. It was about who gets to determine how everyone else lives.
This was not new. It has been a battle in Israel for decades.
But then came the part of the story that is new and deserves far more attention. Walk into Basimta and, at least outwardly, it looks like an ordinary café. No crosses. No Bibles on the tables. No obvious Christian branding. No staff member standing behind the counter announcing the Gospel.
Just coffee.
And that creates an entirely different ethical question. If the organization behind the café has an explicit mission of sharing the Gospel with Jews, why is that understated, and why shouldn’t the customer know that before walking through the door? Christians have every right to share what they believe. But religious freedom does not eliminate the obligation to be transparent.
The identity is largely hidden
If the café were openly identified as being operated by Jews for Jesus, if the staff wore the T-shirts, if the identity were clearly displayed, the customer would know exactly what environment they were entering. That’s honest engagement.
When the identity is largely hidden, however, it begins to look less like transparent evangelizing about which Jews have enough problems, and more like a veiled strategy for lowering the defenses of the very people being approached. Given the complicated history between Christianity and the Jewish people, that distinction matters.
And especially with the reality of widespread Christian support for Israel and the Jewish people, a world in which we coexist daily in our respective life callings and work, where were the Christian voices willing to say so?
Sometimes Christian accountability requires Christians to challenge their own.
Above and beyond Christians not openly questioning the motives and strategy even among those who actively advocate for the Jewish people to accept Jesus as messiah, there’s a deeper theological irony.
Jews for Jesus places enormous emphasis on the Jewishness of Jesus – a first-century Jewish man who lived within the rhythms of Jewish life, including Shabbat.
Jesus certainly challenged interpretations of Sabbath law. He healed on Shabbat. He also defended his disciples when they were accused of violating it. But there is a difference between explaining an action that occurred on Shabbat and intentionally establishing a commercial enterprise designed to operate on Shabbat.
Jesus never authorized that. It’s hard to imagine that were he to come back today, he would patronize such an establishment, much less on Shabbat, any more than he would eat a bacon cheeseburger.
Eventually, after nearly two months of public and weekly controversy that drew widespread national media attention, Basimta decided to close on Shabbat. Just like that.
A huge PR win broadcast across all platforms of Israeli media
The decision was portrayed as caving to ultra-Orthodox, which is surely true, at least in part.
In the media frenzy that occupied numerous hours of radio and TV broadcasts, not to mention social media and other platforms, the Jews for Jesus spokesperson (and presumably the owner of the café) explained their decision as being made in “the love of Jesus.” A huge PR win broadcast across all platforms of Israeli media.
The controversy leaves behind a few uncomfortable realities and questions.
The Christian blind spot: Why was there so little Christian willingness to challenge the methodology of presenting an evangelistic initiative as an ordinary café rather than being transparent about its identity?
The Israeli fault line: Why can a cup of coffee on Shabbat become a proxy battle for the much larger struggle over religious authority, secular freedom, military service, economic responsibility, and the character of the Jewish state? And why did so many Israeli political and civic leaders make the opening of this café specifically, apparently owned by Jews for Jesus with an agenda that is an anathema to most Jews, their cross to die on?
Basimta may have closed its doors on Shabbat. But the questions it exposed are still wide open and deserve a serious public conversation.
The Shabbat coffee is gone. The controversy isn’t.

Omani Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Israeli airport, UAE says

An Omani Flydubai co-pilot had intended to seize a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight and crash it into a terminal at Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport on September 30 in a suicide attack before he was thwarted by the captain, the UAE attorney general said on Friday.
Attorney General Hamad Saif al Shamsi’s statement did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing and contained the most detailed account yet from prosecutors about what they believe to have happened. Flydubai was not immediately available for comment.

It found the suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route and the airport”, the state news agency WAM reported. It is the first public confirmation of the co-pilot’s September 11 inspiration.

massimo dutti reincarnates 16th-century palace as rome flagship store
an olfactory archive, curated design books, and a custom coffee activation connect the fashion retail space to local culture.
16TH-CENTURY PALACE BECOMES flagship for massimo dutti in rome
Spanish fashion brand Massimo Dutti opens its new flagship store within the 16th-century Palazzo Ruspoli in Rome. Spanning over 2,000 square meters (21,527 square feet) along Via del Corso, the retail design exhibits its clothing collections within the historic architecture, pairing the palace’s original features — such as the vaulted ceilings and palatial staircase — with contemporary wooden furniture, large-format rugs, and lightweight displays for fashion.
all images courtesy of Massimo Dutti
preserving historic rome palace vaults and arches
Visitors enter Massimo Dutti’s flagship in Rome by ascending a wide stone staircase that leads into a sequence of arched rooms. Following a heritage study and restoration by specialized artisans, the 16th-century finishes remain visible. Indirect lighting is installed at the base of the vaults to highlight the rhythm of the arches without obscuring the original masonry. The fashion brand uses a material palette of wood and fabric for its understated sofas and display units. In the checkout area, the color palette deepens, and tall bookshelves line the walls to enclose the space.
For the opening, the flagship store hosts an olfactory archive in collaboration with Florentine perfumery Profumoir. Visitors sample the perfumery’s primary fragrance notes from flame-worked glass holders produced by Barcelona-based experimental artist Pia Glasswork. Independent Roman bookshop Leporello Books curates a library of nearly 100 titles on art and architecture for the space, with 20 selections featuring handwritten notes by its founder.
debut of Massimo dutti’s fall/winter 2026 limited edition
The first floor houses the complete men’s and women’s collections, marking the debut of Massimo Dutti’s Fall/Winter 2026 Limited Edition. The garments focus on tailoring, featuring structured jackets, wide-leg trousers, and long coats. The pieces pair leather with knitwear and diaphanous fabrics in a color palette of black, chocolate, gray, taupe, camel, and stone.
The flagship operates with several digital services, including a concierge for delayed collection or hotel delivery, and mobile inventory devices for store staff. Online orders can be prepared for in-store pickup in under two hours. The retail footprint also extends into the city. The brand serves coffee from Caffè Doria at the flagship, while setting up a temporary installation in the courtyard of Palazzo Doria Pamphilj.

Latvia builds a safe space for defence innovators
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:00:28 BST
02:00:28 KST

Latvia has created a state body that can work alongside industry intellectual property without disqualifying the companies involved from later competitions, the deputy commander of NATO Multinational Division North told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Brigadier General Ilmars Lejins said the organisation sits under the defence ministry and is known as the Autonomous Centre, and that it exists to give soldiers and companies somewhere to work together before any contract is in play. Taking part in it is structured so that it cannot count against a firm when procurement begins, which removes the main reason companies hold back from early collaboration.
He was open about how young the arrangement still is and about how little can yet be proved from it. “Are we succeeding? I don’t know yet. It is relatively new. We have done it for one and a half years,” he said, adding that other nations will probably arrive at similar models, where a company can go into a sandbox and build trust without consequences arriving later once money and contracting are involved.
Asked how a user keeps order while so much new equipment arrives at once, he suggested working with the churn instead of against it. “I think that we should embrace chaos for a while, not fight it. Otherwise it’s kind of pointless. We are where we are,” he said.
Contracting models need to change alongside that, in his view, and he was careful to say it is not his job while making clear he holds an opinion on it. The comparison he reached for was the way people buy music.
He said: “We used to be in the military, we want the stuff, we describe the stuff, what we want, we buy the stuff and then we leave industry alone for a while, and then we break it, and then we do that again. We cannot do that anymore. I bought LPs and CDs, that’s how old I am, and then that was my property. I used it on a machine, a player, that was made by several different vendors. But now I stream from Spotify. So I have to go, as a military, into more or less a Spotify agreement with other vendors. How do I write the contract on that one? I do not have shares in Spotify, but it’s a whole new world in contracting and relationship with industry.”
His closing message to the room was about command and control, “What I need as a division commander is C2 networks based on data centric federation. It doesn’t matter if you have the best system in the UK or the best system in America. If it doesn’t work together, it’s pointless,” he said, citing Ukraine’s Delta system as something that works well enough for the people using it.
He also asked for more investment in the people who accredit systems onto networks, a group whose work decides how quickly anything new can be fielded. “In Latvia, they call them the men in black, the security people, the accreditation,” he said. “I would love that they would have more CIS educated people, because it’s the man-made procedures in accreditation of systems.”
Multinational Division North is headquartered in Latvia and commands NATO forward land forces in the Baltic states, which puts it among the first formations to absorb the volume of uncrewed systems now reaching European armies, and gives Riga a reason to get the industry relationship working early.

Does it matter if Jesus actually existed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:00:27 UTC
02:00:27 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at why facts matter for Christians, with Andrew Henry (@religionforbreakfast). You can watch our full hour-long interview at the end.
Why does it matter if Jesus existed?
One of the most common topics in debates about Christianity is the historical accuracy of the Bible.
“Aha! Look, there’s no evidence of a global flood.”
“There’s no way Jericho could have been under siege anywhere around this time!”
For Christians, the most important question, of course, is about Jesus. Did the man exist? Likely. Did he do a lot of the stuff in the Gospels? Likely, with some poetic license. Did he say all those things? Possibly, but everyone needs a good editor. Did he perform miracles? Well, that’s where things get tricky.
The questions of miracles, resurrection, and divine intervention are matters for another day. It’ll probably take more than a day, in fact. No, the question I want to explore in this newsletter is: Why does it matter that Jesus existed at all? Why does it matter whether a flesh-and-blood Jew was really walking around ancient Palestine saying he was the Son of God?
After all, in some religions, it’s a matter of shrugging indifference. A lot of Daoists happily accept that Lao Tzu is not one person but likely an amalgamation of many people or sages across time. Who cares? The Daodejing is still awesome. Many Buddhists will smile at the (usually) Western attempts to chronicle the Buddha’s real life. Who cares? All that matters is that we can walk the path.
So why is Christianity so fact-obsessed? This week, we explore just that.
Go well,
Jonny
Who cares if Jesus existed?
I was wrong.
It happens a lot, and I actually get a strange, intellectual spark of joy when I find out when and how I was wrong. And this week, I was wrong about Christianity.
I was interviewing Andrew Henry, the hugely popular YouTuber and scholar of religion, about common misunderstandings about religion. As you can hear below, we spent a great deal of time debating what makes a religion a religion. It turns out I’m an “essentialist.” A new label to add to the collection.
A country that can’t see its own problem
Malcolm Gladwell weaves a story from a 17th-century knight’s legal troubles to Chicago’s emergency rooms to explore America’s most pressing epidemic: gun violence. Use code MGTHINK for 25% thru 12/31/26.
As we were talking, I got waylaid by a passing point I’d never much thought about: Why is Christian apologetics so concerned with facts? There is a minority belief within Christianity that accepts Jesus is fictional or mythological. But for most Christians today, it matters that Jesus existed and did what the Gospels say he did.
I presented my theory.
“Does it connect to the fact that Christianity has always been a highly proselytizing religion?” I offered. “It involves missionaries, and the disciples, and Christians going out into communities saying, ‘Look, guys, your gods are wrong, my god is right,’ and so therefore I have to present you an argument to convert you.”
And Henry did that thing that all kind, gentle scholars do when someone gets it wrong. He gave me a “Yeah, kinda.”
Yeah, Christianity is “definitely a missionizing religion,” but he added that it was probably more a spiritual, almost magical mission rather than a rational or philosophical one. The missionaries converted people by demonstrating “the power [Christ] claimed to have over demons and evil forces.” In other words, I’d wrongly assumed my conclusion. Why would people — potential converts — in the early years of Christianity be any more interested in “facts” than those elsewhere in the world? They just wanted a religion that worked for them.
So what’s the better answer? Why do Christians care about facts so much today? Well, there are broadly three arguments.
First is the idea of sacred time, which was popularized by Mircea Eliade. The Indian religions like Hinduism, Jainism, and Buddhism see the universe in terms of cycles. The wheel of time turns, and what is here now will come again. Someone like the Buddha — a pure sage guiding us toward the path — will pop up again. In the meantime, bodhisattvas are reborn to help the rest of humanity. And so, the individual body or personality of any one bodhisattva or Buddha is less important than the path itself. In Christianity, though, time is a line, not a wheel, and God steps into it once — as one man, in one place, at one datable moment.
Second, the event of Jesus’ life and death is key to Christian theology. It matters that Jesus beat death — not a spiritual, metaphorical kind of “death of desire” as you might get in Buddhist mythology, but an actual conquest over death. Christians believe we will be bodily resurrected. And so, Christ’s real, provable resurrection has to be the template. Similarly, the role of Jesus’ crucifixion is important because Jesus was the Lamb of God. He was sacrificed to atone for the sins of mankind. God is just — so He cannot let humans off the hook. And Jesus came along to take the punishment on our behalf. If Jesus didn’t exist and wasn’t executed, then humans are still up for punishment. And that isn’t very salvational for a salvationist religion.
Third, and this is Henry’s position, is that Christian apologetics got distracted by philosophical debate. “[Defending factual claims] became particularly salient with the rise of modernism. You have David Hume, who really put out these fusillades against belief in the supernatural, and so in many respects the question of fact-seeking is a hangover of the past 300 years, and less the past 2,000 years — that there really is this need to prove historicity empirically, through empirical methods.”
So, all this fact-obsession may be younger than it seems. Hume drew the battle lines, and the apologists who came after accepted them. From William Paley’s A View of the Evidences of Christianity (1794) to Lee Strobel’s The Case for Christ (1998), which cross-examines the Gospels like witnesses on the stand, Christians will often treat their belief as a hypothesis to prove rather than a creed to accept.
Of course, with a big question like this, none of these will be the full answer. It’ll be a combination, and many other factors to boot. But the question is an interesting one.
If faith isn’t science, and metaphysics is beyond the physical, why does it matter so much what happens in this life? If any Christians are reading, please do add your thoughts! I’ve been wrong once already this week; I’m happy to be called so again.
Sign up for a paid membership to watch my full interview with Henry below.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

Michigan Senate debate: El-Sayed, Rogers spar over Iran, Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

Breadcrumb
Michigan Senate debate: El-Sayed and Rogers spar over Iran and Israel
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers traded barbs on Thursday over Iran and Israel during their first televised debate in the race for Michigan’s open Senate seat, ahead of November’s US midterm elections.
Held in Grand Rapids, Michigan, the debate opened with both candidates being asked whether they would support a pause on the federal petrol tax amid rising fuel prices linked to the war with Iran.
Fuel prices have surged since US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February triggered the conflict, adding to concerns over the cost of living among American voters.
Both candidates backed a pause on the federal petrol tax before turning to their respective positions on the war.
Rogers, who initially supported the US offensive against Iran, has since called for the months-long conflict to end.
The Republican Senate candidate reiterated that position during the debate, as did El-Sayed, who has repeatedly criticised the Trump administration over its handling of the war.
The Democrat also blamed the administration for Iran’s decision to close the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.
“This is what happens when you start wars you never should be fighting,” El-Sayed said.
“We literally taught the Iranian regime that they have a choke on the Strait of Hormuz, and now we’re living in that reality.”
Although Rogers agreed that “we need [the war] to come to an end”, he defended the military campaign, arguing that US attacks had set Iran’s uranium enrichment programme back by “twenty years”.
His remarks echoed claims by the Trump administration that military action was necessary to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Tehran has repeatedly denied US and Israeli accusations that it is seeking to develop nuclear weapons.
The Islamic Republic maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful, while insisting that it will not compromise on its civilian nuclear activities or make structural concessions without the lifting of US economic sanctions.
El-Sayed criticised Rogers for his support of the war and for defending the Trump administration, accusing him of changing his position for political reasons rather than out of concern for Americans’ financial circumstances.
"The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers,” El-Sayed said.
He added moments later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”
El-Sayed and Rogers clash over Israel
During the debate, El-Sayed faced questions over his criticism of Israel’s genocidal military campaign in Gaza, following his recent refusal to say whether he considers Israel or Iran a greater threat to the US in an interview with US cable news network NewsNation.
The candidates hold opposing positions on US military assistance to Israel, which has received more US foreign aid cumulatively than any other country since the Second World War.
Rogers reaffirmed his support for continued US aid to Israel, while El-Sayed called for an end to military assistance, arguing that American taxpayers’ money should instead be directed towards domestic priorities such as education and healthcare.
“He wants unconditional support for a foreign government,” El-Sayed said of Rogers. “I want unconditional support for kids in our schools, unconditional support for our healthcare, childcare.”
The Democrat also blamed Israel for drawing the US into military action against Iran.
“I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in war with Iran,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers, meanwhile, argued that Israel had “the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood”, reiterating his support for the country.
“Is there anything Israel could do that would lose your support?” debate moderator Rick Albin asked.
“Listen, if they’re talking about using nuclear weapons, they would definitely lose my support,” Rogers replied.
Rogers targets El-Sayed over Muslim identity
Beyond their disagreements over foreign policy, the candidates repeatedly traded personal insults.
El-Sayed described his Republican rival as “weak”, “cowardly” and a “sock puppet for the Trump administration”. Rogers, in turn, called his opponent a “glitchy AI chatbot” who was running a “con” and would “say anything to win”.
The pair also challenged each other over campaign donations and their personal finances.
El-Sayed lambasted Rogers over a waterfront property he owns in Florida, while Rogers pointed to a rental property owned by El-Sayed’s wife in the United Arab Emirates.
According to Albin, the candidates continued arguing even when the cameras were off. The moderator repeatedly urged them to maintain order, telling them to “work with me” and adding: “I appreciate your passion, but please, let's try to keep this orderly.”
The debate also covered the trade dispute with Canada, immigration, healthcare, and the cost of living.
However, some of Rogers’ attacks arguably fixated on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and alleged associations with extremist groups.
El-Sayed has repeatedly faced Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, with Trump leading attacks on the Democrat, including labelling him as an “extremist, terrorist sympathizer”.
Trump also claimed his history “goes back to the days of the Jihad” in a post on Truth Social.
During the debate, a discussion about healthcare led Rogers to claim that El-Sayed had “taken money from individuals on his campaign who openly support Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaeda”.
The former US congressman also challenged El-Sayed over his opposition to surveillance cameras operated by Flock Safety, arguing that the technology had helped apprehend people suspected of terrorism.
Rogers then suggested that El-Sayed’s concerns about the cameras warranted further scrutiny.
“Why would that bother you?” Rogers asked. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the terrorism watch list...”
El-Sayed interrupted, challenging Rogers to make explicit the implication he appeared to be suggesting.
“Are you going to go ahead and say that I’m a – go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing about it the whole time. Just say it. Just say it. Go ahead and say it.”
The exchange comes amid repeated attacks on El-Sayed’s Arab and Muslim identity during his campaign, highlighting wider concerns about Islamophobia directed at Muslim and Arab candidates in US politics.
If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim member of the US Senate.
Michigan Senate race could shape control of Congress
A CBS News poll published earlier this week showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 45.6 per cent to 41.4 per cent, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
The race is among those expected to help determine which party controls the Senate following the midterm elections.
The elections will shape the final two years of Trump’s presidential term, with Republicans facing the prospect of losing their current hold on Congress amid the president’s declining popularity and the fallout from the war on Iran.
Trump himself has been holding numerous rallies to potentially reverse the party’s political fortunes.

World day against the death penalty
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:56:41 CEST

World day against the death penalty Fight against the death penalty Statement On : October 09th 2026 On the 24th World Day Against the Death Penalty, 10 October, France reaffirms its absolute opposition to the death penalty everywhere and in all circumstances, and calls for its universal abolition. 2026 is the 45th anniversary of the abolition of the death penalty in France. On 9 October 1981, under the impetus of Robert Badinter, France chose a form of justice that respected human dignity. This commitment, significantly bolstered by its enshrinement in our constitution in 2007, remains at the heart of our action in defence of human rights. In Paris from 30 June to 2 July, France hosted the 9th World Congress Against the Death Penalty, organized by the NGO Together Against the Death Penalty (ECPM) and bringing together nearly 1,300 people from some 100 countries. The Congress provided an opportunity to step up international efforts to bring about universal abolution. On 11 August 2026, in accordance with the commitments made during the Congress, Lebanon became the first Middle Eastern State to abolish the death penalty. Abolition continues to make headway around the world: more than two-thirds of States have now abolished the death penalty in law or in practice; only 17 States went ahead with executions in 2025. This momentum cannot, however, conceal the sharp increase in the number of executions recorded last year, in a limited number of countries. France calls on those States which maintain the death penalty to establish a moratorium on executions with a view to its definitive abolition. It encourages all those States which have not yet done so to adhere to the second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty. Along with its partners and civil society, France will continue taking action in all the multilateral fora to further universal abolition. Abolition of the death penalty

Japan on Friday expressed “deep concern” over the latest US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), saying the measures contradict Tokyo's longstanding support for international judicial institutions.
Japan’s Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reaffirmed Tokyo’s support for international courts, including the ICC, the International Court of Justice and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.
"The measures are incompatible with Japan's consistent position, and Japan is deeply concerned about them," he said, according to a statement posted by the foreign ministry on US social media platform X.
“It is important that the ICC and its States Parties address the challenges facing the Court, so that the Court is administered appropriately,” Motegi said.
The statement said the minister had exchanged views with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Japan’s position on the issue.
Tokyo pledged continued engagement with Washington, ICC President Tomoko Akane and other countries to “work toward strengthening the rule of law in the international community.”
The statement came after Rubio threatened to "end the ICC" unless it stopped what he described as its "threats," urging US allies to "rein in the court."
The US previously sanctioned several ICC officials, including ICC President Akane, a Japanese national, following the tribunal's November 2024 arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Japan is an ICC member, while the US and Israel are not.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi expressed deep concern over US sanctions on the ICC, saying the measures contradict Tokyo's longstanding commitment to international law. "The measures are incompatible with Japan’s such consistent position, and Japan is deeply concerned about them," Takaichi said, reaffirming Japan's support for the court and its role in upholding the international rule of law.
Takaichi said Japan would continue engaging Washington while supporting the ICC's work. "We will continue to reach out to the United States and extend necessary support to the ICC so that the Court can fulfill its role and functions as originally envisaged," she said.

Palestine Action linked to 94% of all UK terrorism arrests
Unknown

01:55:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestine Action arrests make up 94% of all UK terrorism arrests, Home Office data shows
The arrests of pro-Palestine activists have made up the majority of terrorism-related arrests in the UK since Palestine Action was proscribed in 2025, new statistics from the Home Office reveal.
The latest figures show a record high in terrorism-related arrests, with 2,867 arrests made in the year ending June 2026, up from 234 the previous year -- a 1,553% increase. Of these arrests, 94 percent, or 3,630, were tied to alleged support for Palestine Action.
"Supporting a proscribed organisation is illegal. The Court of Appeal found that Palestine Action carried out acts of terrorism and promoted the use of violence," a spokesperson for the Home Office told The New Arab.
The government department added that Palestine Action is "not an ordinary protest or civil disobedience group".
"Its actions are not consistent with democratic values and the rule of law," the Home Office added. "We are backing the police with new powers and record funding, so they have the tools to tackle emerging threats and keep the public safe."
Arrests also rose by 39 percent from the start of the year to March. The Home Office confirmed that 634 arrests were charged under Section 12 or Section 13 of the Terrorism Act 2000 linked to supporting Palestine Action.
Proscription of Palestine Action
The pro-Palestine group was listed as a terrorist organisation on 5 July last year after its members spray-painted a military aircraft at one of the UK's largest air bases. The designation puts the group on the same legal footing as Al-Qaeda, the Islamic State group, and the Wagner Group, among others.
Palestine Action became the first direct action group in British history to be banned under the Terrorism Act.
An appeal against the proscription was initially overturned, but was then upheld in June of this year, with its founder launching another appeal months later.
The ban has condemnation from rights groups, with protests frequently held calling for the ban to be repealed. Many of the protesters demonstrating with the group are pensioners and the elderly, often holding up signs reading, "I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action".
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband recently admitted he didn't think anyone intended "to have those people criminalised".
Several activists from the direct action group have also been convicted as terrorists, despite being arrested before the group was banned.
The United States followed in the UK's footsteps in August, declaring Palestine Action a "terrorist group" and accusing it of "supporting numerous acts of terrorism" since July 2020.

The Guardian view on Labour and the Greens: winning trust takes more than words | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:52:10 UTC
01:52:10 KST

By holding Holborn and St Pancras, Andy Burnham’s Labour has shown it can attract liberal and left-leaning voters. The seat has substantial numbers of young adults, students, professionals and Muslims – offering fertile ground for the Greens’ ecopopulism. However, Labour prevailed. Having won leave-voting Makerfield in June, Mr Burnham can now claim an appeal that bridges Labour’s divided electorate. It’s worth noting that turnout in London was low and Labour’s vote share fell 3.7 points. But that compares with an average 19.3-point fall in four byelections under Mr Burnham’s predecessor. The new leader clearly has bought Labour breathing space and checked the Green advance.
The Greens more than tripled their vote share in the constituency to 33%. But they were beaten. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% in Sir Keir Starmer’s former seat, leaving Zack Polanski’s ambition of entering parliament unfulfilled. For a party that began the year promising to turn voters’ hunger for change into a serious challenge to Labour, this was a sobering moment. The passing of a motion declaring “Zionism is racism” at its conference probably cost the party support – though the result in central London alone cannot definitively say that. There is a separate question of leadership. Mr Polanski now says he would have voted against the motion. Why, then, did he not make his opposition clear when it mattered last weekend?
He intends to remain leader – and the expanded, radical membership has given Mr Polanski a base in the party that likely insulates him from an instant coup. But with calls for his resignation growing, he has to try to stay in the job while restoring confidence in the Greens’ electoral chances. Clouds had emerged on the horizon long before the party’s conference. Its spring polling surge has faded. In March, YouGov put the party second nationally to Reform, on 21%. Mr Burnham has since stolen much of the Greens’ rhetorical thunder by consciously evoking a more leftwing agenda. The party is now in fourth place, polling 10% nationally.
As Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents. Since the beginning of the year his net favourability rating has fallen from -6 to -29. The Greens are not to be discounted. Mr Burnham has yet to turn hope into lasting support. That will depend on what his government delivers, especially as prices rise, rather than whom it defeats.
In an interview with the BBC, Jonathan Bartley, the Greens’ former party co-leader, warned that the influx of members has changed the party and that some newcomers are unaware of its traditions of consensus and opposition to political “purity tests”. Significantly, Mr Polanski’s deputy, Rachel Millward, said that the party structures needed to become “fully democratic and strategic”. This may not be enough for the Green MP Siân Berry, who said she wanted to “fix the serious flaws” in the controversial Zionism motion.
Leadership is missing, and responsibility for that falls squarely on Mr Polanski. He has shown that he can communicate persuasively. Now, if he remains in post, he must show that he can acknowledge what went wrong and build support for changing the controversial Zionism policy. Mr Polanski claims credit for Labour’s leftward turn. But the Green leader now needs to put his own party’s house in order.

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:51:20 EEST
01:51:20 KST

A prosecutor from the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), based on an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), has sent an indictment to court in a case involving the alleged embezzlement of UAH 129 million allocated for the restoration of critical infrastructure in Kamianske district, Dnipropetrovsk region.
Seven people have been charged, including a local businessman alleged to have organized the scheme, the head of the municipal enterprise that commissioned the reconstruction, the director and deputy director of the company that won the tender, the head of an intermediary company used for procurement, a deputy head of the design organization and an employee of a company controlled by the alleged organizer, SAPO said in a Telegram post on Friday.
According to the investigation, members of an organized group helped a company controlled by the alleged organizer win a 2022–2023 tender for reconstruction of a water pipeline in Kamianske district.
Under the contract, the winning company was required to purchase pipes. Investigators found that the pipes were bought from the manufacturer at market prices and then resold to the municipal enterprise at prices more than three times higher, SAPO said.
The alleged scheme caused losses of more than UAH 129 million to the municipal enterprise. The suspects allegedly took control of the funds and disposed of them at their own discretion, the anti-corruption prosecutor's office said.
The alleged organizer and people under his control subsequently laundered the funds by transferring them to accounts of other related companies, SAPO said.
The beneficial owner of the company that won the tender was a prominent local businessman who was wanted by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation for property crimes, SAPO added.

Iran Guards say struck tanker transiting Hormuz via 'illegal route'
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Friday that they had struck a tanker attempting to take an "illegal route" through the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has sought to blockade since the outset of the Middle East war.
Maritime trackers also reported on Friday that an unknown projectile sparked a fire aboard a ship off the UAE coast, but named a different vessel.
In a statement carried by official media, the Guards said Iranian forces "have taken control of the administration of the strait".
"In carrying out this mission, a few hours ago, a giant LPG carrier named NV Sunshine, owned by NatWit, which was attempting to transit via the illegal route south of the Strait of Hormuz, was struck," they added.
Iran has attempted to impose its control over the Hormuz over the course of the war, insisting that vessels seek its permission to cross via its preferred routes.
However, ships have increasingly been willing to risk transiting via an alternative route hugging the strait's southern coast.
Britain's UKMTO maritime agency said on Friday that a ship 13 nautical miles (24 kilometres) off the UAE's Al Jazeera Al Hamra, southwest of the strait, was struck by a projectile, which caused a fire on board.
"Status of the crew, damage assessment and environmental impact are unknown at present. Authorities are investigating," UKMTO said in a statement.
British security firm Vanguard also reported the incident, and identified the vessel as the Panama-flagged crude tanker GEM NO.2.
The incident comes days after a tanker was hit off Qatar, around 500 kilometres (300 miles) west of the vital strait.
Ships in the Gulf and those attempting to transit the strait -- the only maritime route in or out of the oil-rich region -- have come under repeated attack since the US and Israel sparked the Middle East war in late February.
Iran has blockaded the strait ever since, though some vessels do manage to cross, and US media has reported on American military efforts to protect ships on the southern route.
The United States has set up its own counter-blockade of Iranian ports and occasionally fires on vessels linked to Tehran.
Hormuz is vital to the world economy, with around a fifth of the planet's oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the strait before the war began.

US sanctions on ICC spark global backlash, European calls for action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:50:00 UTC
01:50:00 KST

The U.S. faced mounting international criticism Friday over its sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), as European governments, Canada and Japan rallied behind the tribunal and warned that Washington's move threatened international justice and judicial independence.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the U.K., alongside their counterparts from Canada and Japan, expressed strong opposition to the sanctions, warning of serious consequences for the court's operations and personnel.
"We, the undersigned States Parties to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC), reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," the ministers said.
They cautioned that the restrictions, if implemented, would significantly affect the tribunal's work, its employees and their families, while welcoming preparations aimed at maintaining its operations.
The eight countries pledged to maintain dialogue with nations outside the Rome Statute, the treaty establishing the ICC, ahead of the Assembly of States Parties in December.
"We will continue to work together to support the Court's vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability," they said.
The ICC itself denounced the measures as an attempt to obstruct justice and intimidate those cooperating with the tribunal.
The sanctions represent "an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," the court said, warning that they undermine the principle that no individual is above the law.
The tribunal vowed to continue its work despite the restrictions but urged its member states to defend its independence.
"The Court, for its part, will not be deterred," it said, adding that its future also depended on the governments that established it.
The European Commission similarly criticized Washington's decision and pledged to consider measures to protect the tribunal and European businesses affected by the sanctions.
"The EU stands ready to take any necessary measures to enable the Court to carry out its work," the commission said, referring to investigations and prosecutions involving war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen described the sanctions as deeply regrettable but emphasized that a six-month period before their implementation would allow time for negotiations.
"We will stand firm in defence of the Court," he said, adding that service providers could continue working with the tribunal during the transition period.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot called for more decisive European action, urging the EU to activate its Blocking Statute to shield the court from the effects of U.S. sanctions.
"Europe must act," Prevot said, announcing plans to raise the issue with EU foreign ministers and at the upcoming European Council meeting.
German Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig also condemned the decision, highlighting Washington's historic role in establishing international criminal accountability following World War II.
She recalled that the United States had championed the Nuremberg trials against senior Nazi officials, helping lay the foundations of modern international criminal law.
"It is utterly staggering that the US, of all countries, is now setting out to destroy this idea once and for all," Hubig said.
In Washington, Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called the sanctions "unfortunate and short-sighted," accusing the Trump administration of further isolating the United States and undermining efforts to prosecute atrocities in Ukraine and Darfur.
Human rights organizations also criticized the measures, linking them to Washington's opposition to ICC proceedings involving U.S. and Israeli officials.
Philippe Bolopion, executive director of Human Rights Watch, accused the Trump administration of seeking to dismantle the tribunal to protect American and Israeli officials from potential prosecution.
He urged governments, particularly the EU, to take immediate steps to protect the ICC, its employees and those cooperating with its investigations.
James A. Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, similarly described the sanctions as a deliberate challenge to judicial independence and equality before the law.
He characterized the move as part of a broader effort to weaken the international justice system.
The sanctions have intensified tensions between Washington and its European allies over the ICC, which has faced U.S. criticism over its investigations involving American personnel and arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

====================================================================================================

Watchdog Urges Better Alignment Across Pentagon’s Planned GPS Backups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:47:39 UTC
01:47:39 KST

All of the U.S. military services are pursuing capabilities to complement GPS amid concerns that the constellation is increasingly vulnerable to interference, but a new government watchdog report calls for better coordination and prioritization among those efforts to avoid delays and duplication.
Today’s GPS constellation is a mix of new and legacy satellites, the oldest of which are nearly 30 years old. The system has become essential to the entire global economy, affecting industries like agriculture, banking, and transportation, which are dependent on the system for timing and positioning. It’s also a fundamental military capability, particularly important for navigating in remote areas and helping guide missiles and drones.
In recent years, U.S. leaders have sounded the alarm about GPS vulnerabilities, especially jamming and spoofing. Because the Pentagon is dependent on space for precision targeting and communications, signal disruption poses a growing threat. Efforts to modernize GPS satellite, ground, and user equipment have faced repeated delays, exacerbating those concerns.
The Air Force, Space Force, Army, Navy, and Marine Corps have all pursued programs to either augment GPS capabilities or serve as a backup should the constellation be unavailable. For example, the Space Development Agency and the Army are fielding positioning, navigation, and timing, or PNT, satellites in low-Earth orbit, and the Navy is developing a PNT receiver that can calculate a ship’s position without the use of GPS using celestial bodies like stars, planets, and satellites on predictable orbits.
While these efforts have seen various degrees of success, an Oct. 7 report from the Government Accountability Office highlights risks within the current GPS modernization plans and the services’ various alternative PNT pursuits.
“Ineffective coordination of the fragmented interdependent PNT efforts among multiple military services—sometimes across more than one—hampers efficient alignment of those efforts,” GAO says in its report. “Pursuing modernized GPS and complementary PNT technologies to augment GPS requires foresight and planning. Integration timelines for weapon systems are often lengthy, and schedules must be properly aligned for the development of such modernized PNT technologies and their integration into weapon systems.”
As an example, GAO points to efforts to upgrade munitions to use M-code, a specialized, secure GPS signal. If the munitions have an integrated M-code capability before the aircraft, ships and ground platforms that fire them—which GAO says is likely to occur—that could cause synchronization issues before and after launch since positions are usually passed from a platform to a munition.
The report notes that officials has made some steps to consolidate PNT development efforts into joint program offices but argues more is needed. The agency recommends the Army, Navy, and Department of the Air Force identify opportunities to consolidate complementary programs to “ensure better strategic alignment with DOD and the other services” and drive efficiency.
“These efficiencies may improve schedule alignments between interdependent programs and ease the realignment of resources for higher priority programs within the portfolio to ensure that warfighters obtain these necessary capabilities to address current and future threats,” GAO writes.

Pakistan has deployed a “substantial” number of military forces and resources in Saudi Arabia, the country’s foreign ministry said.

However, Khan said it was up to the alliance organisation “to assess the threat perception and operate in accordance with its own mandate.”
Before the trilateral Mecca pact was signed, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had signed a bilateral defence agreement last September, following which “there has again been some deployment,” said Khan, the ministry spokesperson.
Earlier on Wednesday, Pakistani military spokesperson Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told CNN, "The Pakistani troops have been there for decades in multiple capabilities.”
Chaudhry said Pakistani forces were already present in Saudi Arabia across multiple domains but declined to disclose troop numbers or operational capabilities, citing their sensitive nature.
The foreign ministry spokesperson Khan added, "Since 1982, the Pakistan armed forces have been present in Saudi Arabia in one capacity or another, sometimes under logistical arrangements and sometimes as part of training missions.”

Breadcrumb
Drone attack on Erbil camp renews Kurdish fears over Iran War fallout
Two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil on Thursday night, raising fresh concerns about security in Iraq's Kurdistan Region following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces and their air defence systems.
The Kurdistan Region's Counter-Terrorism Service said the attack took place at 22:19 local time in the Kawergosk area of Khabat district, west of Erbil, the regional capital. No casualties were reported.
Local reports said the drones caused material damage near the site, although other accounts suggested they had crashed in an uninhabited area. The extent of the damage remains unclear, and no group has claimed responsibility.
The attack follows more than a month of relative calm in Erbil and has renewed concerns over the region's vulnerability to drone strikes, particularly after US-led coalition forces withdrew their air defence systems at the end of September.
Kurdish officials have repeatedly called for stronger air defences and greater coordination with the federal government in Baghdad, which holds primary responsibility for protecting Iraqi airspace.
A captain in the Kurdish Peshmerga forces told The New Arab that the latest attack highlighted the urgent need for air defence systems capable of intercepting drones, a role previously carried out by the international coalition.
"The renewed attacks make it necessary to accelerate the provision of air defence systems capable of dealing with drones," the officer said, speaking on condition of anonymity. He added that surveillance and interception measures alone could not provide sufficient protection without dedicated defensive capabilities.
The officer suggested the attack could be linked to Iran, citing the nature of targets struck in previous incidents. However, there has been no official confirmation of responsibility for Thursday's attack.
The Kurdistan Region has faced repeated drone and missile attacks in recent months amid escalating tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and associated refugee camps have been among the targets.
Earlier attacks have also affected areas of Erbil and Sulaimaniyah provinces, with Kurdish security authorities reporting the interception of drones targeting civilian and military sites. Some strikes blamed on Iran have killed members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq.
The latest incident comes shortly after the US-led coalition completed its military withdrawal from Iraq under an agreement reached between Baghdad and Washington in 2024.
Coalition forces previously operated air defence systems in the Kurdistan Region that intercepted incoming drones and missiles. Kurdish political and military leaders had warned before the withdrawal that removing those systems without providing replacements would leave the region exposed to further attacks.
The Kurdistan Regional Government has argued that its airspace forms part of Iraq's national airspace and that the federal government must take responsibility for its protection.
Ali al-Harki, a member of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), told The New Arab that the renewed attacks threatened civilians and placed further pressure on the region's security arrangements.
"There is an urgent need for Baghdad to assert its authority over Iraqi airspace and take security measures to prevent further attacks," he said.
"Kurdistan's security is part of Iraq's security, and the Baghdad government cannot distance itself from the responsibility it must assume for protecting the country's airspace."
The attack has also raised concerns about the safety of refugee families living in camps across the region, particularly those associated with Iranian Kurdish opposition groups that have previously been targeted.
Those concerns have grown following the departure of US forces and their defensive equipment from Erbil, which has left regional authorities seeking alternative arrangements to protect civilian areas and critical infrastructure.
With the perpetrators of Thursday's attack still unidentified, Kurdish officials are pressing Baghdad to strengthen air defence capabilities and improve coordination between the Iraqi military and the Peshmerga to prevent further strikes.

Happy birthday to the ROC
Today marks the 115th birthday of the Republic of China (ROC), while on Oct. 1, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) celebrated its 77th birthday.
From a historical and logical perspective, a 115-year-old nation could never be the “descendant” of a 77-year-old nation, let alone recognize a regime that is 38 years younger as its “motherland.”
If we insist on considering age and historical origins, it is actually the ROC that, historically, represents the shared memory of the people of the PRC over 77 years old.
We must not, simply because the word “motherland” easily evokes associations with bloodlines, ancestral origins or cultural roots, blindly accept this country, with a political system opposed to ours, as our motherland.
This year, I happen to be wishing my country a happy birthday as a soldier in military training.
This country can be called in many ways: It can be the ROC (Taiwan), the ROC, or simply Taiwan. Regardless of the name changes, the core fact remains: The ROC has been firmly rooted in Taiwan for 77 years. During this time, the values of democracy and freedom have become inextricably linked to the people of this land, perfectly integrated with their lives.
Through 115 years of democratic trials and tribulations, and 77 years of deep-rooted commitment, our nation has always been here.
Huang Yi-sheng
Taichung

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:29 UTC
01:43:29 KST

Firmus Grid Ltd abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, after the Nvidia Corp-backed data center company failed to lure global investors who have grown increasingly skittish over frothy AI valuations.
It was a dramatic about-face for a company that just days ago was signaling healthy demand for a deal that would have valued it at US$30 billion, up from US$10.5 billion less than three months ago. The canceled deal is a stark example of investor pushback against AI financing terms that some worry have become too generous as global borrowing costs climb and the long-term payoff from the technology remains uncertain.
Firmus, whose business model hinges on a steady influx of fresh capital, will withdraw its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange and consider other funding options, according to a statement yesterday.
Photo: AFP
“Having considered recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions, the board determined that the terms on which the offer could proceed would not appropriately reflect the strength of the company’s business and long-term growth outlook,” it said.
The IPO showed signs of stress soon after books opened for institutional investors this week. The struggles underscored investors’ polarized views on the deal. Some saw the business as well placed to benefit from the artificial intelligence boom, while others are worried about the valuation and existing shareholders potentially flooding the market soon after the debut. Part of the difficulty was convincing potential investors of the steep increase in market value for a company without a proven track record that had revenue of US$51 million in the 2026 financial year.
AI FACTORIES
Firmus, which was looking to raise as much as US$5.5 billion including a greenshoe option, must now find other ways to raise funds to keep its ambitious expansion plans on track. The company aims to build data centers it calls AI factories using hardware from backer Nvidia. It has a pipeline of 912 megawatts, of which only 46MW has been built, according to investor documents seen by Bloomberg.
“Investors just weren’t prepared to pay a sky-high price up front for capacity that’s still largely on the drawing board,” eToro lead analyst for APAC and Middle East Josh Gilbert said. “The timing hasn’t helped either, with higher yields lifting borrowing costs and shrinking what investors will pay today for earnings that sit years down the track.”
Firmus will also explore a potential listing in the US in the longer term, people familiar with the matter have said.
DATA CENTER PIPELINE
The failed deal underscores growing concern over how much capital AI infrastructure companies are demanding from public markets at a time when borrowing costs are rising. Much of Firmus’ valuation was based on the company successfully building a pipeline of data centers across Asia serving customers such as Meta Platforms Inc and OpenAI.
The strain is spreading across credit markets in the US, where a record wave of AI-related borrowing is forcing investors to reassess the risks around some of the biggest technology companies. Nearly US$500 billion of new debt has been priced this year to fund AI infrastructure, while rising financing needs and interest rates have driven up credit-insurance costs and weakened tech debt performance.
“There’s no question investors feel more anxiety recently, as the tech sector rallies despite mounting risk on every other front,” Rayliant Global Advisors head of portfolio management Phillip Wool wrote in a LinkedIn post. “Everything at this point hinges on the virtuous cycle of AI infrastructure spending boosting hardware and hyperscalers’ AI investment exciting shareholders about their own future earnings growth.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:28 UTC
01:43:28 KST

Every day, Shanti Dangol stares down at Nepal’s Trishuli River from her makeshift shelter, searching for traces of the home she lost and wondering when she will have a roof over her head again.
Dangol is among hundreds of people living in tent shelters following a catastrophic Himalayan flood triggered by a mountain and glacier collapse near Nepal’s border with China on Aug. 26.
More than 1,400 people died and over 5,000 remain missing after tsunami-like waves swept through northern mountainous areas, destroying homes, roads, bridges and settlements.
Dangol, a former hotel owner, now lives in a tent in a forest clearing in Betrawati, Rasuwa district.
She shares the plot with 25 other families who also lost their homes.
“Where are we supposed to go? What are we supposed to do? The river now flows where our house once stood,” Dangol said.
Photo: AFP
“Where will the government settle us?”
Dangol lost 18 relatives in the disaster, as well as two four-story houses. Four employees from her hotel are still missing. “We just want somewhere to live, we don’t need anything more,” she said. “That is what worries us more than anything else.”
Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the UN last month that the flooding “was a warning to the world” about the rising dangers of climate change.
Government report shows that more than 7,500 private houses were damaged in the floods.
‘NO PROPER PLACE’
In Rasuwa district alone, more than 1,000 people are in temporary shelters, said Kamal Prasad Pandey, the district’s chief administrative officer.
“We are also equally concerned about their permanent settlement, their hygiene and mental health issues,” he said.
Aarati Magar, 26, who lost her newly opened hotel in the disaster, lives in the same plot in a tent with her daughters, aged eight and three, worrying about their safety and education.
“It is tough to stay here. There is no bathing place and no proper place to live,” she said. For 58-year-old Narayan Man Dangol, the prospect of spending months in a tent is particularly worrying as winter approaches. “I don’t see a situation where we can stay in the tent for a long time,” he said.
“The wind will carry it away, and then it will rain again. This is just cloth. Living inside a cloth house is very difficult,” he said.
He said he had lost his life’s earnings. “Life will never be the same for us, we can no longer work in the fields and earn at this age,” he said.
‘RESTORE THEIR LIVELIHOODS’
Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of Nepal’s disaster agency, said authorities were “moving to the search and recovery phase”, and were working on “transitional shelters and identifying resettlement areas.” Families have also lost businesses, jobs and access to essential services, leaving many uncertain about how they will rebuild their lives.
“Recovery is about much more than rebuilding damaged infrastructure,” said Kyoko Yokosuka, the UN Development Program head in Nepal.
“It is about helping people restore their livelihoods, reopening local economies, restoring essential services and ensuring communities can move forward with dignity and hope,” she said.
For Dangol, the former hotel owner, the immediate concern is finding somewhere safe to live.
“We were victims of this flood, but we don’t want the next generation to be homeless like us,” she said.

Jurist Navi Pillay receives this year’s Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:28 UTC
01:43:28 KST

Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former UN human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, yesterday won the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack.
Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have rejected the findings of the UN commission she led on Gaza. The leaders also have been highly critical of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court; Pillay has worked at both.
Pillay’s work “is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world,” Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jorgen Watne Frydnes said in announcing her win.
Photo: AFP
The committee said it sought to bolster international law at a time of conflict, and Watne Frydnes said Pillay’s award was a message to those seeking to undermine “the international rules-based system and the institutions.”
Pillay, 85, received the news while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, the location of the trials of Nazi war criminals that helped lay the foundations of international law.
“Firstly, at this venue, your applause means a great deal to me,” she said. “You don’t want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this.”
Pillay dedicated her award to “survivors of international crimes,” and called on world leaders to respect international legal institutions.
“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said. “My message to leaders, political leaders, is that ... you have a legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war.”
Pillay chaired the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, which a year ago concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.
The commission also found that the Israeli president, prime minister and former minister of defense “have incited the commission of genocide.”
Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since it was established in 2021, has strenuously denied the accusations.
Pillay has repeatedly rebuffed critics who accused her of antisemitism or allegedly turning a blind eye to the Hamas attacks in Israel.
Under her leadership, the commission also issued reports accusing Hamas of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

Climate hopes shift from politics to the courts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

The political fight against global warming may be losing steam, but the legal battle is heating up. Over the past decade, legal activists have successfully taken a number of national governments to court, triggering the adoption of more climate-friendly policies in countries including the Netherlands, Pakistan, Switzerland, South Korea and others.
“There is momentum for climate litigation in the courts,” said Dennis van Berkel of the Climate Litigation Network, which supports legal action against states and corporations.
In one such victory earlier this week, Australia’s highest court blocked the expansion of a coal mine in New South Wales, citing its climate impact.
Photo: AFP
“Climate change litigation is growing domestically and internationally,” said Margaret Young, a law professor at the University of Melbourne.
On the political front, from Europe to the US, governments have been scaling back climate ambitions and policies, and global climate negotiations at the upcoming COP next month are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels that drive global warming.
But over the past two years, three international courts have affirmed in advisory opinions that countries have legal obligations to address climate change: the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, and the International Court of Justice (ICJ). A fourth opinion is expected from the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights.
“A lot has been achieved in a short period of time,” said Margaretha Wewerinke-Singh, a law professor at the University of Amsterdam who served as a legal expert in proceedings before all three courts.
While an advisory opinion issued by such a court is not legally binding in the same way as a judgment in a contentious case, van Berkel said the legal principles set out in those opinions are already being used in national courts.
“That norm is now flowing back to being picked up by the plaintiffs in different countries (and) used in their litigation,” he explained.
A Paris court cited the ICJ opinion in a ruling in June last year that ordered TotalEnergies to include emissions linked to the use of its products in its corporate vigilance plan. In January, a Dutch court also cited the opinion when it ordered the Netherlands to strengthen its climate plan in a case brought by residents of the Dutch Caribbean island of Bonaire. Both rulings are being appealed.
“Despite what politicians say about the international legal system, judges still respect and apply international law in many countries around the world,” said Sophie Marjanac, legal director at the Redwater Insights think tank.
‘TIGHTENING NET’ FOR OIL FIRMS
When it comes to corporations, the legal precedent is less established than for states, but there is a “tightening net” for oil companies, said Jasper Teulings, who also works for the Climate Litigation Network.
In some cases, years of litigation have led to permits for oil, gas and coal projects being overturned, including in the UK. Norway’s Supreme Court is expected to rule soon on licenses for projects in the North Sea.
And the Supreme Court of the Netherlands is next year expected to rule in a closely watched case brought by the environmental group Milieudefensie against Shell, deciding whether to impose a specific emissions-reduction target on the energy giant.
MAKING POLLUTERS PAY
Another potential breakthrough would be a ruling requiring a major polluter to compensate people harmed or threatened by climate change, wherever they live, in proportion to the company’s greenhouse gas emissions.
German courts moved toward that principle last year in a case brought by Peruvian farmer Saul Luciano Lliuya against energy company RWE. Although they rejected his claim for compensation, the courts left the door open to holding major emitters liable for climate-related payments.
Similar lawsuits are now pending in several countries, including cases brought by Philippine victims of Typhoon Odette against Shell in the UK, residents of Indonesia’s Pari island against cement maker Holcim in Switzerland, and Pakistani farmers affected by 2022 floods against RWE and Heidelberg Materials in Germany.
There have also been setbacks.
Climate groups have lost lawsuits against oil companies in the US. And in New Zealand, the government changed the law to block a lawsuit brought by Maori activist Mike Smith against six domestic companies, but he has vowed to continue the fight.

NBA superstar LeBron James on Thursday delivered a solid first half in his first pre-season game for Philadelphia, although the new-look 76ers fell 114-108 to the New York Nets in Brooklyn.
James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, in July announced that he had signed a two-year, US$8 million deal with the 76ers, ending weeks of speculation over where the four-time NBA champion would land as a free agent after eight seasons and one title with the Los Angeles Lakers.
The 41-year-old, entering a record-extending 24th NBA season, won two titles with the Miami Heat, another with the Cleveland Cavaliers and a fourth with the Lakers, and is aiming to help the Sixers win their first title since Julius Erving led the club to the crown 43 years ago.
Photo: John Jones / Imagn Images
Thursday’s game marked his first chance to line up alongside new teammates Joel Embiid, V.J. Edgecombe, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown — a new arrival from the Boston Celtics.
“It felt a little different,” James said. “Obviously, just wearing a new uniform, but the game is the game.”
“We’re still trying to put each other in a position to be successful and complement each other the best way we can out on the floor, but it’s going to take some time,” he said. “Tonight was a good sample size for us to build on.”
James scored 10 points, connecting on his lone shot from the floor and making all eight of his free-throw attempts. He added four rebounds, five assists and a steal in 18:04 minutes in the first half.
Brown led all scorers with 18 points. Julius Randle had 14 for the Nets, who out-scored the Sixers 37-23 in the third quarter to take control.
However, all eyes were on James, starting with his first signature pre-game chalk-toss in a 76ers uniform.
James smoothly directed the Sixers offense in his time on the floor, making all five of his assists in the first quarter and combining effectively with Maxey.
“I think there was some really good things happening, you know, right off the bat,” 76ers coach Nick Nurse said after seeing his starters together for the first time.
“A bunch of back cuts and good passing et cetera ... there were segments where obviously we turned the ball over a lot ... just the little clunky segments, too. But, again, it’s pre-season, first time they’re together,” Nurse said. “I think you look at it as what’s good and what are the learning experiences, things that we can improve.”
The 76ers have two more pre-season games, both against the Boston Celtics, before opening the NBA regular season away against the New York Knicks — the defending champions — at Madison Square Garden on Oct. 20.
James’ arrival has already found the 76ers battling outside “noise.”
James took to Instagram to refute a report from a play-by-play announcer during the team’s first pre-season game on Monday that James had admonished Embiid for being late to a practice.
“He ain’t been late, so stop the lie,” James wrote.
James said at a team media day last month that such outside hubbub around the 76ers would be “doubled, tripled and quadrupled now that I’m here.”

Taiwan offers much more than tech, Tsai Ing-wen says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

Taiwan offers the global democratic community much more than just semiconductors, former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) told an audience at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution in San Francisco on Thursday, while defending her “boring” leadership style as a necessary asset to find common ground.
Tsai spoke about how Taiwan has managed differences, responded to crises and built societal resilience.
Discussions about Taiwan often focus on semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), cross-strait relations, the risk of conflict and occasionally touch on its popular food and drinks, she said.
Photo: CNA
However, those topics are only part of the story, Tsai said, pointing to the nation’s 23 million people and their experience of building a democracy under challenging circumstances.
“That experience has shaped who we are and continues to shape how we approach the future,” she said.
Democracies face growing challenges from outside and within, as increasingly sophisticated authoritarian influence campaigns coincide with domestic populism and political polarization, she said.
The domestic divisions make it harder to reach a consensus on how to respond to outside threats, she added.
Tsai also warned that advances in AI have lowered language barriers, making it easier to spread disinformation across borders.
“Ill-intentioned actors, especially from outside, use social media platforms to spread false and misleading information to drive a wedge between fellow citizens, between societies and their governments, and even between countries,” she said.
However, decades of external pressure and intense domestic political competition have taught Taiwan how to safeguard democracy while keeping its institutions open and its society resilient, Tsai said.
Taiwan has moved from authoritarian rule to its first direct presidential election in 1996 to become the vibrant democracy it is today, she said.
“That transition taught us how to confront deep political differences without allowing those differences to make democratic progress impossible,” she said.
Managing relations with China has required preparedness and restraint, Tsai said, adding that decades of pressure from Beijing have made Taiwan more resilient and pragmatic.
Although Taiwanese hold differing views on what form relations with China should take, there is a consensus on maintaining the cross-strait “status quo,” avoiding unnecessary provocation, and protecting Taiwan’s democracy and security, she said.
“Democracy, resilience and partnership are the foundation of our collective future,” Tsai said, adding that no amount of threats or coercion would shake Taiwan’s determination to engage with and contribute to the world.
While some people described her as “boring” during her time as president, Tsai said that “being boring can be useful” in an era of increasing political polarization in which provocation attracts more attention than restraint.
This is especially true when needing to ensure Taiwan’s security while finding enough common ground to keep democracy moving forward, she added.
Tsai arrived in the US on Monday and is scheduled to return to Taiwan tomorrow.
Additional reporting by Su Yung-yao

Jose Ramirez belted a two-run home run in the fifth inning and delivered a run-scoring single in the Guardians’ big sixth to help Cleveland win a second straight game in Chicago after dropping the first two games of the best-of-five American League Division Series at home.
Having denied the White Sox’s bid to clinch a playoff series at home for the first time since 1906, the Guardians were to host Game 5 yesterday.
Photo: AFP
“I think it’s going to be crazy,” Ramirez said of the decider.
“It’s going to be incredible energy. For us, it’s going to be the same mindset: Try to win the game and enjoy the environment,” said Ramirez, who followed pinch-hitter Patrick Bailey’s solo homer in the fifth by belting a fastball from White Sox relief pitcher Jordan Hicks into the bullpen for a two-run home run that put the Guardians up 3-2.
“It was Jose Ramirez being Jose Ramirez in the playoffs,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said of the Dominican, whose regular-season success has not always translated into the post-season. “Hicks with a great fastball and Josy got to it ... big moment for him, big moment for us.”
The White Sox edged back in front with a pair of runs in the bottom of the fifth, but Cleveland poured it on in the sixth, sending 10 batters to the plate.
Angel Martinez was hit by a pitch to take first and stole second. He scored on Travis Bazzana’s double.
Bailey, Ramirez, Chase de Lauter and Jo Adell added run-scoring hits.
