Williams was the eighth pitcher to take the mound for the Guardians. The White Sox used seven, with starter Hagen Smith exiting in the first inning after recording two outs, but walking the bases loaded to get the hook after 27 pitches.
Chicago reliever Grant Taylor, who pitched 5-1/2 scoreless innings in the first two games of the series, gave up four runs on four hits without recording an out in the sixth inning.

Giant Taiwan flag flies freely on National Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:23 UTC
01:43:23 KST

Largely banned from display internationally due to Beijing’s objections, a giant Taiwanese flag suspended under a US-made Chinook helicopter and flown over Taipei is one of the most eye-catching moments of Double Ten National Day.
Since 2019, as a way to boost unity amid rising Chinese pressure, the military has every year flown a massive flag beneath one of its tandem-rotor Chinook CH-47SD helicopters over the Presidential Office Building in Taipei while the national anthem is sung during Oct. 10 National Day celebrations.
President William Lai (賴清德) is to give a keynote address mid-morning today, laying out policy objectives and addressing relations with China.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
China has ratcheted up efforts to stop countries engaging with Taipei, including preventing Taiwan’s flag from being displayed at sports events such as the Olympics.
One of the helicopter pilots taking part in rehearsals this week, 40-year-old Lin Chang-cheng (林昶成), said that the flag is a “concrete symbol of national sovereignty.”
“This is especially true given that we have actually suffered a lot of suppression in the international community, so when we see the national flag being displayed, it’s an extremely moving moment,” Lin said at Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport).
National Day is held on the anniversary of a 1911 uprising that led to the overthrow of China’s last imperial dynasty and the establishment of the Republic of China (ROC).
The ROC government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong’s (毛澤東) communists, who proclaimed the People’s Republic of China.
Suspended from a long, weighted cable beneath the helicopter, the 12m-by-18m ROC flag is made out of the same tough, lightweight material used for parachutes.
While the flag is a contested symbol even within Taiwan, especially for those who champion an entirely separate identity from China, catching sight of it flying over Taipei is exciting for those watching from the city’s hills.
“When I see the Taiwan flag, I feel that it represents freedom, democracy and freedom of speech,” said Hsiao Shao-chun, 44, watching rehearsals on Taipei’s outskirts.
During the Cold War, National Day celebrations in Taiwan were heavily military focused, with speeches about “retaking the mainland.”
These days, the event is more about showcasing Taiwan’s soft power and global visibility.

The firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said on Thursday, a stunning revelation about plans for the first military execution in more than 65 years.
The US army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3 after Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said.
Photo: Reuters
Pentagon officials said the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
The revelation about the public nature of the execution — let alone one as violent as a firing squad — has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the US, especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” said Eugene Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails.
Those are benefits that would be useful at a time when Pike’s botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes, she said.
As many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are being seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
“Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner,” he said. “I don’t think that’s what’s motivating this. There’s a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the ‘lethality culture.’”
Elisabeth Semel, codirector of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth’s announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions.
Although there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, “I don’t recall a situation in which it was instigated by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government,” she said.
Semel said she was skeptical that the administration of US President Donald Trump had given a second thought to the legal and social questions presented by the decision.
Hasan, an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment.
He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of fleeing soldiers.
It was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims, Hasan said.
A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial.
Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement.
He could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, but given his behavior at trial, he might not want to.
After firing his lawyers and representing himself, Hasan told jurors he was the gunman. He said little else over the next three weeks, which convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan’s only goal was to get a death sentence.
The military called nearly 90 witnesses, but Hasan rested his case without calling a single person to testify in his defense and made no closing argument. Yet he leaked documents during the trial to journalists that revealed he told mental health workers he could “still be a martyr ” if executed.
Attorney John Galligan, a former military judge who had represented Hasan in several civil matters following his criminal trial, said that according to Hasan, the commandant of the facility brought a chaplain, but no attorney from either the Trial Defense Service or from his civilian defense when he was notified that Trump had signed off on his execution.

Shark attack survivor Mel Ismail recounts his ordeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:19 UTC
01:43:19 KST

As shark attack survivor Mel Ismail fought the predator that severed his leg, he noticed something odd.
“I saw its eye ... a big black eye,” Ismail said. “But it was winking back at me — I was trying to get my fingers in its eye and just pushing its eye as I was being dragged.”
When the shark swam off, he managed to struggle back to shore, the surfer and professional firefighter said in an Australian Broadcasting Corp interview broadcast on Thursday.
Photo: Australian Broadcasting Corp via AP
He was surfing at Glenfield Beach near Geraldton on Australia’s west coast when he was attacked on Sept. 14. He lost his right leg below the knee.
Ismail said he was resting when he spotted a pod of about 20 dolphins before being hit by something big. It was the first time he has spoken publicly about the attack.
“I thought I got hit by a dolphin, initially,” Ismail said. “And suddenly — bang — something grabbed me and dragged me down into the water. And I knew it was a shark.”
Ismail said it looked like the shark winked at him before it bit his leg.
Many sharks, including the white shark and mako shark, do not have eyelids, but when attacking prey, they roll their eyeballs backward into their sockets as a protective measure, exposing a tough layer of white cartilage.
Authorities have yet to determine the species of shark that attacked Ismail.
Alone and bleeding at the back of the surf break, Ismail caught a wave that took him about 20m closer to shore.
Ismail said he was out of breath and losing strength when he spotted surfer Shannan Dunn coming down the dunes on to the beach.
Dunn went to Ismail’s rescue, helping the shark victim on to his board.
Ismail described Dunn as having “eyes like saucers.”
“The first thing he [Dunn] said to me is, ‘Where’s the shark?’” Ismail said. “I said, ‘I don’t know. I’ve got a bit going on here.’”
Once they returned to the beach, an onlooker crafted a tourniquet for Ismail using a leg rope and another onlooker phoned for an ambulance.
A pair of teenagers helped Ismail climb into Dunn’s car and they drove along the beach to meet an ambulance.
“I had a heap of people laughing, keeping me alive, keeping me positive in the back,” Ismail said.
“I gave a few knuckles to the people there, because I was feeling good,” he added. “I started to feel like I [was] going to make it.”
Four days after Ismail was attacked, 63-year-old swimmer Greg O’Neill was fatally mauled by a large white shark. O’Neill was attacked off Sorrento Beach in Perth’s northern suburbs.
Ismail said he intends to return to the surf as a bodyboarder.
There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.
Three spearfishing divers were killed by sharks off the Australian coast in four weeks over May and June. In January, a 12-year-old boy died in a hospital days after he was mauled by a bull shark in Sydney Harbor.
Australia has averaged between two and three fatal shark attacks a year since 2000, the Australian Shark Incident Database showed.

Putin says Caspian Sea shoreline in Russia receded by 20,000 sq km in 20 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:19 UTC
01:43:19 KST

Kanyshai Butun
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Friday that the Caspian Sea’s shoreline in Russia had receded by an estimated 20,000 square kilometers (7,722 square miles) over the past 20 years, warning of serious environmental and economic consequences.
Speaking at the Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, Putin said the sea’s water level was falling by an average of nine centimeters (3.5 inches) annually, threatening biodiversity, fisheries and coastal soil stability.
“Falling water levels have a negative impact on the socio-economic situation in the Caspian region, reduce the investment attractiveness of trans-Caspian logistics corridors, and threaten a decline in the population's quality of life, job losses, and other acute crises,” he said, attributing the decline primarily to climate change.
Putin said Russia was working with regional partners to protect the Caspian ecosystem and supported developing an action plan on fluctuations in the sea’s water level through 2036.
He also backed establishing a special commission to investigate the causes of the decline and develop measures to address its consequences, adding that Russia was preparing a comprehensive research program on changes in the Caspian Sea’s water level through 2030.
Moscow has also proposed creating a digital twin of the sea using artificial intelligence to model water-level changes and improve navigation safety.
He stressed the need for coordinated action among Caspian littoral states to preserve the sea’s ecosystem and ensure sustainable regional development.
“In conclusion, I would like to reiterate that Russia has always advocated—and will continue to advocate—for strengthening and developing cooperation among our states in the interests of preserving the Caspian region’s ecosystem, ensuring its sustainable growth, and improving people's quality of life,” he said.
The meeting was attended by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

Taiwan’s Double Ten reckoning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:17 UTC
01:43:17 KST

On Oct. 10, 1911, gunfire in Wuchang (武昌) shattered the stillness of late-Qing China. What began as a regional uprising quickly ignited a chain reaction across the empire, toppling a dynastic order that had endured for more than two millennia and ushering in one of Asia’s first republics — the Republic of China (ROC). From that moment, the 10th day of the 10th month became a date of epochal significance, not merely in Chinese history, but in the broader arc of Asia’s encounter with modernity.
Yet today, as Taiwan marks Double Ten National Day, the holiday’s meaning has undergone a transformation as profound as the revolution it commemorates. No longer a ritual of nostalgic irredentism or a symbolic claim to a lost mainland, Oct. 10 has become, for many in Taiwan, a celebration of something far more tangible: the nation’s hard-won democracy.
The linguistic footprint of this shift is subtle, but telling. Merriam-Webster, the only major English dictionary to include the term “Double Ten,” defines it as a holiday observed by the ROC to commemorate the 1911 uprising. First recorded in 1940, the term is a calque from the Chinese shuang shi (雙十) — “double tenth,” marking the 10th day of the 10th month. But language, like history, is never static. In Taiwan, the word now carries connotations its early 20th-century coiners could scarcely have imagined.
By the 1960s, the holiday had hardened into a spectacle of revanchist theater. On the 50th anniversary in 1961, Time magazine described the scene in Taipei: 11,000 troops marched past the reviewing stand while 160 jet fighters roared overhead, and Nationalist frogmen swam ashore on an uninhabited island to plant their flags. Then-president Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石) declared that conditions on the mainland resembled those of 1911, predicting imminent uprisings and promising a massive counteroffensive. For Chiang, Double Ten was a rallying cry; for then-Chinese premier Zhou Enlai (周恩來), it was a footnote to what he dismissed as an old-fashioned bourgeois revolution.
However, Taiwan’s own political evolution has rewritten the script. The lifting of martial law in 1987, the first direct presidential election in 1996, and nearly four decades of vibrant democratic practice have gradually stripped Double Ten of its revanchist overtones. The parade names tell the story: from “Chinese Unification” in 1991, criticized as excessively sinocentric, to “National Defense Performance” under former president Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁), “Defense Exhibition” under former president Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九), and, in 2023, the English designation used that year: “Taiwan National Day.” Each renaming reflects a society negotiating its identity, shedding the baggage of a continental past in favor of an island-centered present.
This is not mere semantic gamesmanship. It is the linguistic expression of a deeper truth: Taiwan has become something the 1911 revolutionaries dreamed of, but never saw realized, a functioning liberal democracy in Asia. Its legislature features robust opposition voices. Its press criticizes the government without fear. Its citizens take to the streets not as subversives, but as participants in their own governance. These are not abstract ideals; they are the daily texture of life in a society that completed a peaceful transition from authoritarianism, rare in the region.
To be sure, the holiday remains politically contested. Beijing views any invocation of “Taiwan National Day” as a provocation. Some still mourn the loss of a broader Chinese identity, but for a growing number of Taiwanese, Oct. 10 is less about remembering a revolution on a distant mainland than about honoring their own journey, from martial law to free elections, from isolation to global relevance.
In an era when authoritarianism is resurgent and democratic norms are fraying, Taiwan’s story carries weight beyond its shores. Double Ten, once a symbol of republican aspiration, has become something more urgent: a testament to democratic resilience. The revolution of 1911 opened a door. Taiwan, against all odds, walked through it, and kept walking, all the way to a future its founders could hardly have envisioned. That is the true legacy of Double Ten. Not the restoration of a vanished empire, but the preservation of a living democracy.
Hugo Tseng has a doctorate in linguistics, and is a lexicographer and former chair of the Soochow University English Department.

Vance highlights Microsoft in crackdown on visa abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:14 UTC
01:43:14 KST

US President Donald Trump’s administration accused Microsoft Corp, Adobe Inc and a half-dozen other companies of abusing a US worker visa program and suspended them indefinitely from a longstanding immigration initiative that has served as a crucial talent pipeline for Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
The suspensions, announced on Thursday by US Vice President J.D. Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, also target information technology services giants Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp, Infosys Ltd, Tata, Wipro Ltd, HCL Technologies Ltd and Capgemini SE. Those firms, either based in India or with large operations there, are often called outsourcers for their role offering contract IT work to other businesses.
At a briefing in Washington, Sonderling said there were multiple federal investigations under way into the use of a system that allows US employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.
Photo: Bloomberg
“We are cutting off the head of the snake — the companies that enabled this abuse for decades,” Sonderling told reporters at Thursday’s briefing.
Vance singled out Microsoft, the world’s third-most valuable company, for what he characterized as exploitation of the program.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” he said.
In a statement, Microsoft defended its use of visa programs and said that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information. Adobe and the Indian companies named by Vance and Sonderling did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Vance’s comments assailing Microsoft came hours before Trump honored the company’s chief executive officer, Satya Nadella, with a National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to spotlight US scientific leadership. Just last week, Nadella joined other tech industry leaders at a White House luncheon to discuss safeguards for artificial intelligence.
“Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them, they do a lot of important things,” Vance said. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company. It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.”
The moves announced by Vance and Sonderling take aim at the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, which allows companies to sponsor a foreigner who has been working in the US under the H-1B and other visa holders to become a legal permanent resident, the first step to becoming a US citizen.
Silicon Valley’s reliance on foreign workers has long been a flashpoint in the debate over immigration. Since Trump’s return to office last year, the administration has seized on those concerns and pressed tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers.
As part of that effort, Trump has moved to make it harder for companies to use H-1B visas to attract foreign talent, targeting a major source of workers for the industry. The changes have included proposals for $100,000 filing fees for most candidates and tightening the rules of how the H-1B visas are awarded in an annual lottery, giving priority to companies offering the highest salaries.
Vance urged the US-based companies to shift their policies to employ more US workers.
“Stop defrauding the American worker. Stop importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do,” the vice president said.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:11 UTC
01:43:11 KST

What animal looks like a bird, acts like a mouse, and sounds like the name of a fruit? Meet the kiwi. Native to New Zealand, the kiwi has tiny wings, furry-looking feathers and a long beak, making it strangely cute. Still, it has become one of the nation’s best-known symbols.
Evolution had a hand in shaping the kiwi’s unique look. Millions of years ago, when New Zealand lacked land predators, the kiwi lived in an environment where flight was unnecessary for survival. Gradually, it adapted to a ground-dwelling lifestyle. Its wings shrank into small stubs hidden beneath its feathers, while its flight muscles were replaced by strong legs built for walking and fast running. Its feathers also transformed into hair-like structures that provide perfect camouflage in the forest.
Even its sense of smell evolved in a surprising way. Unlike most birds, which rely mainly on sight to find food, the kiwi depends on an exceptional sense of smell. It developed a long beak with nostrils located at the very tip. While foraging for food, it repeatedly taps its beak against the ground to sniff out insects and worms hidden beneath the soil.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
By the time humans arrived in New Zealand, the kiwi had settled into its own way of life. Its sharp call, which sounds like “kee-wee,” earned the bird its name. Interestingly, the fuzzy fruit we eat was later named “kiwi fruit” because its brown, fuzzy skin reminded people of the bird, not the other way around. Today, the word kiwi still confuses people. Is it a fruit, a nickname for New Zealanders, or a bird? In New Zealand, the answer begins with the bird, a national icon and one of the country’s most recognizable identities.
什麼動物看起來像鳥、行為像老鼠，名字聽起來像水果呢？來見見奇異鳥吧。奇異鳥原生於紐西蘭，牠們有迷你翅膀、看起來毛茸茸的羽毛，還有長長的鳥喙，怪可愛的。不過，牠們成為了紐西蘭最知名的象徵之一。
演化在形塑奇異鳥的獨特外觀上插了一腳。數百萬年前的紐西蘭缺乏陸地掠食者，奇異鳥住在不需要靠飛行生存的環境中。牠們逐漸適應了地棲的生活方式。牠們的翅膀縮小成隱藏在羽毛下的小殘翼，用來飛行的肌肉則被適合步行和快跑的強壯雙腿取代。牠們的羽毛也轉變成毛髮般的結構，能在森林裡提供完美的偽裝。
甚至連牠們的嗅覺也有驚人的演化。與大多數主要仰賴視力來找食物的鳥類不同，奇異鳥依靠的是絕佳的嗅覺。牠們發展出長長的鳥喙，鼻孔位於尖端。在覓食的時候，牠們會反覆用鳥喙敲打地面，以嗅出藏在泥土下的昆蟲和蟲蟲。
等人類抵達紐西蘭時，奇異鳥已經適應了自己的生活方式。牠們宏亮的叫聲聽起來像kee-wee，使其獲得kiwi這個名稱。有趣的是，我們吃的那種毛毛水果後來會被稱為「奇異果」，是因為其棕色的毛毛外皮讓人們聯想到奇異鳥，而非反過來。如今，kiwi這個字仍讓人們感到困惑。是一種水果、紐西蘭人的綽號，或是一隻鳥呢？在紐西蘭，答案始於奇異鳥，牠們是國家象徵，也是紐西蘭最具辨識度的形象之一。
Words in Use
1.evolution n. 演化
evolve vi. 演化
Fossils provide clear evidence of biological evolution.
化石提供生物演化的明確證據。
Animals evolve over time due to changing environments and survival pressures.
動物會因為不斷變化的環境與生存壓力而演化。
2. adapt vi. 適應
adapt to N/V-ing 適應……
Humans have adapted to the fast-paced digital world.
人類已經適應了步調快速的數位世界。
3. shrink vi. 縮小
三態為：shrink, shrank, shrunk。
The sweater shrank after being washed in hot water.
這件毛衣用熱水清洗後便縮水了。
4. muscle n. 肌肉
High-protein diets along with exercise support muscle development.
高蛋白飲食加上運動有助於肌肉發展。
5. transform vi. 改變，轉變
transform into… 轉變為……
The street transformed into a lively market as vendors began selling food there.
攤販開始在街上賣食物時，那裡就成了熱鬧的市場。
Practical Phrases
1. be native to + 地方 原產於某地，某地特有的
Certain rare birds are native to this remote island.
某些稀有鳥類原生於這座偏遠島嶼。
2. have a hand in. . . 影響∕參與……
Many engineers had a hand in designing the bridge.
許多工程師都有參與這座橋的設計。
3. rely on. . . 仰賴∕依靠……
= depend on. . .
I rely on public transport to commute to work every day.
我每天都依賴大眾運輸通勤上班。
4. settle into. . . 適應∕習慣……
Freshmen often need time to settle into university life.
大一新生通常需要時間適應大學生活。
5. remind sb. of N 使某人（聯）想起……
This song reminds me of my high school days.
這首歌讓我想起高中時光。

Shorter season pitched as salary cap battle looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:43:10 UTC
01:43:10 KST

MLB proposed cutting its regular season to 154 games from 162 starting in 2029 during bargaining on Thursday, a plan that the MLB Players’ Association said was tied to a salary cap it firmly opposes.
The proposal, which comes as the league and the union negotiate a new collective bargaining agreement before the current one expires in December, would also expand the Division Series of the playoffs to a best-of-seven from a best-of-five affair.
Shortening the regular season would create a standard weekly off day benefiting player health, the MLB said.
Under its proposal, the higher-seeded clubs in the Wild Card and Division Series would select their opponents beginning in 2027.
The players’ association said it is reviewing the proposed changes.
“Players will weigh in on these proposals and we will respond at the bargaining table,” it said in a statement. “Unfortunately, the league once again made clear that all of its proposals are contingent on players’ agreement to a salary cap, a system that guts player rights and compensation, as well as its other anti-player proposals.”
Other North American leagues have lengthened their schedules in the past few years.
The NHL went to 84 games from 82 this season, and the NFL, which added a 17th game in 2021, wants an 18th.
The NFL players’ union has pushed back.
However, the bigger fight is expected to be over a salary cap, which could lead to a lockout or strike.
In their first proposal in May, MLB owners asked for a hard cap of US$245.3 million, including player benefits, and a payroll floor of US$171.2 million, starting in 2027.
The MLB union has long opposed any form of salary cap.
The collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1.
The last time owners pushed for a cap, players went on strike in 1994.
The 232-day stoppage forced the cancelation of that year’s MLB World Series.

EDITORIAL: Inclusivity is not a token gesture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:08 UTC
01:43:08 KST

A police raid on a gay bar in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) area one week ago prompted a protest by civil groups and members of the LGBTQ community, who characterized the raid as excessively forceful and demanded that police apologize and stop stigmatizing LGBTQ culture.
Police from the Wanhua Precinct raided the bar, Commander D, after obtaining a search warrant following complaints that the venue might be contravening public decency laws. Police said they found people without clothing and seized used condoms, taking 51 people to the police station for questioning and referring the bar’s owner to prosecutors.
The legality of the raid itself is not the issue. Police had obtained a warrant, and authorities have a legitimate responsibility to investigate suspected contraventions of the law. What is far more difficult to justify is how the raid was carried out.
People at the scene said officers ordered them to squat or kneel, prevented them from using their phones and initially refused to let some people put their clothes back on. One person taken in for questioning said they were held for more than six hours after being accused of breaking public decency laws, having removed their shirt shortly before police arrived because the bar was crowded and hot.
There were also allegations that police searched personal belongings and treated large numbers of patrons as suspects. One officer was recorded asking a disabled customer in a restroom how disabled people “manage to have sex in there.”
Police have disputed some of these allegations and said the orders were necessary to secure the premises, prevent interference with the investigation and preserve evidence. However, after reviewing body camera footage, the Taipei City Police Department found that four officers had used inappropriate or discriminatory language.
The lead investigator was disciplined for failing to stop the remarks, while the Wanhua Precinct chief was disciplined for inadequate supervision. Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) apologized to those affected and said police discipline would be bolstered, while emphasizing that everyone, regardless of gender, sexual orientation or identity, should be treated equally.
Those measures are necessary, but they do not answer the deeper concerns raised by the operation.
A search warrant gives police legal authority to enter and search a specified premises. It should not, by itself, give officers unlimited discretion over how they treat the people inside and their property.
The alleged offenses were not violent crimes or an immediate threat to public safety. If the bar or its customers contravened public decency laws, they should be dealt with according to the law. However, law enforcement must still be proportionate to the conduct being investigated.
There is also the broader question about how such operations are planned and supervised. The government should review what circumstances warrant a forceful raid and how officers are expected to execute search warrants under a variety of circumstances. Sensitivity and diversity training should also be improved, particularly when officers are dealing with communities that have historically faced discrimination and stigma.
The Taiwan Alliance to Promote Civil Partnership Rights and other groups said the incident was not simply a matter of individual officers misspeaking or a single instance of excessive enforcement. They described it as the “resurfacing of long-standing homophobia, discrimination and abuse of power” within the police system.
Taiwan became the first in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage in 2019 and has developed a reputation as one of the region’s most LGBTQ-friendly societies. Taipei is preparing to host its annual Pride event on Oct. 31, the largest in East Asia and one that attracts visitors from across the region.
For a community that has long been a target of discrimination and oppression, an aggressive police operation at an LGBTQ venue carries much deeper implications than a few inappropriate remarks. It can reinforce the perception that LGBTQ spaces are inherently suspicious or depraved, and that people who enter them need not be treated with dignity when the state exercises its authority.
Penalizing the officers involved is not enough. Beyond providing the public with a clear account of what happened and explaining the legal basis for the treatment of those detained, the government and police department should outline concrete measures to ensure that misconduct like this does not happen again — and they should do so before the Pride event, rather than simply waiting for the controversy to fade.
The government should ensure that all residents, regardless of their identity, feel safe, respected and equally protected under the law — that is what defines an inclusive city.

China’s targets for growth have become a trap for Xi Jinping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:07 UTC
01:43:07 KST

China’s latest effort to prop up its battered housing market and spur the economy is getting a poor reception. The measures are underwhelming and unlikely to achieve much beyond improving Beijing’s chances of meeting its already restrained growth ambitions.
That is damning the initiative with faint praise. The deeper problem lies in how China measures economic success. The government itself deserves some blame: It does not aspire to beat expectations, merely to meet them. And those expectations are set at the start of each year with the much-heralded unveiling of an economic growth target. China should jettison it.
The negative reception for the real estate package, which includes subsidized loans and support for favored sectors, helps explain why a change of approach would be beneficial. Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) has been trying to nurse the property market back to health for years, with limited success. There is nothing wrong with experimenting when existing remedies are not working. Washington tried repeatedly to contain the subprime crisis in 2007-2009. Several measures proved inadequate before policymakers eventually restored confidence.
However, the criticism also misses a more fundamental point. Investors and businesses still have not fully adjusted to the reality that this is not the China of old. Growth will be slower, more modest and likely to drift lower over time. Beijing’s annual GDP targets can help manage that transition by signaling what policymakers consider an acceptable pace of expansion, but they can also become a trap. By turning that number into a test of economic success or failure, the government encourages policies aimed at hitting the target rather than confronting the deeper problems holding back growth.
There is no sign that major stimulus along the lines of 2008 is in the works. That does not mean a fresh policy push is not needed. What is required, though, is a new narrative. Each batch of data produces much the same picture — and a similar disappointed response: Domestic demand is weak while exports power ahead. Last month’s numbers and third-quarter GDP, due in two weeks, are unlikely to alter that story.
The report card can almost be written in advance. The figures will be judged largely by whether they leave China on course to meet its growth aspirations. Fall too far behind, and calls for another dose of stimulus will intensify; stay on target, and policymakers can afford to wait. In the preceding quarter, the economy expanded 4.3 percent from a year earlier, slightly below the bottom of the 4.5 percent-5 percent range articulated by Xi. The near-universal prescription was for more public spending. But monetary easing looked a distant prospect then, and still does. People’s Bank of China officials have repeatedly stressed that they are in no hurry.
The stated goals get in the way of a dispassionate assessment of China’s economic performance. They establish useful parameters and offer some insight into the expectations of top decision-makers, but they also create an artificial benchmark for what is not merely achievable, but desirable. If the goal looks comfortably within reach, everyone can relax. If it appears distant — or attainable only with considerable effort — the case for stimulus strengthens. Either way, the target ends up driving the interpretation. The numbers rarely get to stand on their own.
Targets do have a useful signaling role. They allow Beijing to indicate the pace of economic growth it wants, and the degree of weakness it is prepared to tolerate. For much of the post-COVID period, the goal has hovered around 5 percent. Moving to a range acknowledges that growth might undershoot that pace and, more broadly, that tougher times lie ahead.
However, Beijing is not solely to blame. Some of the problem lies with those of us assessing China. If the economy is performing poorly, we should say so; that judgement should not depend on whether an official target is met. And there is plenty to criticize. For years, hopes have rested on a rebalancing of growth away from exports and toward domestic demand. It has yet to happen. That is hardly a new critique, but it remains a valid one.
The narrative surrounding China’s economy is stuck. The numbers are not great, but nor are they terrible, assuming they can be believed. Some slowing is only natural: The bigger the economy becomes, the harder it is to keep delivering outsize gains. Government support increasingly seems designed to stabilize the expansion, not accelerate it. As Bloomberg Economics points out, this is not a sprint. A gradual deceleration toward annual growth of around 2 percent over the next decade is increasingly in the cards.
What is needed is a new way of thinking about the world’s second-largest economy, one that does not depend on crystal-ball gazing by cadres. Only then can we judge whether China is doing well, doing poorly or simply muddling through. Don’t expect that breakthrough any time soon. Whether 4.5 percent is comfortably in the bag or tantalizingly out of reach, expect it to dominate discussion of the third-quarter report.
Xi would be well advised to dispense with numerical growth targets. Once the current one has been met, of course.

After two naval jet contracts, Boeing could be turning the page
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:05 UTC
01:43:05 KST

Boeing has won the contract for the US Navy’s next-generation fighter due to years of investment, decades of experience building carrier-based jets and a design approach that closely matched the Pentagon’s push for easier-to-upgrade aircraft, according to people familiar with the competition.
Last week’s win marks Boeing’s second major fighter jet victory after securing the Air Force’s F-47 program last year. The aerospace company bested rivals Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman for the Navy’s F/A-XX fighter contract, worth more than US$20 billion in its initial development phase.
The victories give the company’s defense, space and security division an opportunity to turn the corner on years of costly overruns, delays on military aircraft programs and the high-profile setbacks of its Starliner spacecraft.
“Now all of a sudden, it controls the next half century and beyond of US tactical aircraft,” AeroDynamic Advisory managing director Richard Aboulafia said. “There’s nothing like that in history.”
The Pentagon required competitors for the F-47 and F/A-XX programs — Boeing, Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman — to use common design standards to make later upgrades and modifications easier, in order to respond quickly to changing technology and evolving threats.
“All the industry players did what they were supposed to, but there were varying degrees of embrace and enthusiasm,” a former Pentagon official familiar with the competitions said. “Boeing’s embrace was effective.”
The company also distinguished itself through its use of digital design tools, making it easier for engineers, military officials and maintainers to test changes and refine the aircraft during development, the official said.
The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin declined to comment.
Northrop Grumman said in a statement that it “offered a highly survivable, digitally advanced sixth-generation fighter” in the F/A-XX competition, and it has “requested a debriefing from the US Navy” on the selection process and award decision, a requirement for appealing the Pentagon’s decision.
Winning the programs does not guarantee financial success for Boeing. Several analysts said the outcome will depend heavily on the terms of the contracts, which neither Boeing nor the Defense Department would comment on.
Boeing has lost US$20.5 billion on five fixed-price development programs that left it responsible for cost overruns — the KC-46 tanker, T-7 trainer, MQ-25 refueling drone, Air Force One replacement and Starliner programs.
“If it is fixed price, that’s a warning sign,” Aboulafia said.
Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg has said Boeing will not pursue similar fixed-price development contracts in the future, as it tries to leave those expensive mistakes in the past.
Few details about either aircraft have been released. The F-47 is expected to fly in 2028 and enter service in 2029, with the Air Force planning to buy at least 185 aircraft to replace the F-22. Even less is known about the F/A-XX, which is expected to enter service in the 2030s and eventually replace the Navy’s F/A-18 fleet.
While the development contracts are each worth more than US$20 billion, the production work could generate hundreds of billions of dollars over the lifetime of the aircraft.
After losing the F-35 contract to Lockheed Martin in 2001, Boeing kept its engineering expertise with work on classified projects, as well as F-15 and F/A-18 upgrades. The F-15EX upgrade was considered so good that the Air Force resumed buying the jet years after it had stopped.
After COVID, Boeing spent billions of dollars on new production facilities, engineering capabilities and digital design tools in a bid to win the next generation of US fighter jets.
Boeing argues that developing two advanced fighters in tandem lowers risk due to shared technologies and design features.
“Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly,” Boeing Defense CEO Steve Parker said in a statement. Ortberg tapped the veteran of Boeing’s fighter programs to lead the defense division in 2024.
While important differences remain, both the F-47 and F/A-XX are meant to establish air superiority alongside autonomous drones in a potential conflict with China, TD Cowen defense analyst Roman Schweizer said.

Overseas offices celebrate Double Ten
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Taiwan’s overseas representative offices marked Double Ten National Day with receptions in India, Turkey, the Netherlands, the Philippines and the US, underscoring efforts to bolster diplomatic ties, expand trade and deepen cooperation in technology and other key industries.
Taiwan’s representative office in India on Thursday held a National Day reception in New Delhi, with several hundred people attending, including officials from India, diplomats and Taiwanese businesspeople, the office said.
At the event, Representative to India Chen Mu-min (陳牧民) announced that the Taiwan-India Parliamentary Friendship Association would resume operations.
Photo: CNA
So far, 23 Indian lawmakers have agreed to join the group, which would become an important new force in promoting cooperation between Taiwan and India, Chen said.
Trade relations between Taiwan and India are continuing to grow rapidly, with bilateral trade reaching a record US$12.5 billion last year, he said.
Trade in the first eight months of this year reached US$12.9 billion, a 60 percent increase from the same period last year, he added.
Taiwan’s representative office in Turkey held a National Day reception on Wednesday, with more than 300 guests attending, including Turkish lawmakers from across party lines, senior government officials and diplomats, the office said.
Taiwan hopes to deepen cooperation with Turkey’s public and private sectors by promoting joint ventures, jointly developing artificial intelligence (AI) applications and cultivating high-tech talent, Representative to Turkey Huang Chih-yang (黃志揚) said.
By combining Taiwan’s technological and industrial strengths with Turkey’s strategic location and market advantages, the two sides could build a bridge linking East Asia and the Mediterranean, Huang said.
Taiwan’s representative office in the Netherlands on Wednesday hosted a reception attended by more than 250 Dutch political and business figures and members of the Taiwanese community, the office said.
Representative to the Netherlands Tien Chung-kwang (田中光) thanked the Dutch government and parliament for their firm support of Taiwan, including publicly backing Taiwan’s participation in the WHO at the World Health Assembly in May and sending the Royal Netherlands Navy frigate De Ruyter through the Taiwan Strait in June.
Peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait are in the global interest and particularly important to trading nations such as Taiwan and the Netherlands, Tien said.
The Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in Atlanta, Georgia, held a National Day celebration on Wednesday, with nearly 300 people from the political, academic and business sectors attending, the office said in a statement on Thursday.
The office will continue working with local state governments, chambers of commerce, schools and businesses to bolster cooperation in AI, healthcare, aerospace and disaster resilience, TECO Atlanta Director Lin Chu-en (林主恩) said.
Taiwan-US ties have continued to deepen over the past year, with Taiwan’s economy continuing to grow on demand from high-tech industries, Lin said, adding that the US has become one of Taiwan’s most important trading partners.
Cooperation between Taiwan and six US states — Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina — has become increasingly practical, covering high-tech talent development, scholarships, Chinese-language education, cultural exchanges, research collaboration and industrial investment, Lin said.
TECO Houston also hosted a National Day reception on Wednesday, drawing more than 300 guests from the political, business, academic and Taiwanese expatriate communities in the southern US, the office said in a statement.
Taiwan and the US are working together to build a “joint fleet” by further reinforcing bilateral trade, investment and supply chain integration, TECO Houston Director Yvonne Hsiao (蕭伊芳) said.
By combining Taiwan’s manufacturing strengths with US innovation and talent, the two sides aim to build secure and resilient supply chains for semiconductors, AI and drones, Hsiao said.
Taiwan-US technology cooperation is about helping both sides succeed and promoting the global economy, she added.

Ethiopian federal police yesterday fanned out across the regional capital of Tigray after anti-government forces pulled out, driving in vehicles and calling on residents over loudspeakers to help establish a new administration following the rebels’ withdrawal.
Over the last weekend, government-allied fighters had entered Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, after the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) announced its withdrawal.
The TPLF had joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Fighting escalated late last month, undermining the 2022 peace deal. The rebels seized the Mekelle airport and the city, one of Ethiopia’s largest.
Photo obtained by Reuters
Then on Saturday last week, the rebels said their forces had pulled out — similar to what they did in the previous two-year war, which ended with a peace agreement in 2022, apparently to spare the city from destruction.
Still, local government offices remained shut yesterday in Mekelle as the city awaited new authorities, with police and the government-allied Tigray Peace Force in charge of security. Members of the city’s new civilian administration had arrived with federal police on Thursday, but said they were awaiting instructions.
The Tigray Peace Force imposed an overnight curfew on Wednesday.
No administration had taken office in Mekelle by yesterday morning.
Tigray’s TV and radio stations have been off the air since the TPLF withdrawal.
Ahmed’s government promised to restore banking, electricity, telecommunications and water services, but gave no timetable. It also outlined plans to register people involved in the conflict and help them return to civilian life.
Further north, a government-allied commander and a conflict monitoring group have separately reported Eritrean troops entering Ethiopia, raising fears of a wider conflict.
Eritrean personnel entered Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, Tigray Peace Force commander Ermiyas Ababu said, citing reports from his personnel in the area.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data monitoring group said Eritrean troops crossed the border at Zelambesa on Wednesday and came under drone attack at Guada while traveling toward Idaga Hamus.
It attributed the strikes to Ethiopia’s military.
Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Gebremeskel said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.”
He accused Ethiopia of threatening regional peace through its pursuit of “sovereign access to the sea,” but did not explicitly confirm or deny the crossing.
Eritrea has previously denied Ethiopian allegations that it supports the TPLF — its enemy during the 2020-to-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces.
During that war, the Associated Press documented accounts from survivors and witnesses accusing Eritrean soldiers of killings, rape and looting.
Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki dismissed allegations of abuses by his forces as “a fantasy” in 2023.
Eritrea announced last week that it was severing diplomatic ties after Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara.
Abiy on Monday said landlocked Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.
The Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday said it remained committed to dialogue with its neighbors.

China Youth Corps ruled a KMT-affiliated body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

The Supreme Administrative Court on Thursday upheld a 2018 ruling by the Ill-gotten Party Assets Settlement Committee designating the China Youth Corps (CYC) as an “affiliated organization” of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT).
The decision, which cannot be appealed, means NT$5.61 billion (US$176 million) in assets frozen by the committee would not be returned to the CYC.
The CYC said in a statement late on Thursday that it could not accept the decision and “strongly objected to the court stigmatizing more than 70 years of its public service work as ill-gotten KMT assets.”
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
The KMT condemned the ruling, accusing the judiciary of acting as a rubber stamp for the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) targeting of political opponents.
The Executive Yuan-supervised committee was set up following the 2016 enactment of the Act Governing the Settlement of Ill-gotten Properties by Political Parties and Their Affiliate Organizations (政黨及其附隨組織不當取得財產處理條例) by the then-DPP government.
The law aims to address assets acquired by political parties and their affiliated organizations during the KMT’s authoritarian rule over Taiwan.
In its 2018 ruling, the committee said the CYC benefited from the KMT party-state system’s resources and privileges under martial law and that the KMT controlled the CYC’s personnel, finances and operations until 1999.
It determined that although a leadership change saw the CYC break away from KMT control in 1999, continued ambiguity over asset ownership meant it could not conclude the two organizations had fully separated.
Following the ruling, ownership of 61 plots of land and buildings belonging to the CYC was ordered transferred to the state and the organization’s assets were frozen.
The CYC appealed the ruling, arguing that it was established and initially run by the government in 1952, under the supervision of the Executive Yuan and the Ministry of National Defense, and that its key leaders were appointed through the government rather than by the KMT.
It said that it became an independent civilian organization after ending its affiliation with the Ministry of National Defense in 1969, pointing to the defeat of a KMT-backed candidate in its 1999 leadership election as evidence of its independence.
However, the Taipei High Administrative Court in 2024 ruled that the CYC was effectively controlled by the KMT, despite being formally under the ministry, and that the KMT’s control continued after the CYC became a civilian organization.
The court also agreed with the committee that the CYC’s 1999 break from KMT control did not mean it had fully separated from the party, as asset ownership remained unclear.
In its ruling, the Supreme Administrative Court said it found no reason to overturn the lower court’s decision, citing sufficient evidence and correct application of the law.

Doctor accused of falsifying record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

Allegations that a China-trained doctor is illegally practicing medicine with a fake US medical diploma need to be verified, officials said yesterday, although they did not rule out launching a probe into the matter.
In a post on Threads, a member of the public said that they recognized a Tainan-based internal medicine doctor as an acquaintance who studied medicine in China.
She had cut all ties with her friends shortly after graduating, the post said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The person is practicing medicine with a diploma from the University of California, Riverside under a different name, but records of medical certification for her under either name could not be found online, it said.
Ministry of Health and Welfare Medical Affairs Department Deputy Director Liu Yu-ching (劉玉菁) said that Taiwan does not recognize higher-education qualifications in medical fields from China when it grants doctors’ licenses.
The restriction applies to medicine, dentistry and traditional Chinese medicine, Liu said, citing the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (台灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例).
Holders of a medical diploma issued by foreign countries other than China might qualify for a license to practice medicine if the degree-conferring institution is accredited by the Ministry of Education, she said.
Applicants must study in a field relevant to the type of license they apply for, and meet standards for academic credits earned and scholastic performance before being allowed to take a medical license test, she said.
The evaluation for eligibility to take the test is conducted by a panel of experts, she added.
The applicants must pass a Ministry of Examination-administered certification test to become a doctor in Taiwan, she said.
The health ministry has not verified the accusations on social media against the Tainan-based doctor, she said, adding that officials would, if necessary, seek information from the Ministry of Examination.
The doctor’s medical license would be revoked if the examination authority cancels her qualification after establishing that she had submitted forged documents, Liu said.
The claims that no record of the doctor’s medical license could be found would be investigated, she said.
Deputy Minister of Examination Huang Ching-chang (黃慶章) said that would-be doctors must pass background checks to qualify to sit the license test.
Candidates with Chinese diplomas are not allowed to take the exam, while those who hold degrees from other foreign nations are rigorously scrutinized, including a review of their academic and international travel records, Huang said.
The examination ministry would initiate a probe into the doctor accused of using forged qualifications if it receives a complaint or request for investigation through official channels, he said.
With some exceptions, Taiwan does not recognize academic degrees conferred by China’s Jinan University, which the doctor supposedly attended, because of the institution’s affiliation with the Chinese United Front Work Department, said Liao Kao-hsien (廖高賢), director-general of the Ministry of Education’s Department of Higher Education.
Holders of degrees in medicine, dentistry or traditional Chinese medicine issued by a foreign country must pass an education ministry qualification assessment before taking the national licensing examination, subject to statutory exemptions, Liao said.

GlobalFoundries rallies after US$2bn TSMC deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:50 UTC
01:42:50 KST

GlobalFoundries Inc shares gained as much as 7 percent after the chip manufacturer announced a five-year, US$2 billion deal to provide US production capacity to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電).
Under the agreement, announced on Thursday, GlobalFoundries is to help supply components known as silicon interposers. The US company is to rely on manufacturing at its facility in Malta, New York, and said it has the option to expand capacity “as customer demand grows.”
An interposer is a small layer of silicon that sits between a chip and its packaging. It is home to the wires that carry electronic signals and power needed to make that chip functional. The components are increasingly important as semiconductors become larger and companies combine multiple chips into the same package.
Photo: Bloomberg
GlobalFoundries expects to expand capacity at its Malta facility and establish the first US-based source of silicon interposers supporting advanced packaging technologies, including embedded deep trench capacitor components, it said.
The company expects to begin ramping up volume production of the TSMC components in the first half of 2028.
The multi-year US$2 billion agreement will expand capacity for advanced packaging ecosystem and support growing demand for AI and high-performance computing technologies, GlobalFoundries said.
The deal provides TSMC with an additional US-based source of production at a time when the Taiwanese company is working to expand its US footprint. TSMC is the dominant chip foundry — a business that produces semiconductors for outside customers — and serves clients such as Nvidia Corp, Apple Inc and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.
Shares of GlobalFoundries rose as high as US$51.45, marking their biggest intraday gain in three weeks. The stock had been up 38 percent this year through Wednesday’s close.
GlobalFoundries’ foundry business is generally focused on less sophisticated chips, what it calls “essential semiconductors.” Greater interest in technology like silicon interposers for packaging is giving the company a role to play in more advanced AI components.
“Advanced packaging is becoming increasingly critical to delivering the performance, power efficiency and scale required for next-generation AI systems,” GlobalFoundries senior vice president Ed Kaste said in the statement.

Respect for gay community lacking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:50 UTC
01:42:50 KST

The recent controversy surrounding a police raid on a gay bar on Saturday last week in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) area flies directly in the face of the city government’s long-standing efforts to project an image of Taipei as a diverse and inclusive city. With its rainbow-themed public spaces and tourism marketing, Taipei has long been proud of its support for diverse communities. However, in light of this incident, it must be asked: Should a city’s inclusivity be measured by the number of rainbows on its streets, or by how the authorities actually treat LGBTQ people?
According to the Wanhua Precinct, police were investigating a case involving public indecency in accordance with the law. However, their conduct during the operation has drawn sharp criticism, with reports of patrons being handcuffed, ordered to squat and officers making inappropriate remarks. LGBTQ groups have called on the Taipei City Government to investigate the conduct of the operation and address the stigma and insecurity that the city’s queer venues have long faced.
It is the police’s duty to investigate and crack down on crime, and gay bars should not be treated as spaces beyond the reach of the law. Equally, however, standards regarding due process, human rights and dignity must not be weaker for cases involving LGBTQ establishments. The legal grounds for enforcement and whether its execution respects the principle of proportionality and the dignity of the public are two separate questions. They must both be seriously examined.
Taipei has over the past few years promoted rainbow tourism, but genuine inclusivity cannot exist only within the confines of tourism brochures and event stages. Whether LGBTQ communities receive the same respect as other citizens when it comes to police checks, searches or other exercises of state authority is the real measure of how far we have come on equal rights.
There is no need to rush on pronouncements of guilt. Instead, the Taipei City Government should release full footage from the operation to address the concerns raised. Any misconduct should be dealt with through accountability and corrective action.
The incident should also prompt a review of police training to prevent prejudice from influencing law enforcement. Taipei’s rainbows are decoration; they do not prove that equality has been achieved. When the events are over and the flags have been put away, the real test is whether the city’s LBGTQ communities can retain their full dignity when dealing with the authorities.
Ken is a social worker.

Meta bans ads from TikTok on its apps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

Meta Platforms Inc banned advertisements in the US from ByteDance Ltd (字節跳動), the former controlling owner of TikTok, intensifying the competition with the popular social video site.
On Thursday, Meta began implementing a complete restriction on ads and paid marketing messages placed on its platforms by ByteDance, the Chinese company that remains in charge of key parts of TikTok in the US.
The ban is to take effect in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, according to Meta, and also extend to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries.
Photo: Bloomberg
“We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps,” Meta spokesperson Chris Sgro said in an e-mailed statement. “Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience.”
Meta and TikTok have competed neck-and-neck for years, even with a key imbalance in that rivalry: TikTok has been able to operate in Meta’s most important market, the US, while Meta has been unable to do so in TikTok’s most crucial market, China. However, that competition took a more heated turn in August after Meta agreed to a historic US$18 billion settlement with US states requiring it to implement new safety features for minors across its Instagram and Facebook apps.
Since then, Meta has been pressuring TikTok and Google’s YouTube to commit to making similar changes, suggesting it cannot solve industrywide child safety problems on its own.
TikTok has remained publicly silent on the matter, ratcheting up the tension between the companies as Meta grapples with what it sees as yet another competitive disadvantage.
Last month, TikTok enacted a number of measures to make it harder to shift from its app to other social platforms, including by eliminating dedicated Instagram links from its users’ profiles. It also rejected ads from Meta demanding that TikTok commit to comparable concessions on child safety.
Soon after the settlement with the state attorneys general, Meta ran ads in top newspapers upping its pressure campaign. Meta executives have also called out TikTok publicly for failing to show up at a recent Office of the Surgeon General event on the harms of excessive screen use, and for dropping out of a national security meeting with the House Select Committee on China to avoid broader scrutiny amid its child safety litigation.
Other consumer tech platforms have also introduced friction between its products and its competitors. The Information reported last month that OpenAI told advertising partners that it would not accept ads for image and audio-generation products that competed with its own.

Thailand’s Queen Suthida has flown a Gripen fighter jet solo for the first time, the royal household revealed yesterday, watched by her husband, King Maha Vajiralongkorn, himself a keen pilot.
The 48-year-old queen took off in a single-seat JAS 39C from a military air base in southern Surat Thani Province on Thursday, footage released by the royal household showed.
The outing followed weeks of simulator training at the base and about 10 hours in a two-seat Gripen, media reports said.
Photo: Royal Household Bureau via AFP
A former Thai Airways flight attendant who married the king in 2019, days before his coronation, Suthida began flying in 2010 and has logged nearly 1,190 hours.
She regularly flies as copilot to the king on royal trips, including landing at Bhutan’s notoriously difficult Paro airport, the reports said.
Thailand already operates a squadron of Gripen C/D fighters made by Sweden’s Saab, and last year signed a deal for three Gripen E jets and one Gripen F worth about US$556 million, with deliveries due by 2030.
After she landed, the king handed the queen a bouquet and pinned a Golden Gripen Order patch on her left arm, which reports said made her Thailand’s first female Gripen pilot.

Coast guard struggling to staff its expanding fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:46 UTC
01:42:46 KST

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) has increased its fleet by 21.3 percent since 2022, but is struggling to recruit personnel to crew the vessels, the Legislative Yuan’s Budget Center said yesterday, as the agency is increasingly tasked with countering Chinese “gray zone” incursions.
The CGA increased its fleet from 169 vessels in 2022 to 205 as of July under two vessel-building projects, but its recruitment shortfall has exceeded 30 percent since 2024 and is approaching 40 percent this year, it said.
The fleet added three patrol vessels and 34 patrol boats, while the number of pelagic patrol vessels decreased by one, the report said.
Photo: I-Hwa Cheng, AFP
The larger fleet means the CGA needs to recruit 136 additional personnel this year and 128 next year, plus 15 people annually from 2028 to 2031, it said.
These staffing requirements do not include personnel needed for the Maritime Rights Protection Coast Guard Vessel Construction Plan (海域維權海巡艦艇建造計畫), it said.
From 2021 to last year, the CGA’s annual personnel requirements ranged from 142 to 306 people, while the number of candidates recruited ranged from 140 to 229, and the number who reported for duty ranged from 121 to 208.
The resulting annual shortfall ranged from 21 to 98 people, or 15 to 34 percent of the recruitment target, the report said.
The CGA’s recruitment target for this year is 344 people, an increase of 202 from 142 in 2021, it said.
As of the end of August, results had yet to be announced for the Civil Service Senior and Junior Examinations and the Grade 3, 4 and 5 Special Examinations for Coast Guard Personnel.
The report said it would continue to monitor the number of candidates selected and how many reported for duty.
However, the rate of shortfall for examinations whose results had been announced was about 40 percent, reinforcing concerns over recruitment, it said.
The CGA should draw on the experiences of the US and Japan and make greater use of technology to support coast guard operations, helping to address personnel shortages and maintain its maritime law enforcement capabilities, the Budget Center said.
In response, the CGA said it commissions the Central Police University and Taiwan Police College to recruit and train personnel for its vessels according to schedule, while replenishing its workforce each year through special examinations and other recruitment channels.
To encourage more young people to join, it has increased six types of allowances, including those for seagoing and hazardous duties, and sought budget approval for additional contract positions to recruit vessel operations personnel, it said.
Staffing levels aboard its vessels comply with regulations, it added.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:46 UTC
01:42:46 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) yesterday condemned a senior diplomat facing corruption charges who has not returned since going on a trip to Japan, and said it is preparing to fire him.
Paul Chen (陳盈連), who is a senior diplomat at the ministry’s Institute of Diplomacy and International Affairs and previously served as director-general of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Guam and Taiwan’s representative to Fiji, was indicted by the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office in June on charges of breaching the Anti-Corruption Act (貪污治罪條例).
He is accused of fraudulently claiming NT$3.43 million (US$107,608) in rent subsidies while stationed in Los Angeles and embezzling public property during his tenure in Guam.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
According to a Chinese-language Mirror Media report, Chen pleaded guilty and returned the illicit funds during the investigation.
However, when the Taipei District Court was scheduled to hold a hearing in the middle of last month, it discovered that he had flown to Japan and subsequently traveled to the US.
Chen applied for personal leave to visit Japan from Sept. 12 to 20, but has not returned to Tainan, the ministry said.
The institute made multiple attempts to contact Chen and asked his spouse for assistance, demanding a written explanation by a specified deadline, but received no response, it said.
The ministry said it has therefore officially recorded Chen as being absent without leave for eight days and four hours in accordance with the Civil Service Leave Regulations (公務人員請假規則).
The ministry said it strongly condemns Chen’s failure to return, his continued absence and his refusal to contact his agency while his legal cases are being processed by judicial authorities.
Civil servants are entrusted by the state and should strictly abide by the law and remain dedicated to their duties, it said.
The ministry will convene a performance review committee in accordance with the Civil Service Performance Evaluation Act (公務人員考績法), it said.
As Chen has been absent without leave for more than four consecutive days, the committee is expected to issue him two major demerits, which would result in his immediate dismissal, it added.

Education as a tool for preventing drug abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:44 UTC
01:42:44 KST

As the local elections heat up, the issue of drugs has become a focal point of public discussion. Political considerations are inevitably part of election-related debates — but if they can prompt society to re-examine drug policy, it might not be a bad thing. Rather than arguing over who is tougher on drugs, we should instead consider what constitutes the most fundamental anti-drug policy.
Early approaches to drug control focused heavily on enforcement, punishment and incarceration. However, practitioners found that incarceration alone was not enough to address addiction. Consequently, policies have expanded to incorporate management, treatment and harm reduction.
Drug enforcement disrupts supply, addiction treatment helps people recover and harm reduction minimizes harm to individuals and society — each is a vital part of the equation.
However, drug seizures might represent only a fraction of the drugs in circulation, while addiction treatment requires sustained investment of resources.
Beyond asking how we stop drugs from coming in and how we help people quit after they become addicted, we should take the question one step further: How can we ensure that children never want to try drugs in the first place?
Tainan’s experience warrants attention. Since 2021, the Tainan Bureau of Education has promoted drug awareness campaigns. In 2022, Tainan’s anti-drug program — initiated by a senior prosecutor and backed by the city government — mobilized resources from the judiciary, academia, lawyers and civil society organizations to produce 10 short anti-drug videos for elementary and junior-high schools across the city.
The education bureau also scheduled the videos to be shown at the beginning, middle and end of each semester, supplemented by anti-drug educators and realistic teaching aids featuring emerging drugs. Two minutes might seem brief, but when these messages appear repeatedly in children’s daily lives — serving as a constant reminder that drugs should be avoided — they can help develop an internal framework for making sound judgements about drugs.
Even more encouragingly, some elementary schools have begun developing their own anti-drug education programs, showing that anti-drug efforts have begun shifting from being something government-mandated to a voluntary undertaking on the part of schools. If this grassroots momentum continues to spread, it could foster a culture in which schools, teachers, students and families all play a role.
Hating drugs should mean rejecting drugs and the harm they cause, not discriminating against those struggling with addiction. The central government should continue to provide treatment and opportunities for people with substance abuse disorders to reintegrate into society. For children, the focus should be on building psychological resilience and a strong defense against drugs from an early age.
Once drugs infiltrate society, the costs associated with enforcement and treatment are immense. By contrast, starting with everyday education entails relatively limited costs, but could yield lasting preventive benefits.
If “don’t use drugs” can become as natural a habit and value choice for children as observing traffic lights before crossing the street, only then would we have the kind of anti-drug policy that is worth long-term government investment.
Yang Yung-nane is a professor in the Department of Political Science and vice dean of the College of Social Sciences at Cheng Kung University.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Eswatini’s king yesterday pledged to deepen his country’s “enduring friendship” with Taiwan during a return visit to Taipei after President William Lai’s (賴清德) trip to the southern African nation in May that China tried to block.
King Mswati III arrived early yesterday for a state visit until Saturday next week. He is to attend today’s Double Ten National Day celebrations in Taipei.
The trip is his 20th visit to Taiwan and comes as the two countries celebrate 58 years of diplomatic ties.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Eswatini would continue to advocate for Taiwan’s meaningful participation in the UN, the monarch said.
“We deeply value the enduring friendship and cooperation between our two countries, and we look forward to strengthening these bonds for the benefit of our peoples,” the king told a welcoming ceremony on Liberty Square.
Lai said the two sides had always collaborated from a position of trust and were partners who “support each other and grow together.”
Cooperation with Eswatini has expanded under Taiwan’s diplomatic initiative to promote shared prosperity with its allies, with increasingly close exchanges between the two countries’ peoples, Lai said.
In separate remarks, Lai thanked the king for supporting the establishment of a Taiwan Industrial Innovation Park in Eswatini and expressed hope that more Taiwanese companies would invest there, making the country a gateway to African markets.
The two leaders also witnessed the signing of an agreement on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, which Lai described as a milestone in law enforcement cooperation.
Mswati emphasized turning existing bilateral agreements into practical cooperation and encouraging partnerships between businesses.
“We need to put them into action,” he said, calling for officials to study how the agreements could be implemented effectively.
Mswati’s itinerary includes observing a joint ground-air military exercise alongside Lai, a visit to an agricultural research center and an investment dinner hosted by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) said the king was interfering in China’s internal affairs and “ignoring the long-term interests of his people.”
The former Swaziland is one of just 12 small states, mostly in Latin America, the Caribbean and the Pacific, that have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
In April, Taiwan accused China of pressuring three other African countries to block overflight permission for Lai’s aircraft, causing him to postpone a plan to join celebrations of the 40th anniversary of the king’s accession.
That was the first time a Taiwanese president had canceled an entire foreign trip due to denial of airspace access, an apparent new Chinese strategy to curb the nation’s international ties.
Lai made a surprise trip in May, using an “arrive, then announce” approach.

Pig farms urged to heed rules about feed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

Twenty-four cases of illegal transportation of kitchen waste have been identified so far this year, the Central Emergency Operation Center for African swine fever (ASF) said on Thursday, calling on pig farmers to abide by epidemic prevention regulations.
The government continued to clamp down on the illegal use or transportation of kitchen waste by pig farms after the Mid-Autumn Festival break to prevent ASF, the center said.
As of Wednesday, 24 cases of illegal kitchen waste transportation had been detected so far this year, 22 of which resulted in fines, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Pingtung County Government
The two other cases — in Taichung and Miaoli County — are under investigation, it said, adding that penalties would be issued according to the results.
The 24 cases involved 23 pig farms, with one of the farms caught twice, the center said.
Of the 23 pig farms, six had 200 or more pigs, while 11 had 20 to 199, it said.
The six other farms had 19 pigs or fewer, the center said.
That means 17 non-compliant farms had 199 pigs or fewer, accounting for about 73.9 percent of all non-compliant farms, it said.
Eight non-compliant farms had 20 pigs or more without livestock farm registration, accounting for 34.8 percent, the center said.
The center said it would ask local authorities to conduct follow-up inspections and penalize the eight farms for failing to register in accordance with the Animal Industry Act (畜牧法).
Farms that are not big enough to register should be listed for epidemic prevention management, it said.
Registered pig farms with non-compliance records should be listed for high-risk site inspections based on their kitchen waste sources, transportation routes, operational scale and registration status, it said.
Real-time temperature and video monitoring systems have been installed at 243 pig farms that have permission to feed pigs with kitchen waste, the center said.
GPS trackers have also been installed on 453 vehicles to monitor kitchen waste disposal, it said.
The Taichung City Government during a joint inspection on Friday last week found that a farm with 23 pigs in Longjing District (龍井) was having kitchen waste illegally transported to it, the center said.
The farm also illegally mixed pig feed with rice, ham and large bones, it said.
The Taichung Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office has collected blood samples from three pigs at the farm and confirmed that the samples tested negative for ASF, the center said, adding that a 15-day movement ban has been imposed on the farm.
Since the beginning of this year, transporting kitchen waste to pig farms without prior approval has been subject to a fine of NT$200,000 (US$6,275) for the first offense, NT$500,000 for the second offense, and NT$1 million for the third offense and each subsequent offense as stipulated in revised penalty guidelines issued pursuant to the Act on the Prevention and Control of Infectious Animal Diseases (動物傳染病防治條例), it said.
Farms that feed pigs kitchen waste without prior approval would face fines of NT$200,000 for the first offense and increased fines for subsequent offenses, capped at NT$3 million, as stipulated by penalty guidelines for the Feed Control Act (飼料管理法), the center said.
Those who illegally transport kitchen waste to a pig farm and illegally feed it to pigs would be fined according to the two pieces of legislation, or NT$400,000 for the first offense up to a maximum of NT$4 million for subsequent offenses, it said.
